生存

SURVIVAL

一张绘制于此地最初有人定居时的古老地图显示，一旦海岸线消失，到处都是怪物……

An old map from when this place was first settled shows monsters everywhere, once the shore gives out . . .

——卡尔·菲利普斯，《游泳》

—Carl Phillips, “Swimming”

一天晚上吃饭时，我丈夫给我讲了一个他在北大西洋听到的故事，故事的主角是一艘船和一个差点溺水的人。1984年3月11日深夜，一艘渔船在冰岛南海岸附近群岛中的赫马岛以东三英里处平静的海面上作业。天空晴朗，气温只有零下2摄氏度。船上有五名船员。大副古德劳格·弗里德索尔松只有22岁；他当时正在休息，在甲板下睡觉，被厨师叫醒，厨师告诉他拖网渔具被海底缠住了。弗里德索尔松来到甲板上后不久，就看到船员们正在试图用绞盘把渔具拉上来。其中一根拖网钢丝绷紧在船舷外，把船拉得倾斜得很厉害，海水都开始从栏杆缝隙里涌进来。弗里德索尔松大声发出警告。船长赫约图尔·琼森下令放松绞盘，但绞盘却卡住了。一个涌浪涌入船底，将船掀翻，水手们发现自己被抛入了冰冷的海水中。

One night over dinner, my husband tells me a story he heard about a boat in the North Atlantic and a man who should have drowned. Late on the evening of March 11, 1984, a fishing trawler was working on calm seas three miles east of the island of Heimaey, part of an archipelago off the south coast of Iceland. The sky was clear, the air a wintry twenty-eight degrees Fahrenheit. There were five crew aboard the vessel. Guðlaugur Friðþórsson, the boat’s mate, was just twenty-two years old; he had taken a break and was asleep below deck when he was woken up by the cook, who told him the trawling gear had snagged on the sea bottom. Soon after Friðþórsson arrived on deck, he saw that the crew were trying to winch up the gear. One of the trawl wires was taut over the side, pulling the boat over so far that the sea had begun to wash through the railings. Friðþórsson shouted a warning. The captain, Hjörtur Jónsson, gave instructions to slacken the winch, but then it jammed. A swell ran under the boat, overturning it, and the sailors found themselves pitched into the freezing sea.

两名男子几乎立即溺水身亡，但包括弗里德索尔松在内的其余三人设法抓住了船底龙骨。船很快开始下沉，他们无法放下救生筏。在41华氏度（约6摄氏度）的水中，他们只有不到半小时的时间就会因体温过低而丧命。三人开始向岸边游去。几分钟后，只剩下两人：琼森和弗里德索尔松。

Two of the men drowned almost immediately, but the remaining three, including Friðþórsson, managed to grab hold of the boat’s keel. The vessel quickly began to sink, and they could not release the emergency raft. In the forty-one-degree water, they would have less than half an hour before hypothermia claimed them. The three began to swim toward the shore. Within minutes, only two remained: Jónsson and Friðþórsson.

两人一边游泳一边互相呼喊，互相鼓励。后来，琼森不再回应。弗里德索尔松穿着蓝色工装裤、红色法兰绒衬衫和一件薄毛衣，继续游着，为了保持清醒，他开始和海鸥说话。一艘船游到离他不到350英尺的地方，他拼命地喊叫，但船还是开走了。他仰泳着，目光紧紧盯着岛屿南端的灯塔。最终，他听到了海浪拍打海岸的声音。他祈祷自己不会被礁石撞碎。他发现自己背靠着陡峭的悬崖底部，精疲力竭，口渴难耐，四肢都失去了知觉。他无路可爬，只好转身返回大海，调整方向，继续向南游去，最终上岸。他缓慢地穿过一片布满尖刺、积雪覆盖的熔岩地带，走了超过一英里才到达镇上。途中，他停下来，凿开一个羊粪蓄水池上厚达一英寸的冰层，喝了些水。当他终于到达镇上时，眼前的景象宛如梦境般美好。他敲响了第一户亮着灯的家门。他赤着脚，浑身结满了霜。在他身后……通往房子的路边人行道上，留有一串血淋淋的脚印。

The two men called to one other as they swam, to spur each other on. Then Jónsson stopped responding. Friðþórsson, wearing blue work pants, a red flannel shirt, and a thin sweater, kept swimming, and found himself talking to seagulls to stay awake. A boat came within three hundred and fifty feet of him and he shouted as loud as he could, but it sailed away. He swam backstroke, his eyes trained on the lighthouse at the southern end of the island. Eventually he heard the surf crashing on the coast. He prayed he would not get obliterated on the rocks. He found himself up against the base of a steep cliff, exhausted and terribly thirsty, unable to feel any of his extremities. With no way to climb up, he turned back to the sea, adjusted course, and swam farther south, where he came ashore and made his way slowly across a spiky, snow-covered lava field over a mile into town, stopping to punch through an inch-thick layer of ice on a sheep cistern to get a drink of water. When he finally arrived in town, it seemed to him a splendid dream-vision of life; he knocked on the door of the first home he saw with lights on. He was barefoot and covered in frost. Behind him was a trail of bloody footprints on the sidewalk leading up to the house.

这是一个真实的故事。最终，弗里德索尔松在冰冷的海水中挣扎了六个小时，游了超过三英里半才到达岸边。当他被送到医院时，医生们甚至无法摸到他的脉搏。然而，他并没有出现体温过低的症状，只有脱水的迹象。

This is a true story. In the end, Friðþórsson survived six hours in frigid seas and swam more than three and a half miles to land. When he arrived at the hospital, doctors were unable to discern his pulse. And yet he showed no signs of hypothermia, only dehydration.

弗里德索尔松的身体结构，竟然酷似海豹。研究人员后来发现，他身上覆盖着14毫米厚的脂肪层——是正常人类脂肪厚度的两到三倍，而且更加坚实。这个人与其说是陆地生物，不如说更像海洋哺乳动物。他身上有一种独特的生物构造，正是这种构造救了他：它让他保持温暖、漂浮，并能够继续游泳。许多人称他为现实版的海豹人——冰岛和苏格兰传说中那种半人半海豹的生物。对我而言，他是一个活生生的提醒：我们与海洋的距离其实并不遥远。

Friðþórsson’s body, it turns out, resembled a seal’s. Researchers later determined that he was insulated by fourteen millimeters of fat—two or three times the normal human thickness, and more solid. This man was more marine mammal than terrestrial. He had a biological quirk that saved him: it kept him warm, buoyant, and able to keep swimming. Many called him a real-life selkie—that half-man, half-seal figure of Icelandic and Scottish lore. To me, he is a living reminder that we are not so far removed from the sea.

作为人类，我们行走于大地之上。我们是陆地生物，却拥有水生祖先。我被弗里德索尔松的故事所吸引，是因为我想了解如今还剩下多少那段历史的痕迹。从某种意义上说，所有关于游泳的故事——从希腊神话中的水仙女到2013年从古巴游到佛罗里达的长距离游泳运动员戴安娜·奈德——都是在尝试让我们这些适应陆地生活的人类重新认识水。我们人类并非天生的游泳健将，但我们已经找到了方法，重新获得在数亿年前陆地与海洋分化之前就已存在的能力。

As humans, we walk the earth. We are land creatures with an aquatic past. I’m drawn to stories like Friðþórsson’s because I want to know what remains of that past, today. In a way, all swimming stories—from the naiads of Greek myth to the long-distance swimmer Diana Nyad, who swam from Cuba to Florida in 2013—are attempts to reacquaint our land-adapted selves with water. We humans are not natural-born swimmers, but we have figured out ways to reclaim abilities that existed before that land-sea split in our evolution, hundreds of millions of years ago.

既然进化使我们更擅长在陆地上追逐猎物直到其精疲力竭，为什么我们还要游泳呢？当然，这与生存息息相关：在漫长的进化过程中，游泳帮助我们从一个史前湖岸游到另一个湖岸，躲避天敌；潜入水中捕捞大型贝类，寻找新的食物来源；横渡海洋，定居新大陆；克服各种水上危险，并将游泳视为快乐、愉悦和成就的源泉。今天，我们来探讨一下我们为什么游泳。

Why do we swim, when evolution has shaped us to excel on land by running down prey until it drops from exhaustion? Of course it has to do with survival: Somewhere along the way, swimming helped us to get from one prehistoric lakeshore to another and escape predators of our own; to dive for that trove of bigger shellfish and get to new sources of food; to venture across oceans and settle new lands; to navigate all manner of aquatic perils and see swimming as a source of joy, pleasure, achievement. To arrive at this day, to talk about why we swim.

这本书探讨了是什么吸引我们去亲近水，即便它充满危险，以及我们为何一次又一次地回到水中。在我看来，一旦我们能够游泳求生，游泳的意义就远不止于此。游泳可以是一种疗愈身心、促进健康的活动，是通往幸福的途径。通过团队、俱乐部或共享的、挚爱的水域，一起游泳可以成为一种建立社群的方式。我们只需观察彼此在水中的身影，就能感受到水为玩耍创造了空间。如果我们技艺精湛，游泳可以成为一种竞争的动力，一种在泳池或开放水域中检验自身实力的方式。游泳也关乎心灵。在水中找到节奏，就是通过流动，发现一种全新的存在方式。这关乎我们人类与水的关系，以及沉浸其中如何开启我们的想象力。

This book is an investigation of what seduces us to water, despite its dangers, and why we come back to it again and again. It’s clear to me that once we can swim for survival, swimming can be so much more. The act of swimming can be one of healing, and health—a way to well-being. Swimming together can be a way to find community, through a team, a club, or a shared, beloved body of water. We have only to watch each other in water to know that it creates the space for play. If we get good enough at the thing, it can be an engine of competition—a way to test our mettle, in the pool or open water. Swimming is about the mind, too. To find rhythm in the water is to discover a new way of being in the world, through flow. This is about our human relationship to water and how immersion can open our imaginations.

地球表面超过70%被水覆盖；全球40%的人口居住在距离海岸线不到60英里的地方。本书献给所有热爱游泳、对水充满好奇的人们，无论你是追求速度、距离还是超越自我，无论你被水吸引。本书献给那些响应水的召唤的人们。本书也献给……对于我们这些寻求了解自己的人来说，那种迷失的、安静的存在状态——没有科技，没有哔哔声——可以追溯到我们人类水生起源的时代。

More than 70 percent of the planet is covered by water; 40 percent of the global population lives less than sixty miles from the coast. This book is for swimmers and curious humans of every stripe and age, whether you are drawn to water for speed or distance or transcendence. This is for those who heed the siren call of the water. It’s also for those of us who seek to understand ourselves, that lost, quiet state of just being—no technology, no beeps—dating back to our watery human origins.

我们选择置身于各种各样的水域：海洋、湖泊、河流、溪流、泳池。我们甚至与救生员——这些地方的守护者——之间也萌生了情愫。我的家庭故事就此展开——这不仅仅是因为我的父母在香港的一个游泳池相遇。

We choose to put ourselves in all kinds of waters: oceans, lakes, rivers, streams, pools. We even have a romance with lifeguards, the custodians of those places. At the intersection of these things, my family story begins—and not just because my mother and father met in a swimming pool in Hong Kong.

我五岁就学会了游泳，原因很简单，父母不想让我溺水：在浴缸里、邻居家的后院泳池里、海滩上。小时候在纽约琼斯海滩，我经常在大西洋波光粼粼、波光粼粼的海岸边，那四英尺深的海水里玩耍。我至今仍能清晰地回忆起当时的场景：我和哥哥、堂兄弟们在浅水中上下漂浮，等待着海浪将我们托起。我们用手臂当舵，沿着浪头的方向滑行，最终被抛到水沙交界处那片泡沫翻滚的海面上。然后，我们起身，欢笑，如此往复。

I learned to swim when I was five years old, for the simple reason that my parents didn’t want me to drown: in the bath, in the neighbor’s backyard pool, at the beach. As a kid at Jones Beach, New York, I spent a lot of time in the four feet of water at the scalloped, lacy edge of the Atlantic. I can picture the scene clearly: My brother and cousins and I bob up and down in the shallows, waiting for a wave to come and lift us off our feet. We use our arms as rudders to pilot us along the face of a wave as it breaks, depositing us at the foamy intersection where water meets sand. Get up, laugh, repeat.

我们被那波涛汹涌的海水深深吸引，其他人也一样。在炎热的夏日，尤其是在节假日，琼斯海滩可能会聚集十万多人。救生员们像哨兵一样守卫在高处，戴着反光太阳镜，巡视着熙熙攘攘的人群。

We are mesmerized by that heaving body of water. So is everybody else. On a hot day, and on a holiday, a hundred thousand other people might be there at Jones Beach. Lifeguards sit sentinel at their elevated stations, policing the crowds from behind mirrored sunglasses.

海滩上这样的日子，有一种原始的气息——就像所有动物都涌向水坑。水对我们熙熙攘攘的人群有着磁石般的吸引力。我观察着人们进出水面的情景。有些人只是在那里待着。来此消暑：激情澎湃地进入，迅速离开。有些人会停留片刻，漂浮、嬉戏、游泳。总有人保持距离，根本不下水。但他们依然会来，被海洋的脉动所吸引，沉醉于海浪的拍打声和咸咸的海风之中。

There’s something primal about a day like that at the beach—it’s all the animals heading to the watering hole. Water is a magnet for our teeming throng of humanity. I watch the ways people dip in and out. Some are just there to cool off: electrifying entry, quick exit. Some stay awhile, floating and splashing and swimming. Always there are people who keep their distance and don’t go in at all. But still they come, hypnotized by the pulse of the ocean, alive to the sound of the surf and the smell of the briny air.

我早早就感受到了水的诱惑：滑入美妙的沉浸之中，那种螺旋式的失重感，那种进入静谧水下世界的特权。在琼斯海滩，我获得了进入这世界的资格。我们在那里消磨时光，离妈妈们的蓝色碎花沙滩巾只有几步之遥。游泳间隙，我们互相戏弄，把内裤往里拽，然后把自己埋进沙子里。我喜欢大海仿佛在呼吸，前一刻平静如镜，下一刻便汹涌澎湃，带着我们这团涟漪在地平线上起伏。有一次，一个大浪从后面打过来，把我打得晕头转向。猝不及防，我被掀翻在地，屁股朝下栽了下去。然后，眼前出现了一个绿色的液体房间，被沙子笼罩着。我，游啊游，游向虚无。哪里才是上？四英尺深的水不算多，但也足以让人溺水。

I felt the draw of liquid early on: that slide into lovely immersion, that spiraling weightlessness, that privileged access to a muted underworld. Entry was granted to me there at Jones Beach, where we passed the hours within shouting distance of our moms’ blue-flowered beach towels. In between swims, we gave each other wedgies and buried ourselves in the sand. I liked how the ocean seemed to draw breath, lying placid one moment and rearing up the next, moving us in one rippling mass to and from the horizon. Once, a big wave came and smacked me from behind. Surprise overturning, ass over teakettle. Then, a liquid, green room, clouded by sand. Me, swimming and swimming toward nothing. Which way is up? Four feet isn’t very much water, but it’s deep enough to drown in.

时间仿佛凝固了。我感到肺部灼痛难忍，渴望呼吸。

Time stretched. I wondered about the press of my burning lungs, wishing for air.

时间仿佛在表弟不小心踢了我一脚后重新开始，他游到离我不到两英尺的地方。有了这唯一的参照物，我赶紧挣扎着浮出水面，头发像海藻一样缠在脸上。我尴尬地喘着粗气，环顾四周。发现没人注意到我遇到了麻烦，我便装作若无其事，转身又游回了海里。

Time restarted with an accidental kick to the head, from my cousin swimming not two feet away. Gifted this reference point, I scrambled to the surface, my hair wrapped around my face like kelp. Embarrassed and gasping, I looked around. When I realized that no one had noticed I was in trouble, I pretended that I never was. And I turned right back into the sea.

是什么导致了这种自愿性失忆？我究竟被海水的什么魅力所吸引，以至于能够原谅自己在海边犯下的谋杀未遂罪行，而且如此迅速？几乎每年都有一些人在长岛海滩溺水身亡。那时，我只是个年轻的游泳爱好者，一次又一次地回到那里，只为体验那份魔力：一种仿佛自己是这片并非人类家园的水域的居民的错觉。

What could bring on this voluntary amnesia? What did I find so alluring about the water that I could forgive a murder attempt by the sea, and so quickly at that? Most every year, a handful of people drown at the beaches of Long Island. At the time, I was just a young swimmer, going back for more of the magic: the illusion of being native to an element that is not home to humans like me.

那天的经历一直铭刻在我心中——三十年后，我已长大成人，几乎每天都游泳，既是为了娱乐也是为了锻炼身体。然而，我仍然会思考，究竟是什么更深层、更原始的本能驱使着我们。水既是生之源，也是死之源，这种矛盾的特质深深吸引着我们，我们也摸索出了无数种与水相处的方式。并非人人都会游泳，但每个人都有一段关于游泳的故事。在探究这种普遍的体验时——无论你是否惧怕水，无论你热爱它还是远离它，你终究会在人生的某个阶段与它相遇——我们发现自己正在锻炼着生存本能，凭借着在水中的坚持，悄然取得了某种胜利。我们一起在泳池间穿梭，追寻着绿洲，沉浸其中，寻找着那将我们引向深渊的诱饵。这是一场探索世界的旅程。让我们一起去游泳吧！

What I experienced that day stayed with me—three decades later I’m an adult who swims for pleasure and exercise nearly every day, and yet I wonder about the deeper, more primitive instincts that drive us. We are pulled to the paradox of water as a source of life and death, and we have figured out myriad ways to conduct ourselves in it. Not everybody is a swimmer, but everyone has a swimming story to tell. In the examination of this universal experience—and it is universal, whether you are fearful of the water or not; whether you love it or leave it, you will encounter it at some point in your life—we find ourselves flexing our survival muscles, achieving something quietly triumphant with our persistence in the medium. Together we are pool-hopping, chasing oases, immersing ourselves, in search of the bait that pulls us into the depths. This is an exploration of a world. Let’s go for a swim.

我们先从贝类开始。

We begin with a shellfish.

1

1

石器时代游泳

Stone Age Swimming

鲍鱼不肯离开岩石。我在水下十五英尺的地方，用金属鲍鱼钳戳进鲍鱼壳下方，就在它强壮的足部和它所附着的岩石之间，希望能听到之前承诺的“啪”的一声。结果什么也没发生。

The abalone does not want to come off the rock. Fifteen feet underwater, I jab the metal abalone iron underneath the shell, between the mollusk’s muscular foot and the boulder it’s fastened to, hoping for the pop I’ve been promised. Nothing.

我再次尝试，拼命原地游泳，与来回拉扯的水流搏斗，呼吸都快从鼻子里冒出来了。还是不行。这只鲍鱼显然感觉到了我的存在，紧紧地咬住了我的身体。一旦咬住，我发现几乎不可能把它弄出来。

I try again, my breath beginning to bubble out of my nose with the effort of swimming in place, fighting the currents that are pulling me to and fro. Still nothing. This abalone, evidently sensing my presence, has locked down tight. Once that happens, I am finding, it is nearly impossible to remove.

潜水捕捞鲍鱼是一项充满吸引力却又危险的运动。为了追寻这种难以捉摸的软体动物，我潜入了位于旧金山以北两个半小时车程、人迹罕至、蜿蜒曲折的索诺玛海岸的盐点州立公园。这里的危险重重：冰冷的海水、离岸流、礁石、缠绕的海藻、汹涌的巨浪，还有鲨鱼。尽管如此，几乎每年四月到十一月，仍有成千上万满怀希望的游泳者涌向北加州海岸。他们想尝试一下捕捞鲍鱼。野生红鲍鱼是世界上最大的鲍鱼，只产于北美西海岸。在那里，我可以扮演史前猎人的角色，潜入水中捕捞晚餐，即使我没有任何经验。

Diving for abalone is an attractive but dangerous sport. In pursuit of the elusive mollusk, I’ve submerged myself in the waters of Salt Point State Park, along the solitary, switch-backed Sonoma Coast two and a half hours north of San Francisco. The hazards are many: cold water, rip currents, rocks, kelp tangles, heavy surf, sharks. Still, most every season, April through November, thousands of hopeful swimmers make their way to the Northern California coast to try their hand at abalone hunting. The wild red abalone is the biggest in the world and is found only on the west coast of North America. It’s where I can play the role of prehistoric hunter, swimming down for my dinner, with zero experience.

我持有潜水证，但多年来，所有装备在水中都让我感到幽闭和笨重。在这片海岸，潜水气瓶是违法的，所以鲍鱼潜水员除了憋气和游泳技能外，几乎没有其他工具。这种返璞归真、人与自然对抗的活动，其残酷的现实是，正如护林员所说，这片海岸的每个海湾都是一座坟场：仅在2015年鲍鱼季的前三周，就有四人在鲍鱼潜水中丧生。事实证明，即使是经验丰富的潜水员也无法长时间憋气；习惯了背着满满一瓶空气的人，在面对这一事实时会开始恐慌。在浑浊的海水中，很难保持方向感。涌浪会把你抛向岩石，然后把你卷入大海。

I hold a scuba certification, but over the years all that gear has come to feel claustrophobic and encumbering when I’m in the water. Here on this part of the coast, scuba tanks are illegal, so abalone divers are armed with few tools beyond their breath-holding and swimming skills. The reality of this back-to-basics, man-versus-nature pursuit is that every cove along this part of the coast, rangers say, is a gravesite: in 2015, four people died while abalone diving during the first three weeks of the season alone. It turns out that even experienced divers can’t hold their breath for long; people who are used to wearing full tanks of air start to panic when confronted with this fact. In the murky water, it’s tough to stay oriented. The swell will toss you against the rocks and then suck you out to sea.

但我仍然想尝试。我学会了辨认鲍鱼那波纹状的黑色组织——外套膜——在嶙峋峭壁上的轮廓。我费力地撬开一只，又一只。当我俯身潜入海底，目光锁定目标，最终将一只六磅重的鲍鱼从水中拉出来时，我大脑中一个古老而豌豆大小的区域顿时充满了满足感。我需要双手用力才能把它拉上来，双腿才能推动自己前进；还没等我的头露出水面，我就能感觉到嘴角已经泛起了笑容。

But still, I want to try. I learn to spot the abalone’s rippling lip of black tissue, or mantle, against the side of a big, craggy escarpment. I struggle to dislodge one, then another. An ancient, pea-size part of my brain lights up with satisfaction when I jackknife down to the seafloor, eyes on the prize, and finally hoist a six-pound abalone out of the water. I need both hands to haul it up and both legs to propel me; I can feel the grin forming on my lips before my head even breaks the surface.

我从未有过想猎鸟当早餐，或是追鹿当晚餐的冲动。但当我看到贝类的那一刻，游泳觅食的吸引力便显而易见。我需要理解，游泳的意义远不止于锻炼。那天晚些时候，我在后院里清洗、修整、捶打贝肉——没错，是用石头——直到肉质软嫩，然后在火上烤熟，用我亲手、亲身、亲力亲为地为我的四口之家烹制了一顿饭。我们与食物来源脱节，这是现代生活的一个公认症状。游泳觅食让我得以暂时弥合这种脱节。那天晚上，当我在水槽里洗手，看着水流走时，我想起了海水有节奏地冲刷着海岸线上的岩石，以及看着海水最终流向地平线的那种感觉。

I’ve never felt the urge to shoot a bird for breakfast or run down a deer for dinner. But the direct appeal of swimming for my lunch is clear from the moment I spy the shellfish. There is something I need to understand about the act of swimming for something more essential than exercise. In my backyard later that day, I clean, trim, and pound the meat tender—yep, with a rock—cook it up over a flame, and feed my family of four a meal I’ve prepared entirely with my own hands and breath and body. We are divorced from our food sources; it is a recognized symptom of modern life. Swimming for resources allows me, for a moment, to resolve the disconnect. That evening, when I rinse my hands in the sink and watch the water drain away, I remember the rhythmic sluicing of seawater through the rocks along the shoreline and what it felt like to watch it all flow back toward the horizon.

已知最早的游泳记录出现在沙漠中央。在埃及靠近利比亚边境的撒哈拉沙漠偏远山区吉尔夫凯比尔高原，有游泳者正沿着洞穴的墙壁进行蛙泳。

The first known record of swimming lies in the middle of a desert. Somewhere in Egypt, near the Libyan border, in the Sahara’s remote and mountainous Gilf Kebir plateau, there are swimmers breaststroking up the walls of a cave.

1933年，匈牙利探险家拉斯洛·阿尔马西发现了“游泳者洞穴”，洞穴内藏有大量新石器时代的壁画，描绘了人们在水下的各种姿态。考古学家已将这些艺术作品的创作年代追溯到一万年前。在阿尔马西发现洞穴之时，撒哈拉沙漠并非一直都是沙漠的观点还非常激进。当时的气候变化理论……能够解释从温带环境到贫瘠、极度干旱沙漠转变的理论如此新颖，以至于据说阿尔马西1934年出版的《未知的撒哈拉》一书的编辑不得不插入脚注表示异议。但这些壁画使阿尔马西本人确信，水可能是洞穴附近自然存在的，画中的游泳者就是画家，湖水轻柔地拍打着他们的脚趾。如今是一片沙海的地方，曾经是流水潺潺。他想，如果说一种媒介是液态的生命，那么另一种媒介或许看似是其干涸、颗粒状的对立面，但两者之间确实存在联系。

The Cave of Swimmers, discovered by the Hungarian explorer László Almásy in 1933, contains a trove of Neolithic paintings that depict people in a range of underwater poses. Archaeologists have dated the creation of the artwork as far back as ten thousand years ago. At the time of Almásy’s discovery, the notion that the Sahara had not always been a desert was a radical idea. Theories of a climate change that could account for the shift from temperate environs to barren, hyper-arid desert were so new that the editor of Almásy’s 1934 book, The Unknown Sahara, reportedly felt compelled to insert footnotes stating disagreement. But the paintings convinced Almásy himself that water might have been a natural feature in the immediate vicinity of the cave, that the swimmers themselves were the painters, that a lake lapped their very toes as they worked. Where there is now a sea of sand, there was water flowing. Where one medium is liquid life, the other may seem to be its parched, granular antithesis, he thought, but the two were indeed connected.

事实证明，阿尔马西的推测是正确的。几十年后，考古学家在离洞穴不远的地方发现了干涸的湖床，这些湖床见证了撒哈拉沙漠曾经绿意盎然的时代。他关于沙漠中游泳者之谜的解答最终得到了大量地质证据的证实，这些证据显示，这片土地曾经遍布着古老的湖泊，此外，考古学家还发现了河马骨骼以及许多其他水生动物的遗骸，包括巨龟、鱼类和蛤蜊。这段湿润的时期后来被称为“绿色撒哈拉”。

It turns out, of course, that Almásy was right. Decades later, archaeologists would find dried lake beds not far from the cave, from a time when the Sahara was green. His answer to the riddle of swimmers in the desert would eventually be confirmed with a remarkable abundance of geological evidence showing a landscape once dotted with ancient lakes, as well as the startling discovery of hippo bones and the remains of many other water-dwelling animals, including giant tortoises, fish, and clams. This wet period became known as the Green Sahara.

不久前，我在一期旧版的《国家地理》杂志上读到一篇关于古生物学家保罗·塞雷诺的文章，他进一步证实了阿尔马西的猜想。2000年秋天，塞雷诺在撒哈拉沙漠的另一处区域——位于冲突频发、鲜为人知的尼日尔南部边缘——寻找恐龙化石。在距离该国最大城市约125英里的开阔沙漠中，阿加德兹是他探险队的摄影师之一，他爬上了一处偏僻的沙丘，偶然发现了一大堆骨骼。这一次，这些骨骼既不是恐龙的，也不是河马的。

Not long ago, in an old issue of National Geographic, I read about a paleontologist named Paul Sereno who further confirmed Almásy’s hunch. In the fall of 2000, Sereno was hunting for dinosaur bones in a different part of the Sahara, the southern edge, in conflict-prone, little-explored Niger. In the open desert, some 125 miles from the country’s largest city, Agadez, one of his expedition photographers scrambled up a remote group of dunes—and stumbled across a massive trove of skeletons. This time, the bones weren’t from dinosaurs or hippos.

这些饱受侵蚀、风吹日晒的沙丘显露出数百具人类遗骸，其中还散落着距今约一万年的史前陶器碎片。一些陶器碎片上刻有波浪线，另一些则点缀着圆点。科学家们将这处墓地命名为戈贝罗（Gobero），这是图阿雷格人对该地区的称呼。它是迄今为止发现的规模最大、年代最早的石器时代墓地。事实证明，绿色撒哈拉沙漠正是史前人类游泳者可能存在的理想之地。

These eroding, windswept sand dunes revealed what turned out to be hundreds of human remains, interspersed with prehistoric fragments of pottery that were up to ten thousand years old. Some of the pottery pieces were carved with wavy lines; others were stippled with dots. The burial place, which the scientists called Gobero, the Tuareg tribal name for the area, was the largest and earliest Stone Age cemetery found to date. It turns out that the Green Sahara was exactly the sort of place where prehistoric human swimmers might exist.

在一个寒风刺骨的一月午后，我在芝加哥大学的化石实验室见到了保罗·塞雷诺。他在那里任教已有三十余年。关于石器时代游泳的研究并不多，所以我希望他能帮我描绘出一个史前世界的景象。塞雷诺本人并不常游泳，但他花了大量时间研究恐龙和人类的游泳能力（他是将埃及棘龙确立为已知第一种会游泳的恐龙的科学家之一）。他身上带着几分印第安纳·琼斯的气质——他穿着皮夹克，充满着永不满足的热情，而且他还曾被《人物》杂志评为“全球50位最美人物”之一。

On a bitingly cold January afternoon, I meet Paul Sereno at his fossil lab at the University of Chicago, where he has been a professor for more than thirty years. There isn’t much scholarship specific to Stone Age swimming, so I want him to help me conjure up a picture of this prehistoric world. Sereno doesn’t swim much himself, but he has spent a lot of time thinking about the swimming abilities of both dinosaurs and people (he’s one of the scientists whose research established Spinosaurus aegyptiacus as the first known swimming dinosaur). There’s a dash of Indiana Jones to him—he has the leather jacket and the restless enthusiasm, and he was once voted one of People magazine’s “50 Most Beautiful People.”

我请塞雷诺为我重现一个适合游泳的古代环境。他说，在一万年前的绿色撒哈拉沙漠，戈贝罗就像“沙漠中的代托纳海滩”——一个巨大的、相互连通的浅湖系统，许多湖泊深约十英尺，湖边有沙洲，人们可以由此走到水边。

I ask Sereno to reconstruct for me an ancient environment that was suitable for swimming. In the Green Sahara of ten thousand years ago, he says, Gobero resembled “a Daytona Beach in the desert”—a vast interlinked system of shallow lakes, many of them about ten feet deep, with sand spits that allowed humans to walk out to the water.

科学家将这片水系命名为古戈贝罗湖（Paleolake Gobero）。其最重要的地理特征之一是一侧的断层，它发挥了双重作用。首先，它阻挡了深层地下水，即使长时间不下雨，湖中也始终有水。其次，当降雨或地下水涌出时，断层崖就像一道天然堤坝，环绕着这片区域，并周期性地泄洪以调节盆地的水位。这片浅水系统时而出现时而消失，但它足够稳定，以至于人类在其岸边生活了数千年。这处保存完好的墓葬遗址埋葬着两个不同的人类群体，他们的居住时期相隔一千年，在此期间，湖泊消失，遗址也被废弃。塞雷诺表示，撒哈拉沙漠的这种绿化和干旱化是自大约一万两千年前的末次冰期以来最大的气候变化。

Scientists have named the aquatic system Paleolake Gobero. One of its most critical geographic features was a fault on one side, which did two things. One, it dammed up deep groundwater, so there was always water there even if it didn’t rain for a long while. Two, when it did rain, or when the groundwater welled up, the fault cliff acted as a natural dam flanking the site, with periodic spills to regulate levels in the basin. The shallow aquatic system came and went, but it was stable enough that people lived along its shores for many thousands of years. The pristine burial site contained the remains of two distinct populations of humans, their occupations separated by a period of a thousand years, during which the lake disappeared and the site was abandoned. This greening and drying of the Sahara, Sereno says, was the largest climate change since the last ice age, about twelve thousand years ago.

那里堆积着大量的剥壳蛤蜊壳——数量之多，让塞雷诺认为戈贝罗岛的居民不仅从岸边收集蛤蜊，还一定潜水捕捞过蛤蜊。而且，那里的证据表明，捕捞并非他们唯一的食物来源。他们发现了雕刻的鱼钩和用鳄鱼颚骨制成的精磨倒钩鱼叉尖。塞雷诺和他的团队甚至还发现了四支鱼叉。鱼叉就嵌在湖底。“他们很可能有船，”塞雷诺说，“但我们不知道船长什么样，也不知道是用什么材料做的。而且鱼叉都放在湖底中央很远的地方，我猜他们可能也带着船游过去了。”

There were immense middens of shucked clamshells—so many shells that Sereno thinks the people of Gobero must have dived for clams as well as collected them from shore. And the evidence there suggests that this was not the only means of catching dinner. There were carved fishhooks and finely honed barbed harpoon tips made from the jawbones of crocodiles. Sereno and his team even found four harpoons embedded in the lake bed itself. “They likely had boats,” Sereno says. “But we have no idea what the boats looked like, or what they were made of. And with the harpoons way out in the middle of the lake bed, I’d guess that they probably swam with their boats, too.”

塞雷诺的团队还发现了沉甸甸的平底石头——他们怀疑这些石头是用来捕捞罗非鱼和鲶鱼等鱼类的。在实验室的工作间里，研究人员正在清洗和准备用于展示的材料，他递给我一块这样的石头，那是一个光滑的、带有棕色斑点的椭圆形石头，拿在手里沉甸甸的。在那片湖泊里，古代渔民用鱼叉捕捞了大量的尼罗河鲈鱼，这种淡水巨兽可以长到六英尺长，重达四百多磅。虽然如今这种鱼的数量正在减少，但它仍然是非洲许多地区重要的食物来源。

Sereno’s team also discovered heavy, flat-bottomed stones—what they suspect to be weights for netting fish like tilapia and catfish. In a lab workroom where researchers clean and prepare materials for display, he hands me one of these, a smooth, brown-speckled oval that has a pleasing heft. In that lake, the ancient fishermen speared and landed impressive catches of Nile perch, a freshwater monstrosity that can grow to six feet long and weigh more than four hundred pounds. The species, though in decline today, is still an important food source in many parts of Africa.

在参观这位著名古生物学家的实验室时，我惊讶地发现很多事情。塞雷诺对桌上那些装着珍贵早期人类DNA的试管（装在袋子里，等着送去分析）以及柜子里那些只做了一半准备工作的新恐龙物种（还没命名）都显得毫不在意。如果你也像他一样，好奇心旺盛到根本停不下来，连文书工作都顾不上做，我想你也会把这些东西乱放的吧。

A lot of things surprise me as I poke about the lab of this famous paleontologist. Sereno is pretty blithe about the test tubes of invaluable early human DNA bagged up and sitting on his desk (still waiting to be sent out for analysis) and about the half-prepped new dinosaur species in his cabinet (still waiting to be named). If you have a roaming curiosity that refuses to settle long enough to get hung up on paperwork, I suppose you’d leave those things lying around, too.

“你见过恐龙木乃伊吗？我超爱木乃伊！”他兴奋地叫道，同时邀请我仔细观察一块罕见的恐龙化石，化石上清晰可见恐龙皮的纹理。我用手指轻轻抚摸着化石上的凸起和纹路。我脑海中第一个浮现的画面就是恐龙皮革，而且我根本停不下来。我强忍着没把话说出口。塞雷诺让我亲手触摸实验室里的一切——从锋利的箭头和易碎的陶器，到剑龙的盘子，甚至是霸王龙的遗骸。这种与过去如此近距离的接触，再加上塞雷诺热情洋溢、语速飞快的讲解，简直令人着迷。这是一次短暂的史前之旅。

“Have you ever seen a dinosaur mummy? I love mummies!” he exclaims as he invites me to examine a rare dinosaur fossil that reveals the specimen’s textured hide. I run my fingers lightly over the imprint’s bumps and ridges. The first thing that comes to my mind is dinosaur leather, and I can’t stop myself from blurting it out loud. Sereno allows me to handle everything in the lab—from sharp arrowheads and fragile pottery to a plate from a stegosaurus and even the remnants of a T. rex. This physical proximity to the past, paired with Sereno’s enthusiastic, mile-a-minute commentary, is nothing short of spellbinding. A little side trip to Prehistoric Times.

但是，尽管证据确凿，我们仍然无法确定戈贝罗古湖居民的游泳能力如何——探究人类水生历史的难点在于，痕迹往往转瞬即逝。塞雷诺和他的研究团队能够证明的是，这些生活在绿色撒哈拉的居民过着狩猎采集的生活，他们会根据需要前往其他水池，但大部分时间都待在水边。

But, with all the evidence, we still can’t tell how well the people of Paleolake Gobero swam—the frustrating thing about investigating the trail of humans’ aquatic past is that a wake doesn’t stick around. What Sereno and his researchers can show is that these inhabitants of the Green Sahara led a hunter-gatherer existence, pool-hopping as needed but mostly staying put by the water.

我喜欢想象，早期人类潜水捕捞蛤蜊塔的方式，就像我潜水捕捞鲍鱼一样——没错，他们会踢水、上下颠簸、喘气，但同时也会感到惊奇和喜悦。不难想象那会是怎样一番景象。我想起我的儿子们，他们最快乐的时光莫过于在博利纳斯（Bolinas）——一个位于加州伯克利以北一小时车程的沿海小村庄——退潮的时候。清晨，银色的泻湖上常常笼罩着一层薄雾。孩子们在退潮后露出的泥滩上奔跑嬉戏，跃过深色的沙质小溪。他们在波涛汹涌的大海边缘来回穿梭。他们互相投掷海藻。他们用沙子堆砌金字塔，一边叽叽喳喳地讲述着与他们建造的微型建筑群相关的详细故事，一边将整个建筑群淹没。洪水滔天。我看着它们在水中嬉戏，不断地试探着自己是否适应深水。它们都热爱大海。哥哥菲利克斯已经会游泳一段时间了，但弟弟泰迪仍然对波涛汹涌的海水感到害羞。

I like to imagine that these early humans dove for their towers of clams the way I dove for abalone—with some kicking and bobbing and gasping, yes, but also with a measure of wonder and joy. It’s not so hard to picture how that might have happened. I think about my own sons, who are no happier than when it’s low tide in Bolinas, a little coastal hamlet an hour north of where we live in Berkeley, California. In the mornings, there’s often a low fog hanging over the silvery lagoon. The boys race around on the muddy flats revealed by the receding tide, leaping over darkly sandy rivulets. They dart to and from the edge of a restless ocean. They throw seaweed at each other. They build pyramids of sand, jabbering a detailed backstory to go with the miniature complex they have constructed, before they inundate the whole thing with a mass flood. I watch as they dance in and out of the water, continually testing their comfort with the depths. They both love the sea. Felix, the older, has known how to swim for some time, but Teddy, the younger, is still shy around water that moves of its own accord.

或许几千年前，事情就是这样发生的。一个女孩在古湖边采集蛤蜊。从她记事起，这就是她的工作。她能看到蛤蜊就在深水区边缘。也许那些蛤蜊比她涉水能够到的要大。有一天，她想，如果屏住呼吸，她能不能游过去？于是，她一点一点地尝试，来回游动，用脚趾蹬着沙底，在水面上上下浮动，像青蛙一样踢腿，让脸露出水面。几周过去了，也许几个月过去了。她终于不再只是上下浮动和喘息，而是找到了一种可以持续下去的方法。她学会了如何平静地漂浮，节省体力；也学会了如何像剪刀一样，在发现有希望的蛤蜊时，迅速俯冲下去。她成功地挖掘出了新的食物宝库。其他人也开始模仿她这种上下浮动的方法。

Perhaps it happened this same way, so many thousands of years ago. A girl gathers clams at the edge of a paleolake. It’s been her job as long as she can remember. She can see the clams just beyond the drop-off to deeper waters. Maybe those clams are bigger than the ones she can reach just by wading. One day, she wonders if she could hold her breath to get to them. Little by little, she ventures out and back, out and back, pushing off the sandy bottom with her toes, bobbing at the surface, frog kicking her legs to free her face from the water. Weeks go by, maybe months. The bobbing and gasping eventually give way to something she can sustain. She knows what it is to float untroubled, conserving energy, and what it is to scissor her body and swoop down when she spies a promising mollusk. She finds success in unearthing a new cache of food. Others start to imitate her up-down, up-down method.

能够亲眼目睹来自过去时代的实物，这本身就充满魔力——你可以说：“看，他们就在这里，就在我们此刻站立的地方。”你可以指着一个用河马牙制成的弯曲臂环说：“她戴过这个。”你可以拿起一根尖锐的矛尖，想象那些水猎者潜水、挖掘、游泳的场景。远古人类！和我们一样！

There’s a magic to being able to look at tangible objects from a bygone era—to say, See here. They were here, where we stand, right now. To point at a curved arm bracelet made of hippo ivory and say, She wore this. To pick up the jagged tip of a spear and picture those water hunters diving and digging and swimming. Paleo man! Just like us!

这些早期人类身手敏捷，足以避开与他们共享水域的河马和鳄鱼，而且他们有足够的时间掌握游泳技能，因为他们无需像人类那样四处奔波寻找水源和食物。湖泊及其丰富的动物资源，使得这些社会能够在湖岸边繁荣发展数千年。在同一时期，或许在撒哈拉沙漠的其他地方，那些洞穴壁画的作者们也在游泳。

These early humans were agile enough to avoid hippos and crocodiles that shared the water with them, and they would have had time enough to master swimming, because they weren’t scouring the landscape in search of water or food. The lake, and the animal riches contained therein, made it possible for these societies to thrive for millennia right on its shores. Elsewhere in the Green Sahara, during this same wet period, perhaps those cave painters were swimming, too.

虽然人类游泳的最早证据可以追溯到一万年前，但我们很可能更早掌握了游泳技能。我们现代人类物种——智人（Homo sapiens）——大约在二十万年前由其他现已灭绝的人类祖先演化而来。有证据表明，这些人类祖先也曾出海。2008年，在希腊克里特岛，一个研究团队在南部海岸洞穴附近的岩石阶地上发现了数十万年前的石英石手斧。这些粗糙的工具与之前在那里发现的任何其他工具都不同，它们与直立人（Homo erectus）使用的工具相似，直立人是生活在非洲和欧洲大陆的人类祖先。由于克里特岛与大陆分离已有五百万年之久，这些人类祖先必须通过开阔水域才能到达该岛。这证明，地中海地区的航海民族出现的时间比科学家之前认为的要早数万年。如果没有合适的交通工具，远洋航行是很难实现的。会游泳吗？或者如果你对水不熟悉、不自在的话？

Though the earliest evidence of human swimming dates back just ten thousand years, we most likely knew how to swim much earlier than that. Our modern human species, Homo sapiens, began to evolve nearly two hundred thousand years ago from other species of now-extinct ancestral humans. There is evidence of those ancestral humans going to sea, too. In 2008, on the Greek island of Crete, a team of researchers found quartz stone hand axes that were hundreds of thousands of years old, embedded in rock terraces near cave shelters on the southern coast. The rough tools were unlike any others previously found there and resembled those used by Homo erectus, a species of ancestral human found in Africa and mainland Europe. Because Crete has been separated from the mainland for five million years, those ancestral humans would have had to travel to the island by open water. It was proof of Mediterranean seafaring peoples tens of thousands of years earlier than scientists had previously thought. Open-ocean voyages are pretty hard to pull off if you don’t know how to swim, or if you don’t have comfort and familiarity with the water.

即使是已灭绝的人类近亲尼安德特人，也可能通过游泳觅食。我咨询了研究尼安德特人的英国人类学家克里斯·斯特林格，他是伦敦自然历史博物馆的人类起源专家；他的团队在直布罗陀洞穴中的发现表明，与现代人类生活时期重叠的晚期幸存的尼安德特人在大约2.8万年前灭绝之前，以海洋为生。尼安德特人从河口采集贻贝，屠宰海豹和海豚，并将它们拖进洞穴，在火堆旁烹制食物。尼安德特人是如何捕获这些鱼类、海豚和海豹的呢？我们无法确定他们是否游泳，也无法确定他们是如何游泳的，但洞穴地层中海洋动物遗骸的分布表明，尼安德特人长期以来对沿海资源有着丰富的知识和熟悉程度，这种行为在现代人类出现之前极为罕见。

Even Neanderthals, extinct close relatives of humans, may have swum for their food. I consult the British anthropologist Chris Stringer, who studies Neanderthals and is an expert on human origins at London’s Natural History Museum; his team’s findings from caves in Gibraltar showed that late-surviving Neanderthals, who overlapped with modern humans, lived off the sea about twenty-eight thousand years ago, before they died out. The Neanderthals collected mussels from a river estuary and butchered seals and dolphins, dragging them into caves for food prep by the fire. How did Neanderthals catch those fish and dolphins and seals? We can’t tell if or how they swam, but the distribution of the marine animal remains in the caves’ strata shows that Neanderthals had longtime knowledge and familiarity with coastal resources, a behavior that has rarely been found before modern humans came along.

但如果说潜水捕捞鲍鱼教会了我什么，那就是游泳看起来多么容易——而危险又多么难以察觉。塞雷诺告诉我，戈贝罗最引人注目的发现实际上与游泳和溺水有关：在古湖边缘发现了一处令人动容的三重葬身之处，他的团队将其命名为“石器时代的拥抱”。

But if diving for abalone taught me anything, it is how easy the act of swimming can seem—and how imperceptible the dangers can be. Sereno tells me that the most striking discovery at Gobero actually has to do with swimming, and drowning: a moving triple burial at the edge of the paleolake that his team dubbed the “Stone Age Embrace.”

他描述了发现三具尸体时的情景：一名三十岁的女子和两个分别为五岁和八岁的小孩，他们紧紧地依偎在一起，双手交握。“这是一处壮观的墓葬，三具头骨重见天日，”他回忆起小心翼翼地挖掘头骨的情景时说道。挖掘工作难度很大，团队在挖掘过程中必须谨慎行事。松散的沙子像水一样流动；每次拂去，它都会再次渗回。

He describes what it was like to uncover the three bodies: a thirty-year-old woman and two small children, aged five and eight, lying intimately together with hands intertwined. “It was a spectacular burial, three crania coming to the surface,” he says, recalling the delicate unearthing of the skulls. The team moved carefully during the excavation, which was difficult to perform. Loose sand moves like water; every time you brush it away, it trickles back.

这具尸体的姿态——双臂伸展，双手相握——深深触动了探险队的每一个人。塞雷诺说，这显然是一种仪式性的摆放。后来在现场采集的沙土样本显示，上面曾放置过花朵——一种属于鸡冠花属（Celosia）的植物，属于苋科，花色繁多。尸体下方发现了用硅化木雕刻的箭头。这些箭头经过X光和电子显微镜扫描分析：结果表明它们从未被发射过，很可能是出于某种象征意义而被故意放置在那里的。经检查，骨骼和牙齿上没有发现任何损伤或疾病的痕迹。

The poignancy of the pose—arms stretched to the other, holding hands—affected everyone on the expedition. The arrangement seemed clearly ceremonial, Sereno says. A sample of sand taken at the scene later showed that flowers—a species in a genus called Celosia, part of the amaranth family, that can come in many colors—had been laid down. Arrowheads carved from petrified wood were found underneath the bodies. They were X-rayed and scanned with an electron microscope: the analysis showed that they were never fired, and were probably deliberately placed there for symbolic purposes. When examined, the skeletons and teeth revealed no stress patterns of injury or disease.

塞雷诺问我想不想现在就去见见戈贝罗的人们。他领我来到三合葬墓的挖掘现场，指着箭头、完好的牙齿以及尸体的摆放位置。虽然亲眼目睹这么多触手可及的古生物发现——恐龙、其他古代水生动物——令人震撼，但我发现与人类遗骸的相遇更加震撼人心。我意识到，真正吸引我的是埋藏在泥土中的故事。这石器时代的拥抱，其核心故事你我都耳熟能详：三人（一位母亲和她的孩子们？）同时死去，猝然离世（溺水？），有人（一位慈爱的丈夫和父亲？）有时间举行一场精心设计的葬礼仪式。

Sereno asks me if I’d like to meet the people of Gobero. Right now. He leads me to the excavated display of the triple burial, pointing out the arrowheads, the healthy teeth, the deliberate placement of the bodies. Though being in the presence of so many tangible paleontological finds—the dinosaurs, the other ancient aquatic animals—was profound, I found the encounter with the human remains to be even more so. I realized that it’s the story embedded in the earth with them that captivates me most. The Stone Age embrace is at heart a story familiar to you and me: the three (a mother and her children?) died together, suddenly (drowning?), and someone (a loving husband and father?) had time to perform an elaborate burial ritual.

塞雷诺的话至少证实了我的一些猜测。“什么时候才能摆好尸体的姿势？你得面对尸僵和日晒腐烂的问题，”他解释说。“所以，这算是猝死。在水边。我想应该是溺死在戈贝罗古湖里。”

Sereno confirms at least some of my imaginings. “When can you pose a body? You have to contend with rigor mortis and rotting in the sun,” he explains. “So it was a sudden death somehow. On water’s edge. I think it was the result of drowning in Paleolake Gobero.”

这是一个永恒的故事，讲述了父母最可怕的噩梦。我知道小时候在海滩上玩耍探索是什么感觉。现在，我也体会到了为人父母的感受，看着我的两个小儿子学习游泳，在水边探索。无论过去还是现在，游泳和溺水之间的界限都既令人恐惧又令人兴奋，而且这种感觉始终存在。无论我们掌握了多少游泳技巧，这种感觉都不会改变。

It is a timeless tale of a parent’s worst nightmare. I know what it is to be that child on the beach, playing and exploring. And I know now what it is like to be a parent, watching my two young sons learn to swim and experiment by the water. Then as now, the states of swimming and drowning are terrifyingly, thrillingly porous. It remains that way no matter how well we have mastered the skill.

漫长的旱季与湿润的交替，使得过往的点点滴滴得以保存至今，供我们探寻。三重葬的悲剧是一切的开端；当然，另一个永恒的故事是关于一个被淹没的世界。地球轨道周期性的变化将非洲的季节性季风带到了北方，造就了绿色撒哈拉；戈贝罗遗址是曾经生活在那里的人类的无可比拟的记录。在今天，海平面不断上升，气温波动幅度远超我们以往的记录，这些生命的遗迹对我们而言具有特殊的意义。

Wet periods punctuated by long dry ones also allowed pieces of that past to persist to this day, for us to find. Collapsed into the tragedy of the triple burial is the beginning of everything; another timeless tale, of course, is that of a drowned world. A cyclical variation in Earth’s orbit brought Africa’s seasonal monsoons north and made the Green Sahara possible; Gobero is an unparalleled record of the humans who lived there. The remnants of these lives have special resonance for us today, when waters are rising higher and temperatures are fluctuating above and beyond what we have ever recorded.

我们自身可能很快也会遭受水灾的毁灭性打击，而这一次，我们自身的活动将成为地球表面发生剧烈变化的罪魁祸首。到2030年，人口数量将……预计受洪水影响的人口将增加两倍。在我居住的加利福尼亚州，到下个世纪之交，海平面上升可能超过九英尺，届时加州超过一半的海滩将被冲走。在全球范围内，海平面上升有可能使数亿人沦为难民。

We ourselves may soon be devastated by water, and this time our own activities are the cause of dramatic changes to the surface of the planet. By 2030, the number of people affected by floods is expected to triple. In California, where I live, sea level rise could exceed nine feet by the turn of the next century, washing away more than 50 percent of the beaches of the Golden State. Worldwide, sea level rise has the potential to turn hundreds of millions of people into refugees.

2

2

你是陆地动物

You’re a Land Animal

大多数陆生哺乳动物天生就具备游泳的本能，但人类却不具备。大象、狗、猫（尽管不太情愿）甚至蝙蝠都会游泳（而且游得相当不错）。人类和其他大型灵长类动物，例如黑猩猩，则需要后天学习。一些科学家推测，这与大型猿类的解剖结构进化得更适合在树间荡来荡去有关。在极少数由研究人员训练猿类游泳的实验案例中，它们展现出的是类似青蛙的踢腿动作，而不是其他哺乳动物常见的狗刨式。

Most land mammals possess instinctive swimming ability from birth, but humans do not. Elephants, dogs, cats (albeit reluctantly), and even bats can swim (and pretty well, too). Humans and other large primates, like chimpanzees, have to be taught. Some scientists speculate that this has to do with the way the anatomy of the great apes evolved to be better suited to swinging through trees. In the rare experimental cases in which apes were taught to swim by researchers, they exhibited a froglike kick, instead of the doggy paddle so common in other mammals.

保罗·塞雷诺告诉我，你是从鱼类进化而来的，但现在“你是一种试图游泳的陆地动物。我们称你为次级游泳者。”

You evolved from fish, Paul Sereno tells me, but now “you’re a land animal trying to swim. You’re what we call a secondary swimmer.”

先别太失望。古生物学家尼尔·舒宾解释说，人体结构是古代鱼类、爬行动物和其他灵长类动物的遗留产物。在2014年一部根据他的著作《你的内在鱼》 （Your Inner Fish）改编的纪录片中，舒宾表示：“成为一名鱼类古生物学家是教授人体解剖学的一种非常有效的方式，因为通常一些最好的方法都源于古代鱼类。”我们自身身体的蓝图可以在其他生物身上找到。”鱼类的遗产：它们的鳍，我们的四肢，都起源于同一组细胞。

Don’t be too disappointed just yet. The paleobiologist Neil Shubin explains that the structure of the human body is the legacy of ancient fish, reptiles, and other primates. In a 2014 documentary based on his book Your Inner Fish, Shubin says that “being a fish paleontologist is a very powerful way to teach human anatomy, because often some of the best road maps to our own bodies are seen in other creatures.” The fish’s legacy: their fins, our limbs, all start from the same group of cells.

我们体内留存着一些奇妙的游泳痕迹。如果我们体内还保留着其他动物的记忆，那么某些功能的痕迹自然也会残留下来，并在浸入水中时重新激活。如果你把一个两个月大的婴儿面朝下放入水中，她会屏住呼吸几秒钟，心率也会减慢，以节省氧气。但这并不意味着如果你把她扔进游泳池，她就能游到安全的地方。随着婴儿长大，神经系统发育成熟，这种心率减慢反射——它是包括吸吮和抓握在内的一系列原始或残余反射的一部分——会逐渐减弱。

Within us there are intriguing traces of a swimming past. And if we hold in our bodies the ghosts of other animals, it follows that hints of certain functions remain and reawaken with submersion. If you put a two-month-old facedown in water, the baby will hold her breath for several seconds and her heart rate will slow, conserving oxygen. But that doesn’t mean she’ll swim to safety if you throw her in a pool. As babies get older and their neurological systems develop, that bradycardic reflex—part of a whole suite of primitive or residual reflexes that include sucking and grasping—starts to weaken.

然而，人类是模仿机器。我们通过观察学习：从动作模式到解读我们所遇到的人的情绪，从工具制造和食物偏好到关于公平、交配和语言的观念，无所不包。“理解人类如何进化以及我们为何与其他动物如此不同的关键在于认识到我们是一个文化物种，”进化生物学家约瑟夫·亨里奇写道。他影响深远的研究聚焦于文化进化和基因进化如何相互作用。累积性社会学习——亨里奇称之为我们形成大规模“集体大脑”的能力——是人类独有的。其他动物也展现出社会学习能力，但人类的独特之处在于，它在累积性的文化层面上进行学习，并真正影响着基因进化。

Humans, though, are imitation machines. We learn through observation: everything from movement patterns to reading the emotions of people we encounter, in domains ranging from tool-making and food preferences to ideas about fairness, mating, and language. “The key to understanding how humans evolved and why we are so different from other animals is to recognize that we are a cultural species,” writes the evolutionary biologist Joseph Henrich, whose influential work centers on how cultural and genetic evolution interact. Cumulative social learning—our ability to form large-scale “collective brains,” as Henrich calls it—is particular to us. Other animals exhibit social learning, but humans are singular in doing it on a cumulative cultural level that actually influences genetic evolution.

亨里希用他那本戏谑地命名为“失落的欧洲探险家档案”的案例研究来阐释他的理论：当欧洲探险家被困在某个看似荒凉的新环境中——比如北极或澳大利亚——他们无一例外地死于饥饿、疾病或严寒，除非他们与当地土著居民相遇。这些土著居民体格强健，他们懂得如何在所谓的恶劣环境中生存，而且这种生存方式已经延续了数千年。人类群体相互联系，并积累了个人一生都无法完全掌握的知识：如何制作三倒钩鱼叉，在没有木材的情况下如何生火，如何从有毒植物中提取毒素使其可食用。古考古记录表明，这种文化演进至少在过去28万年中一直在发生——而且在过去的1万年中，这种演进速度显著加快。

Henrich illustrates his theory with case studies from his cheekily named “Lost European Explorer Files”: When European explorers got marooned in some new, seemingly inhospitable environment—the Arctic, say, or Australia—they invariably died of starvation, sickness, or exposure, except in the cases when they fell in with local indigenous peoples. Those locals were robust and healthy; they knew how to thrive in the so-called harsh environment and had for millennia. Human groups connect and build bodies of knowledge that no single individual is smart enough to figure out in one lifetime: how to make a triple-barbed fishing spear, what to burn for fire in the absence of wood, how to leach poisons out of a toxic plant to make it edible. Paleoarchaeological records indicate that this kind of cultural evolution has been happening for at least the last two hundred and eighty thousand years—and that it rapidly accelerated over the last ten thousand of those.

这种文化与基因的协同进化有助于解释我们物种在地球上取得的卓越进化成就。就个体而言，我们并非多么特别或聪明。但我们获取、储存、组织和代代相传不断增长的信息的能力，使我们比任何个人或群体都更聪明。游泳这项技能，以及我们自学游泳的各种方法，正是这种集体文化知识的一部分。就游泳而言，重要的不仅是游泳技巧——正式的指导——还有我们如何通过讲述故事来传达这些知识的重要性。

This culture-gene coevolution helps explain the outstanding evolutionary success our species has had on our planet. Individually, we aren’t all that special or smart. But our ability to acquire, store, organize, and pass on an ever-growing body of information over generations makes us smarter than any one person or group. The practice of swimming, and the different ways in which we teach ourselves to swim, is part of that collective cultural knowledge. When it comes to swimming, it is not just the how-to—the formal instruction—that is critical but also the ways we communicate the importance of that knowledge, through the stories we tell.

简要回顾一下过去两千年来我们为了辅助游泳而发明的各种工具：

A brief history of what we have come up with to aid us in swimming over the last two millennia or so:

公元前 400 年左右，罗马：普鲁塔克描述了一种软木救生衣，罗马将军卡米卢斯派出的一名信使穿着这种救生衣游过台伯河，因为桥被高卢人占领了。

~400 BC, Rome: a cork life jacket, described by Plutarch and worn by a messenger sent by the Roman general Camillus to swim the Tiber because the bridge was in the possession of the Gauls.

十四世纪的波斯：龟壳的半透明外层，用于在潜水采珠时保护眼睛。

Fourteenth-century Persia: the translucent outer layer of a tortoise shell, to protect the eyes while diving for pearls.

十五世纪的意大利：由动物皮制成并充满空气的膀胱，用于水下呼吸，由列奥纳多·达·芬奇设计，他还绘制了游泳脚蹼、呼吸管和其他浮力装置的草图。

Fifteenth-century Italy: a bladder constructed of animal skin and blown full of air, for breathing underwater, designed by Leonardo da Vinci, who also made sketches for swim fins, a snorkel, and other buoyancy devices.

日期不详，日本：一种连接在滑轮上的绳索，日本女海女（ ama）在游泳或呼吸困难时，用它将自己从深处拉上来。

Date unknown, Japan: a rope line attached to a pulley, used by the ama—Japanese free-diving fisherwomen—to reel themselves up from the depths in case of swimming or breathing troubles.

十八世纪的波士顿：发明家兼水上运动专家本杰明·富兰克林发明了椭圆形画家调色板形状的游泳桨，戴在手上，以便游得更快。

Eighteenth-century Boston: swim paddles in the shape of oval painters’ palettes to wear on the hands, from inventor and expert waterman Benjamin Franklin, to go faster.

1896 年，在马萨诸塞州的其他地方：詹姆斯·爱默生获得了一项专利，发明了一种金属框架的“游泳机”，它可以安全地将学生固定在水中，并配有机械手臂和腿部支撑，使身体以适当的划水和踢腿动作移动。

1896, elsewhere in Massachusetts: a metal-framed “swimming machine” to hold a student safely in the water, with mechanical arm and leg supports that moved the body in the appropriate stroke and kick motion, patented by James Emerson.

1908 年，伦敦：一套用优质棉布缝制的带充气阀的游泳圈——以 Swimeesy Buoy 品牌向公众售出了数万个。

1908, London: a set of water-wings sewn from fine cotton material, with valves for inflation—tens of thousands were sold to the public under the brand Swimeesy Buoy.

1930 年，迈阿密：一种用细云杉木条制成的木制泳衣，这种新奇的泳衣旨在鼓励和帮助胆怯的女游泳者漂浮在水面上。

1930, Miami: a wooden swimming costume fashioned from thin strips of spruce, a novelty to encourage and keep timid female swimmers afloat.

2017 年，中国：一款名为 WhiteShark Mix 的小型手持设备，配备双螺旋桨，承诺帮助任何初学者“像冠军一样游泳，成为水中无可争议的明星”。

2017, China: a tiny handheld device with double propellers, the WhiteShark Mix, promises to help any beginner “swim like a champion and become an uncontested star in the water.”

有时我们需要一点帮助。如果说文化是对人类生物学的补充，那么我们的优势就在于我们能够发现问题并创造解决方案。这些发明的名称和描述对我而言，就像一首水生诗篇。它是我们想象力与生物学交融，化不可能为可能的美妙乐章。

Sometimes we need a little help. If the complement to human biology is culture, then our strength is our ability to identify a problem and invent the solution. The names of these inventions and their descriptions are for me a kind of aquatic poetry. It is the sound of our imaginations dancing with our biology to make the impossible possible.

3

3

来自海上游牧民族的启示

Lessons from a Sea Nomad

在东南亚珊瑚三角区的沿海地带，我们得以一窥正在消失的水生社会中的游泳教学场景。最优秀的自由潜水渔民可以潜到两百英尺深的海底，手持鱼叉枪，在海底交替游动和行走——在这样的深度，人类处于负浮力状态——每次持续十分钟，直到找到猎物。他们每天可以在水下待上五个小时。

In the coastal regions of Southeast Asia’s Coral Triangle, we get a glimpse of swimming lessons in a vanishing aquatic society. The best free-diving fishermen can swim down to two hundred feet and stay there, alternately swimming and walking along the ocean floor—humans are negatively buoyant at that depth—spear guns in hand, for ten minutes at a time, until they find their prey. They can spend five hours a day submerged underwater.

在如今的马来西亚、印度尼西亚和菲律宾一带，数千年来，巴瑶族海上游牧民的幼子们甚至在学会走路之前，就已开始接受海洋生活的熏陶。父母祈祷孩子们能拥有与珊瑚礁紧密相连的生存技能。即使是两三岁的孩子也能轻松潜水，双腿有力地蹬水，游向海面，采集小蛤蜊。年长的孩子们在自家的船屋里，教弟弟妹妹们如何漂浮、踢水和寻找鱼儿。

For thousands of years, in what is today Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines, the youngest Bajau sea nomads have been initiated into a life of the sea before they even learn to walk. Parents pray that babies will be blessed with the aquatic abilities they need for a life joined with the reef. Even two- and three-year-olds can dive with ease, their legs flicking powerfully to propel them to collect small clams. From their families’ houseboats, older children teach their younger siblings how to float and kick and look for fish.

最近的研究表明，巴瑶族人的脾脏比与其相关的村民群体大50%。在印度尼西亚大陆，当我们潜入水下时，脾脏会收缩，这是哺乳动物潜水反射的一部分，脾脏会将富含氧气的红细胞释放到全身循环系统中。心率减慢，血管收缩，将血液从四肢引向主要器官。这些能量节约机制启动，使我们能够更有效地利用氧气。

The Bajau have recently been shown to have spleens that are 50 percent larger than those of a related group of villagers on the Indonesian mainland. When we dive underwater, the spleen contracts as part of the mammalian diving reflex, shooting its supply of oxygenated red blood cells into circulation around the body. The heart rate slows, and blood vessels constrict, directing blood flow away from the extremities and toward major organs. These energy conservation measures kick in so we can use available oxygen more efficiently.

海洋哺乳动物，例如海豹，一生大部分时间都在水下度过，与陆生哺乳动物相比，它们的脾脏不成比例地大。脾脏最大的海豹可以潜得更深——可以把它想象成多了一个氧气罐。研究表明，巴瑶族人脾脏肥大是自然选择的结果，而非潜水本身造成的：拥有能产生较大脾脏基因的巴瑶族人往往更容易生存下来，并且拥有更多的后代。即使是从未潜水过的巴瑶族人也具有同样的特征。他们的身体已经进化得更适合自由潜水。

Marine mammals such as seals, who spend much of their lives underwater, have disproportionately large spleens compared with land-based mammals. Seals with the largest spleens can dive deepest—think of it as having an extra tank of air. Research shows that the Bajau’s oversize spleens are due to natural selection, not to diving itself: Bajau people with genes that produce larger spleens tend to survive and have more offspring. Even Bajau who have never been divers have the same trait. Their bodies have evolved to be better at free diving.

虽然巴瑶族人的这种特殊能力是遗传的，但其他一些水生习性却是后天习得的。与巴瑶族类似的自由潜水海上游牧民族，例如居住在水上房屋和沿海高脚屋中的莫肯族——他们生活在如今的泰国和缅甸各地——都拥有特殊的水下视力。研究表明，从小潜水长大的莫肯族儿童的水下视力比我们这些陆地人敏锐两倍。在我们只能看到模糊景象的地方，这些“人鱼”无需借助护目镜或面镜就能轻松地从海底采集蛤蜊和海参。

Though this particular trait of the Bajau is inherited, other aquatic characteristics are acquired. Similar free-diving sea nomads, like the water-dwelling Moken—who also live on houseboats and coastal homes on stilts, in communities throughout what is today Thailand and Myanmar—have a special ability to focus their eyes underwater. The Moken kids who grow up diving have been shown to have underwater vision that is twice as sharp as that of us landlubbers. Where the rest of us see a blur, these mer-people can easily gather clams and sea cucumbers from the ocean floor without the aid of goggles or masks.

我们大多数人在水下视力很差，这是因为弯曲的角膜在陆地上能很好地发挥屈光作用，但在水中却会抵消这种屈光力。海上游牧民族的孩子们在水下能够通过缩小瞳孔来适应这种情况，从而提高他们能看到的细节。起初，人们并不清楚这种能力是遗传的还是后天习得的。但研究人员发现，早期的水下训练可以改变我们所有人。在不到十几次旨在区分水下特定对比图案的视觉练习中，非海上游牧民族的孩子们也获得了持久的、更强的水下聚焦能力。

Most of us see terribly underwater because the refractive power of the curved cornea, which works so well on land, is offset by immersion in water. Sea nomad kids are able to accommodate for that when they are underwater by constricting their pupils, which increases the fine detail of what they can see. At first, it wasn’t clear whether this ability was inherited or learned. But researchers figured out that early immersion training can change all of us. In fewer than a dozen visual practice sessions aimed at distinguishing specific kinds of contrasting patterns underwater, non-sea-nomad kids were able to achieve a lasting heightened ability to focus underwater.

水也以其他方式塑造了这些民族。在这些地方生存不仅需要游泳技能，还需要了解水生环境的运作方式。这些文化会采取措施做好准备。2004年12月26日，印度洋发生特大海啸，造成南亚和东南亚沿海约23万人丧生，莫肯人通过解读水中的迹象而幸存下来。

The water has shaped these peoples in other ways, too. Survival in these places requires not just swimming skills but also an understanding of how the aquatic environment works. These cultures take steps to prepare themselves. On December 26, 2004, when a massive tsunami in the Indian Ocean killed some two hundred and thirty thousand people along the coastlines of South and Southeast Asia, the Moken survived by reading signs in the water.

在泰国沿海偏远的苏林群岛，莫肯族村民在发现海水退去、海岸干涸后，纷纷逃往地势较高的地方。他们警告了所有遇到的人，并在第一波巨浪袭来之前就已逃离。村庄几乎被夷为平地，但所有村民都幸免于难。在苏林国家公园，大约二十几名莫肯族人正在带领游客进行浮潜之旅，这时他们……他们意识到海流异常，便将船驶离海岸，进入更深的水域，最终幸免于难。类似的情况也发生在缅甸管辖水域的一群莫肯族渔民身上；他们发现船只周围海浪剧烈翻腾后，立即驶向更远的海域。附近其他渔民正在捕捞鱿鱼；当海浪猛烈翻滚时，他们被巨浪卷走，葬身大海。

On the remote Surin Islands off the coast of Thailand, Moken villagers fled toward higher ground after someone noticed the sea receding and the shore going dry. They warned everyone they saw and were gone long before the first wave hit. The village was decimated, but all of its residents were saved. In Mu Ko Surin National Park, some two dozen Moken were out guiding tourists on snorkeling excursions when they recognized that the currents were moving strangely; they steered their boats away from the coast into deeper water and survived. A similar thing happened to a group of Moken fishermen out in Myanmar-governed waters; after observing fiercely swirling water around their vessels, they immediately headed further out to sea. Other fishermen in the vicinity were busy with the squid harvest; when the seas rose up with a terrific violence, they were tossed to their deaths.

在这一地区的其他地方，大象惊慌失措地奔向高地。蝉鸣戛然而止。海豚游向深海。这些莫肯人从未亲眼见过海啸，但莫肯族的长者们讲述着“七波巨浪”的传说，据说每两代人就会来一次。他们把其中最大的一波巨浪称为“拉布恩”（Laboon ）——这是一股“净化之浪”，带着毁灭一切的狂怒而来。

Elsewhere in the region, elephants stampeded for higher ground. Cicadas went silent. Dolphins swam toward the depths. None of these Moken had ever seen a tsunami themselves, but Moken elders spoke of the legend of the “seven roller waves,” which come once every two generations. Laboon was the name they had for the biggest of the waves—it was a “cleansing wave,” one that arrived with a fury to consume and destroy.

在太平洋西北地区的原住民和美洲原住民部落的口述传统中，流传着类似的关于突发性海水洪水和大规模溺亡的故事，而日本一千五百年前的海啸记录也证实了这一点。这些故事中蕴含着知识。巴瑶族关于半人半鱼的传说和莫肯族关于七大巨浪的故事，实际上都是关于如何在海上生存的故事。数千年来，在没有文字的情况下，这些民族通过讲故事的方式，成功地传承了对他们的长寿和生存至关重要的水上技能：游泳、潜水、捕鱼、划船等等。通过敏锐的观察力和对海洋环境的深入了解。

Similar stories of sudden saltwater floods and mass drownings exist in the oral tradition of First Nations and Native American tribes in the Pacific Northwest and are confirmed by Japanese tsunami records dating back one and a half millennia. Knowledge is encoded in these stories. Bajau legends about half-fish people and Moken stories about the seven big waves are really stories about how to live a life at sea. Over thousands of years, without a written language, storytelling is how these peoples have successfully passed along the aquatic skills so key to their longevity and survival: swimming, diving, fishing, boating, all of it made possible by keen observation and intimate knowledge of the marine environment.

这些故事教导人们要敬畏海洋。巴瑶族人在潜水前会向海神献祭——用椰壳做成的小船漂浮着一些食物，用树叶包着一支香烟，或者点燃一根香——因为海神有时仁慈，有时残酷。它们喜怒无常，它们的喜怒也影响着波涛汹涌的大海。如果你对它们谦卑——如果你温柔地对待珊瑚，如果你尊重鱼类，并且不索取超过你所需——海洋就会眷顾你。

The stories teach reverence. Before diving, the Bajau make an offering to the ocean spirits—a bit of food floated in a coconut-husk boat, a cigarette in a leaf, a stick of incense—because the ocean spirits can be kind or cruel. They are mercurial, and with their mood goes the mood of the frothing seas. If you are humble before them—if you are gentle with the coral, if you are respectful of the fish and don’t take more than you need—the ocean will take care of you.

这些历史上以游牧为生的渔民如今仍在努力适应不断变化的世界。作为无国籍人士，他们没有公民身份，没有证件，工作机会也寥寥无几，因此被许多政府视为最不堪一击的“漂泊者”。然而，即便巴瑶族和莫肯族的传统生活方式正在逐渐消逝——越来越少的人能够继续以捕鱼为生——他们文化的最后遗迹仍然指引着他们如何在逆境中求生。

The last of these historically nomadic fishermen struggle today to adapt to a changing world, where, as stateless people with no citizenship, no documents, and few options for work, they are perceived by many governments as adrift in the worst sense. And yet, even as the Bajau and Moken ways of life are eroding around them—fewer and fewer are able to continue a life of subsistence fishing—the last vestiges of their culture still tell them how to swim to survive.

我们并非两栖动物，但我喜欢“两栖”这个概念。博物学家洛伦·艾斯利写道，现代科学最伟大的成就莫过于穿越时空的能力——这不仅体现在我们周围世界的具体观察上（例如阅读“裸露的地层”），也体现在我们自身的想象中（“我看到了早期海洋中漂浮的细胞”）。他写道：“那些远古海洋的盐分融入了我们的血液，它的石灰质则存在于我们的骨骼之中。每当我们沿着……行走……”在海滩上，某种古老的冲动会驱使我们脱掉鞋子和衣服，或者像久战后思乡的难民一样，在海藻和泛白的木头间搜寻食物。我们是生理进化的产物，但我们的行为却受到我们对进化史的解读的驱使。

We are not amphibious, but I like the idea of amphibiousness. The naturalist Loren Eiseley wrote that the great accomplishment of modern science was the ability to time travel—not just through the concrete observations of the world around us (reading “seams of exposed strata”) but also through our own imaginings (“I saw the drifting cells of the early seas”). “The salt of those ancient seas is in our blood, its lime is in our bones,” he wrote. “Every time we walk along a beach some ancient urge disturbs us so that we find ourselves shedding shoes and garments, or scavenging among seaweed and whitened timbers like the homesick refugees of a long war.” We are products of physical evolution, but we are driven by our interpretation of that evolutionary history.

许多居住在水边的现代社会，例如荷兰，都已开始意识到海平面上升的问题。我们可以从他们身上学到的游泳知识，就是真正的游泳课：为了获得免费使用公共游泳池的权利，所有荷兰儿童都要参加游泳课，并通过考核获得证书，证明他们能够穿着衣服和鞋子游泳。

The awareness of rising seas is being built into many modern-day societies living waterside, like the Dutch. The swimming lessons we can take from them involve actual swimming lessons: to earn the right to use public pools freely, all Dutch children take classes to get a diploma that certifies their ability to swim in their clothes and shoes.

我被一张引人注目的水下照片深深吸引，照片上是一群穿着全套衣服的荷兰五年级学生在上游泳课。这很合理——他们每天都穿着衣服，不是吗？所以，如果海水来袭，他们就能做好准备。我突然意识到，这种想法与海洋游牧民族传统的适应能力不谋而合：我们应该学会与水共存，而不是如何抵御它。

I am riveted by a striking underwater photo of fully clothed Dutch fifth graders in one of these swimming classes. It makes sense—they wear garments every day, don’t they? And so if the water comes, they will be ready. It hits me that this kind of thinking is in alignment with the traditional adaptiveness of the sea nomads: that we should teach ourselves how to live with water, not how to keep it at bay.

“这就像骑自行车一样，是我们文化的基本组成部分，”荷兰建筑师雷姆·库哈斯曾对《纽约时报》这样说道。荷兰的一切建设和运营都充分考虑到了洪水的可能性；国家水务管理中心负责控制荷兰的日常水流。鹿特丹市长艾哈迈德·阿布塔莱布解释说，他的城市位于荷兰最易受洪水侵袭的地区。一旦洪水来袭，冲垮了他们建立的排水系统，“从河流……”“如果洪水泛滥成灾，我们或许只能从一百人中救出十五个人，”他说。“我们别无选择。我们必须学会与水共存。”

“It’s a basic part of our culture, like riding a bike,” the Dutch architect Rem Koolhaas once told the New York Times. Everything is constructed and conducted with an awareness of the possibility of flood; a national water management center controls the day-to-day flow of water in and out of the Netherlands. The mayor of Rotterdam, Ahmed Aboutaleb, explained that his city lies in the most vulnerable part of the country. In the case of a flood coming in and overpowering the system they have created, “from the rivers or the sea, we can evacuate maybe fifteen out of a hundred people,” he said. “We have no choice. We must learn to live with water.”

我们必须学会与水共存，然后它才会为我们开启无限可能。我们最初游泳是为了在水中生存——在此之前，我们无法将游泳视为其他任何东西。但一旦我们能够生存下来，水对我们而言便能承载更多意义。我们可以与水共存，与水共生。我想起了查尔斯·汤姆林森的诗作《在切南戈湖游泳》，它捕捉到了这种境界。他将游泳描述为在水的怀抱中移动，但要保持觉知。这样做，就能领悟到汤姆林森所写“在执着与执着之间，自由”的真谛。

We must learn to live with water, and then it opens us up to possibility. We first swim to survive the water—we can’t view swimming as anything else until that happens. But once we can survive it, the water can be something more for us. We can live with it, thrive with it. I think of Charles Tomlinson’s poem “Swimming Chenango Lake,” which captures this state of being. He describes swimming as the act of moving in the embrace of water, but mindfully. To do so is to realize what it means to be, as Tomlinson writes, “between grasp and grasping, free.”

4

4

人类海豹

The Human Seal

古德劳格·弗里德索尔松 (Guðlaugur Friðþórsson) 在 20 世纪 60 年代的冰岛，还是个小男孩时就在公共游泳池里学会了游泳。他的家乡岛屿赫马岛 (Heimaey)——意为“家乡岛”——是韦斯特曼纳群岛 (Vestmannaeyjar) 中最大的岛屿，也是该群岛中唯一有人居住的地方。

Guðlaugur Friðþórsson learned to swim as a boy in a public swimming pool in 1960s Iceland. His island, Heimaey—it means “home island”—is the largest of the Vestmannaeyjar, or Westman Islands, and its only inhabited place.

在他给我看的三张当时拍摄的照片中，第一张里，孩子们在泳池边一位教练的注视下，玩着白色泡沫踢水板——这又是当时一项巧妙的游泳发明。照片背景中，泳池高墙之后，可以看到崎岖的火山岛地貌，小镇就坐落在这座岛屿上，小镇也叫韦斯特曼纳群岛。

In the first of three photos he shows me from that time, kids frolic with white foam kickboards, yet another ingenious swimming invention, under the watchful supervision of an instructor stationed at the edge of the pool. In the background, behind the pool’s high-walled perimeter, you can see the craggy volcanic island topography in which the town, also called Vestmannaeyjar, sits.

在第二张照片中，一团团不祥的黑烟笼罩着泳池清冷的蓝色矩形区域及其邻近的红顶白瓦建筑。最后一张照片拍摄于1973年火山爆发期间，炽热的熔岩流淌过小镇。最终，岛上的渔船疏散了这座拥有五千居民的小镇，而古德劳格的家乡——包括……他以前的游泳池——被熔岩吞噬了。（在冰岛，人们通常直呼其名，姓氏只是指你是谁的儿子或女儿，我将在本章中沿用这一惯例。）火山爆发后，人们捐款建造了一座新的游泳馆，馆内设有一系列利用地热能加热的游泳池。

In the second photo, puffs of ominous black smoke hover above the cool blue rectangle of the pool and its neighboring red-roofed, white buildings. In the final photo, taken during the volcanic eruption of 1973, there is an incandescent river of lava flowing through town. In the end, the community of five thousand people was evacuated by the island’s fishing fleet, and this part of Guðlaugur’s hometown—including his old pool—fell victim to the lava. (In Iceland, people are known and addressed by their first names, the surname being simply whose son or daughter you are, a convention I will apply throughout this chapter.) A new swimming hall, built with donations after the eruption, would feature a series of pools heated with the resulting geothermal energy.

1973年的火山喷发之所以引人注目，是因为冰岛决定与熔岩对抗——用巨大的水管抽取冰冷的海水来阻止炽热的熔岩流——以拯救港口。海马岛是冰岛最重要的渔业中心之一，其位于南海岸的关键港口至今仍占全国渔获量的约15%。尽管熔岩吞噬了城镇的大部分地区，但它实际上改善了岛屿乃至整个冰岛赖以生存的港口，使港口入口变窄，更能抵御恶劣天气。火山喷发为海马岛带来了数百万吨火山灰用于铺设街道，地热为城镇建筑提供了长达十年的温暖，并在岛上原有火山的基础上又增添了一座新的锥形火山。此外，火山喷发还使岛屿面积增加了20%，形成了超过百英尺高的陡峭新悬崖。在岛屿东侧，靠近这些荒凉、饱受海浪侵蚀的悬崖底部的地方，就是古德劳格于 1984 年 3 月 12 日凌晨登陆的地方。

The 1973 eruption is notable because Iceland decided to fight the lava—to halt the fiery flow with massive hoses pumping cold seawater—to save the harbor. Heimaey is one of the most important fishing centers in Iceland, with a critical harbor situated along the south coast. Today, its fishing boats still account for about 15 percent of the country’s fish catch by volume. Though lava engulfed much of the town, it actually improved the harbor upon which the island, and Iceland itself, depends, narrowing its mouth and making it more protected from rough weather. It gave Heimaey millions of tons of ash for paving the streets, geothermal heat that warmed the town’s buildings for a decade, and a new conical volcano to go with the one the island already had. It also increased the size of the island by 20 percent, creating steep new cliffs over a hundred feet high. Near the base of these inhospitable, wave-battered cliffs, on the east side of the island, is the place where Guðlaugur came ashore in the wee hours of March 12, 1984.

古德劳格本人被视为冰岛民族性格的象征。作家约翰·麦克菲在《纽约客》杂志上这样描述冰岛人民：“无论形势看起来多么严峻，只要有一线生机，他们就会奋起反抗，而这……”这似乎产生了进化效应，在与熔岩的搏斗中得以体现，而接下来的故事也印证了这一点。”正如你可能猜到的那样，麦克菲接下来讲述的故事是关于古德劳格的。注意这里的措辞：进化效应。这是一种表达冰岛人与众不同的方式，他们拥有非凡的坚韧，并将古德劳格视为他们所珍视之物的典范。

Guðlaugur himself is viewed as emblematic of the national character of Iceland. The writer John McPhee immortalized the people of Iceland in the New Yorker thusly: “No matter how overwhelming a situation might seem to be, if there was any possibility of fighting back they had done so, and this seemed to have produced evolutionary effects, expressed in the battle against the lava, and much confirmed in the following story.” The story that McPhee went on to tell, as you might guess, is Guðlaugur’s. Note the language: evolutionary effects. It’s a way to say that Icelanders are a people apart, that they are extraordinary in their hardiness, that they claim Guðlaugur as exemplary of what they hold dear.

作为冰岛生存与韧性的象征，这无疑是一份沉重的负担。一位在渔业工作的朋友告诉我，他的冰岛同事们至今仍清晰地记得1984年古德劳格渔船沉没的那一天。人们会前往古德劳格搁浅的地方，那里是他不得不重新下水游到可以攀爬过锋利熔岩地带进入城镇的地方。有时，他甚至需要四肢着地爬行。他曾拼命饮水的那个水池至今仍在，上面用多种语言刻着标记。冰岛人究竟还记得多少他的故事？“全部，”他们说。

It’s a heavy load, being Iceland’s epic symbol of survival and resilience. A friend who works in the fishing industry tells me that his Icelandic colleagues vividly remember the day in 1984 when Guðlaugur’s fishing vessel went down. People make pilgrimages to see where Guðlaugur hit land, where he had to turn back into the water to swim to the place where he could climb across the razor-sharp lava fields into town. At times, he had to crawl on all fours. The basin he drank from so desperately is still there, marked in multiple languages. How much of his story is still remembered by Icelanders? “All of it,” they say.

对于生活在海中一小块土地上的人们来说，古德劳格（Guðlaugur）堪称英雄，因为他让他们想起了许多英雄故事：在一部可追溯至公元1300年的冰岛传奇中，讲述了亡命之徒格雷蒂尔（Grettir）的故事。他从德朗盖岛（Drangey）游了七公里到达冰岛大陆。抵达后，他在一个至今仍然存在的温泉中取暖。冰岛的历史是一部记录着无数葬身大海的生命的编年史，有时他们甚至就在离岸几码远的地方丧生。海马岛（Heimaey）长期以来作为渔港的重要性意味着，岛上稀少的人口承受了不成比例的打击。整整一面墙都记录着韦斯特曼纳群岛（Vestmannaeyjar）的历史。博物馆专门收藏了可追溯至1251年的岛屿海岸溺水事件记录。因此，该岛在游泳教育和船舶安全设备（如橡胶救生筏、安全带和救生服）的研发方面一直走在前列。1891年，韦斯特曼纳群岛港口的游泳课程成为常规课程，并一直持续到1934年该镇第一座游泳池建成。1943年，冰岛所有学校都将游泳课程列为必修课。对于韦斯特曼纳群岛来说，2003年是一个特殊的年份，因为该岛没有发生溺水事件。

For a people living on a speck of land in the sea, Guðlaugur is heroic because, well, he reminds them of heroic tales: In an Icelandic saga dating back to the year 1300, there is the outlaw Grettir the Strong, who swam seven kilometers from the island of Drangey to the mainland. When he arrived, he warmed himself in a hot pool that is still there. Icelandic history is a ledger of lives lost at sea, sometimes just a few yards offshore. Heimaey’s longtime importance as a fishing port means that its tiny population has disproportionately weathered the blow. An entire wall of Vestmannaeyjar’s history museum is given over to records, dating back to the year 1251, of drowning incidents off the island’s coast. As a result, the island has been a pioneer in swimming education and in the development of boat safety equipment: rubber life rafts, safety belts, rescue suits. Swimming lessons became routine in Vestmannaeyjar’s harbor in 1891 and were held there until the town’s first pool was built, in 1934. In 1943, swimming instruction was made mandatory in all of Iceland’s schools. For Vestmannaeyjar, the year 2003 was distinctive because no one drowned.

古德劳格之所以能从这场磨难中幸存下来，有两个关键原因——他拥有这副身体，以及他游泳技术高超。单凭其中任何一项都不足以让他脱险。在众多非凡的真实游泳壮举中，古德劳格的经历堪称特殊。在我看来，他的故事是人类生物学与文化之间独特交融的典范。

Guðlaugur survived his ordeal for two critical reasons—because he occupies the body that he does, and because he is a good swimmer. One or the other alone would not have sufficed. In the annals of extraordinary real-life swims, Guðlaugur’s is special. To me, his story is a unique intertwining of human biology and culture.

古德劳格后来与一支冰岛和英国科学家团队进行了一系列科学实验，这些实验确定了他能够在极寒的水中保持接近正常的核心体温，从而加深了我们对体温过低的医学认识，也使他名扬世界。就连我当时在马萨诸塞州担任手术室护士的岳母也在医学期刊上读到了他的案例。记者们称古德劳格为“人形海豹”。事故发生几个月后，国际媒体在他访问美国朋友期间找到了他，《今夜秀》节目也对他进行了采访。 约翰尼·卡森打来了电话。他转过身对朋友们说，他该回冰岛了。

The scientific experimentation Guðlaugur later underwent with a team of Icelandic and British scientists—who determined his unusual ability to retain a nearly normal core body temperature in extreme cold water, contributing to our medical understanding of hypothermia—made him famous the world over. Even my mother-in-law, who at the time was an operating-room nurse in Massachusetts, read about his case in a medical journal. Reporters called Guðlaugur “the human seal.” A few months after the accident, the international media had tracked him down while he was visiting with friends in the United States, and The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson called. He turned to his friends and told them it was time for him to go back to Iceland.

在冰岛，古德劳格堪称传奇人物——在这个仅有33万人口的国家，他曾与比约克齐名——如今却刻意保持低调。他已年过五十，已婚，依然居住在赫马岛。他有两个女儿和五个孙辈。他曾一度重操旧业，以捕鱼为生，但多年来一直在岛上一家大型鱼类加工厂担任工程师。他通常不再接受记者采访，因为过去三十年来媒体的过度关注让他感到非常不自在。

For someone who is so mythic in Iceland—in this country of three hundred and thirty thousand people, there was a time when he was as famous as Björk—Guðlaugur is resolutely off the radar. Now in his mid-fifties and married, he still lives on Heimaey. He has two daughters and five grandchildren. For a time he returned to sea as a fisherman, but for many years now he has worked as an engineer at a large fish processing plant on the island. As a general rule, he no longer talks to journalists, deeply uncomfortable with the attention that the press has brought him over the past three decades.

我们的通信始于我决定无论如何都要给他写封信。我用挂号信寄出；三个星期以来，我一直追踪着它跨越大西洋的行踪。我想，这大概是碰碰运气吧。一天下午，我收到邮件通知，信件已抵达韦斯特曼纳群岛。第二天早上，我的邮箱里收到了一封来自古德劳格的电子邮件。

Our correspondence begins when I decide to write him a letter anyway. I send it via registered mail; over three weeks, I track its progress across the Atlantic. A wing and a prayer, I think. One afternoon, I get the alert that the letter has arrived at its destination in Vestmannaeyjar. The next morning, in my inbox, I receive an e-mail from Guðlaugur.

2012年，以执导马克·沃尔伯格和丹泽尔·华盛顿等明星主演的大制作动作片而闻名国际的冰岛导演巴尔塔苏尔·科马库尔拍摄了一部关于古德劳格的电影。古德劳格的渔船倾覆时，巴尔塔苏尔本人还是个十几岁的少年，但就像其他冰岛人一样，这段记忆深深地烙印在他的心中。“和我们这个小国家里的所有人一样，我为西人岛所有再次失去亲人的人们感到难过，但我同时也对唯一幸存者的消息感到好奇，”巴尔塔苏尔说道。我曾对一家英国报纸说：“这个人是谁？他是什么材质的？”

In 2012, the Icelandic director Baltasur Kormákur, who is best known internationally for big-budget action films starring the likes of Mark Wahlberg and Denzel Washington, made a movie about Guðlaugur. Baltasur himself was a teenager when Guðlaugur’s fishing vessel capsized, but as it has for his fellow Icelanders, the memory looms large. “Like everyone else in our small country, I felt for all the people of the Westman Islands who again had lost men at sea, but I was also fascinated by the news on the sole survivor,” Baltasur told a British newspaper. “Who was this man? What was he made of?”

古德劳格对这部电影带来的重新审视感到不满。他好不容易才开始过上远离聚光灯的生活，但这部电影又把他拉了回来。“等我死了再拍吧，”当电影制作人找到他时，他曾这样说过。我欣赏他的低调和对名利的抗拒。我也理解全球的迷恋。我们被生存故事所吸引，是因为我们希望它们能揭示人性在极端情况下的某些特质。想想《鲁滨逊漂流记》，这是最著名的生存故事之一；作者丹尼尔·笛福曾写道，他很感兴趣的是人在困境中会展现出怎样的性格：“那些能让我洞察人性的行为最能打动我。”

Guðlaugur was unhappy with the renewed scrutiny that the film brought. He had finally begun to settle into a life out of the spotlight, but the movie yanked him back in. “Make the movie when I’m dead,” he’d told the filmmakers when they approached him. I appreciate his reticence and his resistance to fame. I also understand the global fascination. We are captivated by survival stories because we hope they will reveal something about human nature in extremis. Remember Robinson Crusoe, one of the most well-known of all survival tales; the author, Daniel Defoe, wrote of his interest in what emerges of one’s character under duress: “I am most entertained with those Actions which give me a Light into the Nature of Man.”

古德劳格是个寡言少语的人，这一点从我们的邮件往来中我便可知晓。但他的信中偶尔闪现的真知灼见，如同笛福笔下描绘的那样，深深地吸引着我。古德劳格告诉我，游泳能救命；游泳本身就蕴含着自由。于是，我登上了飞往冰岛的航班，去见他本人。

Guðlaugur is a man of few words, something that I gather from our e-mail correspondence. But there are glimmers of insight in his letters that intrigue me in the manner that Defoe describes. Swimming saves lives, Guðlaugur tells me; there is freedom in that. And so I get on a flight to Iceland to meet him in person.

三月一个寒冷而阳光灿烂的午后，我乘坐一架红白相间的小型螺旋桨飞机抵达海马岛。飞机在低矮的海雾中穿行，我透过舷窗望去，只见岛上的双子火山锥逐渐显露出来，起伏壮丽的景色瞬间变得无比真实。而且是立体的。从镇上，我能看到港口边一排排碧蓝色的建筑，古德劳格就在那里工作。那个我通信一年、思念已久的神秘游泳者就在这里，而且他还是个真人，居然也用脸书。（神秘游泳者：跟我们一样。）我们约好第二天下班后见面。

On a cold, diamond-bright afternoon in March, I arrive in Heimaey on a tiny red-and-white propeller plane. On our approach, we fly through a low-lying sea mist; I peer out the window to watch the island’s twin volcanic cones emerge, the dramatic, undulating landscape suddenly real and three-dimensional. From town, I can see the series of turquoise-blue buildings down in the harbor where Guðlaugur works. The mythic swimmer with whom I have been corresponding for a year, and whom I have been thinking about for much longer, is here, and he’s a real guy who uses Facebook. (Mythic swimmers: just like us.) We make a date to meet the next evening after work.

我计划三月份去冰岛，参加“古德劳格游泳”（Guðlaugssund）活动。这项活动由当地航海学院发起，全程6公里（3.7英里），旨在纪念古德劳格以及所有在海上遇难的人们。自事故发生一周年起，韦斯特曼纳群岛的居民每年都坚持举办这项活动。在最初的二十年里，古德劳格会亲临现场公布成绩，并借此机会向冰岛渔船队宣传配备自动救生筏的必要性。

I’ve planned my visit for March so I can attend what’s called Guðlaugssund, or “Guðlaugur’s swim.” In a tradition begun by the local navigation college, there is a 6-kilometer (3.7-mile) swimming event held in Guðlaugur’s honor and for those lost at sea. Year in and year out, ever since the first anniversary of the accident, the citizens of Vestmannaeyjar have faithfully carried out Guðlaugssund. In the first two decades of the swim, Guðlaugur was present to hand out the results, to help publicize the need for self-deploying life rafts among the Icelandic fishing fleet.

现在我前往韦斯特曼纳群岛游泳馆，这座游泳馆是在熔岩流淹没旧泳池后重建的。在这个狂风呼啸、雪花纷飞的早晨，岛上著名的冬季寒风呼啸而过；赫马岛南端曾记录到欧洲最高的风速。我从健谈的艾伦·艾利森那里了解到一些冰岛深厚的游泳文化，艾伦是古德劳格斯松德游泳节的两位组织者之一，他与古德劳格斯松德是一对健谈的对手。艾伦在韦斯特曼纳群岛游泳馆工作了二十年，担任过救生员和泳池经理。

Now I head over to the Vestmannaeyjar swimming hall, the one built after the lava flowed over the old pool. On this blustery, snowy morning, the island’s famous winter winds are howling; some of the highest wind speeds in Europe have been recorded on the southern end of Heimaey. I learn something of Iceland’s deep swimming culture from Guðlaugur’s loquacious opposite, Alan Allison, who is now one of the two organizers in charge of Guðlaugssund. Alan has worked at the Vestmannaeyjar swimming hall for twenty years, as a lifeguard and pool manager.

在抵达赫马岛之前，我花了整整一周的时间游览冰岛大陆的各个公共泳池。这段经历让我明白，即使在冬天——不，尤其是在冬天——几乎每个人都泡在泳池里。冰岛是世界上人均泳池数量最多的国家之一。冰岛甚至还有专门的路标来标示这一点：一个脑袋从两道蓝色波浪中探出来。冰岛几乎每个城镇，无论大小，都拥有公共泳池——通常是露天泳池，而且往往采用地热加热，可以全年使用——​​许多城镇甚至拥有多个大小和温度各异的泳池可供选择。由于赫马岛的风力异常强劲，韦斯特曼纳群岛还配备了一个室内标准泳池。艾伦告诉我，每天，游泳馆里都会迎来来自冰岛各个年龄段、不同背景的人们：上班前的游泳者、体育课上的小学生，以及前来休闲的退休人士。

Before arriving on Heimaey, I spent much of the previous week visiting public pools on the Icelandic mainland. What I came to understand from the experience is that even in winter—no, especially in winter—everybody is in the pool. Iceland is one of the world’s leaders in swimming pools per capita. There’s a special Icelandic road sign for it: a head poking out of two rows of blue waves. Most every town in the country, no matter how tiny, has a public pool—typically outdoors, often geothermally heated for year-round use—and many towns have several options of varying size and temperature. Because of Heimaey’s unusually high winds, Vestmannaeyjar’s offerings include an indoor lap pool. Every day, Alan tells me, the swimming hall sees multiple generations of Icelanders from all ages and backgrounds: the before-work swimmers, elementary schoolers during gym class, retirees coming for their recreation.

在我抵达冰岛前几个月，我在冰岛报纸上读到，有三十名游泳爱好者正在雷克雅未克准备一次游泳探险。没想到，冰岛总统古德尼·约翰内松竟然也来参加了这次游泳活动！当地记者观察到，古德尼总统对这位意外现身的游泳爱好者们不以为意，热情地欢迎了他们，并表示“他毫不怀疑在冰冷的海水中畅游对健康的益处”。游泳结束后，游泳爱好者们受邀前往总统府，在总统的私人温泉池中暖暖身子。

A few months before my arrival in Iceland, I’d read in the Icelandic newspapers about a group of thirty ocean swimmers preparing for a swim expedition in Reykjavík. Who should show up to join the swim but the president of Iceland, Guðni Jóhannesson? Local reporters observed that President Guðni shrugged off his unexpected appearance by welcoming the swimmers and declaring that “he doesn’t doubt the health benefits of taking a dip in cold ocean water.” At the end of the swim, the swimmers were invited to the presidential residence to warm themselves up in the president’s own hot pool.

艾伦说，遍布全国的温泉池是冰岛游泳的独特之处。我们在韦斯特曼纳群岛的室内泳池游了几圈后，便漫步到户外白雪皑皑的地面上，我可以从三个温泉池中选择一个聊天（水温分别为：热、很热、极热）。古德劳格松温泉的另一位组织者斯文尼·古德蒙德松从救生员岗位上下来，加入我们的谈话。他告诉我，温泉池会为当地青少年举办“迪斯科之夜”，届时他会通过户外音响播放流行音乐。（此刻，我们正在听滚石乐队的歌，但他翻了个白眼说：“这些青少年根本不知道滚石乐队是谁。”）温泉池是冰岛人度过漫长黑暗冬季的方式。

Alan says the ubiquitous hot pools throughout the country are what make Icelandic swimming special. After we do our laps inside the Vestmannaeyjar hall, we meander outdoors across the snow-covered ground so I can choose one of three hot pools in which to have a chat (temperature range: hot, very hot, extremely hot). Svenni Guðmundsson, the other organizer of Guðlaugssund, climbs down from his lifeguard station to join our conversation. He tells me that the pool will host “disco nights” for the local teenagers, during which he pipes popular music through the outdoor speakers. (At the moment, we are listening to the Rolling Stones, but “the teens don’t know who the Rolling Stones are,” he says, rolling his eyes.) The pool is how Icelanders survive the long, dark winter.

我们来探讨一下古德劳格松德游泳赛的发展历程，它的起源是这样的：1985年3月，在拖网事故一周年之际，岛上航海学院的20名学生在时任校长弗里德里克·阿斯蒙德松的监督下，身着全套泳衣在泳池中游了6公里。弗里德里克·阿斯蒙德松以严格著称：禁止使用任何漂浮设备，禁止扶池边。在早期，每次比赛的参赛学生人数最多时达到70人，但通常稳定在二三十人，安全始终是重中之重。

We discuss the evolution of Guðlaugssund, which started like this: On the first anniversary of the trawling accident, in March 1985, twenty students from the island’s navigation college swam six kilometers in a pool, fully clothed, under the supervision of the then headmaster, Friðrik Ásmundsson, who had a reputation for strictness: no flotation devices, no holding on to the side of the pool. In those early years, the number of students participating in any given event went as high as seventy, but mostly held steady at two or three dozen, and the emphasis was on safety.

自2000年起，游泳活动向公众开放。高中生参加接力赛，当地企业赞助员工参赛，岛上的游泳队也一直积极参与。参赛队伍相当庞大。渔船船长和其他海员也参与其中。一些游泳选手申请远程参赛，有的来自附近的雷克雅未克，有的则远在西藏和越南。几乎所有人都与冰岛或岛屿有着某种联系。

Beginning in 2000, the swim was opened to the public. High school students swam relays, local businesses sponsored their employees, and the island’s swim team always had a healthy contingent. Fishing captains and other seamen were also well represented. Some swimmers asked to participate remotely, from nearby Reykjavík and as far away as Tibet and Vietnam. Almost everyone had an island or Icelandic connection.

斯文尼的父亲是一艘渔船的船长，他自己也曾在海上度过了五个冬天。他告诉我，他游泳“既是为了纪念古德劳格，也是为了纪念所有没能游到终点的人。我们仍然认为，这次游泳是对所有人的安全警示，提醒大家注意装备，也提醒大家要学会游泳。”他和艾伦已经多次参加过这项游泳活动，既有个人参赛，也曾作为体育中心接力队的成员参与其中。

Svenni’s father is the captain of a fishing trawler, and he himself spent five winters on the sea. He tells me that he swims “for both the memory of Guðlaugur, who did this, and all the guys who didn’t make it. We still think this swim is a reminder for everybody for safety, of equipment and also of swimming.” He and Alan have swum numerous times, both individually and as part of the sports center’s relay team.

艾伦总是热情洋溢地鼓励所有年龄段、各种水平的游泳新手。他解释说，如今这项游泳活动的目的是让人们完成他们原本认为自己无法完成的事情。几个月前，在我第一次和艾伦通电话讨论古德劳格松德游泳活动时，我不知怎么就答应参加。“如果你游不完六公里，”他当时兴高采烈地告诉我，“我会替你游完。”

Alan is unfailingly upbeat in his encouragement of first-time swimmers of all ages and abilities. The aim of the swim these days, he explains, is to have people achieve something they would not have thought they could accomplish themselves.
