Months before, over the course of my first phone conversation with Alan about Guðlaugssund, I somehow ended up agreeing to swim in it. “And if you can’t finish the six kilometers,” he cheerfully told me then, “I’ll finish it for you.”

后来在游泳馆，我看到一个年轻人从热水池边走过，径直走向冷水池——这是唯一一个没有加热的室外泳池。气温只有零下26度，地面结了冰。45度的水冷得难以想象；为了亲身感受一下，我小心翼翼地沿着结冰的斜坡挪动，每走一步都低声咒骂。那是什么感觉？刺骨的寒冷，而且……情况紧急。我的身体仿佛在呐喊着要我逃离。虽然之后我会游完古德劳格松德河全程六公里，但我意识到，这次跳入水中或许是我最接近古德劳格当年游泳时的感受的一次了。

Later at the swimming hall, I watch one young man stroll past the hot pools for a dip in the cold pool—the only outdoor pool that’s unheated. The air temperature is twenty-six degrees, and there’s ice on the ground. Forty-five-degree water is the kind of cold that is hard to imagine; to feel it for myself, I cautiously inch down the icy ramp, swearing under my breath at every step. What does it feel like? Piercing, and urgent. My cells scream for me to get out. Though I will later swim the full six kilometers of Guðlaugssund, it occurs to me that this plunge is probably the closest I’ll ever come to feeling something of what Guðlaugur felt on his swim.

像所有优秀的冰岛人一样，古德劳格小时候经常在海里游泳。他和朋友会像弹珠一样从岛的一端游到另一端，一会儿在港口附近游，一会儿又在灯塔附近游。这两个十岁的孩子从镇上走到赫马岛南端一片绵延的新月形黑沙滩，只需要不到一个小时。他们对此毫不在意，直到他朋友的父亲发现了他们的行为，才限制了他们独自下海游泳。

Like any good Icelander, Guðlaugur often swam in the sea as a child. He and a friend would pinball from one side of the island to the other, swimming near the harbor, then near the lighthouse. It would take less than an hour for the pair of ten-year-olds to walk from town to a sweeping crescent-shaped black-sand beach on the south end of Heimaey. They thought nothing of it, until his friend’s father got wind of it and put limits on their unsupervised ocean jaunts.

我和古德劳格正开着他那辆栗色的福特皮卡，沿着南边的路，经过这片新月形的海滩，朝着岛上的灯塔驶去。那天晚上，在漆黑的夜色和汹涌的波涛中，是灯塔指引他回到了家。今天傍晚，天还没完全黑，太阳低垂，将万物都染上了一层玫瑰金色的光晕，包括古德劳格那浓密的银白胡须。我问他游泳是否依然让他感到快乐。他回答说，他和妻子曾去冰岛西峡湾地区度假，住在一个海边带小型无边泳池的地方。他说，在那个泳池里，他感觉自己就像大海本身。那种感觉真好。

Guðlaugur and I are driving south past this very same crescent-shaped beach, toward the island’s lighthouse, in his maroon Ford pickup truck. On the night of his swim, in the inky darkness and surging waves, the lighthouse is what guided him home. This evening, it’s not quite dusk yet; the sun is low in the sky, bathing everything in a rose-gold tint, including Guðlaugur’s big, silvery beard. I ask him if swimming still feels joyful to him. By way of an answer, he tells me about the time he and his wife went to the Westfjords region of Iceland, where they stayed at a place with a little infinity pool by the sea. Being in that pool, he says, was like being the sea itself. And it felt good.

我们在灯塔下车，穿过一片干涸的、被雪覆盖的草地，走了一小段路。悬崖顶上竖立着一座齐腰高的圆形纪念碑；在其表面那是一块风化的铜盘，上面刻着岛屿地图，标明了我们当前的位置、沉船地点以及距离岸边的距离。狂风呼啸，吹得我的头发扑面而来。古德劳格抬起一只手，指向东南方向的大海。

We get out of his truck at the lighthouse and walk a little way over a field of parched, snow-covered grass. Installed on the cliff top is a waist-high circular memorial; on its surface is a weathered, coppery disc etched with a map of the island, with markings of our current location, the place where the boat went down, and the distance back to shore. The wind is wicked and sharp, whipping my hair into my face. Guðlaugur raises a hand and points southeast toward the sea.

“很多时候，渔船上一旦出了事，所有人都会溺水身亡，”古德劳格说道，“所以没人能说清发生了什么。但那天晚上我们紧紧抓住龙骨时，我们说好，如果我们当中有人能活下来，就告诉他们。”他停顿了一下。“我就是那个活着的人。”在古德劳格松德成立的最初几十年里，他信守了诺言，并且一直积极支持为冰岛所有渔船配备自动展开式救生筏。

“Much of the time, when something goes wrong on a fishing boat, everyone drowns,” Guðlaugur says. “So there is no one to say what happened. But when we were holding on to the keel that night, we said that if one of us made it, we would tell them.” He pauses. “I was there to tell.” He faithfully kept his promise with the early decades of Guðlaugssund and with his vocal support for auto-deploying life rafts for all of Iceland’s fishing fleet.

在岛上的几天里，我们多次驱车长途旅行，沿着空旷的道路蜿蜒而行，这些道路勾勒出荒凉的红色岩石地貌的轮廓。夏季，当地人口激增，因为世界上五分之一的海鹦会回到韦斯特曼纳群岛栖息，同时还有成千上万的游客前来观赏。然而，到了冬季，旅游业基本停滞，岛屿又回到了常住居民的怀抱。古德劳格解释说，在这个小镇上，开车是与熟人进行不受打扰的交谈的最便捷方式。

During my few days visiting the island, we go for several long drives, looping around on empty roads that trace the contours of the stark, red-rock landscape. The local population balloons in summer, when one-fifth of the world’s puffins come back to roost on the Vestmannaeyjar archipelago, along with the thousands of human tourists who come to see them. In the winter months, though, tourism is largely dormant, and the island is returned to its year-round residents. In this small-town place, Guðlaugur explains, driving is the easiest way to have a conversation uninterrupted by someone he knows.

古德劳格在冰岛可谓家喻户晓。“嗯，你看，我一点也不低调，”他略带讽刺地说。他身高六英尺四英寸（约1.93米），身材魁梧，相貌堂堂，留着齐肩的银色卷发和浓密的络腮胡，胡须边缘呈深色。如果你在谷歌上搜索……你可能会觉得，搜索“海明威”和“渔夫”这两个词，搜索结果里应该会出现他，或者长得像他的人。我们发现，附近有一支法国摄制组，他们乘船在附近拍摄一部关于他的纪录片。古德劳格没有和他们交谈，但他知道他们的存在。他接到过来自日本记者的电话。当他回雷克雅未克探望子女和孙辈时，人们经常会在公共场合上前和他握手，询问他近况如何。

Guðlaugur is recognized everywhere in Iceland. “Well, you see, I don’t blend in,” he says wryly. At six-foot-four, he is a broad, striking man, with shoulder-length curly silver hair and a full beard edged with dark. If you Googled “Hemingway” and “fisherman,” you’d expect him, or someone who looks like him, to emerge in the search results. We find out there is a French film crew in the area, out on a boat, making a documentary about him. Guðlaugur doesn’t speak with them, but he knows they’re there. He gets phone calls from journalists in Japan. When he visits his children and grandchildren in Reykjavík, people often come up to him in public to shake his hand and to ask how his life has been.

一天傍晚，我们开车经过，看到两艘鳕鱼渔船的灯光正返回港口。我坚持要停在一家鱼餐馆，好让他让我请他吃饭。出门时，一位面带微笑、发型利落、脚蹬时髦黑靴的女士走了过来，我以为又是他的仰慕者。“我妹妹，”他腼腆地说道，并向我们介绍道。

On one evening drive, we see the lights of two cod-fishing vessels returning to the harbor. I insist that we stop at a fish restaurant so he can let me buy him dinner. On our way out, a smiling woman with smartly cut hair and stylish black boots approaches, and I assume it’s another admirer. “My sister,” he says shyly, introducing us.

我了解到，他住在自己从小长大的那条街上；他的妻子玛丽亚也住在那条街上。他们住在玛丽亚出生的房子里。一天早上，他们邀请我去吃早午餐，玛丽亚带我参观了他们整洁的后院菜园。在菜园后面，古德劳格在做各种各样的东西，比如用渔船的一部分改造了一个高高的柴火炉。他忙于工作、家庭、朋友和旅行。在他出事后的那一年，他曾在纽约州北部的乔治湖游泳，那也是我和丈夫结婚第二天早上横渡的湖。不知怎的，得知这些让我们感觉彼此就像亲人一样。

What I learn is that he lives on the same street where he grew up; his wife, Maria, grew up on that street, too. They live in the house where she was born. One morning, they invite me over for brunch, and Maria shows me the vegetable plots in their tidy backyard garden. Behind the garden, Guðlaugur builds things, like a tall wood stove fashioned from part of a fishing trawler. He is busy with work, family, friends, travels. Once, in the year after his accident, he swam in Lake George, in upstate New York, the lake my husband and I swam across the morning after we were married. Somehow, learning this makes us feel like kin to one another.

在他家的一面墙上，一个显眼的位置，挂着一幅装裱好的画作，是他孙子丹尼尔上幼儿园时画的。那是一幅色彩鲜艳的沙画。画中描绘了蔚蓝的大海、一艘红色的渔船，以及旁边一个在水中游泳的黑色身影。当古德劳格和玛丽亚把这幅画给我看时，我惊讶地发现自己的眼眶瞬间湿润了。

On one wall of his home, in a place of honor, there is a framed piece of art made by his grandson, Daniel, when Daniel was in kindergarten. It’s a brightly colored sand painting of a blue-ocean background, a red fishing boat, and, next to it, the dark figure of a man swimming in the water. When Guðlaugur and Maria show this picture to me, I am surprised by the tears that suddenly prick my eyes.

古德劳格能 告诉我们什么？这是摆在我们面前的问题。但或许更重要的推论是：古德劳格会告诉我们我们想知道的吗？我开始意识到，其他游泳者讲述的关于古德劳格的故事，与他本人告诉我的任何事一样，都揭示了人性的本质。我逐渐明白，我必须亲自去海马岛，才能亲眼见证这两种故事。

What can Guðlaugur tell us? is the question at hand. But perhaps the more important corollary is, Will Guðlaugur tell us what we want to know? I began to realize that the stories other swimmers told about Guðlaugur were just as revealing about human nature as anything the man himself could tell me. And I came to understand that I had to visit Heimaey to witness both kinds of stories for myself.

艾伦·艾利森向我介绍了西格伦·哈尔多斯多蒂尔，一位年轻的教师，她从韦斯特曼纳群岛搬到雷克雅未克，现在是一名游泳教练。三年前，她开始带领孩子们游古德劳格斯海峡。西格伦从十二岁就开始游古德劳格斯海峡，如今她已经三十岁了。“即使我退出了游泳队，我每年还是会独自游一次，以此来传承这项运动，”我打电话给她时，西格伦告诉我，“他（古德劳格）的壮举意义非凡。”她向她的游泳队员们讲述古德劳格的壮举；孩子们完成游泳后，艾伦会从韦斯特曼纳群岛寄给他们签名的证书。听他们讲述，让我更能体会到这段传奇故事中普通人的一面：古德劳格的故事告诉我们，我们游泳是为了生存，也是为了铭记。

Alan Allison introduces me to Sigrún Halldórsdóttir, a young teacher who moved from Vestmannaeyjar to Reykjavík and is now a swim coach. Three years ago, she began to lead her charges in swimming Guðlaugssund. Sigrún started swimming Guðlaugssund when she was twelve years old. She is now thirty. “Even after I stopped swim team, I do the swim every year on my own, to keep it alive,” Sigrún tells me when I phone her up. “It’s a big deal, what he did.” She teaches her swim team about Guðlaugur’s achievement; after the children complete their swims, Alan mails them signed certificates from Vestmannaeyjar. Hearing from them illuminates the Everyman side of this saga: Guðlaugur’s story tells us that we swim for survival, but also that we swim for remembrance.

事故发生后，古德劳格躺在病床上，接受了电视采访，讲述了他的经历。视频里，他面容稚嫩，稚气未脱。他留着稀疏的胡须，身穿白色病号服。他低着头，讲述着海鸥的故事。在他游泳时，海鸥在他头顶盘旋。他跟海鸥说话，请求它们如果可以的话帮忙寻找救援。整夜，海鸥都守候在他头顶。

After the accident, from his hospital bed, Guðlaugur spoke with a television interviewer about his experience. In the footage, his face is young, cherubic. He wears a faint wispy mustache and a white hospital gown. His eyes downcast, he talks about the seagulls, who circled above his head as he swam. He spoke to them and asked them to get help if they could. All night long, they stayed above him.

那位主持医学研究的冰岛医生后来成了他的好朋友。几年前，他们在咖啡馆偶遇。医生告诉古德劳格，他刚参加完一个关于低温症的医学会议。其他许多医生都对他的这位最著名的病人有同样的疑问。“他精神还好吗？”他们问道。人们经历如此巨大的事情后，难免会精神失常。古德劳格告诉医生他没事；他还开玩笑说，他已经够疯了，不可能再疯了。

The Icelandic doctor who conducted the medical studies became a good friend. A few years ago, they met each other over coffee. The doctor told Guðlaugur that he’d just been to a medical conference on hypothermia. Many of the other doctors had the same question about his most famous patient. “Is he all right in the head?” they asked. When people go through something so big, they can go crazy. Guðlaugur told the doctor that he was fine; he joked that he couldn’t get any crazier than he already was.

古德劳格告诉我，在他康复期间，他的父亲在医院病床边的椅子上坐了一个月，寸步不离。古德劳格感到自己必须倾诉。他一遍又一遍地讲述着事故的经过，而他的父亲总是静静地听着。“我想这就是我现在没事的原因，”他告诉我，“我的父亲是个很好的倾听者。”他父亲那优美动人的草书笔迹，满满地记录着古德劳格松德游泳日志，细致地描绘着那个夜晚的种种，并年复一年地记录着游泳活动及其参与者，留给后人。

Guðlaugur explains to me that during his recovery, his father sat in a chair next to his bed at the hospital and didn’t leave his side for a month. Guðlaugur felt compelled to talk. He would relay the drama of the accident over and over again, and his father would listen. “I think that is why I am OK now,” he tells me. “My father was a very good listener.” It’s his father’s startlingly beautiful cursive handwriting that fills the pages of the Guðlaugssund logbook, recounting the events of that night with care and recording the swims and their participants, year after year, for posterity.

在韦斯特曼纳群岛历史博物馆，古德劳格溺水当晚所穿的衣服被悬挂在玻璃柜中。他的母亲保存了这些衣服并小心翼翼地妥善保管；最终，他的妻子将它们捐赠给了博物馆。

At the Vestmannaeyjar history museum, the clothes Guðlaugur wore the night of his swim are hanging in a glass case. His mother saved them and carefully put them away; eventually, his wife donated them to the museum.

“我们都想活下去。我们都有活下去的意志，”博物馆馆长、古德劳格的朋友海尔加·哈尔贝格斯多蒂尔说道。“但我认为，在船沉没之前，他们在船顶上的那次谈话，他们彼此承诺——如果有人侥幸生还，他一定会努力让世界变得更安全、更美好，拯救他人——正是这种信念支撑着他活了下来。”

“We all want to survive. We all have a will to do it,” says Helga Hallbergsdóttir, the director of the museum, and a friend of Guðlaugur’s. “But I think that conversation at the top of the boat, before it sank, they promised one another—that if someone somehow survives, that he will work to make things safer and better, to save others—that’s what kept him going.”

古德劳格并非自愿游向岸边求生。但如果说这件事有什么意义的话，或许在于他凭借游泳得以幸存，从而鼓励了其他人也学习游泳。我问海尔加，为什么近三十五年过去了，岛民们仍然年复一年地坚持游过古德劳格海峡。她说，他的壮举提醒着人们那些未能幸存的人，也提醒着我们自身终将面对的死亡。“我们没有忘记他所做的一切，”她说，“我们非常敬重他。” 这项始于这座岛屿的游泳教学活动，如今已深深融入冰岛的文化基因之中。

Guðlaugur didn’t choose to swim for his life. But if there’s meaning in what happened, perhaps it is that his survival, enabled by swimming, encouraged others to learn to swim, too. I ask Helga why she thinks the islanders still swim Guðlaugssund so faithfully, year in and year out, nearly thirty-five years later. She says that his accomplishment is a reminder of all those who did not survive, and of our own inevitable mortality. “We have not forgotten what he was able to do,” she says, “and we respect him very much for it.” The emphasis on swimming instruction that began on this island, by extension, is now baked into the cultural DNA of Iceland itself.

“游泳池，”赫尔加笑着告诉我，“就是我们的酒吧。”

“The pool,” Helga tells me with a smile, “is our pub.”

这么多年过去了，古德劳格也曾有所保留，他最终为何同意与我交谈？在我们相处的短短几天里，我逐渐明白，那是因为他身上也流淌着冰岛人与生俱来的文化基因。

After all these years, and after all his reservations, why did Guðlaugur agree to talk to me? It becomes clear, in the few days we spend together, that it was because the cultural DNA that lives in his fellow Icelanders lives in him, too.

他特意跟我讲了这个故事：三周前，他去镇上的五金店。从停车场走进店里时，他碰到了一个熟人，一位周末就要满九十岁的老太太。他出价祝她今天过得愉快。她抬头看着他，一脸茫然：我们认识吗？ “我说，‘你不记得我了吗？’”她是他的游泳教练，五十年前在那个老游泳池里教他游泳的那个人。他很少刻意提醒别人自己是谁，但他想让她记得是她教他游泳的。“我说，‘嗯，我后来过得挺好的。’”他停顿了一下，笑了笑。“然后她才明白我是谁。”

He makes it a point to tell me this story: Three weeks before, he’d gone to the hardware store in town. On his way in from the parking lot, he ran into someone he knew, a woman who would be turning ninety years old that weekend. He bid her a good day. She looked up at him without recognition: Do we know each other? “I said, ‘Don’t you remember me?’” She was his swimming teacher, the one who taught him how to swim in the old swimming pool, fifty years before. He doesn’t often go out of his way to remind people who he is, but he wanted her to remember that she’d taught him to swim. “I said, ‘Well, it turned out well for me.’” He pauses and smiles. “And then she understood who I was.”

我清晨早早起床去古德劳格松德。地上覆盖着一层新雪，我在清晨六点的昏暗中走向游泳池，一路嘎吱作响地踩着积雪。

I wake early in the morning for Guðlaugssund. There’s fresh snow on the ground, and I crunch through it on my walk to the pool in the six a.m. gloom.

五名游泳者，四男一女，已经下水了。他们不畏凌晨四点半的严寒，只为完成游泳后还能准时上班。艾伦和斯文尼在裁判台值班，他们把我介绍给坐在泳池边的伙伴、朋友和同事。有些人在数圈数，有些人只是来陪陪我。更多的游泳者陆续到来，准备出发。我赤着脚踩在红色的瓷砖地板上，感觉湿漉漉的。我一边等待泳道空出来，一边想着大家来这里都是为了同一个目标。

Five swimmers, four men and one woman, are already in the water, having braved the predawn cold at four-thirty a.m. so that they could complete the swim and still get to work on time. Alan and Svenni are manning the officials’ table; they introduce me to the partners and friends and coworkers sitting on the pool deck. Some are counting laps. Some are there to keep company. More swimmers show up, ready to go. Under my bare feet, the red tile floor is clammy and damp. As I wait for a lane to open up, I think about how everyone is here for the same thing.

这项传统活动让人想起感恩节的火鸡赛跑和七月四日的趣味跑。三月第二周的一个星期三早上，在这个冰岛小镇的游泳池里，我们通过一项国民运动，向一位伟人以及一个国家的历史致敬。这并非一个全国性的节日。这里没有热狗和烟花，取而代之的是……热咖啡和两百四十圈游泳。这是一种朴实无华的方式，却凝聚着一个社群。但在这份执着中，蕴藏着比游泳馆里三十个人更伟大、更美好的东西。

The routine tradition of it is reminiscent of Thanksgiving Day turkey trots and Fourth of July fun runs. On a Wednesday morning in the second week of March, in this small-town Icelandic pool, we are paying homage to a man, and to a country’s history, through a national pastime. It’s not quite a national holiday. Instead of hot dogs and fireworks, there’s hot coffee and two hundred and forty laps. In a modest, mundane way, this is simply how a community binds itself together. But in the doggedness, there is something bigger and more beautiful than the thirty people in the swimming hall.

当我真正下水后，我发现游泳很大程度上是在我的脑海中进行的。我逐渐适应，慢慢地开始注意到周围的事物。游到两公里时，我看到隔壁泳道的小学校长爬上岸，去上班了。游到三公里时，我闻到了鱼腥味，斯文尼打开了外面的门。鱼粉厂已经开始一天的工作了。游到四公里时，太阳已经升得足够高，阳光透过天窗和侧窗洒进来，呈现出一种绚丽的晚冬柠檬黄。阳光洒在泳道上，也洒进我游泳的水中。

When I do get in the water, I find that the swim is something that largely takes place inside my head. I settle in, and eventually I notice things. At two kilometers, I watch the elementary school headmaster in the next lane haul himself out and head off to work. At three kilometers, I smell fish, when Svenni opens the outside door. The fishmeal factory is up and running for the day. At four kilometers, the sun has risen enough so that it starts to filter through the skylights and side windows, a glorious late-winter lemon yellow. It plays across the lanes and down into the water where I swim.

游到五公里时，我开始感到头晕目眩。我想起了温泉池边的警告：小心！过度使用热水浴缸可能会导致烦躁不安。还剩八圈时，我探出头来，开始蛙泳，同时和正在帮我数圈数的艾伦确认距离。最后，我又游了一圈蝶泳、一圈仰泳、一圈蛙泳和一圈自由泳，只是为了换换口味，也是为了证明我状态依然很好。开始一个小时五十分钟后，我完成了游泳。我给古德劳格发短信，告诉他我为了纪念他完成了这次游泳。能够做到这一点，我感到非常荣幸。他从单位打电话过来，用长辈的语气叮嘱我一定要好好休息。毕竟，这是一次长距离游泳，他说。我想起了……真觉得不可思议，竟然是他跟我说这些。然后我穿过雪地走回酒店，睡了一觉。

At five kilometers, I start feeling giddy. I am reminded of the warning posted by the hot pools: Caution! Excessive use of hot tubs may cause dysphoria. With eight laps to go, I poke my head up and do the breaststroke, double-checking my distance with Alan, who’s counting my laps. I finish with one lap each of butterfly, backstroke, breaststroke, and freestyle, just to mix it up, just to show I am still in good form. An hour and fifty minutes after I begin, I’m done. I text Guðlaugur to let him know that I have completed the swim in his honor. It gives me great pleasure to be able to do this. He calls from work to caution me, in an avuncular way, to make sure I get some rest. It is a long swim, after all, he says. I think about how surreal it is that he’s the one telling me that. Then I walk back through the snow to my hotel and take a nap.

游览冰岛海岸，在泳池边凝望大海：游泳本身就是一种仪式。游泳的仪式感让我们能够通过共同讲述故事和实践，来承受许多苦难。我相信我们传承这一传统的力量。

Visiting the Icelandic coast, contemplating the sea from the perch of a pool: it is swimming as liturgy. The rite of swimming enables us to endure many things through a communal call-and-response of story as well as practice. I believe in the power of how we pass down that tradition.

从一开始，游泳和家庭对我来说就密不可分。这可以说是我的起源故事。1968年夏天，我的父母在香港的一个游泳池相遇。在那短暂的瞬间，他们简直就是老套爱情的化身：他是古铜色皮肤的救生员，她是身着比基尼、拥有一头乌黑长发和一双深邃大眼睛的美女。每当我翻看那时的照片，都忍不住赞叹他们的俊美：他们修长的身姿，以及彼此间充满渴望的眼神。

In many ways, swimming and family were intertwined for me from the start. It’s my own origin story. In the summer of 1968, my parents met in a swimming pool in Hong Kong. For one hot moment, they were the cliché incarnate: he was the bronzed lifeguard, she was the bikini-clad beauty with long black hair and big, serious eyes. When I flip through snapshots of that time, I can hardly bear their prettiness: their slim-limbed stances, the way they looked at each other with such longing.

当然，这种渴望很少能持久。他们维持了那么多年的婚姻——直到我和哥哥都顺利上了大学——期间经历了分居、激烈争吵和冷战，这让这段婚姻变得复杂起来。他们之间似乎唯一的共同点就是年轻的容貌、我们这些孩子和游泳。

Such longing, of course, rarely lasts. That they stayed married as many years as they did—until my older brother and I were safely in college—is complicated by periods of living apart, blowout fights, silent treatments. The only things they had in common, it seemed, were their youthful looks, us kids, and swimming.

认识我和我哥哥的人听到我们说父母是在游泳池相遇时都会笑。我们六岁和五岁的时候就开始在长岛家附近的户外休闲中心游泳。这可以说是我们水上生活的前奏——最终里程尚未记录——那些夏日的清晨，我跟着安迪上游泳课，而我们的母亲则在隔壁泳道练习。她最喜欢的泳姿是蛙泳。我们划水时，可以看到她时不时地探出头来换气，双腿在平静的水面下有力地踢动着。

People who know my brother and me laugh when we tell them our parents met at the pool. We began to swim at ages six and five at the outdoor recreation center near our home on Long Island. As the precursor to a life in the water—the final mileage not yet marked—I spent summer mornings taking lessons with Andy while our mother swam laps in the next lane. Her favorite stroke was breaststroke. As we paddled alongside, we could see her head popping up for breath at regular intervals, her legs executing a powerful frog kick under the calm surface.

下午，父亲有时会加入我们，一起去琼斯海滩。我们沿着堤道从家出发，行驶八英里，一路飞驰，穿过海湾中那些将鱼形长岛与狭长沙洲（也就是海滩）分隔开来的小岛。沙洲的另一边是浩瀚无垠、碧绿如翠的大西洋。我们摇下车窗，让海风吹进我们那辆蛋壳色的1978年沃尔沃旅行车里；退潮时，我们捏着鼻子，忍受着从下方裸露的泥滩上散发出的刺鼻气味。

In the afternoons, my father would sometimes join us, and we’d head down to Jones Beach. We drove the eight miles along the causeway from our house, leapfrogging across the little islands in the bay that separate fish-shape Long Island from the skinny barrier island that is the beach. On the other side of that barrier island was the vast viridian-green expanse of the Atlantic Ocean. We rolled down the windows and let the sea air blast through our eggshell-colored 1978 Volvo station wagon; during low tide, we pinched our noses against the stink that rose from the exposed mudflats below.

大多数时候，父母都会先在水边一起慢跑。跑完后，他们会跳进海里，父亲会独自游到离岸边浪花更远的地方。那是他的舒适区：每一次划水都让他离我们更远，仿佛回到了小时候和父亲、哥哥在香港岛亚热带海滩上自由潜水、捕鱼的日子。母亲会游回来，坐在沙滩巾上，我们时不时会抬头，用手遮住眼睛，寻找父亲在海浪中嬉戏的身影。在那里游泳是成年人的事。每年，我都满怀希望地慢慢靠近他。

Most visits my mother and father would begin with a jog alone together by the water’s edge. At the end of the run they’d jump into the ocean, and my father would finish with a solo swim beyond the shore break. This was his comfort zone: Every stroke pulled him further from us, back in time to the days spent free diving and spearfishing with his father and brother off the subtropical beaches of Hong Kong Island. My mother would come back and sit on the towel, and we’d look up every now and again, shading our eyes, searching out my father’s splashing figure in the waves. Swimming out there was a grown-up thing. Each year I hopefully inched closer and closer to it.

我的父母在水里看起来那么快乐。但在现实生活中，在陆地上，他们却常常争吵不休。妻子是严厉而负责的家长，操持家务，支付账单。丈夫则是那个爱玩爱闹的艺术家，在楼下的工作室里工作，常常熬夜到凌晨四点。他们从未谈论过真正重要的事情：比如他为什么在美国感到孤独，或者妻子怀念养育孩子之外的生活。他们竟然能同意一起游泳，这简直是个奇迹。但在那些沙滩上，或者和我们一起在泳池里的时刻，我相信他们仍然彼此相爱。在水中，那些在家中泾渭分明的角色分工消失了。游泳本身就极具吸引力，而它与维系父母关系的脆弱纽带之间的联系，更让它魅力倍增。

My parents seemed so happy in the water. In real life, on land, they were often at odds. She was the stern, responsible parent who ran the household and paid the bills. He got to be the fun one, the artist who worked in his downstairs studio and stayed up until four a.m. They never talked about the things that mattered: why he felt lonely in America or what she missed of life outside of raising kids. It was a wonder they agreed on swimming. But at those moments on the beach, or in the pool with us, I believed they still loved each other. In the water, the rigid roles that were so defined at home disappeared. The allure of swimming, already powerful, was amplified by its association with the tenuous thing that still held my parents together.

我们曾是一家人，后来却不再是一家人了。我们四人中，除了我，没有人继续游泳。我游过了离婚的痛苦。我游过了大学。我曾受人怂恿，从恶魔岛游了出来。我曾用游泳来康复膝盖手术后的伤病。我曾在婚礼上游过湖。为了帮别人完成一个赌约，我游到意大利的一座修道院又游了回来。我曾用游泳来度过流产的痛苦，也在我的两个儿子出生前的每一天都坚持游泳。三十年的游泳，三十年对平衡的追求，让我始终保持着清醒。游泳带来的生存意义远不止于身体层面。

We were a family, and then we weren’t. No one in our foursome kept swimming except for me. I swam through the divorce. I swam through college. I swam from Alcatraz, on a dare. I swam as rehab from knee surgery. I swam across a lake at my wedding. I swam to an Italian monastery and back, to help settle someone else’s bet. I swam through a miscarriage and on each of the days before my two sons were born. Three decades of swimming, of chasing equilibrium, have kept my head firmly above water. Swimming can enable survival in ways beyond the physical.

像古德劳格人（Guðlaugur）和莫肯人（Moken）这样的古代游泳健将的生存故事，也与我作为一名游泳者息息相关。阅读澳大利亚哲学家达蒙·杨（Damon Young）的著作，帮助我理解崇高感在我们游泳体验中的重要性。十八世纪的哲学家们他解释了崇高之美及其力量，它源于自然界对立力量和理念的交汇：痛苦与快乐、恐惧与敬畏、害怕与兴奋、生命与死亡。杨格写道，今天我们游泳时，那种欣快感“源于生存的激情，而非生存的迫切需要”。我们因此更接近于对生命本身鲜活而深刻的体验。

Survival stories like those of Guðlaugur and ancient swimmers like the Moken have to do with me as a swimmer, too. Reading the Australian philosopher Damon Young helps me to understand the importance of the sublime in our experience of swimming. Eighteenth-century philosophers explained the sublime and its power in the meeting of nature’s opposing forces and ideas: pain and pleasure, terror and awe, fear and exhilaration, life and death. When we swim today, writes Young, that euphoria “comes from the passions of survival, without the desperate need to survive.” We come closer to the acutely vivid experience of life itself.

我们不断进化，我们游泳的原因也在不断变化。

We evolve. Why we swim does, too.

福利

WELL-BEING

如果能游向太阳而死，那该有多美好啊。

How nice it would be to die swimming toward the sun.

——勒·柯布西耶

—Le Corbusier

当今世界顶尖马拉松游泳运动员之一的金·钱伯斯（Kim Chambers）成年后才开始游泳，那是在2009年，为了康复她差点截肢的腿。她告诉我，罪魁祸首是一双高跟鞋——它导致她在旧金山公寓外的楼梯上摔了下来。她记得医生当时对她说：“我们保住了你的腿，但我们不知道你以后还能恢复到什么程度，甚至是否还能恢复。”她花了两年时间才重新学会走路。但她很快就发现自己在长距离游泳方面有着惊人的天赋。

One of the best marathon swimmers in the world today began swimming as an adult, in 2009, to rehab a leg she almost lost to amputation. A high-heel shoe was the culprit, Kim Chambers tells me—it led to a nasty fall down the stairs outside her San Francisco apartment. She remembers the doctors telling her this: We saved your leg, but we don’t know what—if any—functionality you’ll ever have. It took her two years to learn how to walk again. It took much less time to discover that she is freakishly gifted at long-distance swimming.

你可以说金是世界上你不认识的最厉害的游泳运动员。在她遭遇意外七个月后第一次下水游泳，她就从恶魔岛游到了旧金山，横渡了旧金山湾波涛汹涌、暗流汹涌的海面。她现在保持着多项长距离游泳世界纪录，其中包括她在2015年创造的纪录：成为首位独自一人从法拉隆群岛游到金门大桥的女性。这段30英里的旅程始于她滑入漆黑的海水中。午夜时分，她来到了臭名昭著的大白鲨出没的“红三角”海域。她花了十七个小时才完成挑战；在船员的密切注视下，她克服了恶心、狂风和鲨鱼的威胁。一向细心周到的金在前一天晚上就把衣服洗好叠好了；她不想留下凌乱的衣物，万一自己无法返回呢。她是历史上第六位完成“七大洋挑战”（Oceans Seven）的人，这项挑战相当于公开水域游泳版的“七峰挑战”。挑战路线包括英吉利海峡、直布罗陀海峡、莫洛凯海峡（或称卡伊维海峡）、卡特琳娜海峡、新西兰的库克海峡、日本的津轻海峡，以及从爱尔兰到苏格兰的北海峡。之后，她因数百次被水母蜇伤而中毒性休克。

You could say that Kim is the best swimmer in the world whom you don’t know. Seven months after she first got into a pool after her accident, she swam from Alcatraz to San Francisco, cutting across the choppy waters and fierce currents of San Francisco Bay. She now holds multiple world records for distance swimming, including one she set in 2015 by becoming the first woman to swim solo from the Farallon Islands to the Golden Gate Bridge, a thirty-mile journey that began with her slipping into pitch-dark waters just before midnight in the notorious Red Triangle of great white sharks. It took her just over seventeen hours; under the watchful eye of her boat crew, she faced nausea, high winds, and the perpetual menace of sharks. Ever thoughtful, Kim did her laundry and folded it neatly the night before; she didn’t want to leave a mess in case she didn’t make it back. She was only the sixth person in history to complete the Oceans Seven, the open-water swimming equivalent of the Seven Summits. This consists of the English Channel, the Strait of Gibraltar, the Molokai (or Kaiwi) Channel, the Catalina Channel, the Cook Strait in New Zealand, the Tsugaru Strait in Japan, and the North Channel from Ireland to Scotland, after which she went into toxic shock from hundreds of jellyfish stings.

十二月一个阴雨绵绵的早晨，我陪着金在旧金山湾游泳。我想了解一下游泳对她来说为何如此重要，以及她是如何养成这个习惯的。水温清爽宜人，华氏53度，气温48度。“如果哪天没下水，我就感觉不太舒服，”她一边说着，一边和我站在水上公园——海豚俱乐部后面的沙滩上。海豚俱乐部是世界顶级的公开水域游泳和划船俱乐部之一，成立于1877年。它的邻居南端划船俱乐部历史更悠久，成立于1873年。这两个俱乐部都是业界的标杆，一百五十年的历史中涌现出众多奥运选手。它们既是激烈的竞争对手，又是友好的伙伴，而金是这两个俱乐部的会员。“我是家里的老二，”她不好意思地解释道。

One gray, drizzly December morning, I join Kim for a swim in San Francisco Bay. I want to get a sense of the way that swimming is a daily practice for her, and how it got that way. The water temperature is a brisk fifty-three degrees Fahrenheit, the air forty-eight. “The days I don’t get in are the days I don’t feel right,” she tells me as we contemplate the bay from Aquatic Park, the sandy beach behind the Dolphin Club, one of the premier open-water swimming and rowing clubs in the world. It was founded in 1877. Its neighbor, the South End Rowing Club, is even older; it was founded in 1873. Both are institutions, with numerous Olympians on their century-and-a-half-old membership rolls. They are fierce yet friendly rivals, and Kim is a member of both clubs. “I’m a middle child,” she says sheepishly, by way of explanation.

对许多游泳者来说，游泳本身就是一种滋补品。这个词保留了它古老的含义：它是一种恢复剂，一种兴奋剂，旨在带来活力和幸福感。“滋补品”一词源于希腊语“tonikos ”，意为“伸展的”或“用于伸展的”。大约有十几个人已经下水，在轮船、工业码头和高桅帆船交织而成的奇特背景下畅游。雨点点缀着钢铁般的水面，宛如一面液态水银的镜子，映照着上方的天空。这里有一种开阔感。不难想象，这种游泳方式不仅舒展了身体，也舒展了心灵。

For many swimmers, the act of swimming is a tonic, in that old-fashioned sense of the word: it is a restorative, a stimulant, undertaken for a feeling of vigor and well-being. The word tonic comes from the Greek tonikos, “of or for stretching.” About a dozen people are in the water already, swimming against the unlikely backdrop of ships and industrial docks and tall-masted sailboats. Rain pocks the steely surface of the water, a liquid-mercury mirror of the sky above. There is an expansiveness here. It’s not too hard to think of this kind of swimming as stretching the mind as well as the body.

金停下来和斯特拉打招呼，斯特拉是海豚俱乐部一位会员的爱犬，浑身湿透。小狗兴奋地叫着跳了起来，舔着金的脸和手。我呢，即使穿着四毫米厚的氯丁橡胶潜水服，也忍不住瑟瑟发抖。金却毫不在意。她身高五英尺十英寸，身材苗条，笑容灿烂，甩了甩胳膊，除此之外，丝毫没有冷的迹象——只有小狗般渴望下水的热情。这里其他人也和她一样。八十岁的咪咪每天早上都从俱乐部游过来，她一边朝我们咧嘴笑着，一边迈着大步走下木板台阶，走向水边。和金一样，她只戴着泳帽、泳镜和一件薄薄的莱卡连体泳衣。在这里，穿潜水服并不被视为禁忌——俱乐部欢迎所有人——但游泳者们也被委婉地鼓励不穿潜水服。

Kim stops to greet Stella, the sopping-wet dog of a fellow Dolphin Club member. The dog yelps and jumps, licking Kim’s face and hands in excitement. Me, I can’t stop shivering, even in a four-millimeter neoprene wetsuit. Kim is unfazed. Five-feet-ten and willowy, with a high-megawatt smile, she shakes out her arms but otherwise shows no signs of cold—only a puppyish eagerness to get in the water. Others here are of a similar mind. Eighty-year-old Mimi, who swims from the club every morning, grins at us as she strides purposefully down the wood-planked stairs to the water. Like Kim, she is outfitted simply in a cap, goggles, and a thin one-piece Lycra swimsuit. Wetsuits aren’t exactly frowned upon here—the club encourages all comers—but swimmers are gently encouraged to do without.

金至今仍觉得不可思议，自己竟然偶然闯入了她所从事项目的最佳训练基地之一。不过，当初她刚开始加入俱乐部游泳时，只是为了生存。她腿伤的治疗——一次钝器伤导致她腿部一个腔室内压力骤增，需要多次手术减压，还进行了植皮、高压氧治疗，并在旧金山圣弗朗西斯医院的烧伤科接受了一段时间的治疗。两年后，她终于重返工作岗位。“我最担心的是疤痕，”她告诉我，“我的步态很不正常，跑不了步，感觉自己不像自己了。”她用长裤遮住疤痕，穿深色鞋子来掩盖为了支撑步态而穿的笨重矫形鞋垫。

It still amazes Kim that she just happened to stumble into one of the best training grounds there is for what she does. At the time she began swimming with the club, though, she was just trying to survive. The treatment for her leg injury—a blunt force trauma that caused a catastrophic buildup of pressure inside one of her leg compartments—required multiple surgeries to relieve pressure, as well as skin grafts, hyperbaric treatments, and a stint in the burn unit at San Francisco’s St. Francis Hospital. Two years later, she finally went back to work. “I was most worried about the scars,” she tells me. “My gait was off. I couldn’t go for a run. And I didn’t feel like me.” She hid her scars under long pants and wore dark shoes to camouflage the clunky orthotics she needed to support her stride.

她回忆起小时候在新西兰游泳的自由，于是鼓起勇气开始在当地的游泳池游泳——她选择在晚上去，因为她不想让别人盯着她身上的疤痕看。她的第一个目标是游一英里。起初，她的泳姿很糟糕。金的导师，企业家兼投资人维托·比亚拉（Vito Bialla）本人也是一位经验丰富的公开水域游泳运动员，他后来回忆说，他第一次见到金时，她连穿着脚蹼都游不出来。有一天，泳池里有两个游泳者问她有没有想过在海湾游泳。在海湾游泳？她心想。金自1995年以来就一直住在旧金山，但她从未听说过有人在海湾游泳。

She remembered the freedom of being in the water as a child in New Zealand, so she worked up the courage to begin swimming at a local pool—in the evenings, because she didn’t want people ogling her scars. Her first goal was to swim a mile. At first, her stroke was terrible. Kim’s mentor, the entrepreneur and investor Vito Bialla, an accomplished open-water swimmer in his own right, would later say that when he first met her she couldn’t swim her way out of a paper bag with flippers on. One day, two swimmers in the pool asked her if she’d ever thought about swimming in the bay. Swimming in the bay? she wondered. Kim had been living in San Francisco since 1995, but she’d never heard of anyone swimming in the bay.

2009 年末，在一个阳光明媚、气温宜人的日子里，金在水上乐园尝试了一次。尽管天气寒冷，她却全程笑容满面。第二个月，她加入了海豚俱乐部。她称之为冒险家的秘密社团，成员来自各个年龄段、各种收入水平。有时候，这需要……而当她在街上认出其他成员时，她说：“那是因为他们终于穿上了衣服。”我和金初次见面时，她即将年满四十；如今，她毫不避讳地谈论自己的疤痕。她给我看她的右腿，整齐的疤痕勾勒出移植的皮肤轮廓，这些皮肤取自她的大腿上部，用来修复小腿周围受损的组织。“水是我的老师。它是我的避难所。你可以经历糟糕的一周，但来到水边，你会感到身心得到净化。你赤裸裸地——所有的伪装都被剥离。”我开始明白，这些疤痕就像一张地图，记录着她如何重塑人生。

On a crisp fifty-four-degree day in Aquatic Park, in late 2009, Kim gave it a try. Despite the cold, she couldn’t stop smiling the whole time. She joined the Dolphin Club the next month. She calls it a secret society of adventurers, populated by individuals of all ages and incomes. Sometimes it takes a while for her to recognize a fellow member on the street: “It’s because they’re wearing clothes for a change,” she says. When Kim and I first meet, she is on the verge of turning forty; these days she has no qualms about talking about her scars. She shows me her right leg, neat tracks circumscribing the skin graft that was taken from her upper thigh to repair the traumatized tissue around her calf. “The water has been my teacher. It is my sanctuary. You can have a shitty week, but then you come to the water and feel cleansed. You’re naked—all the artifice is stripped away.” I begin to understand that the scars are a map of how she rehabilitated her life.

我们第一次一起游泳的那天早上，金拍着手，发出欢呼声，这无声的叫喊仿佛是一种祝福。“准备好了吗？”她问。我们纵身跃入水中，奋力划向阿尔卡特拉斯岛。

The morning of our first swim together, Kim claps her hands and hoots, the wordless sound a kind of blessing. “Ready?” she asks. We dive in and stroke our way toward Alcatraz.

5

5

水疗法

The Water Cure

18世纪50年代，本杰明·富兰克林在伦敦任职期间，每天都会在泰晤士河游泳。冷水浴在当时是一种非常流行的疗法，这位科学家、发明家和博学多才的文艺复兴式人物，在其漫长的一生中，大部分时间都热衷于裸泳。当时的英国人饱受一种作家所描述的“各种疾病的折磨……发烧、消化不良、忧郁症、神经抽搐、震颤，甚至愚钝，都是当时的流行病。” 治疗都市生活带来的种种健康问题的“新奇药”是什么呢？答案是：冰冷的海水。于是，英国的海滨度假胜地应运而生——并非为了日光浴或嬉戏玩闹，而是为了将自己浸泡在冰冷的海水中，享受这神奇的疗愈。这仿佛是整个国家的一次集体洗礼。

While posted in London in the 1750s, Benjamin Franklin swam daily in the Thames. The cold bath was a corrective much in vogue, and the scientist, inventor, and all-around Renaissance man was an avid skinny-dipper for much of his long life. Brits at the time suffered from what one writer has called “a mess of maladies . . . fevers, digestive complaints, melancholia, nervous tics, tremors, and even stupidity were the epidemics of the day.” The new wonder drug prescribed for the nasty health effects of urban living? Cold seawater. And thus the English seaside resort was born—not for sun worshipping or frolicking, but for dunking oneself in the cold miracle cure of the ocean. It was the collective baptism of a country.

回到大西洋彼岸，水疗在19世纪的美国蓬勃发展。公众对医疗机构的不信任导致人们热衷于用水疗法治疗各种疾病，从骨折到伤寒。甚至在1851年，纽约市还开设了一所水疗法医学院。到南北战争爆发时，超过当时全国有两百家水疗法诊所，一本专门介绍该主题的期刊拥有数万名订阅者。

Back across the pond, water therapy became big business in nineteenth-century America. Public distrust of the medical establishment led to the fervent adoption of the water cure for everything from broken bones to typhus. There was even a hydropathic medical school, opened in New York City in 1851. By the outbreak of the Civil War, more than two hundred water cure clinics were operating around the country, and a journal dedicated to the subject had tens of thousands of subscribers.

一位历史学家写道：“水疗病人坐在水中，浸泡在水中，站在水下任由水浇灌，敷着湿毛巾，裹着滴水的床单，吃着极其简陋的食物，当然，这些食物也都要用水送服。” 那时到处都是水——大多是用来浸泡的，有时也用来饮用。（每天喝八杯水的处方就是那个时代的遗迹。）冷水被誉为包治百病的灵丹妙药。发烧时把头浸在水里！流鼻血时闻一闻冷水！用冷水漱口可以戒掉嚼烟的恶习，恢复健康的唾液分泌！

“Water cure patients sat in water, submerged themselves in water, stood under water as it was poured over them, wore wet compresses, wrapped themselves in dripping sheets, and ate a meager diet washed down, of course, with water,” writes one historian of the practices. It was water, water everywhere—mostly for immersion but sometimes to drink. (The prescription of eight glasses of water a day is a relic from this time.) Cold water was proclaimed the sovereign remedy for every ailment. Dunk your head in it for a fever! Sniff it for a nosebleed! Take a cold mouth-bath to cure yourself of the filthy habit of tobacco chewing and restore a healthy salivary flow!

游泳是水疗法的关键。在约1851年出版的八卷本《水疗法百科全书》中，“游泳浴”被誉为对所有人都有益的“保健”和“卫生”方法，同时也被证明“对某些慢性疾病具有显著的治疗效果”。当我翻阅这本五百多页的百科全书时，发现其中对河浴、海绵浴和波浪浴的详尽论述既令人眼花缭乱又引人入胜。无论你是肺结核导致肺部虚弱，还是饱受慢性便秘的折磨，游泳都能有所帮助——增强并打开肺部，激活松弛的腹部肌肉，并（咳咳）促进肠道蠕动。各种宣传册铺天盖地而来，鼓吹海水游泳可以延年益寿。

Swimming was critical to the water cure. In the eight-volume Hydropathic Encyclopedia, published circa 1851, the “swimming-bath” is prescribed as “health preserving” and “hygienic” for all persons, but also as “eminently therapeutic in some forms of chronic disease.” As I flip through the encyclopedia’s five hundred plus pages, I find its exhaustive discussions of river, sponge, and wave baths to be both mind-numbing and fascinating. Whether you were weak in the lungs from tuberculosis or suffering from chronic constipation, swimming would help—to strengthen and open up the lungs, to get those lax abdominal muscles going and (ahem) move things along. Pamphlets rained down on the public prescribing saltwater swims for longevity.

我们对水作为万能药的信赖可以追溯到远古时代。埃及皇室成员沐浴在添加了精油的水中，中国和日本的传统也推崇温泉的药用价值。古希腊人对各种水疗法进行了深入研究。欧里庇得斯写道：“大海能恢复人的健康”，他对此深怀感激，因为据说他曾因在海中溺水而治愈了狂犬病。这种结合了水和窒息的疗法被称为“水手疗法”，是古代治疗狂犬病的一种著名方法。狂犬病的一个症状是恐水症，人们认为及时用水可以治愈它。（尽管欧里庇得斯如此认为，但事实证明这种方法并不有效。）希波克拉底和亚里士多德都非常推崇海水浴。罗马人会先泡在热水池里，然后跳进冷水浴池（一种令人精神振奋的冷水浴），以收缩毛孔，让沐浴者在疗程结束后感到神清气爽。

Our trust in water as a cure-all goes back to the ancients. Egyptian royals bathed in water laced with essential oils, and Chinese and Japanese traditions extolled the medicinal effects of thermal springs. The Greeks went deep in their examination of every type of water therapy. Euripides wrote that “the sea restores men’s health”—with great personal gratitude, since he was allegedly cured of rabies with a near drowning in the ocean. Called the “sailors’ method,” this combination of water and asphyxia was a celebrated ancient treatment for the disease. One symptom of rabies is hydrophobia, and it was thought that a timely application of water would cure it. (Euripides notwithstanding, it did not prove to be an effective remedy.) Hippocrates and Aristotle were big fans of hot seawater baths. Romans would soak in hot water pools, then hop into the frigidarium—a bracing cold-water bath—to close the pores and leave bathers refreshed at the end of the regimen.

在人们长期以来推崇将身体浸泡在水中以求健康的这段历史中，支持者们大多并不确切地知道其中的原理。但他们知道什么感觉很好。

For most of this history of immersing our bodies in water for wellness, proponents didn’t know exactly what they were talking about when it came to why. But they knew what felt good.

金·钱伯斯对水疗法的来历知之甚少，但她受伤后急需康复。2007年的某一天，她摔倒了，头部撞到地面，腿撞到楼梯底部的一个大陶瓷罐上。“我的耐痛能力很强，”她告诉我，“所以我当时觉得这没什么大不了的。”“肯定是一大块淤青。”她勉强开车去上班，腿肿胀得几乎是正常大小的两倍。到了办公室，她就晕倒了。在医院，外科医生在她的腿上切开了两处切口，以缓解肿胀对神经的损害。直到术后她才醒过来，医生告诉她一个可怕的消息：她可能再也无法行走了。

Kim Chambers doesn’t know much about the murky history of the water cure, but she was desperate to recover after her injury. When she fell that day in 2007, she smacked her head on the ground and struck her leg on a big ceramic pot at the bottom of the stairs. “I have a really high pain tolerance,” she tells me, “so I just thought it was going to be a nasty bruise.” She managed to drive to work, her leg ballooning to nearly double its normal size. At the office, she collapsed. At the hospital, surgeons sliced open her leg in two places to relieve the swelling that was destroying her nerves. She didn’t wake up until postsurgery, when her doctors reported the grim news that she might never walk again.

绝望是什么样子，感觉如何？它看起来像触目惊心的红色伤疤。它感觉像羞耻，像迫切想要掩盖跛行的渴望。它感觉像绝望。因此，它与孩子在海滩游泳时那种无拘无束的快乐截然相反。

What does despair look like, feel like? It looks like angry red scars. It feels like shame, the urgent desire to hide a limp. It feels like desperation. It is the opposite, then, of the unfettered joy of a child swimming at the beach.

金之所以强迫自己去游泳池，就是为了寻找那种快乐。当病人时间长了会让人厌倦——两年的医生预约、止痛药、全天候的物理治疗。在她第一次在旧金山湾游泳的那个早晨，她终于瞥见了另一个世界。“很少有人会拍下自己重生的视频，”金说，“但我有。和我一起游泳的那些家伙拍下了我，一个浑身发抖、瘦骨嶙峋、伤痕累累的女人，即使浑身湿透也只有一百二十磅。但我脸上却挂着他们见过的最灿烂的笑容。” 我突然想到，那些找到上帝的信徒当然会拍下自己重生的视频。他们获得了新生——通常是在水中，通过洗礼。

That joy is what Kim was after when she made herself go to the pool. Being a patient gets old after a while—two years of doctors’ appointments, pain meds, full-time physical therapy. On the morning she swam for the first time in San Francisco Bay, what she finally found was a glimpse of an alternate reality. “Not a lot of people have video footage of their rebirth,” Kim says. “But I do. The guys I was swimming with filmed me, this shivering, skinny, broken woman who was a hundred and twenty pounds soaking wet. But I had the biggest shit-eating grin on my face that they’d ever seen.” It occurs to me that religious people who find God, of course, do have videos of their rebirth. They are born again—oftentimes in water, with a baptism.

金开始在海湾冰冷的海水中游泳后，她注意到自己严重神经损伤的右腿有了变化：感觉好多了。她当时有个想法，也跟医生们提过。“当你下水时，血液会从四肢流向内脏器官，以保护它们。”“冷水，”她用她那轻快的新西兰口音解释道。那天晚上，在我们下班后长时间的电话交谈中，她这样说道。（除了训练和环游世界参加游泳比赛之外，她直到最近还在软件公司Adobe担任社区参与总监。）“是不是有可能，当你再次暖和起来之后，血液涌回四肢时，你就得到了某种形式的氧疗？氧气在体内循环的速度是不是更快了？”她的医生们表示，他们也认同这种说法，因为在水中，氧气的循环速度比金静坐不动甚至在陆地上运动时都要快得多。结果是：与前两年相比，她的神经再生速度明显加快。

After Kim started swimming in the cold waters of the bay, she noticed a change in her severely nerve-damaged right leg: it had more feeling in it. She had a theory that she ran by her physicians in those early days. “All the blood is sucked from your extremities to protect your organs when you get in that cold water,” she explains, in her lilting New Zealand accent, during one of our marathon phone calls after work one evening. (When she’s not training or traveling the world for swims, she has until recently been working as a director of community engagement for Adobe, the software company.) “Couldn’t it be possible that when the blood rushes back into those extremities after you warm up again, that you’re getting a kind of oxygen therapy? That there’s a higher rate of it being flushed around your body?” Her doctors said they could see the validity in it, with oxygen circulating at a much faster rate than if Kim were sedentary or even exercising on land. The result: her nerves were regenerating at a swifter pace relative to that of the previous two years.

为了厘清围绕水的种种真相与迷思，我采访了德克萨斯大学心血管衰老研究实验室主任、运动机能学教授田中博文博士。他研究人体如何运动、愈合和衰老。凭借他的研究工作以及在日本——这个由众多岛屿组成的国家——的成长经历（在日本，所有小学生都必须学习游泳），田中博士热情洋溢地倡导游泳有益健康。

To tease apart the tangle of truth and myth around water, I call up Dr. Hirofumi Tanaka, director of the Cardiovascular Aging Research Laboratory and professor of kinesiology at the University of Texas. He studies how our bodies move, heal, and age. By virtue of his work, and his upbringing—in the string of islands that is Japan, where learning to swim is required of all schoolchildren—Tanaka is an effusive, enthusiastic proponent of swimming for health.

田中实验室率先开展了游泳对两大衰老标志——高血压和关节炎——的影响的新研究。“在过去的四五年里，发生了一件奇妙的事情——我们发现游泳的效果实际上超过了步行或骑自行车，”他告诉我。“我们以前谁也不知道这一点。”陆上运动训练后血压可降低5到7个点。他发现，游泳平均可使血压降低9个点——在血压领域，这意义重大。游泳还能降低动脉僵硬，动脉僵硬是指动脉壁弹性降低，增加心肌压力的一种状况。

Tanaka’s lab has pioneered new research on swimming’s effects on two of the biggest hallmarks of aging: high blood pressure and arthritis. “Over the last four or five years, a funky thing happened—we realized that the effects of swimming actually surpassed the magnitude of the effects of walking or cycling,” he tells me. “None of us knew that before.” Average reduction in blood pressure after land-based exercise training is five to seven points. Swimming, he found, reduces blood pressure by an average of nine points—in the blood-pressure world, that’s significant. It also decreases arterial stiffness, a condition in which the walls of your arteries become less elastic and add strain to the heart muscle.

水对身体的压力在游泳健身中发挥着重要作用。当你浸入水中时，水会将血液从四肢推向心脏和肺部；这会暂时升高血压，使心肺功能更加活跃。这个过程可以增强心血管系统的效率和耐力，长期下来有助于降低血压。此外，游泳时，水还能为肌肉提供温和的全方位阻力。

The pressure of water itself on your body plays a part in swimming for health. When you immerse yourself in water, it pushes blood away from the extremities and toward your heart and lungs; this temporarily elevates your blood pressure and makes your heart and lungs work harder. The process builds efficiency and endurance in the cardiovascular system, leading to lower blood pressure over time. And when you swim, the water provides gentle, all-around resistance for your muscles to work against.

田中说，游泳有一种不分年龄的魅力：更多的人都能参与其中，而且能游得更久。在日本这个老龄化程度较高的国家，游泳非常受欢迎。甚至还有专门描写游泳的日本漫画。田中喜欢登上东京晴空塔——这座高达2080英尺（约740米）的世界最高塔——因为在晴朗的日子里，你可以俯瞰城市屋顶上波光粼粼的游泳池。

There’s an element of agelessness to swimming, Tanaka says: more bodies can do this, and for longer. In Japan, a nation of old people, swimming is hugely popular. There is even a subset of Japanese manga, or comic books, dedicated to swimming. Tanaka loves to go up to the top of Tokyo Skytree—at two thousand and eighty feet, it’s the tallest tower in the world—because on a clear day you can look down and see all the swimming pools glinting on the city’s rooftops.

人们一直认为游泳是治疗关节炎的好方法，但缺乏科学依据。2016年，田中和他的合作研究人员发表了一篇论文，给出了明确的肯定答案。“如果你观察那些……”田中医生说：“对于关节炎患者来说，主要问题是疼痛和功能障碍。他们每天都饱受慢性疼痛的折磨。游泳训练后，疼痛程度显著降低。即使患者身处水中，我们在陆地上评估的功能——例如行走和从椅子上站起——也得到了显著改善。游泳是我们能推荐的最佳运动，因为它能刺激活动能力（而且不会引起疼痛）并促进血液循环。” 这些游泳研究是在冷水泳池中进行的，也就是普通的游泳池，水温通常在华氏80度（约摄氏27度）以下。

Swimming had always been assumed to be good treatment for arthritis, but there was no science to back it up. In 2016, Tanaka and his co-researchers published a paper that provided a definitive yes. “If you look at patients with arthritis, the major issues are pain and function,” Tanaka says. “They suffer from chronic pain on a daily basis. After swimming training, the pain levels went down substantially. And even though the patients were in water, the functions we assessed on land—walking, standing from a chair—improved substantially. Swimming is the best exercise we can prescribe because it stimulates mobility—without pain—and circulation.” The swimming studies were done in cool water pools, that is, regular swimming pools, which are typically eighty degrees and below.

所以金·钱伯斯的直觉是对的：每天在凉水中游泳能显著改善她的血管功能——也就是促进血液在体内健康循环，输送到受损部位——其效果甚至超过了跑步或骑自行车。而且，或许最重要的是，游泳不会引起疼痛。

So Kim Chambers’s instinct was right: swimming in cool water every day boosted her vascular function—the healthy circulation of blood around the body, to the damaged parts that needed it—even more than running or cycling would have. And, perhaps most important, without the pain.

“如果我不游泳，疼痛就会加剧。如果我越来越痛苦，我的生活将会怎样？”作家梅丽莎·洪在一篇关于与慢性疼痛共存的文章中，将游泳描述为一种每日的忍耐。自从头痛在她脑中扎根以来，泳池成了她暂时摆脱疼痛的唯一场所。在那里，她能从“不听使唤的身体”中获得片刻的解脱。游泳会痛，但不游泳更痛。

“If I don’t swim, the pain grows. If I’m in more pain, what will become of my life?” In an essay on living with chronic pain, the writer Melissa Hung describes a swim as a daily act of endurance. In the years since a headache has taken up permanent residence inside her skull, the pool is the place where pain leaves center stage, if only briefly. It’s where she finds momentary relief from “a body that will not behave.” Swimming hurts, but not swimming hurts more.

富兰克林·罗斯福总统患有小儿麻痹症；在任期间，他在白宫安装了一个游泳池，每天游泳数次进行康复治疗。约翰·肯尼迪总统则饱受持续不断的背痛折磨。罗斯福一生饱受疾病折磨，但他酷爱游泳池，午餐和晚餐前都要游泳。罗斯福的游泳池至今仍保留在那里，位于现在的新闻发布室下方。

President Franklin D. Roosevelt suffered from polio; while in office, he had a swimming pool installed in the White House and swam for therapy several times a day. President John F. Kennedy, who endured near-constant back pain and a life of excruciating health miseries, loved the pool so much he swam before lunch and dinner. FDR’s pool remains there today, beneath what is the press pool briefing room.

浮力、漂浮、失重。自由。这些是我们用来谈论游泳的词语。巧合的是，我们也用这些语言来谈论我们在这个物质世界中努力追求的轻盈感和身心健康吗？

Buoyancy, floating, weightlessness. Freedom. These are the words we use to talk about swimming. Is it a coincidence that this is also the language we use to talk about the lightness of being, the wellness of being, that we strive for in this corporeal world?

在海豚俱乐部楼下，船屋和前楼梯入口之间，墙上贴着亨利·大卫·梭罗《瓦尔登湖》中的一句引言：“每天都要彻底更新自己；一遍又一遍地这样做，直到永远。”

Downstairs at the Dolphin Club, between the boathouse and the front stairway entrance, there’s a quote from Henry David Thoreau’s Walden posted on the wall: “Renew thyself completely each day; do it again, & again, & forever again.”

“每次下水，你都会感觉焕然一新，”一天，我们站在船屋楼上的窗户边，眺望着海湾，金对我说。整个冬春两季，我们都会定期见面游泳。这天早晨，风雨交加，水面波涛汹涌。“我们都会有心情低落、心碎难过的时候。但当你潜入水中，就像按下重启键一样。它让我头脑清醒了很多。”每次下水，海水仿佛都能映照出她的感受，并做出相应的回应。“所以我每天都要下水。”

“You do renew yourself every time you’re out there,” Kim tells me one day, as we look out at the bay from the upstairs window of the boathouse. Over the course of the winter and spring, we continue to meet up periodically for swims. On this particular morning, it’s proving to be a stormy start, and the water is turbulent. “We all have bad days and heartache and heartbreak. But you submerge yourself in that water, and it’s like pressing the reset button. It has given me tremendous clarity.” Each time she gets in, it’s as if the water reflects how she feels and responds in kind. “That’s why I have to do it every day.”

从法拉隆群岛游到太平洋30英里外的海域，对金来说，这是深海如何迫使人彻底臣服的终极体现。正如她常说的，岛屿周围五英里半径的海域是大白鲨的“客厅”。她只不过是个过客，匆匆而过。她曾作为法拉隆群岛首支全女子接力队成员打破纪录，之后又作为首位独自游泳的女性，不顾危险，如果可以，她恨不得每天都去那里游泳。她有时会利用周末时间去岛上游玩，只是为了游泳。

Swimming from the Farallon Islands, thirty miles out in the Pacific, was for Kim the ultimate extension of how being in deep water could force a kind of surrender. As she likes to put it, the five-mile radius around the islands is the great white sharks’ living room. She’s just a visitor, passing through. After her record-breaking swims as part of the first all-female relay team from the Farallons and then as the first solo woman, despite the danger, she would swim there every day if she could. She sometimes takes a weekend jaunt out to the islands, just to swim.

“我的所有感官都被唤醒了，”她说。“我能闻到海洋生物的气息。那种感觉就像身处六千或一万英尺深的海水中，而你只是个渺小的人，在水面上游弋。”企业家维托·比亚拉曾形容在法拉隆群岛游泳就像同时置身天堂和与魔鬼对话。金说，这片海域的躁动不安深深吸引着她。“你不知道水下有什么。周围都是海豹和海鸟。你知道自己不应该出现在那里，鲨鱼随时可能从天而降。那种身处边缘、与自然如此紧密相连的感觉，真是令人着迷。”

“All my senses are ignited,” she says. “I can smell the sea life. That feeling of being in water that’s six thousand or ten thousand feet deep, and you’re just this tiny person swimming on the surface.” Entrepreneur Vito Bialla has described swimming at the Farallons as akin to being in heaven and talking to the devil at the same time. The restlessness of the seascape, Kim says, is captivating for her. “You don’t know what’s swimming underneath you. The seals all around, and the birds. You know you’re not supposed to be there, and a shark could come out of nowhere. It’s tantalizing to be on that edge, to be that connected.”

在事故发生前，金自称是个控制狂——对自己的身材、外貌和体重都极度在意。她在硅谷有一份收入丰厚、工时很长的工作。“我以前是个肤浅的人，”她说，“我接受过古典芭蕾舞训练，我的世界观里一切都非常严谨。”学习游泳意味着学会放手，学会在充满不确定性的环境中茁壮成长。

Before her accident, Kim was a self-described control freak—about her body, about her appearance, about her weight. She had a job in Silicon Valley with long hours and good money. “I was a superficial person,” she says. “I was classically trained as a ballerina, and everything in my world view was very disciplined.” Learning to swim meant learning how to relinquish control, to thrive in a space of uncertainty.

她为每一次长距离游泳都做了充分的准备，但现在她觉得最刺激的莫过于纵身跃入水中，对即将发生的一切一无所知。“我们生活在陆地上，以为自己知道接下来会发生什么，”她告诉我，“但其实我们并不知道。我已经学会了顺其自然。这感觉太棒了。”既自由又可怕，但你会觉得自己像个现代探险家。很少有人下过法拉隆群岛的水域。你就像个宇航员一样。” 2016年，金被授予探险家俱乐部会员资格，该俱乐部成员包括宇航员和探险家，例如埃德蒙·希拉里爵士、丹增·诺尔盖、西尔维娅·厄尔、尼尔·阿姆斯特朗、莎莉·赖德、索尔·海尔达尔和珍妮·古道尔。

She works hard to prepare for each big swim, but she now finds nothing more exhilarating than jumping in and not knowing what will come. “We live a life on land, and we think we know what’s going to happen,” she tells me, “but we don’t. And I’ve learned how to surrender. It’s so freeing, and so scary, but you feel like this modern-day explorer. Not many people have gotten into the water in the Farallons. You’re like an astronaut out there.” In 2016, Kim was inducted into the Explorers Club, which includes among its members astronauts and explorers, including Sir Edmund Hillary, Tenzing Norgay, Sylvia Earle, Neil Armstrong, Sally Ride, Thor Heyerdahl, and Jane Goodall.

在晨泳的过程中，我从金那里了解到，每天在海湾游泳是她直面心魔的时刻。然后，她与心魔握手言和。十年前，她曾被认为再也无法行走。然而，如今她却在自己从未听说过的游泳项目中，保持着多项世界纪录。抗拒那些让我们感到不舒服的事情是人之常情。但她却在克服不适、探索彼岸的过程中，发现了非凡之处。

During the course of our morning swims, I learn from Kim that the daily swim in the bay is where she confronts her demons. Then she shakes their hands. Ten years ago, she was someone who wasn’t supposed to walk again. And yet here she is, a multiple world-record holder in a discipline that, back then, she didn’t even know existed. It’s human nature to resist doing things that are uncomfortable for us. But she finds something extraordinary in pushing through the discomfort to see what’s on the other side.

有一年秋天，我决定从恶魔岛游到旧金山。我是受人怂恿才这么做的。我印象最深的，是曾经参加过一次夜间游览这座岛屿监狱的经历。由于恶魔岛离旧金山市中心很近，囚犯们常常被水对岸的生活声所困扰。当城里的居民举办新年派对，他们的狂欢声飘过冰冷湍急的海湾时，岸边似乎离囚犯们近得令人发狂。这是一种极致的折磨——近在咫尺的煎熬。

One fall, I decided to swim from Alcatraz to San Francisco. I did it on a dare. What I remember most about a nighttime tour I once took of the island prison is the fact that, given the nearness of Alcatraz to downtown San Francisco, inmates were often haunted by the sounds of life across the water. When city residents held New Year’s Eve parties and their reveling carried across the cold, current-roiled bay, the shore seemed maddeningly close to the prisoners. It was the ultimate torture—that of proximity.

阿尔卡特拉斯岛荒凉崎岖，面积不足一平方英里。岛上处处皆是圣路易斯令人惊叹的景色。旧金山，浩瀚的海湾，还有锈红色的金门大桥。奥隆尼族的口述历史告诉我们，阿尔卡特拉斯岛曾被原住民用作隔离之地，用来惩罚那些违反部落法律的人。当你身处其中，尤其是在夜晚，你就会明白。置身于如此广袤的地方，感到自己的渺小也就不足为奇了。

Alcatraz’s barren, craggy island is less than a square mile in area. Everywhere there are astounding views of San Francisco, the expansive bay, and the rust-hued Golden Gate Bridge. Ohlone oral history tells us that Alcatraz was used by the indigenous people as a place of isolation, to punish those who violated tribal law. When you are there, especially at night, you understand. It makes sense that you would feel small anchored in a place so big.

在阿尔卡特拉斯岛（绰号“岩石”）作为联邦监狱运营的近三十年间——从1934年到1963年，由于所有物资（包括淡水）都必须通过船只运输，成本飙升，最终关闭——它关押着众多高危囚犯，其中包括阿尔·卡彭、罗伯特·斯特劳德（又名“阿尔卡特拉斯的鸟人”，因其早年在莱文沃斯监狱服刑期间成为一位受人尊敬的鸟类学家而得名）以及罗伊·加德纳，这位美国著名的火车大盗和当时最臭名昭著的越狱高手。加德纳于1934年被转移到阿尔卡特拉斯岛，他成功上诉获得赦免，并于1938年7月获释；次年，他出版了一部轰动一时的自传。他将这本书命名为《地狱之岛》（Hellcatraz ），以这座对他影响至深的地方命名。又过了一年，他自杀身亡。

In the nearly three decades that Alcatraz, known as the Rock, was a functioning federal prison—from 1934 to 1963, when it closed due to the skyrocketing costs of having to bring in everything by boat, including fresh water—it held high-risk prisoners, including Al Capone, Robert Stroud (aka the Birdman of Alcatraz, so called because he became a respected ornithologist during his earlier incarceration at Leavenworth penitentiary), and Roy Gardner, the great American train robber and the most notorious escape artist of his time. Transferred to Alcatraz in 1934, Gardner successfully appealed for clemency and was released in July 1938; the next year, he published a sensational autobiography. He named the book after the place that marked him: Hellcatraz. In another year, he would be dead, by suicide.

岩石监狱（The Rock）是个能让人发疯的地方。作为一座监狱，它曾是臭名昭著的恐怖之地。它的设计目的就是为了让囚犯屈服。据记载，这里共发生过十四起越狱事件，涉及三十六名囚犯。其中最臭名昭著、计划最周密的，莫过于弗兰克·莫里斯和安格林兄弟于1962年6月发起的越狱行动。他们用削尖的勺子挖地道逃出牢房；在床上留下了毯子和事先准备好的假人头。他们用光了肥皂、卫生纸，甚至连自己的头发都没了。夜深人静之时，他们乘坐一个用五十件偷来的雨衣做成的充气筏跳入水中。这三人至今下落不明，但最近一项利用计算机建模和当时历史潮汐信息的研究显示，他们或许有机会避免被卷入大海，而这机会窗口非常短暂。他们有可能在金门大桥北侧的海岬上岸——潮水退去后，他们登陆的残骸很可能被冲到天使岛上——事实上，联邦调查局正是在那里发现了一支桨和与他们相关的个人物品。尽管如此，最可能的结果是体温过低，最终溺水身亡。

The Rock is a place that can drive you mad. As a prison, it had a storied menace. It was designed to break you into submission. All in all, there were fourteen separate documented escape attempts involving thirty-six prisoners. Of these, the most infamous and exhaustively planned attempt was that of Frank Morris and the Anglin brothers, in June 1962. They tunneled out of their cells using sharpened spoons; in their beds they left blankets and dummy heads constructed out of soap, toilet paper, and their own hair. In the dead of night, they entered the water in an inflated raft made from fifty stolen raincoats. The three men were never found, but a recent study using computer modeling and historical tide information from that date shows a very narrow window of opportunity in which they could have avoided being sucked out to sea. It is possible that they were able to get out of the water in the headlands north of the Golden Gate Bridge—debris from this landing would likely have washed up on Angel Island after the tide turned—and this in fact was where the FBI found a paddle and personal items linked to the men. Still, the most probable outcome was hypothermia, and drowning.

1962年12月，一名囚犯约翰·保罗·斯科特成功地从岛上游到了金门大桥南端的炮台角。斯科特是唯一被证实的囚犯游泳上岸的案例。人们普遍认为，岛上的水温（通常低于60华氏度）、湍急的水流（流速往往达到6节甚至更快）、锋利的岩石（足以将人割成碎片）以及鲨鱼（无需赘述）都使得这项任务徒劳无功。但斯科特证明并非如此。

One inmate, John Paul Scott, succeeded in swimming from the island to Fort Point, on the southern end of the Golden Gate Bridge, in December 1962. Scott’s was the only confirmed case of a prisoner reaching the shore by swimming. The water temperature (typically below sixty degrees), vicious currents (often moving at six knots or faster), sharp-edged rocks (that could slice you to ribbons), and sharks (enough said) were believed to make the task futile. Scott proved it wasn’t.

他和另一名囚犯用偷来的橡胶手套做了游泳圈（两人在厨房干活；斯科特的同伙在越狱过程中摔断了脚踝，几分钟后就被抓获）。斯科特最终在退潮时被冲到福特角，被发现时已经昏迷不醒。他因体温过低被四名青少年殴打。在普雷西迪奥医院短暂治疗后，他被送回了阿尔卡特拉斯监狱。

He and another prisoner had fashioned water wings from stolen rubber gloves (the two worked on kitchen duty; Scott’s co-conspirator broke his ankle during the prison break and was captured within minutes). Scott ended up beached at Fort Point during an ebb tide and was found unconscious, suffering from hypothermia, by four teenagers. After a brief stay at the Presidio hospital, he was taken back to Alcatraz.

我们竟然选择在距离旧金山海岸仅一英里半的狭小土地上建造一座最高安全级别的联邦监狱，这无疑反映了我们集体的一些信念。我们建造像雷克岛监狱那样的监狱——它夹在布朗克斯区和皇后区之间，距离纽约拉瓜迪亚机场的跑道只有几步之遥——还有像恶魔岛监狱那样紧邻我们城市的监狱，而我们却因为周围有水域环绕就认为它们很安全。

Surely it says something about our collective beliefs that we chose to put a maximum-security federal prison on a speck of land barely a mile and a half offshore from San Francisco. We build jails like Riker’s Island—sandwiched between the Bronx and Queens and within shouting distance of the runways at New York’s LaGuardia Airport—and prisons like Alcatraz tantalizingly close to our cities, and we believe them to be secure because of the water surrounding them.

但早在20世纪20年代，岛上的游泳者就已经开始在阿尔卡特拉斯岛附近水域进行试探性游泳了。在被改建为联邦监狱之前，阿尔卡特拉斯岛曾被军方用作防御工事和拘留中心（美国内战初期，南方邦联的战俘就被关押在那里）。1933年，也就是阿尔卡特拉斯岛正式成为联邦监狱的前一年，17岁的阿纳斯塔西娅·斯科特（与囚犯约翰·保罗并无亲属关系）——她的父亲是驻扎在岛上的一名军士——在一艘划艇的陪伴下，用43分钟从阿尔卡特拉斯岛游到了旧金山。她是历史上第一个完成这项壮举的女性。随后不久，另外两名旧金山游泳者多丽丝·麦克劳德和格洛丽亚·西格利亚诺也完成了这项壮举，以抗议将该岛改建为联邦监狱的决定。麦克劳德用了两个小时完成了往返的游泳。这三位女性都是游泳健将，并且了解潮汐情况。当然，他们成功的关键还在于，他们并非要么被迫在夜幕掩护下逃脱，要么只能靠监狱的伙食勉强维持生存，几乎没有任何运动。

But swimmers on the outside had been testing the waters around Alcatraz since at least the 1920s. Prior to its conversion to a federal prison, Alcatraz was used by the military both as a fortification and as a detention center (Confederate POWs were housed there early in the American Civil War). In 1933, the year before Alcatraz opened as a federal penitentiary, seventeen-year-old Anastasia Scott (no relation to the prisoner John Paul), whose father was a sergeant stationed on the island, swam from Alcatraz to San Francisco in forty-three minutes, accompanied by a rowboat. She was the first woman on record to make the swim. Two other San Francisco swimmers, Doris McLeod and Gloria Scigliano, followed shortly thereafter, to protest the decision to turn the island into a federal prison. McLeod completed a two-way crossing in two hours. All three women were excellent swimmers with knowledge of the tide conditions; also critical to their success, of course, was the fact that they were not required to escape under cover of darkness or to subsist on a prison diet with little to no exercise.

为了从恶魔岛游过去，我和朋友史蒂夫在水上公园附近的水域进行训练，那里是大多数恶魔岛游泳路线的终点；从这里可以游到开阔的海湾，感受一下水流的强度。我们第一次在那里游泳时，我感到一阵恶心——先是胸口发紧，然后是多年来游泳时从未有过的那种焦虑。我呼吸困难。我不知道这应该归咎于刺骨的寒冷，还是因为潜水服的束缚感。我们停下来踩水，互相确认状态时，史蒂夫对我露出了灿烂的笑容。“放松，”他看到我的表情后说，“深呼吸。”

For our swim from the Rock, my friend Steve and I took up training in the waters around Aquatic Park, the end point for most Alcatraz swims; from this spot you can venture into the open bay and get a feel for the strength of the currents. The first time we swam there, I experienced a queasy discomfort—it started with a tightness in my chest and a genuine anxiety of the kind I had not felt for years when it came to swimming. My breath did not come easy. I did not know if I should attribute that to the cold, which felt unexpectedly crushing, or to the wetsuit, which felt unexpectedly confining. Steve smiled widely at me when we took a break to tread water and check in with each other. Relax, he said when he saw my face. And breathe.

到了游泳当天早上，我已经做好了应对寒冷的准备，也熟悉了退潮时海湾水流以令人不安的速度将人拉向开阔海域的情形。我知道集装箱船看起来可能很远，但几秒钟之内就会出现在眼前。我们的船长加里·埃米奇是一位公开水域游泳传奇人物，他后来完成了从阿尔卡特拉斯岛到旧金山的第一千次游泳，并打破了世界纪录。我让自己做好准备，听从史蒂夫的建议：放松，深呼吸。

By the morning of the swim itself, I had tried to prepare myself for the cold, and I was familiar with the way the bay’s currents pull you with unnerving speed toward the open ocean on an outgoing tide. I knew that container ships could seem far away but come upon you in a matter of seconds. Our boat pilot, Gary Emich, was an open-water swimming legend who would go on to break a world record with his one-thousandth swim from Alcatraz to San Francisco. I had conditioned myself to follow Steve’s advice: Relax, and breathe.

那天我们六个人一起游泳。水温57华氏度，微风拂面，水面波光粼粼。我们早上九点前就到了阿尔卡特拉斯岛，然后跳了下去。正值涨潮，冰冷的海水刺得我喘不过气来。我们重新集合，最后一次向船和船夫挥手告别。那天早上拍的照片里，我面带微笑。照片里的我看起来比实际感觉暖和，阳光在我的反光泳镜上闪着银光。我们转向城市方向，游了起来。

There were six of us swimming that day. The water temperature was fifty-seven degrees, the surface chopped with a light wind. We arrived at Alcatraz before nine a.m. and jumped in on a flood tide. The chilly water had a bite that managed to steal my first breath away. We regrouped for one last wave at our boat and its pilot. In photos from that morning, I am smiling. I look warmer than I felt, the sun glinting silver on my reflective goggles. We turned for the city and swam.

随着划水的进行，我逐渐找到了节奏，游泳不再像是一场搏斗。每一次呼吸、划水、划水、呼吸的循环都轻松自如，规律而舒适。我们早已做好了准备。入水时紧绷的胸口感觉放松下来，我开始从容应对周期性的涌浪，不再焦虑不安，而是以热情而精准的蛙泳腿绕过每一道浪花。

As I stroked through the water, I fell into a rhythm, and suddenly the swim didn’t feel like a fight. There was an ease, a comforting regularity, to each round of breath, stroke, stroke, breath. We were prepared for it. The tight band that squeezed my chest upon entry loosened, and I began to greet the periodic cresting wave with aplomb instead of anxiety, skirting each rise of foam with an enthusiastic and carefully timed frog kick.

除了偶尔被海藻缠住之外，我们成功地避开了与海洋生物的任何不愉快或危险的遭遇。（唉，最近那里似乎出现了海狮咬人的事件。）从独特的鱼眼视角眺望金门大桥和恶魔岛，提醒着我们，我们正在努力加入一个精英俱乐部。四十五分钟转瞬即逝，我们突然就到了水上公园。埃米奇宣布这次旅行非常棒。

Other than the occasional rogue seaweed tangle, we managed to avoid any undesirable or hazardous run-ins with marine life. (Alas, sea lion bites have recently become a thing there.) The unusual fish-eye angle to the Golden Gate Bridge, and to Alcatraz, were reminders of the rarefied club in which we were earning membership. The forty-five minutes passed swiftly, and suddenly we arrived at Aquatic Park. Emich proclaimed it an excellent time.

6

6

我们血管里的海水

Seawater in Our Veins

每天都下海游泳，你的身体就会逐渐适应海水的温度、节奏和变化。水温53度时，你会感觉像吃了冰淇淋一样头疼；水温50度时​​，你的手腕骨头会隐隐作痛。金和她的海豚俱乐部成员以及南区居民，每天都能凭感觉把水温精确到一度。“你觉得今天多少度？59度？”有一天，她在水里自言自语地问我。我问她为什么这么想，她说因为感觉太舒服了。“是啊，我敢打赌肯定是59度。还没到60度……咱们游过去看看温度计吧。”（当然，她说得没错。）

Get in the ocean every day, and your body will calibrate itself to the medium’s moods, rhythms, temperatures. At fifty-three degrees, you get the ice cream headache. At fifty degrees, the bones in your wrists ache. On any given day, Kim and her fellow Dolphin Clubbers and South Enders can call the water temperature to within a degree, just by feel. “What’d you think it was today? Fifty-nine?” she wonders aloud to me in the water one day. When I ask why she thinks so, she says it’s because it feels wonderful. “Yeah, I would bet a lot of money on that. It’s not quite sixty . . . Let’s swim over and check the thermometer.” (She’s right, of course.)

人类胎儿在子宫内吸入和呼出羊水，帮助肺部形成。我们有所谓的鳃裂，它们最终会成为我们颌骨和呼吸道的一部分，其形态是水生鳃呼吸脊椎动物进化遗迹。海水的矿物质含量与人类血浆非常相似，以至于我们的白细胞可以在海水中存活并发挥功能一段时间。我沉浸在脑海中的画面中……这就是我们血管里循环着海水这种并非异想天开的想法。

Human fetuses inhale and exhale amniotic fluid in utero, helping to form the lungs. We have so-called gill slits that become parts of our jaws and respiratory tracts, the form of which are evolutionary relics of aquatic, gill-breathing vertebrates. Seawater is so similar in mineral content to human blood plasma that our white blood cells can survive and function in it for some time. I delight in my mental picture of this, the not-so-fanciful notion that we have seawater circulating in our veins.

自从古德劳格三十多年前意外落入海中以来，科学界发现了其他一些在极寒水域中拥有非凡适应能力的人。其中就包括传奇的公开水域游泳运动员琳恩·考克斯，她是第一个游过白令海峡的人；1987年，她从阿拉斯加游到苏联，当时水温低至零下1摄氏度。（《纽约时报》的头条标题是“漫长的寒冷之旅”。对她的接待情况的报道是：“那是一场简单的海边野餐，一场优雅的沙滩茶会，但对这位贵宾来说，到达那里却并非易事。”）第二年，古德劳格和考克斯在同一份学术期刊上发表了一篇学术简报，探讨了北极游泳发展成为一项体育运动的潜力。

Since Guðlaugur’s involuntary plunge into the sea more than three decades ago, science has been introduced to other humans with unusual adaptive abilities in extremely cold water. There’s Lynne Cox, the legendary open-water swimmer who was the first to swim the Bering Strait; she swam from Alaska to the Soviet Union in 1987 in water that dropped as low as thirty-eight degrees. (The headline in the New York Times read Long, Cold Swim. Her reception was reported thusly: “It was a simple seaside picnic, a genteel tea party on the beach, but to get there took some doing for the guest of honor.”) The following year, Guðlaugur and Cox appeared in the same academic journal, in a scholarly brief about the potential for Arctic swims to become a sport.

2002年，考克斯在南极洲32华氏度（约1摄氏度）的海水中游了一英里多——她是史上第一个做到这一点的人。2007年，她又在格陵兰岛迪斯科湾低于27华氏度（约零下3摄氏度）的海水中游泳。美国女性的平均体脂率在22%到25%之间。据估计，考克斯的体脂率高达35%；更重要的是，她的体脂分布非常均匀。除了保暖之外，这件“内置潜水服”还能让她在海水中保持中性浮力，这意味着她只需消耗极少的能量就能在海洋中保持最佳游泳姿势。和古德劳格一样，考克斯也参与了医学研究，为研究人员提供了治疗多发性硬化症的新方法。（冷水游泳可在浸入后的数小时内显著减轻痉挛）并改善心脏、脊髓和脑损伤的医院治疗程序（冷却身体可以减轻肿胀和创伤）。

In 2002, Cox swam more than a mile in thirty-two-degree water in Antarctica—she was the first person ever to do so. In 2007, she swam in Disko Bay, Greenland, in water that was below twenty-seven degrees. The average American woman has a body fat percentage that ranges between 22 and 25 percent. Cox’s body fat has been estimated at 35 percent; more significantly, it is very evenly distributed around her body. In addition to keeping her warm, this “internal wetsuit” provides her with neutral buoyancy in seawater, which means she can expend very little energy to maintain optimal swimming position in the ocean. Like Guðlaugur, Cox has participated in medical studies, opening researchers’ eyes to new ways to treat multiple sclerosis (cold water swimming can dramatically reduce spasticity for a number of hours following immersion) and to improve hospital procedures around heart, spinal, and brain injuries (cooling the body can reduce swelling and trauma).

例如，通过研究考克斯的手浸入冷水中时的血液流动情况，医生们学会了如何更好地制定手术方案。科学家们还发现，考克斯浸入冷水后，她的核心体温实际上会升高。看看她进入冷水按摩浴缸时的表现：短短两分钟，她的体温就能使水温升高两华氏度。（古德劳格没有接受过此类测试。）

By studying the specifics of blood flow into Cox’s hand while it was immersed in cold water, for example, doctors learned how to better plan for surgeries. Scientists also found that with immersion in cold water, Cox’s core body temperature actually goes up. See what she can do when she enters a cold-water Jacuzzi: in two minutes, her body heat warms the water by two degrees Fahrenheit. (Guðlaugur has not undergone this kind of testing.)

还有一位英国-南非混血游泳运动员刘易斯·普格，他被誉为游泳界的埃德蒙·希拉里爵士。他曾在北极、珠穆朗玛峰的融水湖以及南极的罗斯海游泳。研究普格的科学家发现，他的核心体温甚至在入水前就开始升高，最高可达华氏101度（约摄氏38度）。南非开普敦大学的运动生理学家蒂姆·诺克斯教授最早注意到这种反应。他在《柳叶刀》杂志上将其称为“预期性产热”：即在运动前产生热量。这是普格多年来冷水训练形成的巴甫洛夫式条件反射。

And there’s the British–South African swimmer Lewis Pugh, who is nicknamed the Sir Edmund Hillary of swimming. He has swum in the Arctic, in a meltwater lake on Mount Everest, and in Antarctica’s Ross Sea. Scientists studying Pugh have found that his core body temperature rises even before he hits the water, reaching temperatures as high as one hundred and one degrees Fahrenheit. Professor Tim Noakes, a sports physiologist from the University of Cape Town, South Africa, first noted this response. In the Lancet, he called it “anticipatory thermogenesis”: the creation of heat before an event. It’s Pugh’s Pavlovian response, from years of cold-water conditioning.

至于我们其他人，我们的身体在冷水中会发生什么变化？我问长寿研究专家田中博文，是否有关于冷水游泳与健康的长期研究。“我们知道当……时，身体会产生反应，也就是潜水反射。”“把脸浸入冷水中——皮肤里的血管会收​​缩，心率会急剧下降，”他说。“但我们还没有很多关于长期在寒冷环境中运动的研究。”然后他跟我讲了ama（一种游泳训练项目） 。

As for the rest of us, what happens to our bodies in cold water? I ask Hirofumi Tanaka, the longevity researcher, if there are any long-term studies of cold-water swimming and health. “We know the response, the diving reflex, when you put your face in cold water—the blood vessels in your skin constrict and your heart rate drops like crazy,” he says. “But we don’t have a lot of research in terms of chronic exposure to exercise in the cold.” Then he tells me about the ama.

几年前，田中回到日本，研究日本和韩国的传奇女性自由潜水员——海女（ama） 。“海女”在日语中意为“海洋之女”。她们传承着该地区两千多年来捕捞贝类的传统，从十三四岁就开始潜水；田中研究的这群海女平均年龄为六十五岁。与东南亚的摩肯族海族一样，海女们通过代代相传的故事，将她们的技能和对海洋重要性的知识传承下去。和摩肯族的孩子一样，捕捞贝类的潜水活动也改变了她们的身体。她们每天潜水多达两百次，一年四季如此。田中说，就血管功能而言，她们“非常强壮”。

A couple of years ago, Tanaka went back to Japan to study the ama, the legendary female free divers of Japan and Korea. Ama is Japanese for “women of the sea.” Carrying on this region’s more than two-thousand-year-old tradition of hunting for shellfish, the women begin diving at age thirteen or fourteen; the group Tanaka studied was composed of sixty-five-year-olds on average. Like the Moken sea nomads of Southeast Asia, the ama pass on their skills and knowledge about the importance of the sea in stories told over generations. As with the Moken children, the practice of diving for shellfish changes their physical bodies, too. They dive up to two hundred times a day, every day, year-round. When it comes to vascular function, Tanaka says, they are “sky-high.”

海女每天都要经历数百次潜水反射。田中一直想知道，海女的动脉结构和功能是否已经进化得与其他潜水哺乳动物相似。他发现，与居住在同一渔村的其他成年人相比，这些女性的心率明显更低，动脉僵硬程度也更低。然而，她们却患有听力损失——五十年的冷水环境也会对身体造成不利影响。

The ama are exposed to the diving reflex on a daily basis, hundreds of times a day. Tanaka had wondered if the ama’s arterial structure and function had adapted to resemble that seen in other diving mammals. He found that the women had significantly lower heart rates and less arterial stiffness when compared to other adults living in the same fishing village. They did, however, suffer from hearing loss—fifty years of exposure to cold water has adverse effects, too.

虽然科学研究远未完成，但越来越多的研究表明，浸泡在水中具有治疗益处。温水浸泡尤其如此。冷水游泳也有诸多益处——研究表明，在90华氏度（约32摄氏度）的水中浸泡一小时（头部露出水面），可以降低心率和血压，促进放松。而同样时间在57华氏度（约14摄氏度）的水中浸泡，则能使新陈代谢率提高350%，多巴胺水平提高250%。此外，其他研究表明，经常进行冷水冬泳可以显著减轻参与者的紧张、疲劳和疼痛，并改善整体健康状况。

The scientific picture is far from complete, but there’s a growing body of research on the therapeutic benefits of immersing ourselves in water. Warm-water immersion has its perks, too—studies show that one-hour head-out immersion in ninety-degree water lowers heart rate and blood pressure, promoting relaxation. But immersion in fifty-seven-degree water for the same period boosts the metabolic rate by 350 percent and dopamine by 250 percent. And when it comes to actually swimming in that water, other research shows that regular cold-water winter swimming significantly reduces tension, fatigue, and pain among participants—and improves general well-being.

我只需翻阅海豚俱乐部自身的档案，就能找到令人信服的游泳健身照片。早在1974年，杰克·拉兰——这位打造了著名健身帝国的传奇人物——就曾拖着一艘划艇，从阿尔卡特拉斯岛游到俱乐部，全程不到90分钟，而他的双腿和双手都被镣铐锁住。在当天的一张黑白照片中，体格健壮的拉兰高举着他那肌肉发达、戴着手铐的手腕，仿佛在庆祝胜利，他当时已经接近水上公园。那时他60岁。到了70岁，拉兰再次被镣铐锁住，在长滩港游了一英里半，拖着70艘载有70名乘客的船只。

I need to look no further than the Dolphin Club’s own archives for convincing snapshots of swimming health. Back in 1974, Jack LaLanne—he of the famed fitness empire—swam while towing a rowboat behind him from Alcatraz to the club in less than ninety minutes, all with his legs shackled and his arms manacled. In a black-and-white photo from that day, the astonishingly robust LaLanne holds up his handcuffed (and well-muscled) wrists in triumph as he nears Aquatic Park. He was sixty years old. When LaLanne was seventy, shackled and manacled again, he swam a mile and a half in Long Beach Harbor, towing seventy boats with seventy passengers.

拉兰每天都游泳。因此，他被授予海豚俱乐部终身荣誉会员称号也就不足为奇了。他于2011年去世，享年96岁。

LaLanne swam every day. No surprise, then, that he was made an honorary lifetime member of the Dolphin Club. He died in 2011, at the age of ninety-six.

在一个更现代的清晨，在水上公园，冰凉的海水拍打着我们的肩膀，我问金，她是否认为某些体型的人在海湾里表现更好。一项关于人体运动能力的新研究表明，与精英跑步运动员不同，精英游泳运动员可以利用不同的体型取得优异成绩。不同距离的运动员体型各异；一项对2012年伦敦奥运会跑步运动员的分析显示，200米短跑运动员的体型明显大于马拉松运动员，但例如，相应的50米自由泳短跑运动员与10000米公开水域马拉松运动员的体重却相近，无论身高或性别如何。看来，所有体型的人都能在水中游得不错。但如果水温较低呢？“嗯，理论上说，在冷水中会产生更多的棕色脂肪，”金解释道，我们停下来踩水聊天。“棕色脂肪燃烧能量并产生热量，而白色脂肪则不会。”她笑着耸了耸肩。“至少我是这么听说的。”

On a more contemporary morning at Aquatic Park, the cold water sloshing around our shoulders, I ask Kim if she thinks certain bodies tend to do better in the bay. New research into human physical performance shows that elite swimmers, unlike elite runners, can excel with different body types across all distances; an analysis of runners in the 2012 London Olympics revealed that 200-meter sprinters were significantly larger than marathoners, but the corresponding 50-meter-freestyle pool sprinters, for example, shared a similar body mass with 10,000-meter-open-water marathoners, regardless of height or sex. All bodies can do well in water, it seems. But what about when the water is cold? “Well, the theory is that you get more brown fat from being in cold water,” Kim explains, as we pause to tread water and chat. “Brown fat burns energy and generates heat, and white fat doesn’t.” She laughs and shrugs. “Or so I’m told.”

那次游泳之后不久，我驱车向南行驶五英里，穿过一座桥，来到一座高耸入云的未来主义建筑前。这座建筑的屋顶花园可以俯瞰金门公园。我走进梶村慎吾博士的办公室，和他聊了聊脂肪、冷水和健康之间究竟有何关联。他是加州大学旧金山分校一位屡获殊荣的生物化学家，他领导的实验室致力于研究如何改造脂肪细胞对抗肥胖和代谢疾病。梶村博士是一位略带稚气、举止轻松、笑容可掬的男子，他对动物如何适应环境非常着迷。他小时候在东京郊区长大，那时的工作就是捕鱼为生，比如捕沙丁鱼或比目鱼。他说，如果他不是一名科学家，他会在旧金山当一名渔民兼寿司师傅。

Not long after that swim, I drive five miles to the south, cross a bridgeway to a soaring futuristic building with rooftop gardens overlooking Golden Gate Park, and duck into the office of Dr. Shingo Kajimura to talk to him about what fat, cold water, and health could possibly have to do with each other. He’s a prize-winning biochemist at the University of California, San Francisco, who runs a lab that is trying to engineer the way fat cells fight obesity and metabolic disease. A boyish man with a relaxed manner and a ready smile, Kajimura is fascinated by how animals adapt to their environment. As a kid growing up in the Tokyo suburbs, his job was to catch fish for dinner: sardines, say, or flounder. If he wasn’t a scientist, he says, he’d be a fisherman and a sushi chef in San Francisco.

他对鱼类适应能力的早期好奇心——例如，鲑鱼如何从淡水游到咸水，或者鲶鱼如何在污水中生存——使他对以下方面产生了兴趣：哺乳动物能够适应寒冷的环境。“那时我住在密歇根州，总是想着寒冷，”他坦言。但这却是一件偶然的事，因为它让他对脂肪的前沿科学产生了兴趣。

His early curiosity about fish adaptations—how salmon can swim from freshwater to saltwater, for example, or how catfish can thrive in dirty water—led to an interest in how mammals could adapt to cold conditions. “I was living in Michigan back then. I thought about cold all the time,” he admits. But it was serendipitous, because it got him interested in the cutting-edge science of fat.

梶村给我讲了一个关于两种脂肪的故事：人类和其他哺乳动物一样，天生有两种脂肪。白色脂肪储存能量，棕色脂肪燃烧能量，产生热能。冷水游泳结合了长期的冷水环境和运动，这两者都能使白色脂肪“褐变”——转化为所谓的米色脂肪——并加速新陈代谢。

Kajimura tells me a tale of two fats: Humans, like other mammals, are born with two kinds of fat. White fat stores energy. Brown fat burns it, creating heat energy. Cold-water swimming is a combination of chronic cold exposure and exercise, both of which are known to have a “browning” effect on white fat—turning it into what’s called beige fat—and revving up your metabolism.

当然，新陈代谢是个热门话题。梶村经常接到来自洛杉矶和纽约健身房的电话。“他们会问，‘我们想在寒冷的天气里开始练瑜伽——这对你来说好吗？’”他笑着说。“我会说，‘这要看情况。’在寒冷的天气里锻炼对某些人有益，但对另一些人则不然。”他知道这并不是一个简单或令人满意的答案，但是——嗯，这就是科学。

Metabolism, of course, is a hot topic. Kajimura gets calls all the time from gyms in LA and New York. “They say, ‘We’d like to start yoga in the cold—is that good for you?’” he says, laughing. “I say, ‘It depends.’ Exercising in the cold is good for some people, but not others.” He knows that it’s not a neat or satisfying answer, but—well, that’s science.

梶村教授指出，白色脂肪细胞几乎90%都是脂质——它是我们储存能量的地方。相比之下，棕色脂肪细胞是人体内线粒体最丰富的细胞之一——它们是我们燃烧能量的“燃料引擎”。在实验室对小鼠的研究中，运动会诱导白色脂肪褐变，低温会进一步加速这一过程；这种米色脂肪能够保护小鼠免受肥胖和糖尿病的侵害，即使喂食高脂肪饮食，它们也能保持苗条健康。但由于这项科学研究尚属新兴领域——棕色脂肪直到2009年才被证实存在于成年人体内——这些过程的分子机制目前仍不清楚。

White fat cells are almost 90 percent lipid—it’s where our stores of energy live, says Kajimura. Brown fat cells, by contrast, are among the most mitochondria-rich cells in the human body—they are our fuel-burning engines. In the lab’s studies with mice, exercise induced the browning of white fat, which was increased further by cool temperatures; this beige fat protected the mice from obesity and diabetes, and they were able to stay lean and healthy even when fed a high-fat diet. But because the science is so new—brown fat was only proven to exist in human adults in 2009—the molecular level of these processes is not yet clear.

婴儿出生时体内含有大量的棕色脂肪。“由于婴儿肌肉发育不足，无法在寒冷时通过颤抖来产生热量，因此棕色脂肪对于调节体温至关重要。”梶村解释道。他给我看了一张科学插图：一个婴儿的背部和颈部被涂成棕色，这些区域富含棕色脂肪。大部分棕色区域看起来就像一条围在脖子上的冬日围巾。

Babies are born with lots of brown fat. “Since babies don’t have enough muscle to shiver when they’re cold to generate heat, brown fat is very important to regulate body temperature,” Kajimura explains. He shows me a scientific illustration: a human infant, shaded with brown areas on the back and neck, where brown fat deposits are rich. The major coverage area resembles nothing so much as a winter scarf draped around the neck.

但到了五六十岁，棕色脂肪会急剧减少，这与年龄相关的肥胖密切相关。“大多数人在这个年龄段都会增重，但这并非因为他们吃得更多，”梶村说。“这让我们非常着迷。体重增加是因为能量消耗下降。我们并不完全了解其中的原因，但我们推测棕色脂肪的减少是导致体重增加的原因之一。那么，究竟是什么因素在起作用呢？即使棕色脂肪已经减少，我们能否通过生成新的、能够燃烧能量的棕色脂肪来逆转体重增加呢？”

But there’s a dramatic decline in brown fat when we reach our fifties and sixties, and it correlates neatly with age-related obesity. “Most people gain weight at this time, and it’s not because they’re eating more,” Kajimura says. “It’s very fascinating to us. You gain weight because your energy expenditure goes down. We don’t fully understand why, but we speculate that the loss of brown fat contributes to it. What are the factors? Can we reverse the gain by creating new types of energy-burning brown fat even after you lose it?”

寒冷刺激会引发身体的应激反应：当你感到寒冷时，身体会通过增加血流量、血管生成和循环来代偿。虽然寒冷是消耗能量最有效的方式之一——甚至比运动更有效——但它对心脏却有害，因为寒冷会刺激血管收缩，导致血压升高。“老年人在冬季清晨容易中风，”梶村告诉我。“寒冷刺激对健康人有益，但对心脏病患者则不然。运动也是如此——如果你有心血管疾病风险，举重或剧烈运动对你没有好处。我们不能把寒冷刺激应用于心脏疾病患者。”或者说，这并非适用于所有人的普遍疗法。这取决于你的年龄、健康状况和家族病史。”

Cold exposure results in a stress response in our bodies: when you feel cold, your body compensates with blood flow, and blood vessel formation and circulation. But while the cold is one of the most efficient ways to burn energy—even more than exercise is—it’s lousy for your heart, because cold stimulates vasoconstriction, and your blood pressure goes up. “Old people get strokes early in the morning in the wintertime,” Kajimura tells me. “Cold exposure is beneficial to healthy people but not for people with heart trouble. It’s the same for exercise—weight lifting or intense exercise is not good for you if you have cardiovascular risk. We can’t apply or generalize this as a therapy for everyone. It depends on your age, how healthy you are, your family history.”

但梶村觉得游泳和冷水的协同增效对健康非常有吸引力。“我小时候在日本，冬天奶奶总会让我出去玩，”他回忆道。奶奶的命令是：孩子们必须在寒冷的户外玩耍。她说，脱掉上衣，这样医生就不会来了。

But Kajimura finds the synergistic health pairing of swimming and cold water a tantalizing idea. “When I was a kid in Japan, my grandmother would send me outside to play in the wintertime,” he recalls. Her command: Kids had to play outside in the cold. Take off a shirt, she said, and that would keep the doctor away.

“我跟俄罗斯西伯利亚的人们聊过，他们经常跳进冷水里，”梶村有些疑惑地说。“从心血管角度来看，这很糟糕，但人们意识到这样做也有好处——增强免疫力，提高对病毒的抵抗力。但我们还不确定其中的原因。”具体的机制尚未完全明了，但相关证据正在不断积累。
