“I’ve talked to people in Siberia, Russia—they jump into cold water all the time,” Kajimura says, a bit wonderingly. “It’s terrible from a cardiovascular standpoint, but people realize that there is something good about this—immunity, viral resistance. But we’re not sure why that is.” The specific mechanisms are still not completely understood, but evidence is accumulating.

2012年，俄罗斯在西伯利亚广袤地区的秋明市一个冰封的湖面上举办了首届冬季冰泳比赛。组织者在冰面上凿出了四条25米长的泳道。来自世界各地的游泳运动员飞来参赛；其中就包括居住在南非的以色列冰泳运动员拉姆·巴凯，他于2009年创立了国际冰泳协会，旨在规范冷水公开水域游泳。

In 2012, Russia held its first winter ice swimming competition in the middle of a frozen lake in Tyumen, a town in the vast region of Siberia. Organizers cut four 25-meter lap lanes into the ice. Swimmers flew in from all over the world to compete; the Israeli ice swimmer Ram Barkai, who lives in South Africa and founded the International Ice Swimming Association in 2009 to standardize cold open-water swimming, was one of them.

比赛首日，面对刺骨的寒冷，巴尔凯和他的队友们强忍着“想要喝得酩酊大醉的强烈冲动”，他在当天的记录中写道。第二天，气温降至零下22度。华氏度——前一天比赛结束后留在外面的湿毛巾冻得笔直，像立柱一样。水温保持在冰点，华氏32度。就在巴尔凯被叫回去参加一公里预赛之前，他看到一位俄罗斯女子完成了她的耐力游泳比赛，她昂着头，不戴泳镜，以蛙泳姿势游完了全程。

Faced with the astounding cold on the first day of competition, Barkai and his fellow swimmers suppressed “an extremely strong urge to drink ourselves silly,” he writes in an account of that day. On the second day, the air was minus twenty-two degrees Fahrenheit—wet towels left out after the previous day’s races froze and stood straight at attention. The water temperature held at the freezing point, thirty-two degrees. Just before Barkai was called back for his one-kilometer heat, he watched a Russian woman finish her endurance swim, swimming breaststroke with her head up, without goggles.

“她的睫毛冻得硬邦邦的，睁不开眼，”巴凯写道。“他们几乎是把她拖到桑拿房里，慢慢地帮她解冻眼睛。鼻子里的水分也冻得硬邦邦的。呼吸就像慢慢地、浅浅地吸入芥末一样。任何暴露在冰冷空气中的胡须或长发都会立刻冻住。” 但他注意到，水看起来却出奇地诱人。

“Her eyelashes froze solid and she couldn’t open them,” writes Barkai. “They basically dragged her to the sauna to slowly defrost her eyes. Moisture in the nose froze solid. Breathing was like inhaling wasabi in slow shallow intakes. Any facial hair or long hair exposed to the icy air just froze immediately.” Yet he notes that the water looked surprisingly inviting.

巴尔凯将赛后的感受——皮肤像龙虾一样红，身体不受控制地颤抖——描述为一种强烈而充满活力的生存状态：“寒冷和游泳会给人带来一种兴奋感和健康活力，除非亲身经历，否则很难解释这种感觉。”

Barkai describes the post-race prize—skin lobster-red, body uncontrollably shivering—as the feeling of being intensely, vigorously alive: “The cold and the swim gives one such a rush and sense of health and vigor which is hard to explain unless you have done it.”

当我从南非的家中拨通巴凯的电话，询问他关于冰泳养生之道时，他笑了。“有些人会说这简直是极端的不健康行为，”他说，“很多医生都告诉我，我早就该死了。”但他依然在世界各地追逐冰雪，追求他所谓的“疯狂运动”，为了体验他在西伯利亚那一天经历中所描绘的那种令人心潮澎湃的感受。他最近刚从同一地点再次游泳回来，并想让我知道，十年的冰泳经历让他感觉更加强健。

When I get him on the phone from his home in South Africa to ask him about ice swimming for wellness, Barkai laughs. “Some people would argue that this is extreme un-wellness,” he says. “I’ve been told by so many doctors I should have been dead long ago.” But he continues to chase ice around the world, in pursuit of his “mad sport,” for the heightening experience that he describes in his account of that day in Siberia. He recently returned from another swim in the same place and wants me to know that a decade of ice swimming has only made him feel more robust.

到 2018 年初，已有超过 250 人完成了经认证的“冰泳一英里”——在 41 华氏度或更低的水中游一英里或更远。

By the beginning of 2018, more than two hundred and fifty people had swum a certified “ice mile”—a mile or more in forty-one-degree water or colder.

回到梶村的办公室，我们对在西伯利亚冰层中凿出的泳池游泳的想法感到惊叹。“我想，凡是杀不死你的，都会让你更强大，”梶村若有所思地说。“我以前觉得这都是些哲学理论，但从临床角度来看，这或许是真的。”

Back in Kajimura’s office, we marvel at the idea of swimming in a pool cut into the Siberian ice. “I guess whatever doesn’t kill you makes you stronger,” Kajimura says thoughtfully. “I used to think it was all philosophical, but it might be true from a clinical standpoint.”

游泳相关常见（及不常见）健康问题的词汇表：

A glossary of common (and not-so-common) health ailments associated with swimming:

游泳耳：游泳后耳内残留的水引起的耳道细菌或真菌感染（用滴耳液治疗以减轻炎症和对抗感染）。

swimmer’s ear: a bacterial or fungal infection of the outer ear canal brought on by water that stays in the ear after swimming (treated with ear drops to reduce inflammation and fight infection).

外生骨疣：耳道内骨骼的异常生长，由频繁接触冷水和大风环境引起，常影响冲浪者和潜水员（一旦生长物阻塞耳道，则需要手术治疗）。

exostosis: an abnormal growth of bone within the ear canal that is caused by frequent exposure to cold water and windy conditions, often affecting surfers and divers (once the growth blocks the ear canal, the condition requires surgery).

隐孢子虫病：一种由顽强的、耐氯寄生虫引起的胃肠道和呼吸道疾病，是游泳池和水上乐园中最常见的感染（大多数免疫系统健康的人无需治疗即可康复）；

cryptosporidiosis: a gastrointestinal and respiratory illness caused by a hardy, chlorine-resistant parasite, and the most common infection at pools and water parks (most people with healthy immune systems recover without treatment);

海虱：一种会蜇人的微小水母幼虫，经常被困在皮肤和泳衣之间的缝隙中，引起瘙痒的皮疹和水疱（皮质类固醇或抗组胺药可以帮助减轻症状的严重程度）。

sea lice: stinging microscopic jellyfish larvae that often get trapped in the space between skin and swimsuit, causing itchy rashes and blisters (corticosteroids or antihistamines can help alleviate the severity of symptoms).

足癣，又称香港脚：常见于世界各地潮湿的更衣室和游泳池，由真菌引起，导致出现鳞状红色皮疹（可用抗真菌药物治疗）。

tinea pedis, or athlete’s foot: common in damp locker rooms and swimming pools the world over, caused by a fungus that results in a scaly red rash (treated with antifungal medication).

军团病：一种严重的肺炎，由军团菌污染游泳池、热水浴缸、按摩浴缸和其他水系统引起（及时使用抗生素治疗至关重要）。

Legionnaires’ disease: a severe form of pneumonia caused by the Legionella bacterium when it contaminates swimming pools, hot tubs, whirlpools, and other water systems (prompt treatment with antibiotics is critical).

肌腱炎，又称游泳肩：肩关节周围连接肌肉和骨骼的纤维索因重复运动而引起的常见炎症（建议进行交叉训练、拉伸、力量训练和休息）。

tendinitis, or swimmer’s shoulder: a common inflammation of the fibrous cords connecting muscle to bone around the shoulder joint due to repetitive motions (cross-training, stretching, strength training, and rest are recommended).

游泳引起的肺水肿：肺部突然出现过多液体，导致呼吸困难，可能与剧烈游泳和冷水浸泡有关（治疗包括氧疗和监测）。

swimming-induced pulmonary edema: a sudden onset of excess fluid in the lungs that results in difficulty breathing and may be related to strenuous swimming and cold-water immersion (treatment includes oxygen therapy and monitoring).

头发变绿（这是真的！）：是由于泳池水中氯与铜和其他硬金属发生反应造成的；绿色的氧化金属会被头发吸收（小苏打可以有所帮助）。

green hair (it’s a thing!): results from the reaction of chlorine with copper and other hard metals found in pool water; green-tinged oxidized metals are absorbed by hair (baking soda can help).

尾蚴性皮炎，又称游泳者瘙痒症：是由对生活在淡水湖泊和池塘中的鸭子和其他鸟类常见的穴居寄生虫的过敏反应引起的皮疹（炉甘石和抗组胺药可以减轻瘙痒，但相信我，它们作用不大）。

cercarial dermatitis, or swimmer’s itch: a rash caused by an allergic reaction to burrowing parasites common in ducks and other birds that dwell in freshwater lakes and ponds (calamine and antihistamines can reduce itching, but believe you me, they don’t do much).

你可以叫我“满身疙瘩的新娘”，我丈夫就这么叫我。照片上看不出来，但十年前，就在我们当着一百位至亲好友的面互诉衷肠的时候，我全身都长满了细小的疹子，从头到脚（痒得要命）。

You can call me the Bumpy Bride. My husband does. You can’t see it in the pictures, but a decade ago, at the very moment of our heartfelt declarations before a hundred of our closest friends and family, my skin was completely covered in a fine, full-body rash. Head to (miserably itching) toe.

在一个阳光明媚的夏日午后，我们在阿迪朗达克山脉靠近纽约州和佛蒙特州交界处的乔治湖畔一块狭长的沙洲上举行了婚礼。乔治湖以其清澈见底的湖水而闻名——湖水干净到纽约州将其列为饮用水源。我身上的疙瘩是对通常生活在湖中水禽体内的微小寄生虫的过敏反应——那种令人毛骨悚然的皮疹，也就是游泳者瘙痒症。

On that bright summer afternoon, we were married on a spit of land overlooking Lake George, in the Adirondack Mountains near the New York–Vermont border. It’s a lake known for its pristine water—so clean that New York State classifies it as drinking water. The bumps were an allergic reaction to the microscopic parasites that normally live in the waterfowl that frequent that lake—the rashy horror that is swimmer’s itch.

为了做我热爱的事，我忍受过各种各样的叮咬：在澳大利亚游泳，在墨西哥冲浪，在巴拿马潜水。我去过蚊虫肆虐的北极夏季海滩，也去过沙蝇横行的夏威夷海滩。每次回来，我身上都带着发痒的红色“勇气勋章”——游泳者瘙痒症。我努力接受这一切：游泳是第一位的，痛苦是第二位的。然而，这些虫子似乎在某种程度上定义了我。在婚礼誓词中，我的丈夫当着证人的面宣称，他无法保证保护我免受“陆地和海洋中叮咬蜇人的生物”的侵害。但他承诺会尽力而为。

I’ve endured all manner of welts to do what I love: swimming in Australia, surfing in Mexico, scuba diving in Panama. I’ve visited mosquito-filled Arctic summer beaches and sandfly-infested Hawaiian beaches. Always I return bearing itchy red badges of courage. Swimmer’s itch. I try to own it: the swimming comes first, the suffering second. Still, these bugs define me somehow. In his wedding vows, my husband declared before witnesses that he could not promise to protect me from the “biting, stinging creatures of land and sea.” But he promised to try.

戴安娜·奈德从古巴游到佛罗里达，由于脸部被水母蜇伤，回来时面目全非。琳恩·考克斯是第一个在众多地方游泳的人，其中包括鲨鱼和海蛇出没的好望角。马丁·斯特雷尔，这位身穿泳裤的斯洛文尼亚英雄，游过了……亚马逊河——长达三千三百英里，到处都是食人鱼——人们冒着被寄生虫、黄貂鱼和牛鲨咬死的痛苦风险。

Diana Nyad swam from Cuba to Florida and emerged unrecognizable because of jellyfish stings to her face. Lynne Cox was the first to swim in so many places, among them the Cape of Good Hope, patrolled by sharks and sea snakes. Martin Strel, the Slovenian “hero in a Speedo,” swam the piranha-infested Amazon—all three thousand three hundred miles of it—risking the most agonizing of deaths by parasites, stingrays, and bull sharks.

上述大部分疾病都是温水疾病，我想这算是一种幸运吧，因为至少我可以退到其他更冷的水域，比如旧金山的水域，这对像我这样的游泳者来说可能特别有益。

Most of the aforementioned are warm-water afflictions, which I guess is a kind of luck, because at the very least I can retreat to other, colder waters, like those of San Francisco, which might just be specifically salutary to a swimmer like me.

大家都说冷水游泳对身体有益，我决定脱掉潜水服。如果八十岁的咪咪都能做到，而且游得那么轻松自如，那我至少也应该试试，对吧？

With all this talk of how cold-water swimming can be good for you, I decide that I’ve got to lose the wetsuit. If eighty-year-old Mimi can do it, and with such aplomb, I should at least try it, right?

又是一个清晨，这次是在三月中旬，我来到了海豚俱乐部。瓢泼大雨中，海湾的水温却升到了近乎温暖的56华氏度（约14摄氏度）。不知为何，我每次去公开水域游泳似乎都会遇到下雨，这导致每次下水和离开时都感觉浑身湿冷，实在令人不快。当我到达水上公园查看情况时，水里空无一人。我心想，是不是雷雨天气吓跑了游泳的人。这时，金开着她的黑色路虎车来了，兴奋地跳下车。“哇！”她欢呼道。听从她的建议，我把一壶热姜茶放进储物柜，准备游泳后在桑拿房里喝。“这能帮你暖和过来，”她说，“不过别担心，你肯定游得很好！”

Another early morning at the Dolphin Club, this time in mid-March. In the midst of a colossal downpour, the water temperature in the bay has ticked up to an almost balmy fifty-six degrees. Somehow it seems to always be raining when I go open-water swimming, which makes for the unfortunate circumstance of clammy arrivals and departures. There isn’t a soul in the water when I get to Aquatic Park to assess the conditions. I wonder if the reports of thunder and lightning are keeping swimmers away. But then Kim drives up and hops excitedly out of her car, a black Land Rover. “Whoo!” she crows. On her advice, I go to stash a thermos of hot ginger tea in my locker for drinking in the sauna post-swim. “It’ll help warm you up afterward,” she says. “But don’t worry, you’ll do great!”

一波又一波身着泳装的人们跟着我们走出更衣室，来到沙滩上。南区居民们熙熙攘攘地聚在一起。我和海豚俱乐部的成员们兴致勃勃地聊着天，大家站在齐膝深的浪花里，讨论着水况。（当我问一位名叫凯特的中年游泳者，她如何形容这两个俱乐部时，她坦言海豚俱乐部“就像和父母住在一起——我们比较保守。南端俱乐部就像兄弟会，他们更冒险。”站在凯特旁边的是她的朋友，一位南端俱乐部的成员，听到这话哈哈大笑。）

A steady stream of swimsuit-clad bodies rolls with us out of the locker rooms and onto the sand. South Enders mingle convivially with Dolphin Clubbers as everyone discusses the conditions while standing knee-deep in the lapping water. (When I ask one swimmer, a middle-aged woman named Kate, how she’d characterize the two clubs, she confides that the Dolphin Club is “like living with your parents—we’re more conservative. The South End is like the frat house. They’re more risky.” Standing next to Kate is her friend, a South Ender, who laughs appreciatively at this.)

金得意洋洋地向周围所有人宣布我的首次游泳：“这是邦妮。她今天第一次不穿潜水服游泳！”我无力地挥了挥手。一阵问候、自我介绍和一些玩笑之后，她们一个接一个地出发了。然后轮到我了。我用拇指最后擦拭了一下泳镜内侧，绷紧核心肌群，纵身跃入水中。

Kim proudly proclaims my maiden voyage to anyone within earshot: “This is Bonnie. She’s swimming without a wetsuit today for the first time!” I wave weakly. After a chorus of hellos, introductions, and a bit of trash talk, they all set off, one by one. Then it’s my turn. I give the inside surface of my goggles one last swipe with my thumbs, steel my core muscles, and take the plunge.

刚游过一百码，我的皮肤表面就开始出现一种奇特的刺痛感——就像冰火交融，灼烧着我的全身。这种感觉持续了大约六十秒。然后——嗯，我就感觉好多了。我们绕着海德公园码头游了一圈，然后转向与海岸线平行，沿着一排浮标向西穿过海湾，朝着水上公园码头游去。游动过程中，金时不时发出她标志性的欢呼声——大约每十几次呼吸就叫一声，以此来表达她对整个过程的热情。

Immediately, as I stroke through the first hundred yards, the surface of my skin starts generating a peculiar prickly heat—it’s a kind of ice fire, flaming its way all over my body. It lasts for about sixty seconds. And then—well, I feel fine. We swim around Hyde Park Pier and turn parallel to the shore, following a line of buoys west across the cove toward Aquatic Park Pier. Our swim is punctuated every now and again by Kim’s signature whoops—every dozen breaths or so, to mark her enthusiasm for the whole venture.

金不止一次告诉我，在清澈冰凉的海水中畅游的感觉棒极了，“就穿着我们与生俱来的衣服，再加一点莱卡面料。” 这话一点没错——穿上这身衣服，我感觉不仅好，而且棒极了，感觉自己充满活力。天空放晴。我们在远处的浮标旁停了下来，那个浮标上插着旗子，还放着温度计，我们互相确认一下。其他游泳者也来到旗子旁，我们一起踩水，就像在开一场小型茶话会。这时，我已经完全感觉不到冷了。“因为你是第一次，所以我们慢慢来，”金提醒道，“我知道你能游得更远，但是你会经历体温下降。你上岸后体温会继续下降，那时候你才会真正感到冷。” 事实证明，说到寒冷，最大的威胁并非游泳本身，而是游泳后的体温下降。

More than once, Kim has told me that there’s a high to being in the rousingly crisp water, “with just what we came into the world with and a bit of Lycra.” And it’s true—in my skin, I feel more than fine. I feel great, amazing, alive. The sky clears. We pause at the far side buoy, the one planted with a flag and a thermometer, to check in with each other. Other swimmers join us at the flag, and as we tread water together, it’s like a little tea party out there. By then, I don’t feel the cold at all. “We’ll take it easy since it’s your first time,” Kim cautions. “I know you can swim longer, but you’ll get afterdrop. Your body temperature will keep dropping after you get out, and that’s when you’ll get really cold.” Turns out when it comes to cold, the biggest threat isn’t the swim itself but the afterdrop that follows.

沿着浮标返回俱乐部的路上，我交替使用自由泳和蛙泳，欣赏着沙滩和游泳者的景色。然而，一丝不安却始终萦绕在我的心头。我不禁想起在冰冷的北大西洋中遭遇的古德劳格，以及来自长岛——我的家乡——的龙虾渔民约翰·奥尔德里奇：2013年，奥尔德里奇在蒙托克海岸附近的一个深夜落水，在72华氏度（约22摄氏度）的海水中，他用绿色橡胶靴作为漂浮物，在水中挣扎了12个小时才得以幸存。在如此寒冷的海水中待那么久，究竟是怎样的体验？他们是在冰冷的海水中意外落水，而我们却在这里享受游泳的乐趣。我的25分钟初体验就这样结束了，伴随着一阵潮汐般的肾上腺素飙升。但当我们到达沙滩时，我的左手小指开始像爪子一样与我的手掌分离，仿佛是一种警告。

On the buoy trail back to the club, I alternate between freestyle and breaststroke, enjoying the view of the sandy beach and its swimmers. Still, at the edge of my consciousness, there’s a little lurking worry. I can’t help but think about Guðlaugur in the freezing North Atlantic, and of John Aldridge, the lobsterman from Long Island, my own home island: in 2013, Aldridge fell overboard in the middle of the night off the coast of Montauk and survived the next twelve hours in seventy-two-degree water by using his green rubber boots as flotation devices. What must it have been like to be out there for so long, in the cold? They were accidental swimmers in their cold-water ordeals, and here we are doing it for fun. My twenty-five-minute maiden journey is over like that, with a tidal adrenaline rush. But as we hit the beach, my left pinky finger starts to separate from the rest of my hand in a clawlike configuration, almost as a warning.

淋浴时，余温扑面而来。我拼命地把水龙头拧到最高，但还是暖和不起来，也止不住地发抖。无论我把旋钮拧多大，我的牙齿都会打颤。当我揉搓胳膊和腿时，我的下巴开始紧咬。

In the shower, the afterdrop arrives. I furiously crank the faucet toward H, but I can’t get warm or stop shivering no matter how far I turn the knob. My teeth chatter. As I rub my arms and legs, my jaw begins to clench.

巧合的是，长期会员、重症监护专家托马斯·纳克顿（Thomas Nuckton）正是在海豚俱乐部（Dolphin Club）开展研究，研究对象包括其他游泳者，研究内容涉及体温过低和体温下降现象。美国海岸警卫队现行的溺水生存表格和计算机程序实际上引用了纳克顿的一项研究，该研究利用与海豚俱乐部游泳者共同开发的方法，量化了沉船幸存者的生物物理参数。过去二十年来，他的研究揭示了体温下降现象：即使游泳者离开水面后，体温仍会继续下降，轻度体温过低（比正常体温低几度）相当普遍。由此可见，公开水域游泳者，尤其是初学者，最好放慢速度，仔细监测身体的反应，尤其是在游泳结束后。2015年，瑞士研究人员对经验丰富的冰泳一英里游泳者进行了一项研究，他们效仿纳克顿的研究方法，发现体温过低实际上是在参与者完成游泳后才出现的。

The Dolphin Club, as it happens, is where longtime member Thomas Nuckton, an intensive care specialist, made a sideline of studying hypothermia and afterdrop in his fellow swimmers. The current U.S. Coast Guard immersion survival tables and computer programs actually reference one of Nuckton’s studies, which quantifies a shipwreck survivor’s biophysical parameters with methods that were developed with Dolphin Club swimmers. His work over the past two decades illustrated the afterdrop phenomenon: body temperatures continue to go down even after swimmers get out of the water, and mild hypothermia, a couple of degrees below normal, is fairly common. The takeaway: open-water swimmers, especially beginners, would be well advised to take it easy and carefully monitor their bodies’ responses, especially after a swim is over. In a 2015 study of experienced ice-mile swimmers, Swiss researchers who followed in Nuckton’s footsteps found that hypothermia didn’t actually set in until after the participants had finished their swims.

最后，在桑拿房里待了大约十分钟后，沉浸在温暖的谈话和友好的氛围中，我的四肢终于开始恢复知觉。接下来的行程——和金去咖啡馆吃早餐，然后去见一位写作伙伴——我为自己的成就感到由衷的自豪。之后，我沿着水边散步，欣赏着阴郁的海湾，潮湿的海水在灯光下摇曳。我想，今天我没穿潜水服就游了过去。我笑了笑。我自己也逐渐适应并警觉起来，能够感受到海湾的脉搏，仿佛那是我自身脉搏的回响。

Finally, after about ten minutes in the sauna, nestled in the warm conversation and camaraderie that thrives there, I begin to regain control of my extremities. And as I go about the rest of my day—to a café for breakfast with Kim, and then off to meet a writing buddy—I feel a secret pride in my accomplishment. Later, I walk along the waterfront and observe the moody bay with its damp and flickering light. Today I swam out there with no wetsuit, I think. I smile to myself, newly attuned and alert to the pulse of the bay as an echo of my own.

我为什么要这么做？我意识到，那是因为我也想敲敲天堂之门，和魔鬼聊聊天。

Why did I do it? I realize that it’s because I want to knock on heaven’s door and have a chat with the devil, too.

我从小就害怕死亡。我记得清明节的时候，道教徒会扫墓祭拜住在布鲁克林的曾祖父。我们烧香烧纸钱，好让我的曾公子有钱在天上花。然而，真正让我铭记这些扫墓经历的，并非我们做什么、为什么这样做，而是恐惧。对黑暗的恐惧，对无法解释的未知的恐惧；对虚无的恐惧。这种对死亡的深深焦虑一直伴随着我。即使我现在已经长大成人，它仍然会在夜里把我惊醒。

I have been afraid of death since I was very small. I remember visiting my great-grandfather’s grave in Brooklyn during the spring Qingming festival, when Taoists honor their dead with ancestral grave sweeping. We burned incense and joss-paper ingots so my bok-gung could have ghost money to spend in heaven. What defined those visits for me, though, was not the story of what we were doing and why we were doing it. It was fear. Fear of the dark, inexplicable unknown; fear of not being. That deep anxiety over dying has stuck with me. Even though I am now grown, it’s what jolts me awake in the night.

在开阔水域游泳是直面这种恐惧的一种方式——更接近那种想要活下去、想要抵御死亡的渴望，却不必真正面对死亡的恐惧。也许这是一种预演。大海深邃而陌生。它蕴含着一种能量，一种危险的元素，需要我们放下自我，这使得在汹涌的海水中游泳成为一种神圣的仪式。这是一个适合我们去探索人类心灵深处的陌生感和恐惧的环境。我们的双脚仿佛被抽空；脚下是深不可测的深渊。我们会经历恐惧的时刻。当我们再次踏上旧金山的陆地时，安全感便会恢复。虽然我出水时会颤抖，但随之而来的是一种强大的、坚韧不拔的活力，一种……身体上的强健。还有，简而言之，就是感恩，我竟然能够感受到这一切。

Swimming in open water is one small way of confronting that—of getting closer to the fire of wanting to stay alive, of warding off death, without the terror of having to do it for real. Maybe it’s a kind of dress rehearsal. The sea is a deep, alien place. There’s an energy to it, an element of danger that requires a giving over of the self, that makes swimming in heavy water a kind of sacrament. It is a suitable environment to engage with the deep strangeness of the human mind and its fears. Our feet are taken out from underneath us; there are unknowable fathoms below. There are moments of terror. Safety is restored when we set foot on land again back in San Francisco. Though I shiver upon emerging, with the accomplishment comes a powerful sense of hale and hardy vigor, of physical fortitude. And gratitude, quite simply, that I get to feel this at all.

现在，每次我开车经过海湾大桥、沿着海滨行驶或驶过金门大桥时，我都会停下来重新审视海湾。每天早上去旧金山上班的路上，我可能会花几分钟时间沉浸在这片景色中。或者，我会看到傍晚的海水泛着粉红色的光泽，然后想象它白天的感觉。是冰冷刺骨，还是阳光温暖得足以让人下水时感到如丝绒般柔滑舒适？

Now, every time I drive on the Bay Bridge, along the waterfront, or over the Golden Gate Bridge, I pause to reconsider the bay. For a few minutes each morning on the way to my office in San Francisco, I might lose myself in the landscape. Or I might see the evening water shelled with pink and wonder how it felt earlier that day. Was it charged with cold, or had the sun warmed it enough to give one’s entry something like a velvety comfort?

7

7

开放水域，遇见敬畏

Open Water, Meet Awe

我们沉浸于自然世界，因为自然世界总能唤起我们的敬畏之心。每天清晨七点，数百名游泳爱好者聚集在澳大利亚悉尼著名的曼利海滩，进行公开水域游泳。他们游过约半英里（约800米）的海湾到达谢利海滩，然后折返。当地人称之为他们的“唤醒仪式”。

We submerge ourselves in the natural world because the natural world has a way of eliciting awe. Every morning at seven a.m. in Sydney, Australia, hundreds of swimmers gather at the city’s famous Manly Beach for an open-water swim. They swim about half a mile across a bay to Shelly Beach. Then they turn around and swim back. The locals describe it as their “wake-up call.”

游泳者们戴着亮粉色的泳帽。这支队伍由一群中年女性组成，她们希望互相鼓励，勇敢地游过这段距离的开阔水域。澳大利亚作家兼广播员朱莉娅·贝尔德在一篇关于她与这群人每日出游的文章中，描述了她们游泳时欣赏沿途风景的方式：“大多数时候，在这长达一英里的路线上的某个地方，都会聚集着一群人，手臂指向水下巨大的蓝石斑鱼、白色的海豚、变色的乌贼、须鲨……甚至还有小小的海龟和海马。” 贝尔德还特别提到了在水下游弋的成群的暗色鲸鲨：“鲨鱼的统称是‘颤抖’，这并非没有道理。”

The swimmers wear bright pink swim caps. The squad was started by middle-aged women who wanted to gain courage from each other to swim that distance across the open water. In an essay about her daily outings with the group, the Australian writer and broadcaster Julia Baird observes the way they watch the scroll of scenery as they swim: “Most days, at some spot along the mile-long route, heads will cluster, arms pointing down under the water at enormous blue groupers, white dolphins, color-changing cuttlefish, wobbegongs . . . even tiny turtles and sea horses.” Of the gangs of dusky whale sharks that swim beneath, Baird takes note: “There’s a reason a collective term for sharks is a shiver.”

有些日子，游泳者会被水母、暗流和巨浪拍打。（我大学时在悉尼留学，经常去曼利游泳，可以证明那里的水母有多么令人不快。）有些日子，鲸鱼会来。那感觉就像一次宗教体验。

Some days the swimmers are lashed by jellyfish and currents and powerful surf. (When I was a college student studying abroad in Sydney, I swam frequently at Manly and can attest to the unpleasantness of the jellyfish.) Some days the whales come. It’s akin to a religious experience.

“当你的双臂在浩瀚的海洋边缘环绕、摆动、拉扯时，你的思绪也会随之飘荡，”贝尔德写道。随着漂向更深的水域，自由随之而来，一种名为敬畏的感知转变也随之而来。“敬畏，”她继续说道，“当你目睹令人惊叹、深不可测或超越自身的事物时所体验到的敬畏，会拓展和深化我们对时间的理解。”

“As your arms circle, swing, and pull along the edge of a vast ocean, your mind wanders,” Baird writes. With the drift into deeper waters comes freedom and the shift in perception that is awe. “Awe,” she continues, “experienced when you witness something astonishing, unfathomable, or greater than yourself, ventilates and expands our concept of time.”

我们感到轻盈，仿佛悬浮在空中。时间以一种美好的方式慢了下来，我们感觉自己拥有了更多的时间。斯坦福大学和明尼苏达大学的心理学家，在研究员梅兰妮·鲁德的带领下，已经证明，体验过敬畏之后，我们更有可能帮助他人，也更容易放松身心，对生活感到满意。当我问鲁德她的研究发现时，她解释说，敬畏的体验会增强我们对当下的关注。“它能让人们专注于自身和周围正在发生的事情，”她说。敬畏的影响甚至超越了当下——它让我们感到时间充裕，不再那么焦躁，更加慷慨。它帮助我们成为更好的自己。谁不想要这样的自己呢？

We feel light, suspended. Time slows down in the best way, and we feel that we have more of it. Psychologists at Stanford University and the University of Minnesota, led by researcher Melanie Rudd, have shown that after experiencing awe, we are more likely to help others and to be relaxed and satisfied with life. When I ask Rudd about her findings, she explains that the experience of awe heightens our focus on the present. “It captivates people’s attention with what is currently happening with them and around them,” she says. And the effects of awe are striking even beyond the moment—it makes us feel more time-rich, less impatient, more generous. It helps us to be our better selves. And who doesn’t want that?

回到太平洋彼岸的旧金山，一天早晨，我和金正在游泳，突然一只海鸥在我自由泳游到一半的时候，一头撞在了我的肩膀上。我吓得差点从泳衣里跳出来，然后我大声喊金：“我觉得刚才有只鸟撞到我了！”我难以置信地说道。

Back on the other side of the Pacific in San Francisco, Kim and I are swimming one morning when a seagull pegs me on the shoulder, mid freestyle stroke. I nearly jump out of my swimsuit in surprise, and then I call out to Kim. “I think a bird just hit me,” I exclaim, incredulous.

“那是他们的游泳池，”金笑着回答。“我们只是傻瓜，以为我们能进去游泳。”

“It’s their swimming pool,” Kim answers, laughing. “We’re just the fools who think we can swim in it.”

根据我们人类的定义，游泳是一种持续不溺水的状态。 《牛津英语词典》强调的是利用四肢推动身体在水中前进，并保持漂浮在水面上的姿势。溺水则是指因浸入水中（身体在水面以下）并吸入水中而死亡。我们从远古时代就知道，这两种状态之间的界限非常模糊；当我们不注意时，它就会变得模糊不清。

Swimming is, by our human definition, a constant state of not drowning. The Oxford English Dictionary emphasizes the propulsion of the body through water with one’s limbs and a position afloat on the water’s surface. To drown is to die through immersion or submersion—the body under the surface—in water and inhalation of that water. We know from the most ancient of times that the boundary between the two states of being is thin; it grows permeable when we’re not looking.

一位朋友向我推荐了劳登·温赖特三世1973年的经典之作《游泳之歌》。这首歌描绘了在海洋、泳池和公共水库中畅游的夏日体验。温赖特歌颂了游泳带给我们的自由欢呼。然而，即使是这首欢快的歌曲也提醒我们，游泳的界限依然存在：

A friend turns me on to Loudon Wainwright III’s 1973 classic “The Swimming Song.” It’s all about the quintessential experience of summer swimming in oceans, pools, and public reservoirs. Wainwright celebrates the whoop-of-joy freedom that swimming grants us. And yet even this buoyant song reminds us of the boundary line:

今年夏天我去游泳了。

This summer I went swimming

今年夏天我可能溺水了

This summer I might have drowned

但我屏住呼吸，踢着脚。

But I held my breath and I kicked my feet

我挥动着手臂

And I moved my arms around

然后它继续说道：

Then it continues:

我往伤口上撒盐，往眼睛里灌氯气。

I salt my wounds, chlorine my eyes

我是一个自毁倾向的傻瓜

I’m a self-destructive fool

这里需要谨慎。然而，我们仍然在那条界线附近徘徊，因为那里有值得一看的东西。

There’s caution here. And yet we dance near that line anyway, because there’s something there to see.

在纪录片《鱼人》中，导演基思·马洛伊采访了冲浪者、潜水捕鱼者、游泳者以及其他与海洋息息相关的人，生动地描绘了海洋如何改变了他们的生活。这些人生活在水中，不仅享受着海洋带来的感官刺激，也沉浸于海洋所孕育的独特视角。在人生的某个阶段，他们都情不自禁地谈到，海洋如何让他们对自身脆弱的生存状态有了更深刻的认识。

In the documentary Fishpeople, filmmaker Keith Malloy interviews surfers, spearfishers, swimmers, and others to create a vivid picture of how their lives are transformed by the sea. These are people who live in the water for all of its sensory immediacy and also for the outlook it fosters. At some point or another, they all feel compelled to speak about how the ocean brings them to a hyperawareness of our precarious existence.

年轻的塔希提岛冲浪者马塔希·德罗莱特（Matahi Drollet）从小就在著名的特阿胡普（Teahupo'o）冲浪点练习，视频中他正驾驭着自己冲过的一些最大的管浪——其中就包括那次让他名扬四海的冲浪。那次冲浪被拍摄下来，并于2015年赢得了比拉邦（Billabong）赞助的奖项。当时他只有十六岁。对于那次惊心动魄的冲浪经历，他如何评价呢？“我当时以为自己要死了，”他带着一丝难以置信的笑声说道。

The young Tahitian Matahi Drollet, who grew up surfing the storied Teahupo’o surf break, is shown blasting through some of the biggest barrels he’d ever surfed there—including the ride that garnered him worldwide acclaim when it was caught on film and won an award sponsored by Billabong in 2015. He was sixteen years old. His commentary on the vivid experience of this wave? “I thought I was gonna die,” he says, with a little disbelieving laugh.

影片中还有一幕：在瓦胡岛长大、从小跟父亲学习自由潜水和鱼叉捕鱼的冠军级鱼叉捕鱼运动员基米·沃纳，与一条巨大的鲨鱼平静地游动，她抓住鲨鱼的背鳍片一会儿，然后才返回水面。“这很危险。我很害怕，”她谈到自己长时间待在水下时说道。她记得父亲曾告诉她，如果感到害怕，就放松下来——记住怎么游泳。

In another scene from the film, the champion spearfisher Kimi Werner, who grew up on Oahu and learned free diving and spearfishing from her father, swims calmly with a huge shark, holding on to its dorsal fin for a spell before departing back to the surface. “It is dangerous. I am scared,” she says of all the time she spends underwater. She remembers her dad telling her this if she ever got scared: Just relax—and remember how to swim.

马洛伊的另一个拍摄对象是琳恩·考克斯，她是包括金在内的许多游泳运动员的偶像。当然，考克斯拥有……她保持着数十项重要的公开水域纪录；1977年，她成为首位绕过南非好望角的游泳者，她从陡峭的悬崖上攀下，进入汹涌澎湃的20英尺巨浪中，巨浪一次又一次地将她抛回沙滩。我问她，公开水域是如何塑造她的世界观的。她说，她把身处海洋比作“对当下生命的敏锐感知”。你出海时期待着一些新鲜事物，但你并不一定知道那会是什么。在泳池里来回游动则完全不同。“身处海洋，”考克斯告诉我，“你随时都可能成为食物链的一部分。”

Another of Malloy’s subjects is Lynne Cox, a hero to so many swimmers, including Kim. Cox, of course, holds dozens of major open-water records; in 1977, she was the first to swim around the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa, entering the water by climbing down a sheer cliff and into surging twenty-foot surf that repeatedly threw her back to the sand. I ask her about how open water has shaped her world view. She says that she equates being in the ocean with “an acute awareness of your life, in the moment.” You go out there expecting something new, but you don’t necessarily know what that will be. Being in the pool, going back and forth, is not the same. “Being in the ocean,” Cox tells me, “you could become part of the food chain at any moment.”

理解这种邻近性，这种存在状态之间的渗透性，会让人感到慰藉。当澳大利亚冲浪先驱戴夫·拉斯托维奇（Dave Rastovich）将置身海洋描述为“有意义的玩耍”——无论是游泳、冲浪还是漂浮在充气筏上——我完全理解。“我父亲去世后，我仍然继续去海里，”他说——正是这一点让他最终接受了生与死。

The understanding of this adjacency, this porousness between states of being, can be comforting. When the pioneer Australian surfer Dave Rastovich describes being in the ocean as “meaningful play”—whether it’s swimming, surfing, or floating on an inflatable raft—I get it. “When my dad died, I just kept going in the ocean,” he says—it was what made the difference in his acceptance of life and death.

金·卡戴珊至今仍记得，她曾与一群海豚一起，游过库克海峡——新西兰南北岛之间的一片水域——全程十七英里。那是2012年3月，也是她第一次真正意义上的单人探险，同时也是她成功完成“七大洋”耐力游泳挑战的第一步。当时她的祖父身体欠佳，她觉得回到故乡，为了纪念祖父而游泳，意义非凡。

Kim remembers swimming seventeen miles across Cook Strait, a stretch of water between the North and South Islands of New Zealand, with a pod of dolphins. It was her first real solo expedition, in March 2012, and the first of her successful Oceans Seven endurance swims. Her grandfather was in ill health, and she felt that it would mean something to return to her home turf and swim in his honor.

小时候，金经常和当农民的祖父母一起在海边度过暑假。她和祖父母关系很亲密。她称呼祖父为“波帕”。大海对她而言，最让她想起的莫过于惬意地坐在海浪里，晒得通红，直到第二天醒来才知道自己晒伤的程度。每当要去冰淇淋店的时候，祖父母都会大声喊叫。那些日子仿佛永无止境。如今，当她再次游泳时，她仿佛又回到了童年那段自由自在的时光。

As a girl, Kim spent summer holidays at the beach with her grandparents, who were farmers. She was close with her grandfather, whom she called Poppa. What the ocean recalls for her more than anything is sitting contentedly in the waves, being sunburned as hell, and not even knowing until the next day the degree of the burn. Her grandparents would shout when it was time to go to the ice cream store. The days felt endless. When she swims now, she feels a sensory connection to a time in her youth when there was that freedom.

在库克海峡，金的船夫告诉她，每六个游泳者中就有一人会遇到鲨鱼。她当时很紧张，但游到一半，一群海豚出现了。这是她第一次与海豚一起游泳。“它们在我周围吱吱叫，就像在说：‘救兵来了！ ’”她回忆道。她兴奋地回应着，仿佛回到了十二岁。海豚在她周围和水下快速游动，陪伴了她将近一个小时。她在海峡里没有看到任何鲨鱼，她认为这是因为海豚在保护她。

In the Cook Strait, Kim’s boat pilot told her that one in six swimmers encounters sharks. She was anxious, but mid-swim, dolphins showed up. It was the first time she’d ever had the experience of swimming with them. “They were squeaking around me, like, The cavalry is here!” she remembers. She chirped back excitedly, channeling her inner twelve-year-old. The dolphins zipped around and below, escorting her for just under an hour. She didn’t see any sharks out in the strait, and she thinks it was because the dolphins were protecting her.

之后，金径直走到爷爷的床边。“我最引以为豪的是能够躺在爷爷身边，给他看我和海豚一起游库克海峡的视频，”金告诉我。他曾参加过二战，患有创伤后应激障碍，但动物和大自然都能让他平静下来。金很感激能和他分享这段游泳的经历。他已经无法说话了，但他对她微笑，让她知道他听到了。不久之后，他便在家中去世了。

Afterward, Kim beelined to her grandfather’s bedside. “What I’m most proud of is being able to lie next to Poppa and show him the video of me swimming the Cook Strait with the dolphins,” Kim tells me. He’d fought in World War II and suffered from post-traumatic stress, but animals and nature both calmed him. Kim was grateful to be able to share her swim with him. He could no longer talk, but he smiled at her to let her know he’d heard. Not long afterward, he died in his home.

金去世几个月后，他游过了莫洛凯海峡，即夏威夷莫洛凯岛和夏威夷群岛之间的海峡。瓦胡岛。游到尽头时，她看到并听到座头鲸在向她歌唱。“在夏威夷，他们称之为‘ aumakua’ ——那是你的祖先在跟你说话，”她告诉我。那次游泳中还有海豚。它们带来的能量让她感觉彼此同在，她并不孤单。这种感觉很原始。她能尝到水中的生命气息；能闻到旁边船上柴油的味道。她专注于眼前的双手。夜晚，微小海洋生物发出的生物荧光在她指尖闪烁，如同闪光。专注于手指让她感到冥想。这让她感到安全。清澈的海水抚慰着她；深呼吸让她平静下来。

A few months after his death, Kim swam the Molokai Channel, between the Hawaiian islands of Molokai and Oahu. At the end of that swim, she saw and heard humpback whales singing at her. “In Hawaii, they call that aumakua—that’s your ancestors speaking to you,” she tells me. There were dolphins on that swim, too. The energy they brought made her feel like they were all in it together, that she wasn’t alone. It felt primal. She could taste the life in the water; she could smell the diesel from the boat next to her. She concentrated on her hands in front of her. At night, the bioluminescence emitted by tiny marine creatures fluttered off her fingertips like glitter. Focusing on her fingers was meditative. It made her feel safe. The clarity of the water soothed her; the deep breathing steadied her.

在《我将永远栖居于水中》一文中，作家莉迪亚·尤克纳维奇将游泳的本质描述为“大量吸入空气，这口气使人能够在水中自由游动，仿佛我们从未离开过那片可以呼吸的蔚蓝大海”。你可以将其解读为对那片可以呼吸的蔚蓝大海的向往——我们当中又有哪位游泳者不曾如此渴望过呢？——但你也可以将其解读为对维系我们存在的要素的肯定：我们呼吸的空气，我们所需的空气，即便我们正将脸浸入水中。

In the essay “I Will Always Inhabit the Water,” the writer Lidia Yuknavitch describes swimming as being defined in large part by “the great intake of air, a breath that keeps a human able to move through water as if we were not gone from our breathable blue past.” You can read this as a yearning for that breathable blue past—and what swimmer among us has not longed for this—but you can also read it as an affirmation of what keeps us us: the air we breathe, the air we need, even as we put our faces in the water.

我们在水中呼吸的节奏似乎会改变我们。深呼吸的研究尚处于起步阶段，但我们知道这种呼吸节奏具有舒缓作用——我们的呼吸模式与引发焦虑反应的神经中枢之间存在反馈回路。当我们……压力过大时，我们往往会呼吸短促而急促；如果我们深而慢地呼吸，就能抵消压力，抑制我们的警觉系统。由此可见，我们的唤醒中枢和呼吸中枢是相互关联的。游泳尤其能激活深呼吸。这是这项运动的特点：深吸一口气，屏住呼吸，然后慢慢呼出。

Something about the rhythm of how we breathe while we’re in the water changes us. Deep breathing research is in its infancy, but we know that this pace of breath is soothing—there’s a feedback loop between our breathing patterns and the nerve centers that fire our anxiety responses. When we’re stressed, we tend to take short, rapid breaths; if we breathe deeply and slowly, that counteracts the stress and dampens our alarm system. In this way, our arousal and breathing centers are reciprocally linked. Swimming is particular in its activation of deep breathing. It’s the nature of the exercise: you take a big breath, hold it, and then release it slowly.

金的肺活量异常大，或许正是进行深而慢呼吸的理想之选。我们初次见面那天，她指给我看她锁骨上方的一个地方，那里曾被一位针灸师误扎了一针，导致她的肺塌陷。正是这副肺活量，让她在探险游泳中游得更远。

Kim has unusually large lungs, perhaps the ideal bellows for big, slow breaths. On the day we first met, she showed me the spot above her collarbone where an acupuncturist once poked a needle into her lung by accident and collapsed it. Those lungs carry her far when it comes to expedition swims.

因此，呼吸让游泳如同动态冥想。我们吸一口气，屏住呼吸，划水，滑行，然后再吸一口气。在呼吸的间隙，思绪涌现——思考每一次划水、每一次踢腿、每一次呼吸。随着游泳水平的提高，我们对游泳的刻意思考逐渐减少，思绪得以释放，自由驰骋。与此同时，身体也在运转。我们注意到周围的一切：水的流动、水温的变化、游泳的轻松与否。我们既保持着高度的感知，又摆脱了身体的束缚。

The breaths, then, make swimming like moving meditation. We take a breath. We hold. We pull, and glide. We take another breath. In between breaths, the thinking happens—about each stroke, each kick, each breath. As we become better swimmers, there is less conscious thinking about swimming and our thoughts are released, free to wander as they may. All the while, the body works. We notice things: how the water moves, what the temperature is like, whether the swimming feels easy or difficult. We are at once hyperaware and loosed from our bodily constraints.

“在水中游泳是我唯一感到自由的状态，”尤克纳维奇写道。她曾是一名竞技游泳运动员，并撰写了大量关于游泳对身心健康的文章，尤其是在她年纪渐长之后。她说，水能帮助身体记住生命和时间都是流动的：“我看起来有点笨拙、软弱，衰老且臃肿。但把我放进水里……”把我放在水里哪怕十秒钟，我也会向你证明，身体可以是你想要的任何样子。”

“Swimming in water is the only state of being I know where I feel free,” writes Yuknavitch. A former competitive swimmer, she has written at length about swimming for well-being, especially as she ages. Water, she says, helps a body remember that life and time are fluid: “I look a little lumbering and soft, aged and lumpy. But put me in water . . . put me in water for even ten seconds, and I will prove to you that a body is anything you want it to be.”

我问长寿研究专家田中，游泳对老年人的身体究竟有何益处。他回答说，游泳能带来失重感，让身体在运动中免受陆地运动带来的疼痛和损伤，还能带来凉爽和浮力，从而减轻炎症，支撑身体。还有一点，也是最重要的一点。

I ask Tanaka, the longevity researcher, what makes swimming so good for aging bodies. Weightlessness, he says. Physical activity without the pain and damage of land-based impact. Coolness, and buoyancy, to reduce inflammation and support the body. And one more thing, the most important thing.

“我会告诉你游泳与其他所有运动方式最大的区别。”我认真地听着。“人们更喜欢游泳。”我等着。就这？他接着说了一个我们都心知肚明的事实：很多人新年都会立志要锻炼；六个月后，一半的人就放弃了。但游泳在这方面却有着巨大的优势。“我们会评估人们的情绪状态，”田中解释说，“在跑步、骑自行车和游泳这三种运动项目中，人们普遍认为游泳带来的乐趣最高。”换句话说，人们坚持游泳是因为他们喜欢它。游泳是美国第二大最受欢迎的休闲活动，仅次于散步。但游泳却能真正让我们暂时摆脱日常生活的束缚。

“I will tell you the one thing that distinguishes swimming from all other forms of exercise.” I listen carefully. “People enjoy it a lot more.” I wait. That’s it? He goes on to relate something we all know in our bones to be true: Tons of us have New Year’s resolutions to exercise; after six months, half of us drop out. But this is where swimming has a huge benefit and advantage. “We do assessments of mood state,” Tanaka explains. “And with identical exercise programs in running, cycling, and swimming, people place the highest enjoyment in swimming.” In other words, people keep swimming because they like it. Swimming is the second most popular recreational activity in America, outranked only by walking. But swimming is the one that quite literally takes us out of our element.

我们游泳，逃离日常生活的束缚。“在水里感觉很轻快，”金说道，“它唤起了我们成年后早已遗忘的玩乐天性。”我想起了今天早上泳池里那位表情严肃的老人，他突然从泳道下方潜入水中的情景。他缓缓下沉，双臂伸展，仿佛拥有无限的时间。我想起下午家庭游泳时孩子们在泳池里的情景，他们脸上洋溢着无比的喜悦。游泳让我们重新找回玩耍的乐趣。

We swim, and we get out from under the thumb of the everyday. “There’s a giddiness to being in that water,” Kim observes. “It connects with a playfulness that we forget about as adults.” I think about the way that the serious-looking older man in the pool this morning dove under the lanes on his way out, spiraling down to the bottom, arms outstretched, as if he had all the time in the world. And I think about children in the pool during afternoon family swim, their elation so palpable. Swimming is a way for us to remember how to play.

有一次，在秋夜的浓重黑暗中，我乘船环游不列颠哥伦比亚海岸附近的岛屿，突然从船尾纵身跃入未知的深渊——那一刻，冰冷的海水漆黑一片，仿佛无法穿透——只为有机会做一个闪着磷光的雪天使。当我踩水时，周围绽放出朵朵闪烁的生物荧光，宛如一场水上灯光秀。当我爬出水面，用力搓揉双臂时，火花四溅。

Once, in thick autumn darkness while sailing around the islands off the coast of British Columbia, I jumped off the back of the boat and into the unknown—the icy water in that moment looked impenetrably black—just for the chance to make a phosphorescent snow angel. Clouds of glowing bioluminescence bloomed around me as I treaded water, a kind of aquatic light show. When I climbed out of the water and rubbed my arms vigorously, sparks flew.

冲浪运动员戴夫·拉斯托维奇说，这就是我们沉浸其中的奇妙之处：“我们忘记了我们所熟知的身体，我们只是……游泳。”

This is the wonder for which we immerse ourselves, says the surfer Dave Rastovich: “We forget our bodies as we know them and we just . . . swim.”

多年前，我和一位挚友在夏威夷各地游玩，巩固了我们大学时建立的友谊。我们的旅程从他家乡瓦胡岛开始。我们也去了其他岛屿，比如考艾岛。在考艾岛，我们曾在波利哈莱海滩涉水进入太平洋。波利哈莱海滩是一片偏僻的白色沙滩，绵延十七英里，位于一条漫长崎岖的土路尽头，仿佛是与世隔绝的世外桃源。

Years ago, a close friend and I cemented a friendship that began in college by splashing our way around Hawaii, starting on his home island of Oahu. We visited other islands, too, like Kauai, where we waded into the Pacific at Polihale Beach, a remote seventeen-mile stretch of white sand at the end of the long, rutted dirt road that seemed as far away as you can get from anywhere.

我们在波涛汹涌的碧蓝海水中畅游，我印象最深的是那种海水仿佛有重量的强烈感觉。此后的几年里，我开始欣赏开阔的水域——无论是海洋，还是大到足以形成自身生态系统的湖泊。海浪——如同一个独立的生命体。我认为游泳是一种了解一个地方的亲密方式，这种亲密感是我在其他任何方式下都无法获得的。

We swam in that heaving body of aquamarine, and what I remember most is the profound feeling that the ocean water had weight. In the years since, I’ve come to appreciate open water—an ocean, a lake big enough to generate its own waves—as its own animal. I see swimming as a way to get to know a place with an intimacy that I otherwise wouldn’t have.

在某个地方游泳的乐趣可以是日常的、例行的、熟悉的。1779年，詹姆斯·库克船长的一位副官在航海日志中赞叹夏威夷土著居民的游泳能力：“妇女们可以游到船上，然后在水里待上半天。”他观察到，在夏威夷、波利尼西亚以及太平洋其他一些历史悠久的岛屿文化中，男女老少似乎从出生起就“几乎是两栖动物”。这无疑是我对游泳者自由自在的描述中最动人的一笔。

The pleasures of swimming in a place can be everyday, routine, familiar. In 1779, a lieutenant of Captain James Cook’s admired the native Hawaiians’ swimming abilities with an entry in his ship’s log: “The Women could swim off to the Ship, & continue half a day in the Water”; in Hawaiian, Polynesian, and other enduring island cultures of the Pacific, he observed, the men, women, and children seemed “almost amphibious” from birth. This is as lovely a description of the freewheeling freedom of swimmers as any I have come across.

在旧金山湾游泳时，我能感受到那种自由，但我也同样清楚湾岸边时刻存在的危险。寒冷的海水让开放水域的体验更添一份紧张感。“你不属于这里，”金直截了当地告诉我，“但你还是来了。”寒冷的海水让游泳就像是对身体的一次紧急演习。“当你身处水中时，身体会本能地做出战斗或逃跑的反应，”她解释道，“所有的一切都在告诉你你不应该这样做。然而你仍然会去做。”讽刺的是，游泳的一些益处恰恰来自于我们敢于尽可能接近这种生存之战。这就是它的崇高之处：敬畏与恐惧交织在一起。那些恐慌的瞬间，恐惧如闪电般闪现，却又令人醍醐灌顶，振奋人心。下水本身就是对死亡的一种小小的挑战。

I feel that freedom when I’m swimming in San Francisco Bay, but I am just as aware of the hazards that are ever present at its edges. Because of the cold, there’s another layer of intensity to the open-water experience. “You don’t belong here,” Kim tells me, matter-of-factly, “but you do it anyway.” With the cold, the swim is like a fire drill for your body. “It’s fight or flight that’s engaged when you’re in that water,” she explains. “Everything is telling you that you shouldn’t be doing what you’re doing. And yet you still do it.” Some of the benefits of swimming derive, ironically, from daring to come as close as we can to this very fight for survival. That’s the sublime: the awe and the terror, together. Those moments of panic, the electric flashes of fear, are elucidating, exhilarating. The act of getting in is a small defiance of death itself.

在1937年的散文《海底》中，蕾切尔·卡森以优美的笔触将海洋描绘成人类思考生命之间浩瀚关联性的切实途径。“个体元素消失于视野之外，却又在不同的化身中不断重生，仿佛获得了某种物质上的永生，”她写道。无论是鲸鱼的耳骨还是鲨鱼的牙齿，都无关紧要。“在这浩瀚的宇宙背景下，某种动植物的生命周期并非独立完整的戏剧，而只是无尽变迁全景中短暂的一瞬。”我们都与这浩瀚相连，我们在海洋中的存在不过是沧海一粟，一声呼喊，指向虚空。

In her 1937 essay “Undersea,” Rachel Carson eloquently described the ocean as a tangible way for humans to contemplate the vast interconnectedness of life. “Individual elements are lost to view, only to repair again and again in different incarnations in a kind of material immortality,” she wrote. It doesn’t matter if it’s the ear bones of whales or the teeth of sharks. “Against this cosmic background the lifespan of a particular plant or animal appears, not as drama complete in itself, but only as a brief interlude in a panorama of endless change.” We’re all connected in this vastness, and our presence in the sea is but a blip, a shout into the void.

我们还是会大声喊叫。

We shout anyway.

为了追求极致，一个人究竟会付出多大的努力？在海豚俱乐部的桑拿房里，金正在酝酿着她的计划：成为史上第一个横渡七大洋并攀登七大洲最高峰的人。这令人兴奋不已，尤其因为她将不得不再次依靠那条右腿来攀登这些山峰。她已经在加利福尼亚州和科罗拉多州的两座海拔超过14000英尺（约4267米）的山峰上进行了练习攀登。她仍然坚持每天早上游泳。唯一的区别是，她现在晚上会在楼梯机上锻炼。

To what lengths will one person go to chase the sublime? Back in the sauna at the Dolphin Club, Kim is cooking up plans to be the first person ever to swim the Oceans Seven and climb the Seven Summits. It’s a thrilling prospect, not least because she will have to rely on that right leg again to carry her up those peaks. She has made practice runs up two fourteeners—fourteen-thousand-foot-plus mountains, that is—in California and Colorado. She still spends her mornings swimming. The only difference is that she now spends her evenings climbing the StairMaster.

2017年10月，她给我发了一条短信，我读完后不由自主地欢呼出声：她刚刚登顶乞力马扎罗山，这是她征服的第一座山峰。接下来的几个月里，她势头强劲，12月又征服了澳大利亚的科修斯科山，1997年又征服了阿空加瓜山。一月份，她前往安第斯山脉，全身心投入到登山训练中。她每周去健身房好几次，背着一个装满鸟食的五十磅重的背包。她的目标是德纳利峰，然后是珠穆朗玛峰——她想要组建一支全部由女性组成的夏尔巴人登山队。她的下一个目标是：成为陆地和海洋探险界的终极冒险家。

In October 2017, she sends me a text, and I reflexively whoop out loud when I read it: she has just climbed to the top of Mount Kilimanjaro, the first of her summits. As she powers through the next few months—knocking off Australia’s Mount Kosciuszko in December and Mount Aconcagua, in the Andes, in January—she dives headfirst into mountaineering training. She hits the gym several times a week, carrying a fifty-pound backpack full of birdseed. She has Denali in her sights, and then Everest—she wants an all-female Sherpa team. Her next goal: to become known as the ultimate adventurer, of land as well as sea.

游泳让她走到今天，让她拥有了这样的梦想。它治愈了她的身心，让她焕发出前所未有的活力和健康。在桑拿房里，金的目标对其他人来说还是个秘密。但她记不清自己还告诉过谁，所以她请求桑拿房里的每个人都替她保密。

Swimming is the means that got her here, to even dream of such a thing. It healed her, body and soul, and brought her to a new state of exuberant health. At that moment in the sauna, Kim’s goal was a secret—well, from the public, anyway. But she couldn’t remember who else she’d told, so she asked everyone in the sauna to keep it close.

尽管金最初开始游泳探险是为了找回失去的自我——在几乎失去肢体后重拾自我——但随着时间的推移，她的动机发生了变化。通过游泳，她的注意力逐渐转移到自身之外的世界。她说，独自游泳并非孤独。

Though Kim first set off on her swim expeditions to regain a sense of self she’d lost—to revive herself, in the wake of almost losing a limb—over time that motivation changed. Through swimming, her focus gradually pulled back to take in the world beyond herself. She says there’s nothing solo about a solo swim.

“让这些游泳活动超越个人意义，这让我感到无比快乐，”她说。她最近两次重要的游泳活动都与团结人们有关。2016年11月，她带领一支游泳队横渡以色列和约旦之间的死海——这是有史以来第一次有人完成这项壮举——旨在强调这两个国家为应对该地区气候变化所做的努力。“我们就像在做游泳科学实验，”她说。“我不得不把凡士林涂在我以前想都不敢想的地方。盐分像酸一样灼伤我的眼睛。”她表示愿意重来：她的目标是促使以色列和约旦政府合作，让她完成这次游泳挑战。她成功了。

“There’s a joy in making these swims bigger than myself,” she says. Two of her last major swims had to do with bringing people together. In November 2016, she led a team of swimmers across the Dead Sea between Israel and Jordan—the first people ever to complete that swim—to highlight what the countries were doing to combat climate change in the region. “We were like a swimming science experiment,” she says. “I had to put Vaseline in places I would never have dreamed of putting it. The salt burned my eyes like acid.” But she would do it all again: Her goal was to get the Israeli and Jordanian governments to cooperate and let her do the swim. She succeeded.

六个月后，那次经历让她重拾信心和希望，准备迎接下一次挑战。2017年5月5日，金与来自世界各地的11名游泳健将组成团队，从圣地亚哥的帝国海滩出发，绕着现有的美墨边境墙游了6英里，最终抵达墨西哥的蒂华纳。他们与人权组织“蜂鸟”（Colibrí）合作，该组织致力于寻找在越境过程中丧生的人，无论他们选择的路线如何。她的搭档是墨西哥游泳运动员安东尼奥·阿圭列斯；几个月后，他成为继金之后第七位完成艰苦卓绝的“七大洋”公开水域挑战的人。

The experience gave her heart and hope, six months later, to do the next swim. On Cinco de Mayo, 2017, Kim swam six miles around the existing border wall from the United States to Mexico, with a team of eleven other swimmers from around the world, from San Diego’s Imperial Beach to Tijuana. They worked with the human rights organization Colibrí, which identifies people who have died in the crossing, no matter what the route. Her co-leader was the Mexican swimmer Antonio Argüelles; a few months later, he would go on to be just the seventh person, after Kim, to complete the arduous Oceans Seven open-water challenge.

金得到了美国海岸警卫队、海关与边境保护局以及墨西哥海军的合作——在美墨边境政治局势紧张的当下，这堪称一项壮举。她亲自给每个人打了电话，强调这次游泳并非出于政治目的，而是为了我们共同的人性。

Kim had the cooperation of the US Coast Guard and Customs and Border Patrol as well as the Mexican Navy—a colossal feat in this era of contentious border politics between the United States and Mexico. She phoned up everybody herself, emphatic that the swim was not about politics but about our common humanity.

当她游上蒂华纳的海滩时，看到一百多名墨西哥小学生在悬崖上欢呼雀跃，他们穿着印有支持游泳活动的T恤。特蕾莎修女的话浮现在她的脑海：“我一个人无法改变世界，但我可以向水面投掷一块石头，激起层层涟漪。”金心想，这真是一个绝妙的比喻，它诠释了水如何将我们所有人联系在一起：水的共通性，水的共同性。她也想激起涟漪。

As she swam up onto the beach in Tijuana, she saw more than a hundred Mexican schoolchildren on the cliff cheering and wearing T-shirts supporting the swim. Mother Teresa came to mind: “I alone cannot change the world, but I can cast a stone across the waters to create many ripples.” It wasn’t a bad metaphor, Kim thought, to understand the way that water connects us all: the commonality of it, the communality of it. She wants to make ripples.

金和其他游泳运动员在水中受到了墨西哥海军的迎接，他们被安排办理相关手续。他们脸上洋溢着光彩，百感交集。金筋疲力尽地游到船边，但她脸上带着笑容，用一种邻里般的友好语气问道，是否可以借一杯糖，引得大家一阵哄笑。

Kim and the other swimmers were received in the water by the Mexican Navy, to process their paperwork. Their faces were radiant; they were feeling every emotion. Kim swam up to the boat, exhausted, but she grinned and asked, in a neighborly way, to great laughter, if she might borrow a cup of sugar.

社区

COMMUNITY

越过他们所经历的浪潮，他们终于出现了，并肩而立，彼此相距六英尺，稳步向岸边游去，直到下一波浪潮到来，让他们可以冲浪或迎浪而上。

Beyond the wave they had gone through, they finally showed, side by side, still six feet apart, swimming shoreward with a steady stroke until the next wave should make them body-surf it or face and pierce it.

——杰克·伦敦，《卡纳卡冲浪》

—Jack London, “The Kanaka Surf”

男人漂浮在泳池中，如同酷热海洋中的一粒清凉。正午的烈日已然消散，沙漠的空气中只留下一丝余温。傍晚时分，正是游泳的最佳时间。抬头望去，只见棕榈树环绕着巴洛克风格的露天泳池，为池边休憩的人们提供一片荫凉。转头望去，可以看到高低错落的跳台，以及露台上精美的手工瓷砖。纵身跃入那层层叠叠、深邃迷人的蓝色池底，他仿佛置身于加勒比海。

The man floated in the pool, a speck of cool in a sea of hot. The brutal midday sun had burned off, leaving a lingering warmth in the desert air. Late afternoon, early evening—these were the best times to swim. If he looked up, he could see the palm-fringed canopy of the trees that lined the baroque, open-air pool, offering merciful shade to those seated at the edge. Turning his head, he could see the diving platforms of varying stratospheric heights and the exquisite handcrafted tile that lined the terrace. If he dove down, into the rich, layered blue depths, he could pretend he was in the Caribbean.

如果他漂浮时，以某种方式保持头部姿势，将耳朵浸入水中，就可以避免听到射击练习的持续声音：一种永不停歇的敲击声pakapakapakapaka 。

If, while floating, he held his head in a certain way, submerging his ears, he could avoid hearing the constant sound of firing practice: a percussive pakapakapakapaka that never let up.

尽管我现在对撒哈拉沙漠的绿色古湖泊了如指掌，但在沙漠中游泳仍然像是一种梦幻般的幻想。约瑟夫·“杰伊”·泰勒本人也常常有这种感觉。在被称为世界上最热的地方——巴格达。地球上，夏季气温可超过一百二十度。但尽管被沙漠环绕，巴格达本身却是一座绿树成荫的城市，坐落在蜿蜒的底格里斯河畔，河岸边长满了柳树、棕榈树和白杨树。

Even though I know all about Green Sahara paleolakes by now, swimming in the desert still sounds like a kind of fever dream. The man, Joseph “Jay” Taylor, often felt that way himself. In Baghdad, which has been called the hottest place on earth, temperatures can exceed a hundred and twenty degrees in the summer months. But despite being surrounded by desert, Baghdad itself is a green city, situated along the winding Tigris River, its banks lined with willows, palms, and poplars.

在河流蜿蜒曲折的一处，坐落着萨达姆·侯赛因的皇家宫殿及其露天泳池。这座宽敞的泳池是这位独裁者为了取悦他那两个酷爱游泳、犯下滔天罪行的儿子而下令建造的。泳池形状不规则，呈豆荚状，最长处达33码（约31米），池畔装饰华丽，包括气势恢宏的灯光喷泉、枝繁叶茂的高大树木，以及一座规模宏大的石柱圆形大厅。

At one of the serpentine bends in the river you will find Saddam Hussein’s royal palace and its outdoor pool. The expansive swimming pool was commissioned by the dictator to please his two murderous sons, who were fond of swimming. It had an irregular bean shape, thirty-three yards at its longest, and a magnificent poolside decor that included dramatic lighted fountains, tall, leafy trees, and a pillared stone rotunda of heroic dimensions.

2008年至2010年间，杰伊作为美国外交部文化专员驻巴格达。那段时期伊拉克局势动荡不安。美国大使馆位于皇家宫殿内——其正式名称为共和宫，这是侯赛因在全国各地战略要地建造的众多宫殿和豪宅之一（据统计共有81座）。每座宫殿都配有游泳池，这在沙漠中无疑是财富的象征。共和宫是这位独裁者招待来访国家元首的住所。他本人并不居住于此，但宫殿拥有258个房间和广阔的庭院。杰伊在任期间，这座宫殿是绿区的核心，国际社会——包括军人、外交官和平民——都居住于此。这里被认为是当时最安全的地方。在巴格达，杰伊上任的头几个月，该地区不断遭到炮击，造成大量人员伤亡。

Between 2008 and 2010, Jay was stationed in Baghdad as a cultural attaché for the US Foreign Service. It was a volatile period in Iraq. The US Embassy was situated on the grounds of the royal palace—its official name was the Republican Palace, one of the many palaces and opulent homes that Hussein had built in strategic locations around the country (eighty-one, by one count). Each of them had a pool, an unequivocal sign of wealth in the desert. The Republican Palace was the residence where the dictator liked to entertain visiting heads of state. He himself did not live there, but it had two hundred and fifty-eight rooms and sprawling grounds. At the time Jay was there, the palace anchored the Green Zone, where the international community resided—military, diplomats, and civilians alike. It was deemed the safest place in Baghdad, though the first few months of Jay’s tenure saw incessant shelling of the zone, with numerous casualties.

在这里，露天游泳池的想法，说得委婉点，简直有点异想天开。尤其是像这样，装饰着十八英尺高的喷泉，还挂着落地式吊灯供夜间游泳的游泳池。杰伊简直不敢相信自己竟然能在这里游泳，尽管有好几次，他不得不在空袭警报响起时从深水区跳下去，浑身湿漉漉地爬进混凝土掩体，周围震耳欲聋的迫击炮声让他喘不过气来。

Here, the idea of an outdoor swimming pool seemed, to put it mildly, a little cuckoo. Especially one like this, adorned with eighteen-foot fountains and lighted with standing chandeliers for nighttime swimming. Jay couldn’t believe that he got to swim in it, even if on more than one occasion he had to jump out of the deep end at the scream of an air-raid siren and, still dripping, clamber hastily into a concrete bunker as the boom boom of exploding mortars vibrated around him.

他每天都游泳，而且他并非唯一一个热爱泳池的人。一些胆大的士兵会利用高高的跳台，并将他们的壮举发布到社交媒体上。但大多数人只是喜欢下水游一会儿，坐在池边闲聊几句。杰伊偶尔会看到其他游泳者在泳池里游来游去。其中有一位在联合部队服役的女警——她的自由泳姿优美流畅，而且当她停下来和人聊天时，会说一口迷人的浓重澳大利亚口音。

He swam every day, and he wasn’t alone in his love for the pool. Daring soldiers made use of the tall diving platforms and posted their exploits on social media. But mostly people just liked to get in, paddle around a bit, sit at the edge, shoot the shit. Jay would occasionally see other swimmers doing laps. There was this one woman who served Joint Forces detail—she had a graceful freestyle stroke and, when she stopped to chat, a charmingly thick Australian accent.

游泳课于一天晚上开始。杰伊锻炼完后，看到了他的同事安德里·兰博拉马纳纳。兰博拉马纳纳来自马达加斯加，体格魁梧，是个十足的壮汉。他在陆地上是一位经验丰富的拳击手，但在水里却笨拙地扑腾着，动作剧烈得让杰伊担心他会溺水。

The swimming lessons began one evening when Jay, after his workout, spotted his colleague Andry Rambolamanana. A tank of a man from Madagascar, Rambolamanana was an experienced kickboxer on land, but in the water he was flailing, thrashing so violently that Jay feared he might drown.

“安德烈，你在干什么？”杰伊问他。

“Andry, what are you doing?” Jay asked him.

“只是游泳而已，老板！”兰博拉马纳纳回答道。

“Just swimming, boss!” Rambolamanana replied.

杰伊主动提出收兰博拉马纳纳为徒。接下来，他又招收了来自保加利亚的瓦利亚·克拉斯捷娃和桑迪。扬尼克，也是来自马达加斯加的。不久之后，陌生人开始到杰伊的办公室询问游泳课，于是他每周开设两节初级班。厨师、司机、翻译、维和部队士兵、直升机飞行员：来自世界各地、各种背景的人都想让杰伊做他们的游泳教练。来自洪都拉斯的梅林·埃斯皮纳尔；来自印度的因德拉尼·帕尔；来自乌克兰的玛卡·贝拉泽；来自黎巴嫩的迈·沙欣；来自墨西哥的JP·桑塔纳。这简直就是一个小型联合国，一个由从未学过游泳的人组成的全球大家庭。他们称他为杰伊教练，并自称为“巴格达游泳队”。

Jay offered to take on Rambolamanana as a student. Next he signed up Valya Krasteva, from Bulgaria, and Sandy Yannick, also from Madagascar. Before long, strangers started inquiring at Jay’s office about swim lessons, and he set up two beginner classes a week. Cooks, drivers, translators, peacekeeping troops, helicopter pilots: People from all over the world, from all kinds of places and backgrounds, wanted Jay to be their swim coach. Merlin Espinal, from Honduras; Indrani Pal, from India; Maka Beradze, from Ukraine; Mai Shahin, from Lebanon; J. P. Santana, from Mexico. It was a miniature United Nations, a global diaspora of people who had never learned to swim. They called him Coach Jay. And they called themselves the Baghdad Swim Team.

杰伊教练是我的笔友。我们开始通信是因为他读了我写的一篇文章，文章里我把游泳当作远离网络——尤其是数字网络——的最后避难所。他回信给我，提出了相反的观点，认为游泳是一种建立社群、增进友谊、在共同的爱好中找到慰藉的方式。2009年，他因在战时教授游泳课程而受到时任国务卿希拉里·克林顿的嘉奖。

Coach Jay is a pen pal of mine. We began corresponding after he read an essay that I’d written about swimming as the last refuge from connectivity—the digital kind. He wrote to me to argue the opposite, that swimming is a way to form community, forge bonds, and find solace in a common pursuit. In 2009, he received an award from then Secretary of State Hillary Clinton for his service to the community in teaching all those wartime swimming lessons.

我很好奇那些最终来到巴格达却从未学过游泳的人。我也很好奇，为什么我们有些人会游泳，而我们当中又是什么阻碍了我们？是什么力量让我们远离水，而这些力量是否与我们来自哪里都一样？

I wondered about all those people who ended up in Baghdad never having learned how to swim. And I wondered, how is it that some of us get to swim, and what stops those of us who don’t? What forces keep us out of the water, and are they the same no matter where you come from?

这篇文章讲述了游泳如何将我们联系在一起，又如何将我们分隔开来。

This is about how swimming has brought us together, and how it has kept us apart.

8

8

谁可以游泳？

Who Gets to Swim?

在美国，游泳池是一种特权。历史上，人们对水有着复杂的情感。刻意地混杂在一起——无论男女、贫富、肤色——都会引发各种各样的恐惧。作为一个社会，我们基于这些恐惧，将不同的群体隔离开来。

In America, the pool is a privilege. People have historically had complicated feelings about water. Mixing in it deliberately—as men and women, as rich and poor, as black and brown and white—can stir up all kinds of fears. As a society, we’ve kept different groups apart based on those fears.

公共游泳池在二十世纪初开始在纽约和芝加哥等大城市迅速普及。历史学家杰夫·威尔特斯在其引人入胜的美国游泳池社会史著作《争夺之水》中写道，在整个进步时代，出于卫生考虑，游泳池成为了黑人、白人和移民不分种族共同游泳的场所。这些早期的市政游泳池本质上是为工人阶级社区建造的巨型浴缸；它们还将那些在公共水域嬉闹、衣着暴露的青少年从公共水域中隔离出来，因为在炎热的夏日里，孩子们总是会闹腾。不过，男女游泳是分开的，并且隔天轮流进行。

Public pools first proliferated in big cities like New York and Chicago at the turn of the twentieth century. Throughout the Progressive Era, swimming pools were places where blacks, whites, and immigrants swam together, regardless of race, in the interest of hygiene, writes the historian Jeff Wiltse in Contested Waters, his engrossing social history of the swimming pool in America. These early municipal pools were in essence giant bathtubs for working-class neighborhoods; they also corralled rowdy, half-naked youths away from public waterways, where they were perceived as nuisances (on a hot summer day, kids will be kids). Men and women, though, were separated and swam on alternating days.

到了20世纪20年代，情况发生了变化：城市开始建造更大的休闲游泳池，其主要目的是供公众休闲而非公共沐浴。在城市主导的鼓励社区社交的举措下，男女老少和家庭终于可以一起游泳了。其中最著名的游泳池包括旧金山的弗莱什哈克游泳池（Fleishhacker Pool），这是一个长达一千英尺的巨型海水游泳池，在1925年开放时，由于规模庞大，需要救生员划着小船巡逻；还有阿斯托利亚游泳池（Astoria Pool），这是一个宏伟的装饰艺术风格的游泳和跳水综合体，俯瞰着皇后区和曼哈顿之间的东河，于1936年开放。从20世纪20年代到50年代，每年有数千万人光顾全国各地的市政游泳池——他们是为了娱乐而来。

By the 1920s things had changed: Cities began building larger recreational pools that were intended primarily for public leisure instead of public bathing. Men, women, and families were finally permitted to swim together, in the urban-led effort to encourage community socializing. Marquee pools included Fleishhacker Pool in San Francisco, a thousand-foot-long saltwater pool so gigantic that it required lifeguards in rowboats when it opened in 1925, and Astoria Pool, a grand art deco swimming and diving complex overlooking the East River between Queens and Manhattan that opened in 1936. Between the 1920s and the 1950s, tens of millions visited the country’s municipal pools each year—and they did it for fun.

杰伊教练本人在20世纪50年代初，还是个孩子的时候就在巴尔的摩市中心的基督教青年会（YMCA）学会了游泳。那是一个老旧的室内瓷砖游泳池，孩子们在狭小的空间里大声喧哗、嬉戏玩闹，嘈杂声此起彼伏。那是基督教青年会的黄金时代，小孩子们不用穿泳衣。四岁时，杰伊游泳比走路更自在。游泳对他的母亲来说很重要；他们一家经常去马里兰州度假胜地海洋城那绵延十英里的美丽海滩度假。

Coach Jay himself learned to swim as a boy at a YMCA in downtown Baltimore in the early 1950s, in an old tiled indoor pool that reverberated with the particular mayhem of children shouting and splashing in a confined space. It was the golden age of the Y, when young kids didn’t have to wear swimsuits. At four years old, Jay was more comfortable swimming than walking. Swimming was important to his mother; the family took vacations to the glorious ten-mile stretch of beach in the resort town of Ocean City, Maryland.

巴尔的摩郊区的社区游泳俱乐部如雨后春笋般涌现，杰伊也曾是当地游泳队的一员，直到后来成为一名救生员。在塔夫茨大学攻读政治学期间，他利用暑假时间在巴尔的摩一家游泳池担任管理工作，并教授游泳和救生课程。

Community swim clubs proliferated in the Baltimore suburbs, where Jay swam on his local team until he became a lifeguard. While in college at Tufts, studying government, he spent summers managing a pool in Baltimore. He taught lessons in swimming and lifesaving.

但在同一时期，前所未有的混合男女在休闲泳池的混杂加剧了人们对种族融合的由来已久的恐惧。尽管泳池抹去了阶级界限，但种族界限却进一步加深，最终导致了骚乱和种族隔离。从匹兹堡到圣路易斯，黑人游泳者在泳池中遭到白人人群的袭击。在纽约市哈莱姆区的一个泳池，住在附近几个街区的黑人和波多黎各人因为担心白人游泳者的暴力威胁而不敢进入。

But during those same decades, the unprecedented mixing of men and women in recreational pools intensified the old fears of interracial mixing. Though class lines had been erased at the pool, race lines hardened even further, resulting in riots and racial segregation. Black swimmers were attacked by white crowds in pools from Pittsburgh to St. Louis. At one Harlem pool in New York City, blacks and Puerto Ricans who lived just blocks away were deterred from entrance by the threat of violence by white swimmers.

在20世纪50年代和60年代，游泳池以及其他水域成为了公民不服从运动的场所。全美各地的黑人以“涉水抗议”的方式抗议被禁止进入公共海滩，他们成群结队地出现在全是白人的海边或湖边沙滩上游泳。至少有一次这样的“涉水抗议”在密西西比州比洛克西市以白人暴徒的暴力镇压告终；这场名为“血腥涉水抗议”的事件发生在1960年复活节星期日，地点就在比洛克西的公共海滩上。直到八年后，一位联邦法官裁定密西西比州墨西哥湾沿岸的海滩对所有人开放，黑人进入海滩的权利问题才得以解决。

In the 1950s and 1960s pools became sites of civil disobedience, and so did other aquatic spaces. Blacks across America protested being barred from public beaches with “wade-ins,” showing up to swim en masse at all-white beaches by the ocean or the lake. At least one of these wade-ins, in Biloxi, Mississippi, ended in violence at the hands of a white mob; the Bloody Wade-In took place on Easter Sunday in 1960, on Biloxi’s public beach. The question of beach access for blacks wasn’t settled until eight years later, when a federal judge ruled that Mississippi’s Gulf Coast beaches were open to everyone.

这不仅是一场争取进入权的斗争，更是一场争取休闲娱乐权的斗争，无论肤色如何。许多活动家将游泳池和海滩视为这种自由的终极象征。在人们交融的身影中，在与他人共享同一片水域的行为中，蕴含着丰富的意义。这些意义诉说着接纳。然而，当种族隔离最终实现时，结果却并非总是如人们所愿。在美国各地的城市里，游泳池开始变得空荡荡，这无疑是一场悲剧。“1950年至1970年间，数百万人……”威尔特斯写道：“许多美国人选择不再去市政游泳池游泳。”这是白人游泳者对公共空间的“大规模放弃”，与此同时，有能力的人则建造了私人俱乐部和自家后院游泳池。不出所料，社会分化变得更加根深蒂固。

This was a fight not just for the right of access but for the right of recreation, of leisure, no matter what your skin color. Many activists saw pools and beaches as the ultimate symbols of that freedom. In the mingling of bodies, in the act of sharing the same water with others, you can read volumes. The volumes speak of acceptance. But when desegregation did happen, it wasn’t always with the hoped-for results. In cities all across America, pools began to empty, and you can read that as a tragedy. “Between 1950 and 1970, millions of Americans chose to stop swimming at municipal pools,” writes Wiltse. It was a “mass abandonment” of public space by white swimmers, accompanied by the construction of private club and backyard pools for those who could afford it. Social divisions, not surprisingly, became even more entrenched.

历史上公共游泳池的匮乏也导致美国存在着至今仍然存在的种族游泳能力差距。黑人儿童溺水的概率是白人儿童的五倍。而且，就像许多其他事情一样，经济状况也对游泳能力的培养起着至关重要的作用：在美国，家庭年收入低于五万美元的儿童中，近80%的人游泳能力很差或根本不会游泳。

The historic lack of access to public pools also left America with a racial gap in swimming ability that persists today. Black children drown at a rate five times that of white children. And as with so many other things, money also has a heavy hand in the way swimmers are made: in the United States, nearly 80 percent of children in families with a household income of less than fifty thousand dollars have no or low swimming ability.

到了上世纪80年代，也就是我在长岛长大的时候，郊区富裕家庭的后院泳池已经成了标配。正如威尔特斯所说，后院泳池的兴建是因为业主“想要回归家庭，将家庭置于社区之上”，而美国为所有人服务的众多公共泳池却因使用率低和资金不足而关闭，其中许多也年久失修。

By the 1980s, when I was growing up on Long Island, suburban backyard pools had become the rule for families with means. As Wiltse puts it, backyard pools were installed because their owners “wanted to turn inward and privilege family over community,” while more and more of America’s numerous public pools, which provided for everyone else, were closed due to lack of use and funds. Many of them fell into disrepair.

我家很幸运，离社区游泳池不远，而且游泳池设施齐全。八岁那年，父母让我二选一：踢足球还是加入游泳队。我和弟弟都选择了游泳队。我和安迪都厌倦了被踢得腿疼，而且我们本来也不太喜欢足球。接下来的十年，我们都泡在了游泳池里。我们和两英里外一支充满活力的当地队伍一起游泳。我们不仅热爱游泳本身，也热爱和我们一起游泳的孩子们。那种归属感，让我们感到无比亲切。这就是我们的归属。我们结下了跨越城镇、文化和收入阶层的深厚友谊。

My family was lucky enough to live not too far from one of these community pools, one that was not in disrepair. When I was eight years old, my parents gave me a choice: soccer or swim team. I chose swim team, as did my brother. Andy and I were tired of getting our shins kicked, and we didn’t much like soccer, anyway. We spent the next ten years swimming with a scrappy local team two miles away. We loved not just swimming but also the kids we swam with. The feeling of belonging. This was our tribe. We made lasting friendships that crossed towns, cultures, and income brackets.

和我们镇上不一样，弗里波特游泳池里种族多元化。在那个游泳池里，有棕色皮肤和黑色皮肤的人。在那个游泳池里，孩子们不会用手指抠眼角，也不会嘲笑我的姓氏。在那个游泳池里，和各种各样的人在一起，我的身体开始以一种美好的方式真正属于我自己。

Unlike our own town, the Freeport pool was racially diverse. In that pool, there were brown and black bodies. In that pool, kids did not jam up the corners of their eyes with their fingers or make fun of my last name. In that pool, with all those other kinds of bodies, my body started to feel like mine in a way that was good.

那支队伍还有一点——它是男女混合的。最初公共泳池禁止男女混浴，正是出于对这种现象的担忧：不同种族、性别和背景的人们混在一起。对我们来说，事情并没有那么复杂。只不过是泳池边的青春期罢了。每天，我们都沉浸在荷尔蒙和水的混合快感中。身体彼此吸引又排斥，拉扯又推搡，所有人都被邀请一起跳进这片充满无限可能的氯气池中。这就是自由。这是一扇通往未来的窗户，让我们远离家庭、父母和规矩的束缚。氯气散发着令人心醉的兴奋气息。我们可以玩一些我们并不完全理解的东西。

Another thing about that team—it was coed. The original prohibitions at public pools were put in place in fear of this very thing: people of different races, genders, and backgrounds mixing together. For us, it was not so complicated as all that. Just puberty on the pool deck. Every day, we sipped from the heady cocktail of hormones and H2O. Bodies simultaneously attracted and repelled, pulled and pushed, all invited to jump together into one chlorinated rectangle of possibility. This was freedom. It was a window open to the future, away from the strictures of home, parents, rules. Chlorine carried with it an appealing whiff of excitement. We could play at something we did not quite understand.

9

9

迷你联合国

A Mini United Nations

杰伊到伊拉克才三天，就从睡梦中惊醒，发现朋友JP·桑塔纳的假肢放在家门口。就在一秒钟前，杰伊还在忙着洗他在巴格达的第一批衣服，把它们放进他那辆联邦紧急事务管理署（FEMA）的拖车里，拖车就在使馆工作人员居住的营地附近。然后迫击炮弹爆炸了。爆炸把杰伊撞到墙上，他当场昏了过去。JP——他来接杰伊吃晚饭——也被炸飞到三十英尺外的路上，失去了一条胳膊。

Jay had been in Iraq just three days when he woke up in a daze and found his friend J. P. Santana’s prosthetic arm on his doorstep. A second before, Jay had been juggling his first load of Baghdad laundry, depositing it in his FEMA trailer, just inside the complex that housed most of the embassy staff. Then came the mortar blast. It threw Jay against a wall, and he blacked out. It blew J.P.—who’d come by to collect Jay for dinner—thirty feet down the road, minus his arm.

JP朝Jay大喊：“让我听听你的声音！我没事，你还好吗？”Jay大声回应说没事。JP自己的拖车被夷为平地。街对面的一名男子被撞身亡。

J.P. yelled to Jay. “Let me hear your voice! I’m OK, are you OK?” Jay shouted back in the affirmative. J.P.’s own trailer was obliterated. A man across the street was killed.

杰伊说，如果JP再晚到杰伊家门口一会儿，“如果他当时决定去洗澡，他可能就没命了。”

If J.P. had been just a little bit later to Jay’s door, “if he’d decided to shower,” Jay says, “he would have been dead.”

在尘土和瓦砾中，JP找到了他的假肢。美国陆军特种部队迅速赶到，封锁了遇难者的拖车。他们将尸体抬走。JP的拖车仍在冒烟，已被警戒线围住。士兵们告诉JP和杰伊一个小时后再来。除了等待别无他法，两人只好前往宽敞的食堂用餐。食堂门外放着一个装满沙子的油桶，武装人员必须向桶内射击——咔哒咔哒——以证明枪里没有子弹。

Amid the dust and debris, J.P. retrieved his prosthetic arm, and US Army Special Forces quickly arrived to seal off the trailer of the man who was killed. They carried the body away. J.P.’s trailer, still smoldering, was cordoned off. The troops told J.P. and Jay to come back in an hour. With nothing else to do but wait, the two men headed to dinner at the cavernous mess hall. Outside the door was an oil drum full of sand, into which armed personnel were required to discharge their weapons—click click—to show that they weren’t loaded.

“奇怪的是，即使是第一次遭遇那样的爆炸，我们也会爬起来说，‘哦，希望他们还有肉饼，’”杰伊摇着头告诉我。“因为你还能做什么呢？你只能振作起来，继续生活下去。”

“The odd thing is, even the first time being in a bombing situation like that, we just get up and say, ‘Oh, I hope they still have meatloaf,’” Jay tells me, shaking his head. “Because what can you do? You just pick up life and go on.”

战争时期，人们渴望回归正常生活。去市场买菜，和朋友们聚餐，翻看婴儿照片。我记得我朋友的母亲曾在越南当过战地护士，她说在混乱中保持规律的生活对她来说至关重要。人际关系更是不可或缺。“这是一种向世界证明的方式，”她告诉我，“我们生命中一些重要的东西还没有被摧毁。”

During times of war, people seek normalcy. Going to market, hosting dinner with friends, looking at baby pictures. I remember my friend’s mother, who served as a combat nurse in Vietnam, saying that routine in the midst of chaos was important to her. Relationships were essential. “It was a way of showing the world,” she told me, “that something vital hadn’t yet been knocked out of us.”

2008年，在美国领导的伊拉克战争五年后，尽管为了控制教派冲突而大幅增兵，巴格达局势依然动荡。但人们心中仍怀有乐观：伊拉克富布赖特项目在中断数十年后重新启动，杰伊的任务是寻找有潜力的伊拉克青年知识分子，让他们有机会赴美攻读高级学位。他乘坐直升机前往各大学，头戴军用头盔，身穿30磅重的防弹背心，因为空运远比陆路安全。士兵们必须时刻穿着制服，身着迷彩服，携带武器，除非他们在健身房或游泳池锻炼。

In 2008, five years after the US-led invasion of Iraq, Baghdad was unstable, despite a significant surge in troops to control sectarian violence. But still there was optimism: after decades of suspension, the Iraqi Fulbright program was resurrected, and Jay was tasked with finding promising young Iraqi intellectuals who were interested in completing advanced degrees in the United States. He flew to universities by helicopter, wearing a military helmet and a thirty-pound armored vest, because transport by air was far safer than traveling on the ground. Soldiers had to be in uniform at all times, outfitted in camouflage fatigues and carrying weapons, unless they were working out in the gym—or in the pool.

杰伊的大部分时间都待在宫殿里那间巨大的绿厅里。这间厅以前是接待大厅，后来被用作公共事务办公室。它最引人注目的特色包括五十英尺高的天花板、被篷布遮盖着的侯赛因的浮夸画像，以及就在厅外波光粼粼的壮丽水池。杰伊作为一名公共事务官员，接受的训练包括：如果遭到袭击，该如何在大楼内应对。用胶带止血；必要时割开地毯包裹伤员；然后把他们拖出去。

Jay spent many of his days in the palace’s cavernous Green Room. A former reception hall, it was then serving as the office of public affairs. Among its most prominent features were fifty-foot ceilings and vainglorious portraits of Hussein, covered in tarps—and that glorious pool, glinting just outside. Jay’s training as a public affairs officer included what to do in the building in case of attack. Use duct tape to stem bleeding. Cut out the carpet if needed to wrap any injured personnel; drag them out.

“那些建筑宏伟壮丽，气势恢宏，”杰伊说道。他本人衣着整洁，一丝不苟。他浅棕色的头发和胡须都修剪得一丝不苟。我去马里兰州拜访他时，他对伊拉克的记忆如同他的胡须一样清晰如昨。“宫殿里的一切，尽管在我们到达之前很多文物已被搬走，但所有细节都堪称一流。木工、盥洗室，甚至连门铰链都无一例外。空间巨大，堪比国会图书馆。到处都是大理石，到处都是枝形吊灯。”

“The buildings were magnificent, monumental,” Jay says. In person, he cuts a tidy figure. His sandy hair and mustache are carefully trimmed, and when I visit him in Maryland, his memories of Iraq are as precisely rendered as his facial hair. “Everything in the palace, even though lots of artifacts had been torn out before we got there, all the details were of the highest quality. The mill work, the lavatories, even the door hinges. The spaces were enormous, on the scale of the Library of Congress. Marble everything, chandeliers everywhere.”

杰伊的工作时间一半在公共事务办公室，一半在文化事务处，后者位于两英里外另一座较小的宫殿里。人们称那座宫殿为“小宫殿”。那里也有一个游泳池，据说是侯赛因的儿子们建造的。为了往返于两座宫殿之间，杰伊骑着一辆绿色的蒙塔古伞兵折叠自行车——和空降兵在阿富汗使用的型号一样；他们可以骑着它从直升机上跳伞，落地后立刻骑走。他懒得戴头盔。

Jay split his time between the public affairs office and the cultural affairs section, located in another, smaller palace about two miles away. People called that one the “little palace.” It, too, had a pool, supposedly put in by Hussein’s sons. To cover ground between the two palaces, Jay rode a green Montague paratrooper folding bike—the same model that airborne soldiers used in Afghanistan; they could drop from a helicopter with it and ride off as soon as they landed. He didn’t bother to wear a helmet.

游泳一直是一种逃避现实的方式：身体上的，精神上的，心理上的。如果真是这样，那么还有什么地方比战区更适合游泳队呢？每个人都有朋友被炸死，自己也都死里逃生过。濒死体验能把人紧紧联系在一起。事后一起跳进泳池，在意识到自己还活着的延迟反应中，那种兴奋之情便会涌上心头。

Swimming has always been a means of escape: physical, spiritual, mental. And if that’s true, then what better place is there for a swim team than a war zone? Everyone had friends blown up and their own close calls. Near-death experiences are the kind of thing that knits you together. Get in a pool together afterward and, in the delayed-reaction realization that you’re still alive, exuberance bubbles to the surface.

“沙漠尘土造就了绝美的日落——看到这样的日落，人们的本能反应就是停下来欣赏，”杰伊回忆起那段时光时说道。“但在巴格达，令人毛骨悚然的是，这也是迫击炮袭击的绝佳时机，因为这意味着当美军武装直升机搜寻你时，地面尘土飞扬，他们很难发现你。所以，每当出现格外美丽的日落时，你就可以预料到迫击炮弹会落下。”

“The desert dust would create these gorgeous sunsets—the human instinct when you see one is to stop and look,” Jay recalls of that time. “But what made it eerie in Baghdad is that it’s also a wonderful time to mortar, because it means that when the US attack helicopters go looking for you, it’s a little bit dusty, so they can’t see you as well. So when it was an especially beautiful sunset, you could expect that mortars would fall.”

这就是战区扭曲的逻辑。

That’s the screwed-up logic of a combat zone.

杰伊教练开始在宫殿泳池里带领来自马达加斯加的安德里和来自保加利亚的瓦利亚进行训练，帮助安德里放慢他疯狂的风车式划水速度，并帮助瓦利亚摆脱她古老划水方式的束缚。

Coach Jay began leading drills in the palace pool with Andry from Madagascar and Valya from Bulgaria, helping Andry to slow his frenetic windmill down and Valya to escape the tyranny of her archaic strokes.

杰伊在绿区待了十个月后，整个美国社区从侯赛因的宫殿搬到了刚刚竣工、戒备森严的新大使馆大院。当局决定将宫殿和绿区归还给伊拉克人；希望宫殿及其游泳池最终能供普通民众使用。虽然搬迁意味着要告别豪华的游泳池，但杰伊发现新馆里有一个25码长的游泳池。室内标准泳池，全天24小时开放。游泳课也由此正式开始。

Ten months into Jay’s stay, the entire US community in the Green Zone moved from Hussein’s palace into the just-completed and impressively fortified New Embassy Compound. The decision had been made to give the palace and the Green Zone back to the Iraqis; the hope was that both the palace and its pool would eventually be used by ordinary citizens. Though the move meant leaving the lavish pool behind, Jay found that the new facility had a twenty-five-yard indoor lap pool, open twenty-four hours a day. It was then that the swimming lessons began in earnest.

短短两周内，杰伊教练的游泳学员人数就翻了三倍，然后又翻了一番：从四个人增加到十二个，再到二十四个。之后，人数又继续翻了三倍，翻了一番又一番。安德里和瓦莉娅带来了他们的朋友，他们的朋友又带来了他们的朋友。大多数学员都是初学者，技术虽然粗糙，但总算掌握了游泳技能。

In the space of two weeks, Coach Jay’s swimming students tripled, then doubled again: from four pupils to twelve, then twenty-four. Then they tripled and doubled some more. Andry and Valya brought their friends, and their friends brought their friends. Most were beginners, their skills raggedy but existent.

新泳池的后墙几乎全是玻璃，外面是一条巴格达现代风格的宽阔步行长廊，连接着住宅楼、办公楼、体育馆和餐厅。从长廊上可以看到人们在游泳。“我想我们不可能找到比这更好的广告了，”杰伊说道。安德里也在文化事务部门工作，协助杰伊处理富布赖特项目和其他学术及专业交流项目。两人在绿区周围张贴了一些关于课程的告示，课程每周三天，上午和下午都有。

The back wall of the new pool was mostly glass, and outside, a Baghdad-modern version of the broad pedestrian esplanade connected housing blocks and offices to the gym and dining hall. From the walkway, you could see people swimming. “I guess we couldn’t have asked for better advertising,” says Jay. Andry worked in the cultural affairs section, too, assisting Jay with the Fulbright and other academic and professional exchange programs. The two men put up a few announcements around the Green Zone about the lessons, which were held three days a week, with morning and afternoon sessions.

游泳实验开展几个月后，杰伊和安德烈坐在办公室里，对课程的火爆反响感到有些震惊，不禁思考他们究竟开启了什么。游泳队完全是他们自愿组织的，是在他们日常工作之余完成的。但随着越来越多的人加入，他们感到有必要开设更多课程来满足需求。

A couple of months into the swimming experiment, Jay and Andry found themselves sitting in the office more than a little stunned at the overwhelming response to the lessons and wondering just what it was they’d started. The swim team was an all-volunteer effort on their part, organized in addition to their normal job duties. But as more swimmers joined, they felt compelled to hold enough classes to keep up with the numbers.

一群新学生出现了，他们以前从未下过水。一些穆斯林女性甚至从未在公共场合穿过泳衣。她们告诉杰伊，除了保龄球，她们从未有机会尝试过任何运动。她们手里拿着兰兹安德（Land's End）的商品目录，问他该买什么样的泳衣。杰伊自己在这方面也没有经验，便迅速把所有关于泳衣款式的问题都转给了他的孟加拉裔朋友兼文化事务部门的同事因德拉尼。因德拉尼帮助每一位初次下水的学生挑选了保守的两件式泳衣或速比涛（Speedo）背心式泳衣。

A new group of students appeared, people who had never before been in the water. A few of the Muslim women had never worn swimsuits in public. They told Jay that they’d never had the chance to do any sport except bowling. They arrived clutching Land’s End catalogs and asked him what swimsuits to buy. Absent firsthand experience in the matter, Jay quickly referred all fashion questions to Indrani, his Bengali friend and colleague in the cultural affairs section, who helped each first-timer with the selection of a conservative two-piece or Speedo tank suit.

杰伊给每个游泳者都分配了一个号码。最初，瓦莉娅是1号，安德里是2号。每个新来的游泳者都会被分配一个班上已有的伙伴。每个人，即使是经验丰富的游泳者，都会以同样的方式开始：往脸上泼水，吹泡泡，然后以流线型的超人姿势蹬壁。这营造了一种平等主义的氛围——这意味着，三周前还是初学者的人，现在就可以担任教练的角色。杰伊会在泳池边或水中指导；很快晋升为副教练的安德里也会这样做。

Jay gave every swimmer a number. In the earliest days, Valya was swimmer number one; Andry was number two. Every new swimmer was assigned a buddy already in the swim class. Everybody, even if experienced, would start off the same way: splashing water on their faces, blowing bubbles, pushing off the wall in a streamlined Superman pose. It built a culture of egalitarianism—it meant that someone who three weeks earlier was a beginner could then be in the position of teacher. Jay would be on deck or in the water, offering instruction; Andry, who quickly rose to deputy coach status, would do the same.

为了让训练更有趣，他们玩了一些游戏。杰伊教救生技巧，他的课程计划也别出心裁。他喜欢老电影，甚至老电影也能成为训练的素材。“我们会玩《纳瓦隆大炮》的游戏——你知道，就是1961年格里高利·派克主演的那部战争电影？”他告诉我。他会让所有游泳者无声地游动，大部分时间都潜入水中，只用手撑着。他们的眼睛露出水面。然后他会关掉泳池的灯，如果游泳者的头露出水面太高，他和安德里就会用排球敲他们的头。

They played games to keep it entertaining. Jay taught lifesaving and got inventive with his lesson plans. He loved old movies, and even old movies could form the basis for drills. “We’d play Guns of Navarone—you know, after that 1961 war movie with Gregory Peck?” he tells me. He’d have all the swimmers swim soundlessly, mostly submerged, with just their eyes above the water. Then he’d kill the lights at the pool, and he and Andry would bop swimmers on the head with volleyballs if their heads rose too high out of the water.

《纳瓦隆大炮》！在战区！这其中蕴含着黑色幽默。他们笑个不停。（他还在笑。）

Guns of Navarone! In a war zone! There was dark humor in that. They could not stop laughing. (He’s still laughing.)

一位身材魁梧的南非保安专家曾问他是否可以带他的训练犬——一条体态优美、肌肉发达的罗德西亚脊背犬——一起来参加游泳训练。杰伊很遗憾地告诉他，泳池里不允许带宠物。

Once a burly South African security specialist asked if he could bring his training dog—a sleek, muscular Rhodesian ridgeback—to attend swim practice with him. Jay was sorry to have to tell him that no pets were allowed in the pool.

他们依然来了。一条新的班车线路开通，方便工作人员从小宫殿前往游泳池。每次训练都有二三十名游泳者参加，现在军人游泳运动员也开始出现了。有些是年轻的海军陆战队员，他们想改进泳姿。另一些是三四十岁的职业军人，他们即将退役，希望利用自己辛苦锻炼的体能，在退役后参加铁人三项比赛。尽管学员们的体能和能力各不相同，杰伊都能为他们提供指导。他渐渐意识到，尽管他喜欢游泳本身，但他最享受的还是教学。

Still they came. A new shuttle bus route was launched to more conveniently transport personnel from the little palace to the pool. Two or three dozen swimmers regularly attended each session, and now military swimmers started to show up. Some were young Marines looking for stroke refinements. Others were career military men and women in their thirties and forties who would soon be completing their service and wanted to take advantage of their hard-earned fitness by competing in triathlons in civilian life. Though his swimmers’ stamina and abilities varied, Jay had pointers for them all. It began to dawn on him that as much as he liked swimming itself, it was the teaching he enjoyed most.

杰伊订购了一些装备包，准备给他的游泳队员们穿戴：泳帽、泳镜、踢水板。他一直很喜欢教人游泳时使用的各种创意工具和技巧——比如用乒乓球在水面上吹气，帮助队员们放松、集中地呼吸；又比如用浮力板，让队员们感受臀部在水中旋转时的“滴答”声。“有些游泳队员，比如……”“那些来自秘鲁或尼泊尔的保安，他们太穷了——生活艰辛，把所有的钱都寄回家，”杰伊说。“有人愿意送他们一顶帽子或一副两美元的护目镜，对他们来说意义重大。”他自掏腰包买了这些装备。

Jay ordered grab bags of equipment to outfit his swimmers: caps, goggles, kickboards. He’d always loved the creative tools and tricks that went along with teaching someone to swim—the ping-pong balls that you could blow across the water to encourage a relaxed, focused breathing rhythm, or the pull buoys that let you feel the tick-tock motion of your hips as they rotated in the water. “Some of the swimmers, like the security guards from Peru or Nepal, they were so poor—they lived a hard life and sent all of their money home,” Jay says. “The fact that someone would give them a cap or a two-dollar pair of goggles meant a lot.” He paid for the gear out of his own pocket.

我们今天在美国所熟知的游泳队起源于英国。游泳在英国于19世纪初发展成为一项集体运动。虽然上个世纪英国已经形成了海滨文化，但当时人们主要将沐浴和游泳视为保持卫生和健康的方式，而非竞技运动。英国第一座市政游泳池——圣乔治浴场——于1828年在利物浦开放，之后又陆续建成了许多其他游泳池。

The swim team as we know it in America has its roots in England, where swimming emerged as a collective sport in the early 1800s. Though a seaside culture had developed in the previous century, it centered mostly on bathing and swimming for hygiene and health, not for competition. The first municipal pool in England, the St. George’s Baths, opened in Liverpool in 1828, and a slew of others followed.
