早期的游泳俱乐部开始在私立寄宿学校兴起，其中包括伊顿公学；那里的学龄男孩们会记录他们在苏格兰湖泊和英格兰河流中的集体游泳经历。到了19世纪40年代初，伊顿公学本身就要求学生必须具备游泳技能，并登记了通过和未通过游泳测试的学生名单。伊顿公学在英国游泳运动中堪称先驱，以至于几十年后，该校的游泳老师出版了一本名为《伊顿式游泳艺术》的精装烫金图文手册。当时最重要的游泳俱乐部是国家游泳协会（NSS），它由一位名叫约翰·斯特拉坎的葡萄酒商在伦敦创立。19世纪30年代，NSS大力宣传游泳的益处，并在九曲湖和泰晤士河组织比赛，以激励公众参与。

Early swimming clubs began to form at private boarding schools, including Eton College; the school-age boys there kept records of group swimming adventures in Scottish lochs and English rivers. By the early 1840s, the college itself had a swimming requirement and kept a registry of those who did and did not pass the swimming test. Such a pioneer was Eton in English swimming that a few decades later the college’s swimming teacher would publish an illustrated, gilt-edged handbook called The Art of Swimming in the Eton Style. The most significant swimming club of the era was the National Swimming Society, founded in London by a wine merchant named John Strachan. In the 1830s, the NSS hailed the salutary benefits of swimming, and organized races in the Serpentine and the Thames Rivers to inspire the public.

其中一场比赛的奖品是银杯和鼻烟盒。（多么典型的英国式做法！）国家游泳协会最终将银牌颁发给当时在牛津、格拉斯哥等地成立的其他地方游泳协会，作为他们比赛的奖品。协会成员还提供免费课程，但仅限男性公众参加。直到1859年，在颇具影响力的作家和社会评论家哈丽雅特·马蒂诺的倡导下，公共游泳池才开始为女性游泳者预留特定的时间和日期。

In one race, the prizes were silver cups and snuffboxes. (How very English!) The NSS eventually gave out silver medals to other local swimming societies that were being formed at the time—in Oxford, in Glasgow—to use as prizes in their own races. Its members also provided free lessons, but only to the male public. It was not until 1859, with the advocacy of the influential writer and social essayist Harriet Martineau, that select hours and days were set aside for female swimmers at public swimming baths.

“英国女性有四肢，生活在岛屿上，她们会远航，会进行海水浴，需要在学校和家里进行水上运动，还会乘船出海——总之，她们面临着与水相关的普遍风险，”马蒂诺在1861年出版的一本散文集中，以略带讽刺的口吻写道。正因如此，她问道，难道她们没有权利像男性一样学习游泳吗？在维多利亚时代，少女时期对身体羞耻感的挣扎并非小事，马蒂诺关注的是性别对个人健康造成的负面影响。当时，英国已经出现了一些女子游泳学校，但马蒂诺提出了一个坚定的普世建议：所有儿童都应该从小学习游泳。

“English women have four limbs, and live in an island, and make voyages, and practice sea-bathing, and need exercise in the water at school and at home, and go out in boats—in short, run the universal risks in regard to water,” Martineau wrote, with a somewhat wry tone, in an 1861 book of essays. Because of this, she asked, don’t they have a claim to be taught to swim, just as men do? The girlhood struggle with physical modesty was no small thing in the Victorian era, and Martineau was concerned with the negative influence of gender on one’s state of health. At the time, a few swimming schools were opening up in England for women, but Martineau had a firm universal prescription: swimming lessons for all children from a young age.

她曾观察过巴黎塞纳河畔一家公共浴场里的女孩们学习游泳，她们从头到脚都穿着泳衣，腰间系着绳子，教练竟然是男性！她希望英国女孩也能拥有同样的机会。然而，在女孩游泳这件事上，马蒂诺遇到了不少根深蒂固的禁忌。别忘了，几个世纪以来一直流传着“让女巫游泳”或将……在十九世纪的英国，将一名被怀疑是女巫的人捆绑后扔进水中——如果她沉入水中溺亡，则证明她无罪；如果她浮起来，则证明她有罪——这种做法并非闻所未闻。但马蒂诺坚持己见。“在世界上大多数国家——实际上在地球上大部分有人居住的地方——孩子们一学会走路就会游泳，甚至更早，”马蒂诺观察到。她写道，从埃及到蒙古，再到美洲原住民和波利尼西亚，“人类是两栖的。” 这又一次印证了这一点：两栖能力的理想状态，被描述为全世界每个人都渴望拥有的状态。

She’d observed girls learning to swim at a Parisian public bath moored in the Seine, all made possible with head-to-toe clothing, waist belts attached to a rope, and male (gasp!) instructors. She wanted the same opportunities for English girls. Martineau was up against more than a few stubborn taboos when it came to girls’ swimming. Remember that the centuries-old practice of “swimming a witch,” or throwing a suspected witch into water while bound—if she sank and drowned, she was innocent; if she floated, she was proved guilty—was not unheard-of in nineteenth-century England. But Martineau persisted. “In most countries in the world—actually over the greater part of the inhabited globe—the children swim as soon as they walk, if not earlier,” Martineau observed. From Egypt to Mongolia to indigenous America and Polynesia, she wrote, “the human being is amphibious.” There it is again: the ideal of amphibiousness, described as a desirable state for, well, everyone the world over.

然而，在19世纪的英国，游泳传统才刚刚起步，全国各地数百家俱乐部开始致力于推广游泳运动。其中一些俱乐部至今仍然存在，例如成立于1864年的蛇形游泳俱乐部（Serpentine Swimming Club）和成立于1869年的水獭游泳俱乐部（Otter Swimming Club）。随着市政游泳池在英格兰各地的开放，休闲游泳者的数量也随之增加。

In nineteenth-century England, though, swimming traditions were just getting started, as hundreds of clubs across the country took up the cause of promoting swimming. Some of these still exist today: the Serpentine Swimming Club (founded in 1864), the Otter Swimming Club (1869). The numbers of casual recreational swimmers increased as municipal pools opened all over England.

1875年8月，世界上最早的国际游泳英雄之一横渡英吉利海峡的英国蒸汽船船长马修·韦伯横渡了英吉利海峡，成为历史上首次成功横渡英吉利海峡的游泳健将。英法之间的最短距离为21英里，但韦伯的之字形路线使实际距离几乎翻了一番。他那和蔼可亲、留着小胡子的脸庞后来被印在了火柴盒上。八年后，在加拿大，韦伯试图横渡尼亚加拉大瀑布脚下的尼亚加拉河，却不幸溺亡于漩涡之中。然而，游泳的热潮已经蔓延开来：到1890年，英国、德国和法国都成立了业余游泳协会。在世界各地，最初以捕鱼、采集和集体沐浴为生的传统，经过曲折演变，最终形成了正式的俱乐部，人们可以在那里学习游泳。这些俱乐部大多是人们一起练习游泳的场所。

In August 1875, one of the world’s first international swimming heroes emerged: Matthew Webb, a British steamship captain, made the first successful swimming crossing of the English Channel. The distance between England and France is twenty-one miles at its shortest, though Webb’s zigzag course made it nearly double that. His genial, mustached face ended up on matchbooks. Eight years later, in Canada, Webb attempted to swim across the Niagara River at the foot of Niagara Falls and drowned in a whirlpool, but the fever had caught: by 1890, amateur swimming federations had formed in England, Germany, and France. Around the world, what began as fishing and foraging traditions and communal bathing customs evolved, in their own circuitous fashion, to formalized clubs where people could learn to swim. Mostly they were places to practice the sport, together.

看来，哈丽雅特·马蒂诺的愿望最终还是实现了：就参与人数而言，游泳是当今英国最受欢迎的运动。在研究早期游泳课程时，我偶然发现了一张拍摄于1906年9月的黑白老照片。照片中，两个金发碧眼的小孩被吊在泰晤士河中，他们被绳子绑着的，实际上是超大的木制鱼竿。鱼竿由两位男教练举着，他们弯着腰，手臂绷紧，镜头定格了他们教学的瞬间。背景中，一队划艇载着衣着整齐的成年人（是家长？还是路人？），他们都戴着帽子，其中一人撑着阳伞，在远处安全地观察着孩子们的游泳课。

Harriet Martineau, it would seem, had her way after all: when it comes to practice and participation, the most popular sport in England today is swimming. In my research into early swim lessons, I came across a vintage black-and-white photo taken in September 1906. It shows two tiny towheaded children suspended in the Thames River from what are essentially oversize wooden fishing poles tied with rope. The poles are held aloft by two male teachers, bent over and arms tensed, frozen by the camera mid-instruction. In the background, a flotilla of rowboats conveys fully clothed adults (parents? passersby?), all with hats and one with a parasol, in safe and distant observation of the lessons.

我环顾四周，唯一打破静止——在我看来，它以某种难以言喻的方式充满活力——的，是一个年纪稍大、圆脸的孩子，他漂浮在水面上，介于前景中的小孩子和背景中的小船之间。我想，这个孩子正是这些课程和努力的最终成果，淋漓尽致地展现在我们眼前。他咧嘴笑着，挣脱束缚，自由自在地游弋。

As I examined the scene, the only bit that resisted stillness—that seemed to me kinetic in some ineffable way—was the space occupied by an older, round-faced child who bobs in the water between the small children in the foreground and the boats in the background. That child, I thought, is the end result of these lessons and labors, on full display. Grinning, untethered, and swimming free.

每年有37.2万人溺水身亡。这意味着每天每小时都有超过40人溺亡。2014年，世界卫生组织发布了一份关于溺水的全球报告，启动了首个全球战略预防计划。他们的努力。他们的目标：将溺水视为一项公共卫生挑战。

Every year, 372,000 people die from drowning. That’s more than forty people every hour, every day. In 2014, the World Health Organization released a global report on drowning to launch the first worldwide strategic prevention effort. Their goal: to target drowning as a public health challenge.

当然，会游泳并不意味着就不会溺水。导致溺水事故的因素有很多；例如，一些研究表明，如果孩子接受过游泳训练，父母在孩子下水时反而会放松警惕。但绝大多数溺水事故发生在低收入和中等收入国家，这些国家的人们每天都与水密切接触——比如渔民、沿河运货的农民，或者从井里或池塘里取水的孩子。即使在一些游泳传统深厚的地方，游泳培训也仍然不足。例如，在泰国，现代生活的侵蚀严重削弱了莫肯族海上游牧民族延续数百年游牧潜水和捕鱼传统的能力，近年来，世界卫生组织不得不设立系统化的游泳项目，以提高年轻一代的游泳技能。

Just because you know how to swim, of course, doesn’t mean you won’t drown. There are all kinds of factors that contribute to drowning incidents; for example, there is some research that shows parents are less attentive to their young children in water when those children have had swim instruction. But the vast majority of drownings happen in low- and middle-income countries where people have close, daily contact with water—among fishermen, say, or farmers ferrying their goods by river or children fetching water from a well or pond. Even in places with a strong swimming lineage, swim instruction is lacking. In Thailand, for example, where the encroachment of modern life has severely eroded the ability of Moken sea nomads to continue their centuries-old nomadic diving and fishing traditions, the World Health Organization in recent years has had to establish structured swimming programs to boost swimming skills in younger generations.

同样，在非洲东南沿海的岛国马达加斯加，游泳也是一种奢侈。安德里·兰博拉马纳纳的家庭并不富裕。但安德里小时候，他的姑姑问他母亲能否带他去一所私立天主教学校参加游泳课。上课时，教练让所有孩子在泳池边排成一排，然后让他们一个接一个地跳进水里。

Similarly, in Madagascar, an island nation off the southeast coast of Africa, swimming is a luxury. Andry Rambolamanana’s family did not have money. But when Andry was a boy, his aunt asked his mother if she could bring him to a swimming course held at a private Catholic school. At the class, the instructor lined all the children up at the side of the pool. Then he told them, one by one, to jump in.

“我永远不会忘记他，”安德里告诉我。“因为那次经历太可怕了！我们第一次跳水！我们根本不会游泳。但老师告诉我们，如果我们……”“别下去，他会来抓我们的。”六岁的安德烈颤抖着，眼泪在眼眶里打转，站在水边，怎么也下不了水。教练走过来，一把抓住他，抱着安德烈跳了下去。水里顿时充满了泡泡、泪水和恐惧。安德烈对之后的事情几乎没什么印象了。“我甚至不知道自己是怎么上岸的，”他说，“但我再也没下去过。”

“I will never forget him,” Andry tells me. “Because the experience was horrible! Our first time! To jump! We did not know how to swim at all. But the teacher told us that if we did not do it, he would come for us.” Trembling and near tears, six-year-old Andry stood at the edge, unable to will himself to get in the water. The instructor came up, grabbed him, and jumped in while clutching Andry. There was a whirl of bubbles and tears and terror. Andry doesn’t remember much after that. “I don’t even know how I got out of the water,” he says, “but I did not get back in.”

那个瑟瑟发抖的小男孩安德里，如今已长成了身材高大、体格健壮的男人。他肩膀宽阔，一头乌黑的卷发，气场十足。我们视频聊天时——他现在住在巴黎，而我在旧金山——他总是笑容满面，笑容灿烂，整个画面都充满了他的活力。然而，当他讲述自己第一次接触水的经历时，他似乎突然变得沉默寡言，仿佛回到了记忆深处。但这对于他在巴格达的经历至关重要——他能告诉我的关于游泳的最好方式，就是描述自幼以来游泳对他而言的意义：一件可怕的事情。

Andry the shivering child grew into Andry the big, athletic man. With massive shoulders and curly dark hair, Andry cuts an imposing physical presence. When we video chat—he is in Paris, where he now lives, and I am in San Francisco—he fills the frame with his bubbly cheer and wide grin. As he shares the story of his first experience with water, though, he seems to shrink into himself, retreating somewhere in his memory. But it is critical backstory to his experience in Baghdad—the best way he can tell me about swimming is to describe what it was to him since he was a child: a scary thing.

他天生擅长陆地运动。在马达加斯加首都塔那那利佛上大学时，安德里热爱所有运动；除了练习自由搏击，他还打篮球，并和一位跆拳道高手朋友一起上课。每周三下午，学校会免费向学生开放体育设施，安德里也正是在那时重拾了他昔日的“宿敌”——游泳池。

He was gifted on land. At university in Antananarivo, the capital of Madagascar, Andry was fond of all sports; in addition to being a kickboxer, he played basketball and took classes with a friend who was a taekwondo master. On Wednesday afternoons, the university offered students free use of its athletic facilities, and that’s when Andry reacquainted himself with his old nemesis—the pool.

这么多年过去了，他坚定地告诉自己：我必须学会游泳。安德里开始独自去游泳池，没有教练指导，只是随意地玩水，疯狂地扑腾。经过几天或几周的耐心尝试，他终于能够……他游完了整个泳池。“但是真的太累了，因为我使出了浑身解数才游起来！”他瞪大了眼睛告诉我。他的肩膀颤抖着；他比划着自己笨拙的划水动作，然后发出低沉的、男低音般的“嘿嘿嘿”笑声，自嘲地笑着。

After so many years, he told himself sternly, I must learn swimming. Andry began going to the pool, without instruction, doing his own thing, splashing like crazy. After some days or weeks of patient trial-and-error, he was able to go the whole length of the pool. “But it was very exhausting, because I’m making all my effort to get movement!” he tells me, eyes wide. His shoulders quake; he pantomimes his flailing stroke and laughs, a deep, bass-toned heh heh heh, at himself.

安德里抵达巴格达时，他的游泳经验正是如此。2007年底，他比杰伊早几个月到达。当安德里第一眼看到侯赛因的宫殿泳池时，他惊呆了。那时，驻扎在巴格达的军人和安保人员早已见惯了这里的奢华，他们的行为也与此相符——也就是说，他们对这种奢华嗤之以鼻。他们跳入水中，趾高气扬地四处走动。“他们感觉自己好像拥有这里的一切，”安德里说。但他心怀敬畏。“对我来说，我简直不敢相信。我们竟然可以在这里游泳？！ ”

That’s precisely the level of swimming experience he brought to Baghdad when he arrived in late 2007, a few months before Jay did. When Andry laid eyes on Hussein’s palace pool, he was dazzled. By that time, the army and security guys working in Baghdad were familiar with the opulence, and acted accordingly—meaning they thumbed their noses at it. They did cannonballs and strutted around. “They kind of felt like they owned the place,” Andry says. But he had reverence. “For me, I couldn’t believe it. We can swim here?!”

安德烈第一次见到杰是在工作场所。作为新人的赞助人，他是第一个带杰熟悉绿区的人，开着高尔夫球车带他来回转悠。杰来的第三天，杰和JP被炸飞的时候，安德烈就在拖车旁边。每天晚上九点或十点左右，安德烈都会想办法去游泳池。杰通常已经在那里游泳了。安德烈就会开始他那笨拙的“风车式”游泳动作。

Andry first met Jay at work. As a sponsor for newcomers, he was the first to show Jay around the Green Zone, driving him back and forth in a golf cart. He was there by the trailers on Jay’s third day, when Jay and J.P. got blown up. Every night, around nine or ten p.m., Andry tried to get to the pool. Jay would already be there, doing his laps. Andry would start his inelegant windmilling.

“我不知道他在观察我，”安德里说，“然后有一天晚上他问我：‘你到底在干什么？’”他笑着回忆道，“我当时只想游到泳道尽头。”杰伊示范了一些他教给所有初学者的小技巧：试着吹泡泡。适应把头浸在水里的感觉。练习。先是静止漂浮，然后轻轻踢腿漂浮。安德里按照杰伊的指示做了，他立刻感觉到了不同。“变得更容易了，动作也更自然了，”安德里说，“就是这样开始的。”

“I didn’t know he was observing me,” Andry says, “and then one evening he said, ‘What the heck are you doing?’” He laughs at the memory. “I really just wanted to go to the end of the lane.” Jay demonstrated the little things that he showed to all his beginning swimmers: Try blowing bubbles. Get comfortable with your head in the water. Practice floating while still, then floating with a small kick. Andry did as Jay said, and he felt the difference immediately. “It became easier, the flow was more natural,” Andry says. “And that’s how it started.”

安德烈一点一点地进步。他的力量增强了，柔韧性也随之提高。他第一次能够游完一圈而不感到疲惫；在杰伊的鼓励下，他不知不觉又游了三圈。

Little by little, Andry made improvements. He developed flexibility to go with his strength. For the first time, he could do a lap without being exhausted; with Jay coaxing him to keep going, he swam three more without even realizing it.

安德烈在六个月内就学会了四种比赛泳姿。在他34岁生日那天，他一口气游了34个来回。不久之后，杰伊就让安德烈去指导军队的游泳队员。安德烈心里忐忑不安：我该怎么教这些人呢？他们比我厉害多了。但他效仿杰伊冷静沉着的做法：他为高级组制定了一套训练计划，带领队员们进行练习，并仔细观察他们的表现。他努力向杰伊学习。随着越来越多的游泳队员加入，安德烈发现杰伊真正的天赋在于能够给予每个来游泳的人信心。有些人从未下过水，有些人甚至不敢把脸浸入水中，还有些人连一圈都游不完。所有这些恐惧都可以被克服。“这就是方法。玩水。吹泡泡。像超人一样。”

Andry learned all four competition strokes within six months. On his thirty-fourth birthday, he swam thirty-four lengths nonstop. Soon Jay had Andry coaching the military swimmers, too. Andry had his doubts: What am I going to do with these guys? They’re so much better than I am. But he followed Jay’s levelheaded example: he wrote up a plan of exercises for the advanced group, ran the swimmers through their drills, and observed them carefully. He tried to emulate Jay. As more swimmers came, Andry saw that Jay’s real talent was in giving confidence to whoever showed up. There were people who had never been in the water. There were people who were afraid to put their faces in. There were people who couldn’t complete a lap. All those kinds of fears could be conquered. This is how you do it. Play with the water. Blow bubbles. Be like Superman.

“我就是这么做的，”安德里告诉我，“我把这些知识传授给了别人。”

“And that’s what I did,” Andry tells me. “I passed along that knowledge.”

一天，两人驾车经过通往小宫殿前的最后一个检查站时，美国国际开发署遭到直接袭击。隔壁就是美国国际开发署（USAID）的营地。警报声响起，高亢的“寻找掩护”警告声刺耳响起，迫击炮弹开始落下，一切都近在咫尺，令人胆寒。杰伊和安德里跳下车，四处寻找掩护。安德里设法躲进了屋里，却和杰伊失去了联系。他开始惊慌失措。震耳欲聋的炮火声持续不断，但他仍然不见杰伊的踪影，也无法通过电话联系到他。

One day both men were driving through the last checkpoint before the little palace when there was a direct hit on the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) compound next door. The sirens went off, the big-voice “TAKE COVER” warnings blared, and the mortars started dropping, all terrifyingly close. Jay and Andry exited their cars and ran for cover. Andry managed to get inside but lost track of Jay. He began to panic. The resounding booms continued, but still he did not see Jay anywhere and could not reach him on the phone.

袭击稍稍减弱后，安德里立刻冲出大楼去找杰伊。他找到了朋友——一记爆炸把杰伊震得沿着巷子滑行，撞到水泥墙上，杰伊虽然有些晕眩，但还算安然无恙——安德里把他拖了进去。

As soon as the attacks lessened in ferocity, Andry came tearing out of the building to look for Jay. He found his friend—one blast had sent Jay skittering down the lane into a cement wall, a little stunned, but in one piece—and dragged him inside.

安德里谈起杰伊以及他们在巴格达共度的时光时，声音哽咽了。他的眼眶湿润，说话也变得谨慎起来。杰伊教练让安德里·兰博拉马纳纳明白，不可能的事情也能变成可能。“我从未告诉过他，”安德里说，“但我一直把杰伊教练当成我的父亲。他是我各方面的导师。”

As Andry talks about Jay and the time they shared in Baghdad, something snags in his voice. His eyes grow damp, his words deliberate. Coach Jay showed Andry Rambolamanana that the impossible was possible. “I never told him this,” Andry says, “but I think of Coach Jay as my dad. He is my mentor in every way.”

10

10

混乱与秩序

Chaos and Order

大多数人来巴格达都是一年一签——比如说，一名游泳运动员可能在队里待几个月就离开，然后又会有其他人加入。杰伊教练在巴格达驻扎的两年间，他的游泳队队员人数增长到了两百多人。

Most people came to Baghdad on one-year assignments—a swimmer might be with the team for a couple of months, say, before cycling out, but then someone else would join. Over the two years that Coach Jay was stationed in Baghdad, his swimming roster grew to more than two hundred people.

有些游泳运动员格外引人注目，比如像JP Santana那样充满活力、势不可挡的选手。JP身材魁梧，体格健壮，性格桀骜不驯。十几岁时，他不慎抓住高压电线，失去了右臂的下半部分。虽然他从小就学会了游泳，但身上还是留下了烧伤的疤痕。“在那之后，我不敢再下水了——说实话，是害怕，”JP说。“我都忘了怎么游泳了，所以当Jay开课的时候，我第一个就去报名了。”

Certain swimmers stood out, like the irrepressible force of nature that was J. P. Santana. A lively, squarely built man with a defiant streak, J.P. lost the lower part of his right arm from grabbing a high-voltage power line as a teenager. Though he’d learned to swim as a child, he was left with burn scars all over his body. “I was shy about getting back in the pool after that—afraid, really,” J.P. says. “I’d forgotten how to swim, so I was first in line when Jay opened the classes.”

他右肩的肌肉伤痕累累，灵活性也不如左肩，这让他怀疑自己是否还能重返泳池。“一进泳池，我就开始拼命游，生怕自己会直接沉到池底，”他回忆道。“我从杰伊身上学到的是，我需要在游泳和生活中找到平衡。”

His right shoulder muscles, scarred and less flexible than his left, made him wonder if he could get back to swimming at all. “Once I hit the pool, I started to swim desperately, afraid I would go straight to the bottom,” he remembers. “What I learned with Jay is that I need to find that balance—in swimming and in life.”

2008年4月，正值美军“增兵”时期，新大使馆尚未启用。在持续炮击期间，情况变得十分危急，包括JP和Jay在内的文化事务工作人员不得不睡在办公室里，那里比简陋的铁皮房车要安全得多。“我们断水半周，每天吃的都一样。一位伊拉克朋友对我说：‘现在你明白伊拉克中产阶级的生活了吧。’”JP回忆道，“但我们很幸运。我们当时唯一担心的就是：别被火箭弹炸死，用手帕擦擦身子，然后连续一周吃同样的饭菜。”他补充说，与前线部队面临的困境或伊拉克民众的日常生活相比，“我们真是太幸运了。”

During the month of April in 2008—the “surge” in US military activity—the New Embassy Compound was not yet open. When things got hairy during a sustained period of shelling, the cultural affairs staff, including J.P. and Jay, had to sleep in the office, which provided more hard-shell protection than the flimsy, tin-can residence trailers. “We were without water for half a week, food was the same every day, and an Iraqi friend told me, ‘Now you see how it is for the middle class in Iraq,’” J.P. remembers. “But we were lucky. Our only concerns were: don’t get killed by a rocket, clean yourself with a handkerchief, and eat the same meal for a week.” Compared to what the troops were facing in the field or Iraqis in their everyday lives, he adds, “We were blessed.”

获准回到自己的房车里，就像从监狱里被释放出来一样。那时，在泳池里游泳的感觉简直令人无比兴奋。

Being allowed back into their personal trailers was like being let out of prison. Being in the pool, then, felt like nothing short of exhilaration.

“平衡，”JP曾告诉我，“在游泳和生活中都要保持平衡。”战争的残酷和沉重让人渴望一丝轻松。杰伊本人尤其被成群结队来到游泳池的年轻士兵们所吸引。无论他们是正式入伍服役还是从事安保工作，这都是他过去所认识的一群截然不同的人。“这些年轻人非常坚韧，习惯于执行长达十八个小时的任务，”杰伊说道。他们会回到胜利营——所有战斗人员的大本营，城市巡逻队员和狙击手——身上散发着硝烟味，他们会把武器支起来。“你觉得他们最喜欢、最不容错过的电视节目是什么？”他问我。“当然是《吉尔莫女孩》。”

“Balance,” J.P. had told me, “in swimming and life.” The grim, weighty strictures of war make one long for a little levity. Jay himself was especially struck by the young soldiers who came in droves to the pool. Whether they were enlisted in official military service or under security contract, it was a different population of the world than he’d known in the past. “These were very hard young guys, accustomed to going on eighteen-hour missions,” Jay says. They’d come back to Camp Victory—the home base for all those combat, urban-patrol, and sniper-detail Marines—smelling of cordite, and they’d prop their weapons up. “What do you think was their favorite, can’t-miss TV program?” he asks me. “Gilmore Girls, of course.”

游泳训练结束后，军人游泳队员们会重新穿上制服。在这样一个等级森严、社会秩序井然的地方，杰伊开始认真思考游泳是如何将人们剥离到最本质的状态的。“比起打网球，游泳时你失去的自我认同感还要多。你只剩下皮肤、泳帽和泳镜，”他说。“游泳服是最基本的——他们的其他身份都隐藏了起来。两个军人，你根本分不清谁是军官，谁是士兵。”

After swim practice, the military swimmers would get back into uniform. In a complicated place that was so reliant on hierarchy and social order, Jay began to think hard about the way that swimming stripped people down to their bare elements. “You lose even more of your normal identity than if you got dressed for tennis, for example. You’re just skin, cap, goggles,” he says. “The outfits for swimming are at the bare minimum—their other identities aren’t visible. With two military people, you can’t tell who’s the officer and who’s the enlisted man.”

这比他意识到的要重要得多。他尤其想到了那些贫困的秘鲁卫兵，他们成千上万地被雇佣来为美国大使馆和战区提供安全保障。“让他们摆脱那种生活，来学习游泳，就像他们日复一日保护的美国人和其他外国人一样。能够拥有同样的特权，意义非凡。”

That was a bigger deal than he’d realized. He thought in particular of the impoverished Peruvian guards, hired by the thousands to bring security and safety to American embassies and combat zones. “For them to shed that, and come learn swimming, just like the Americans and the other foreigners they guard day in and day out. To have that same privilege, it meant something.”

听着杰伊、安德里和JP的讲述，我真切地体会到在国际水域上游泳课的意义。“在其他任何地方，你都看不到这么多士兵、外交官、伊拉克人和其他国家的人聚在一起，”杰伊教练谈到泳池和他的学员时说道。在水中，差异消失了。混乱变成了秩序。我想起了金告诉我的话，在水中，我们会卸下伪装，回归本真，而这让我们……以最基本的方式彼此相见。在使馆区广阔的范围内，游泳池及其中的课程如同祈祷的召唤，具有强大的中心力量。这是一种在人性深处，通过某种交流来认识人性的方式。

Listening to Jay and Andry and J.P. gives me a sense of what swim lessons in international waters can do. “Nowhere else was there such a mingling of soldiers, diplomats, Iraqis, and other nationalities,” Coach Jay says of the pool and his swimmers. Differences fell away in the water. Chaos turned to order. I remember what Kim told me about being stripped down to our essential selves in the water and how it allows us to see each other in the most basic way. In the far-flung landscape of the embassy compound, the pool and the lessons in it had the focal power of a call to prayer. It was a way to recognize humanity, in a place of deep inhumanity, through a kind of communion.

在杰伊待在巴格达的中期，许多伊拉克人已经不再在绿区工作，因为与美军、美国国际开发署或大使馆有任何瓜葛都变得危险起来。怀疑和误解从四面八方袭来。你是间谍吗？你的收入是否可疑？你会为了美国而抛弃伊拉克、你的家人和传统吗？融入问题一直存在，而且至今依然存在。但一些伊拉克员工仍然留在美国国际开发署，他们乘坐班车去游泳池上游泳课。在游泳池里，他们有机会避免被区别对待，无论是正面的还是负面的。他们可以像其他人一样游泳、学习。

By the middle of Jay’s stay in Baghdad, many Iraqis had stopped working in the Green Zone because it had become dangerous to be affiliated with the American military, USAID, or the embassy. Suspicion and misunderstanding came from every front. Were you a spy? Were you making a suspicious amount of money? Were you going to abandon Iraq and your family and traditions for America? There was, and continues to be, the problem of integration. But some Iraqi staff remained at USAID, and they rode the shuttle over to the pool to take swim lessons. Being in the pool was an opportunity to not get singled out for attention, be it positive or negative. They could swim, and learn, just like anyone else.

那是一件意义深远的事，它改变了我的视角，改变了我的可能性，改变了我在这个世界上可以成为什么样的人。随着我对巴格达游泳者了解的加深，我开始注意到水是一个特殊的空间，而受邀进入这个空间对各种群体来说都意味着什么。我观看了一些关于跨性别游泳者和自闭症游泳者的纪录片，了解游泳池如何为他们的身体和心灵带来自由。进入水中就像是重获力量——“一种宁静的力量”，一位游泳者在纪录片《游泳俱乐部》（讲述伦敦一个跨性别游泳团体的故事）中这样说道。而对于那些终于有机会游泳的自闭症游泳者来说，这更是一种莫大的体验。加入了新泽西州珀斯安博伊的泽西锤头鲨队，让他们能够与其他所有人竞争，我看到了游泳如何通过社群给予他们自信。

It was a profound thing, an altering of perspective, of possibility, of who you could be in the world. As I learn more about the Baghdad swimmers, I start noticing how the water is a privileged space and what an invitation to that space can mean for all kinds of tribes. I watch documentaries about transgender swimmers and autistic swimmers and how swimming pools mean freedom for their bodies, their minds. Entry into that water can feel like a restoration of power—“a serene power,” one swimmer says, in the documentary The Swimming Club, about a transgender swimming group in London. And for autistic swimmers who finally have a team—the Jersey Hammerheads of Perth Amboy, New Jersey—that allows them to compete with everyone else, I see how swimming gives confidence through community.

在杰伊看来，他在巴格达最大的成就就是让他的这群乌合之众难得有机会聚在一起，在同一个泳池里。当然，问题也不少。有个家伙整天戴着泳镜偷看水下的女人，还有几个男人过来坐在池边围观，但杰伊毫不客气地把他们赶走了：“来了就得游。我们可不喜欢偷窥的人。”（他有安德里的魁梧身材撑腰，还有几个身强力壮的战斗人员撑腰。）

As Jay sees it, his greatest achievement in Baghdad was providing his motley crew the rare opportunity to be together, all in the same pool. Not that there weren’t issues. There was one man who spent his time with goggles on looking at women underwater, and several other men who came and sat at the edge of the pool, spectating, but Jay dispatched them firmly: “If you come, you have to swim. And we don’t take kindly to oglers.” (He had Andry’s bulk, plus the looming presence of a couple of combat servicemen, to back him up.)

为了组织巴格达游泳队并缓和队员间的社交摩擦，杰伊教练不仅借鉴了他在巴尔的摩担任游泳教练的经验，还运用了他毕生在非洲和中东从事文化联络工作的经验。谈到冲突，杰伊想起了他在开罗任职的那段日子，当时各国代表为了参加阿拉伯联盟会议而苦苦挣扎。其中一次会议甚至以一场食物大战告终。“在巴格达，至少没人会指责对方在泳池里撒尿，”他淡淡地说道，“尽管他们心里可能这么想。”

To organize the Baghdad swimmers and smooth their social frictions, Coach Jay drew on his experience as a swim instructor in Baltimore but also on his life’s work as a cultural liaison in Africa and the Middle East. Talking about conflicts reminds Jay of his time serving in Cairo, when representatives of different countries struggled to get through Arab League meetings. There was one that ended in a food fight. “In Baghdad, at least nobody accused each other of peeing in the pool,” he notes dryly, “even though they might have thought it.”

对安德里来说，最初只是玩耍的事情，却意外地成为了他通往另一个世界的重要出口。“这就像读书一样——当你沉浸其中时，你就与世隔绝了，”他告诉我。对于一个曾经他从未经历过战争，能够消失对他来说至关重要。

In Andry’s case, something that started out as play surprised him by becoming an essential escape hatch to somewhere else. “It’s like reading books—when you’re in it, you’re not in the world outside,” he tells me. For someone who had never before experienced war, being able to disappear was critical to his well-being.

“当人们问起马达加斯加时，我会告诉他们我们不懂战争，”他轻笑着说。“我们根本不知道战争是什么。即使在法国人来占领马达加斯加的时候，我们也只是顺水推舟地把国家拱手让给了他们。这虽然是个玩笑，但说实话，我们不像其他国家那样对冲突感同身受。”

“When people ask me about Madagascar, I tell them we don’t know war,” he says with a light laugh. “We don’t know what that is. Even back in the time when the French came to take the country, we just gave it to them. It’s a joke, but we honestly don’t have that kind of feeling of conflict as much as other countries do.”

在变幻莫测、动荡不安的战时世界里，泳池、游泳课和游泳队就像是稳定的压舱石。杰伊教练于2010年离开巴格达，安德里不久也随之离开。“据我所知，军方有人试图接管游泳课，但他让游泳变得索然无味，”杰伊说道。此后，游泳课只持续了一个月左右就再也没有恢复过。如今，巴格达游泳队的成员们早已各奔东西。杰伊仍然从事文化交流项目和中东事务方面的工作。他正忙着在自家车库里造一艘船，一艘13英尺长的吉米小艇，配有舷外机，非常适合巴格达和缅因州的水域。他仍然会在家附近的游泳池游泳，那游泳池离他位于巴尔的摩郊外的家只有300码远。安德里和妻子以及蹒跚学步的儿子住在巴黎十五区。

In the world of wartime—unpredictable, unstable, and fickle—the pool, the lessons, and the team provided stabilizing ballast. Coach Jay left Baghdad in 2010, and Andry soon followed. “Someone from the military side tried to pick up the lessons, but he made it no fun, as I understand it,” Jay says. The swimming lessons lasted a month or so after that and never began again. Today, the Baghdad Swim Team has scattered. Jay still works on cultural exchange programs and Middle East issues. He’s busy building a boat in his garage, a thirteen-foot Jimmy Skiff with an outboard, nice for waters there and in Maine. He stills swims at his neighborhood pool, just three hundred yards from his house, outside Baltimore. Andry lives with his wife and toddler son in Paris, in the 15th arrondissement.

最近，杰伊带女儿莉齐去法国游玩。他们特意去了当地建于20世纪30年代的历史悠久的市政游泳池。安德烈至今还保留着从巴格达带回来的满满一柜子的泳镜和游泳装备。杰伊说，等安德烈准备好了，他就能教他的孩子游泳了。男孩学会了游泳。在墨西哥华雷斯，JP Santana 至今仍然每周游泳两到三次。泳池是他艰难岁月里最美好的回忆之一。“对我来说，游泳课就像一缕阳光，带来快乐，”他说。“我们边境的人会说‘la cherry en el pastel’，意思是蛋糕上的樱桃。或者像我一位伊拉克朋友会说的那样：‘羊头盖饭上的羊头’。”

Recently Jay took his daughter, Lizzie, to France for a visit. They sought out the city’s historic municipal pools, built in the 1930s. Andry still has a locker full of goggles and swimming equipment from Baghdad. Jay says that when Andry is ready, he will have all he needs to teach his little boy how to swim. And in Juarez, Mexico, J. P. Santana is still swimming two or three times a week. The pool is one of his best memories from a tough time. “To me, the swimming classes were like an accent of joy,” he says. “We border people say la cherry en el pastel, the cherry on top of the cake. Or as an Iraqi friend would say: the lamb’s head at the top of the biryani.”

不久前，我用谷歌地球俯瞰巴格达，尤其对共和国宫及其昔日辉煌的泳池念念不忘，泳池曾被茂盛的棕榈树荫蔽。如今泳池已干涸，如同周围的沙漠般干燥，但你仍然可以看到池边那些阴凉的角落，想必曾有一群孤独的游泳者在此驻足喘息，相遇相知。

Not long ago, I zoomed around Baghdad using Google Earth and lingered on the bird’s-eye views of the Republican Palace and its once-glorious pool, shaded by lush palm trees. It’s drained of water now, as dry as the surrounding desert sand, but you can still see the shady perches along the edge of the pool where, once upon a time, a group of lonely swimmers paused for breath, and found each other.

竞赛

COMPETITION

自然界中没有任何一种激情比站在悬崖边颤抖着，一心想纵身跃下的人的激情更加急躁。

There is no passion in nature so demonically impatient as that of him who, shuddering on the edge of a precipice, thus meditates a plunge.

——埃德加·爱伦·坡，《反常的恶魔》

—Edgar Allan Poe, “The Imp of the Perverse”

我认为鲑鱼是游泳的终极高手。“鲑鱼幼苗：五到十周大，正在游泳。”这是我在一幅鲑鱼生命周期图解中看到的一句话，它出乎意料地打动了我。鱼生来就会游泳，这是它们的本能。但鲑鱼的生命周期中蕴含着一种独特的挣扎，这与人类努力学习游泳的经历有着惊人的相似之处。对鲑鱼来说，这种挣扎早在五周大时就开始了，这些小鱼儿在向下游游向大海的过程中仍然十分脆弱。它们躲在岩石下，同时还要捕食水生昆虫的幼虫和若虫。

I think of the salmon as the ultimate swimmer. “Salmon fry: five to ten weeks old and swimming.” It’s a caption I discovered on an illustration diagramming the salmon life cycle, and it unexpectedly moved me. Fish, of course, are born to swim. It’s what they do. But there is a beautiful struggle in the life cycle of the salmon in particular, and a compelling analogy for the human struggle to swim at all. For the salmon, it starts as early as five weeks of age, the tiny fish still vulnerable as they wend their way downstream to the ocean. They are hiding under rocks and at the same time hunting for nymphs and insect larvae on which to feed.

鲑鱼的生命周期堪称奇迹，是自给自足和顽强生存的完美典范——换句话说，就是生存之道。鲑鱼的生命始于河流，最初是淡水鱼。最终，它们会经历幼鱼阶段，改变生理结构以适应咸水环境，然后游向开阔的海洋，在那里度过成年生活。我们并不确切知道鲑鱼在海洋阶段的活动范围；加利福尼亚的不同鲑鱼物种分布范围广泛，遍及北太平洋。还有白令海。但这里是鲑鱼生长和探索的地方，它们会在开阔的海洋中生活长达八年。然后，它们会返回最初栖息的淡水水域。不难理解为什么北美西北海岸的原住民在他们的神话中如此崇敬鲑鱼；在这些文化中，鲑鱼象征着本能、决心和新生。在这里，鲑鱼也是主要的食物来源。在这里，人类的生命周期依赖于鲑鱼的生命周期。

The salmon life cycle is nothing short of miraculous, an elegant example of self-sufficiency and persistence—in other words, survival. A salmon begins life in a river, as a freshwater fish. Eventually, the fish smolts, changing its physiology to adapt to salt water, and swims out to the open ocean to spend its adult life. We don’t know exactly where a salmon roams during the ocean phase; the different species of salmon in California distribute expansively over the North Pacific and the Bering Sea. But this is where a salmon grows, and explores, spending up to eight years in the open sea. And then it returns to the fresh water from which it came. It’s easy to see why the aboriginal peoples along the northwest coast of North America hold the salmon in high regard in their mythology; in these cultures, the fish symbolizes instinct and determination, and renewal. Here, the salmon is also a primary food source. Here, the life cycle of the human is dependent upon the life cycle of the salmon.

当鲑鱼准备返回出生地——那条淡水河时，它会再次发生转变。根据品种和性别，它会长出驼峰、犬齿，或者像拳击手一样长出钩状的鼻子，以彰显自己的统治地位。有些鲑鱼还会改变颜色，从淡银蓝色变为深红色。最终，鱼儿会游回那条出生河流的入海口。一旦进入淡水，它便停止进食。由于环境的影响，它会变成另一种生物，唯一的目的就是逆流而上，回到出生地。只有最强壮、最适应环境的鲑鱼才能到达河流的上游，在那里产卵，然后通常会死去，留下它们的尸体滋养着河水。于是，生命再次开始。

When a salmon is ready to return to the freshwater river of its birth, it is transformed again. Depending on species and sex, it will grow a hump, or canine teeth, or it will develop a hooked nose—a bit like a prizefighter, in preparation for asserting its dominance. Some change color, from a pale silvery blue to a deep red. Eventually, the fish navigates its way back to the mouth of that very same natal river. Once it reaches fresh water, it stops eating. It becomes, by virtue of environment, something else, with the singular goal of muscling its way upstream to the place where it was born. Only the strongest and the fittest can make it to the upper reaches of that river, where it spawns and usually dies, leaving behind its body to enrich the waters. And so life begins again.

鲑鱼是人类水上生存追求的绝佳象征。对我而言，游泳的故事也是一个适应的故事。我们努力适应水生环境。有些人甚至为了实现目标而改变自己的身体。然而，对于我们大多数人来说——当然，除了像古德劳格斯（Guðlaugurs）这样的游泳健将——生存的动力已经让位于竞技。竞争是我们……体验评估并穿越一个充满魅力却又极其不适宜居住的环境的冒险之旅。只有坚持不懈的努力，我们才能最终征服它。

The salmon is a handy symbol for human aquatic strivings. For me, the story of swimming is also one of adaptation. We work to inhabit this element. Some of us also alter our bodies in pursuit of a goal. For most of us today—apart from the Guðlaugurs of the world, that is—survival as motivation, though, has given way to sport. Competition is how we can experience the adventure of assessing and moving through an attractive but decidedly inhospitable environment. It is only with sustained effort that we can master it.

对于人类游泳运动员来说，什么是竞争？很难界定游泳霸主地位的争夺，因为我们可以用各种各样的最高级来定义它——最长、最冷、最深、最快。

For human swimmers, what is competition? It’s hard to know where to draw the lines around a contest for swimming supremacy, because we can define it in terms of all kinds of superlatives—longest, coldest, deepest, fastest.

游泳不仅是一项有用的技能，可以用来捕鱼，也可以用来战斗。我们可以从游泳作为战时技艺的起源中了解游泳比赛的本质。从古埃及到古希腊，游泳技能在古代文明中备受推崇；柏拉图曾宣称，“不懂文字或不会游泳”就等同于缺乏正规教育。希罗多德描述希腊人是游泳高手，因此当他们的船只在与波斯人的战斗中被摧毁时，他们能够逃到岸边（相比之下，他几乎是幸灾乐祸地宣称，“许多蛮族人因为不懂游泳而溺水身亡”）。

Swimming is a useful skill with which to fish, yes, but also to fight. We can learn something of the nature of swimming competition from its origins as a wartime art. The ability was held in high regard in ancient civilizations from the Egyptians to the Greeks; to be ignorant of “either letters or swimming,” Plato declared, was to lack a proper education. Herodotus described the Greeks as expert swimmers and thus able to make their escape to shore when their ships were destroyed in battle with the Persians (by contrast, he proclaimed, almost gleefully, “great numbers of the barbarians, from their ignorance of this art, were drowned”).

逃离沉船、渡河、躲避敌人：自古以来，游泳作为一种武术的巨大价值显而易见。公元前880年的浮雕艺术作品描绘了一位亚述国王率领军队渡河的场景，战士们头朝上站在疑似充气的兽皮上游泳。在罗马帝国，青年军事训练包括在台伯河沐浴和游泳。尤利乌斯·凯撒被誉为一位技艺精湛的水上高手，并因此备受赞誉。希腊历史学家在其为凯撒所作的传记中也提到了这一点。普鲁塔克记载，公元前48年冬，在亚历山大战役中，一位将军为了躲避埃及人的追击，纵身跃入大海，一手拎着随身物品，一手拼命划水，最终游到一艘船边。游泳在后来的军事行动中发挥了关键作用，例如公元69年罗马征服不列颠的战役。

Escape a sinking ship, cross a stream, flee your enemy: swimming’s great value as a martial art since time immemorial is clear. Bas-relief artworks dating to 880 BC show an Assyrian king leading his army across a river with warriors swimming head up on what are thought to be inflated animal skins. In the Roman Empire, youth military training included bathing and swimming in the Tiber River. Julius Caesar was described, with much admiration, as a gifted waterman. In his biographical account of Caesar, the Greek historian Plutarch wrote of the general at the battle of Alexandria, during the winter of 48 BC, escaping the Egyptians by leaping into the sea and swimming—belongings in one hand, stroking furiously with the other—to the shelter of a ship. Swimming would prove key in later military campaigns, as in the Roman conquest of Britain in AD 69.

曾经被誉为军事技艺的运动，最终演变为一项竞技艺术，人们先是为祭祀神灵或祖先而进行，最终发展成为纯粹的竞技运动。正如鸣枪可以作为赛跑的发令枪一样，曾经激烈的战斗也可以转化为体育竞技。

What was once praised as a military art eventually became celebrated as an athletic art, performed in honor of the gods or ancestors and, finally, in pure contest for its own sake. In the same way that firing a pistol can be repurposed to signal the start of a race, the ferocious drive of battle could now be directed toward sporting competition.

像金·钱伯斯、琳恩·考克斯和路易斯·普格这样的公开水域游泳运动员，也可以起到一种桥梁的作用，帮助我们理解如何在竞技的语境下重新定义游泳中的耐力和探索精神。挑战激流险滩的尝试从未间断——这些尝试往往以死亡告终，或者至少与死亡擦肩而过。

Open-water swimmers like Kim Chambers, Lynne Cox, and Lewis Pugh can also serve as a kind of bridge, to help us understand how endurance and exploration in swimming can be reframed in the context of competition. There has never been a shortage of attempts to swim some tumultuous body of water—often resulting in death, or near to it.

2007年7月的一个清晨，普格站在北极海冰边缘，想起了他的母亲。她是对的。他即将要做的事非同寻常。就在他即将成为第一个横渡地理北极点的人时，他却愣住了。并非因为寒冷——尽管零下1.8摄氏度（华氏29度）的低温足以让这里成为人类游泳过的最冷的水域之一——而是因为一种挥之不去的生存恐惧。他心想，一个人本来就不应该能在北极点游泳。尽管如此，他还是纵身一跃，身上只穿着一条泳裤。

One July morning in 2007, Pugh stood on the edge of the Arctic sea ice and thought of his mother. She was right. What he was about to do was not normal. Just as he was poised to become the first person to swim across the geographic North Pole, he froze. Not from cold—even though the subzero temperatures (-1.8 degrees Celsius, or 29 degrees Fahrenheit) would make it among the coldest waters any human had ever swum in—but from a creeping existential fear. One shouldn’t be able to swim at the North Pole in the first place, he thought. Still he leapt, wearing just his Speedo.

2003年，普格辞去了海事律师的工作，决心成为一名公开水域游泳的先驱。他梦想着游过峡湾，绕过荒凉的海岬，游过那些从未有人涉足的冰山。“就像水上的沙克尔顿一样，”一天晚上，他通过视频聊天从南非开普敦的家中告诉我，他笑着说。“在我看来，这是我们三个人之间的比赛：我、马丁·斯特雷尔和琳恩·考克斯。他们比我先出发，把所有温暖的水域都占了，只剩下我独自面对冰冷的水域。”

In 2003, when Pugh quit his job as a maritime lawyer and set out to be a pioneer open-water swimmer, he had a vision of swimming down fjords and around wild capes and past icebergs where nobody else had ever dreamed of swimming before. “Like an aquatic Shackleton,” he says with a laugh, one evening via video chat with me from his home in Cape Town, South Africa. “In my mind, it was a race between the three of us: me, Martin Strel, and Lynne Cox. They started before me and they took all the bloody warm stuff, so I was left with the cold stuff.”

当然，这只是玩笑话：在普格开始挑战极限之前，考克斯已经在世界各地挑战冷水游泳的极限，并创造了数十年的世界纪录。考克斯告诉我，她并不认为自己是在和任何人竞争；她说，她的游泳始终关乎人类的能力和冒险精神。尽管她并不认同这种说法，但我们大多数人还是会不自觉地用纪录来衡量世界，而我们谈论公开水域游泳成就的方式也反映了这一点。虽然普格本人声称他并不以传统意义上的方式参与竞争，但他承认自己是一个极具竞争心的人。近年来，他将这种竞争精神引导到了另一个方向，利用那些定义探险家的最高级形容词——最佳、最伟大、第一——来为自己谋利。

This, of course, is tongue-in-cheek: By the time Pugh started, Cox had been pushing the limits of human endurance and setting world records in cold-water swims around the world for decades. Cox tells me that she doesn’t see herself as being in a race with anyone; her swims, she says, have always been about human ability and adventure. Despite her resistance to that portrayal, most of us are not immune to thinking about the world in terms of records, and the way we talk about open-water swimming achievements reflects this. Though Pugh himself claims that he doesn’t compete in the traditional sense, he admits that he is a highly competitive person. In recent years, he has channeled those impulses in a different direction, using the superlatives that define an explorer—best, greatest, first—to his advantage.

“第一名至关重要，”普格告诉我。他的意思是，为了赢得人们对他事业的支持，他必须做到第一。在冷水游泳比赛中成为最强者、第一个冲过终点线，对他来说只是达到目的的手段。这是他吸引人们关注、让人们从宏观角度看待问题的方式。我们的星球正面临气候危机。北极游泳的象征意义显而易见：他能够游过一个原本不可能游过的地方，一个曾经冰封的地方。2015年，他在南极罗斯海的壮举——在刺骨的寒冷海水和凛冽的寒风中——促成了他与俄罗斯部长们的会晤，最终帮助消除了俄罗斯对建立世界上最大的海洋保护区的最后阻力。

“Being first is everything,” Pugh tells me. By this he means that to win support for his cause, he must be first. Being the best, the first, in cold-water swims is a means to an end. It is his way to get people to pay attention, to give a sea-level view of our planet in climate crisis. The symbolism of the North Pole swim was clear: that he could swim across a place that you shouldn’t be able to swim across, that used to be frozen. His 2015 swim in Antarctica’s Ross Sea, in paralyzingly cold waters and severe wind chill, led to meetings with Russian ministers that helped remove the nation’s remaining resistance to the establishment of the largest marine protected area in the world.

“对我来说，”普格说着，扬起眉毛以示强调，“这是一场创造力的较量。”他朝餐厅的方向示意，餐桌上铺着一本展开的、厚厚的地图册，其超大的书页向任何懂得欣赏它的人诉说着无限的可能性。

“For me,” Pugh says, raising his eyebrows for emphasis, “it’s a competition in creativity.” He motions toward his dining room, where the table is covered with a sprawling, open atlas, its oversized pages spelling possibility to anyone who knows how to recognize it.

但对我们大多数人来说，比赛的意义在于速度。它是在泳池中进行的追逐，在可控的条件下，穿着规定的服装。它是奥运会游泳比赛的比赛方式，衡量标准始终是时间：你能游多快。

For most of us, though, competition is about speed. It’s the chase, framed by a pool, in controlled conditions, with regulation attire. It is swimming competition the way it is conducted in the Olympics, for which the metric has always been the clock: how fast you can go.

11

11

飞溅与冲刺

The Splash and Dash

在奥运游泳项目中，没有比50米自由泳速度更快的项目了。它的别称是“水花四溅”。选手只需在跳入水中时吸一口气，就能游完泳池的一整个来回。许多世界级游泳选手在20到24秒内都不会换气，因为那样会减慢他们的速度。这场比赛容不得半点多想。目标再简单不过：以最快的速度从泳池的一端游到另一端。

There is no faster event in Olympic swimming than the 50-meter freestyle. Its nickname is “the splash and dash.” One length of the pool, on just the one breath with which you dive. Many world-class swimmers in this event don’t take another breath in the twenty- to twenty-four-second duration, because it would slow them down. There’s no time to overthink this race. The objective couldn’t be simpler: get from one end of the pool to the other as fast as possible.

达拉·托雷斯从小就爱争第一，她总是和兄弟姐妹比赛看谁先到餐桌，谁先到车里，谁先到妈妈生日那天给她打电话。托雷斯41岁时，已经三次宣布退役。但那几次退役并没有让她真正重返赛场。她在马萨诸塞州的家中通过电话告诉我，竞争早已融入了她的生命。

As a child, Dara Torres always had to be first, racing her siblings to the dinner table, to the car, to call their mother on her birthday. When Torres was forty-one years old, she had already retired from swimming three times. But those retirements didn’t stick. Competition, she tells me by phone from her home in Massachusetts, is ingrained in her very being.

她的第三次复出让她第五次参加了奥运会，即2008年北京奥运会——她是第一位参加如此多届奥运会的美国游泳运动员。41岁的她，是奥运会历史上年龄最大的游泳运动员。作为参考，她在北京奥运会的队友中有一位是当时23岁的迈克尔·菲尔普斯。托雷斯在1984年赢得了她奥运生涯的第一枚金牌，那一年菲尔普斯出生。

Her third swimming comeback brought her to her fifth Olympics, in Beijing, in 2008—the first American swimmer ever to compete in that many Games. At forty-one, she was the oldest Olympic swimmer in history. For context, one of her teammates in Beijing was Michael Phelps, who was twenty-three at the time. Torres won the first gold medal of her Olympic career in 1984, the year before Phelps was born.

但她来北京不是为了打破年龄纪录，而是为了赢得冠军。她凭借惊人的复出一路杀进女子50米自由泳决赛，并以最快成绩晋级决赛，领先于年龄不到她一半的选手。最终获得该项目铜牌的澳大利亚选手凯特·坎贝尔当时只有16岁。托雷斯的两岁女儿泰莎当时在佛罗里达的家中。“总有一天，我的女儿会通过这场比赛了解我，”托雷斯心想。凭借出色的资格赛成绩，她获得了决赛中梦寐以求的位置：第四泳道，中间两条泳道之一，视野极佳，可以俯瞰两侧的对手，还能免受池边水流的干扰。

But she wasn’t in Beijing to set age records—she was there to win. Her extraordinary comeback brought her to the final of the 50-meter freestyle, for which she qualified with the fastest time, ahead of women less than half her age. Cate Campbell of Australia, who would go on to win the bronze medal in the event, was just sixteen years old. Torres’s two-year-old daughter, Tessa, was home in Florida. Someday, this is the race my daughter will watch to know who I am, Torres thought. Thanks to her speedy qualifying time, she earned coveted placement in the final: lane four, one of the two middle lanes, with the best vantage point of her competitors on either side, and shielded by them from the slosh of the gutter.

在这项最考验爆发力的短跑项目中，年轻就是优势。为运动员提供力量的快肌纤维——这些力量包括快速反应的起跳跳水、全力以赴却又气喘吁吁的划臂动作、强劲有力的打腿以及冲刺入池壁所需的爆发力——在25岁以后会迅速减少。（负责耐力的慢肌纤维则会保留得更久一些。）目前男子和女子50米自由泳的世界纪录保持者在创造纪录时分别是22岁和23岁。在这项比赛中，第一名和第四名之间的差距往往只有百分之一秒。

In this sprintiest of sprint events, youth is an advantage. Fast-twitch muscle fibers, which supply the power—for the quick-response starting dive, the all-out, breathless controlled chaos of the arm stroke, the robust motor of the flutter kick, and the propulsive through-the-wall finish that’s required to win—decrease rapidly past age twenty-five. (Slow-twitch muscle fibers, which govern endurance, stick around a little longer.) The current male and female world record holders in the 50-meter freestyle were twenty-two and twenty-three years old, respectively, when they set their records. It’s a race where first and fourth are separated by mere hundredths of a second.

说到游泳，比赛部分……总是让我感到不安。我不太喜欢比赛，而且至今仍然无法完全理解它，所以我承认很难写出来。一想到比赛我就觉得恶心。即使是小时候，只要想到比赛，我就会在同一场比赛中跑好几次厕所，肠胃都快要崩溃了。要么战斗，要么逃跑！我喜欢赢，也喜欢游得快，但我却搞不懂如何控制其他那些让身体进入那种足以击败对手的兴奋状态的因素。

When it comes to swimming, the competition part has always unnerved me. I don’t like it all that much, and I still can’t quite make sense of it, so I admit it’s hard to write about. Thinking about racing makes me feel queasy. Even when I was a kid, contemplating a race would send me to the bathroom more than once during a single meet, my intestines in revolt. Fight or flight! I liked winning, and I liked swimming fast, but I couldn’t figure out how to control all the other stuff that went along with getting your body into the revved-up state required to slay your rivals.

为了理解这种内在驱动力，我找到了达拉·托雷斯。她是个好胜心极强的女人，她向我坦白，绿灯亮起时她会猛踩油门，不让其他车插到她前面。“我得努力提高开车速度，毕竟我有孩子了。” 她也是个好胜心极强的女人，很长一段时间里，除非能赢，否则她根本不想游泳。紧张和内脏的抗拒？当然，这很烦人，但在通往巅峰的道路上，这只是微不足道的小事。“达到巅峰，与世界上最优秀的游泳运动员同场竞技”——这才是她热爱的。她如此热爱游泳，以至于无法抗拒。

It’s in the interest of understanding this inner drive that I seek out Dara Torres. Here is a woman so competitive that she floors it at the green light, she confesses to me, so other cars can’t get in front of her. “I’m trying to be better with driving fast, since I have kids and all.” Here is a woman so competitive that for the longest time she didn’t care to swim unless she was winning. The nerves and the gut in revolt? An annoyance, surely, but a minor one on the way to being the best. “Getting to the top of your game, being there with the best swimmers in the world”—that is what she loved. She loved it so much she couldn’t stay away.

我记得2008年看过那场50米决赛的电视转播；在和托雷斯谈话之前，我又看了一遍录像。托雷斯站在起跑器后，耸了耸宽阔的肩膀，甩了甩修长的双腿。她深吸一口气，挺直了她近六英尺高的身躯，嘴角微微扬起，带着一丝坚定的神情。她修长而肌肉紧绷的双臂绷紧，伸手去调整印有美国国旗和“TORRES”字样的黑色泳帽。用醒目的白色大字写着。人群疯狂地欢呼着。她望着小巷，目光聚焦在静谧的河面上，以及那片清澈的矩形水面，然后掰了掰指关节。

I remember watching the television coverage of that 50-meter final in 2008; I went back to the footage before Torres and I talked. Torres waits behind the starting blocks, shrugging her broad shoulders and shaking out her long legs. She takes a deep breath and draws up her nearly six-foot frame, making a determined little wrinkle of her mouth. Her lean, muscled arms tense as she reaches up to adjust her black swim cap, printed with the American flag and “TORRES” in bold white letters. The crowd is cheering madly. She looks down the lane, focusing on its stillness, its clear, rectangular span of water, and cracks her knuckles.

她突然平静下来。我准备出发了。

Suddenly, she is calm. I’m ready to go.

在1896年于雅典举行的首届现代奥林匹克运动会上，游泳项目赫然在列。此前，罗马皇帝狄奥多西一世在一千五百多年前就以异教崇拜为由禁止了这项运动（古代奥运会最初是为了祭祀奥林匹斯诸神而举办的）。四个比赛项目，四个国家参赛：匈牙利、希腊、奥地利和美国。在一个阳光明媚的四月清晨，游泳比赛在雅典西南部的比雷埃夫斯半岛上的泽亚湾清澈的海水中举行。两万名观众到场观赛，其中包括东道主匈牙利国王乔治一世。

In the first modern Olympic Games, held in Athens in 1896 after being banned by the Roman emperor Theodosius I more than one and a half millennia before as pagan cult worship (the ancient Games were originally performed in honor of the gods of Olympus), there was swimming. Four events, four countries: Hungary, Greece, Austria, the United States. On a bright April morning, the swims were held in the brisk waters of the Bay of Zea, just southwest of Athens on the Piraeus peninsula. Twenty thousand spectators were in attendance, including the host country’s monarch, King George I.

参赛者乘船进入海湾，然后跃入水中，奋力游回岸边。那时，“自由泳”仅仅意味着你可以使用任何泳姿。在其他体育项目中占据绝对优势的美国，却在这项比赛中颗粒无收；据一位亲历者描述，直到发令枪响，美国游泳运动员才意识到春季冰冷的地中海的残酷现实。对一些人来说，冰冷的海水带来的冲击让他们瞬间麻木。18岁的匈牙利游泳运动员阿尔弗雷德·哈约什赢得了100米和1200米两项比赛的冠军。他后来告诉记者：“我的求生欲望完全战胜了求胜的欲望。”（也许他……）（这是一个生存与竞争最终走向圆满结局的案例。）没有女性竞争者。

Participants were taken out into the bay by boat. Then they leaped off the vessel and swam furiously back to shore. Back then, “freestyle” simply meant that you could use whatever stroke you wanted. The United States, so dominant in other sporting disciplines, was shut out of the medal count; by one firsthand account, the American swimmers were “blissfully unaware” when it came to the realities of the icy Mediterranean Sea in spring until the crack of the starting pistol. For some, the shock of the cold water brought on a kind of momentary paralysis. The eighteen-year-old Hungarian swimmer Alfréd Hajós won both the 100-meter and 1,200-meter races. He later told reporters, “My will to live completely overcame my desire to win.” (Perhaps his is a case in which survival and competition were conflated for a happy end.) There were no female competitors.

1908年，国际泳联（FINA）在伦敦奥运会期间成立，旨在规范国际游泳比赛。其创始成员国共有八个：英国、比利时、丹麦、芬兰、法国、德国、匈牙利和瑞典。FINA至今仍在履行这一职责。在FINA成立四年后的斯德哥尔摩奥运会上，女子游泳项目首次亮相奥运会，但当时美国女子游泳队并未参赛。

In 1908, the Federation Internationale de Natation, or FINA, was formed in London during the Olympics to regulate international competition in the sport, with eight founding nations behind it: Great Britain, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Hungary, and Sweden. It still does that job. In Stockholm, four years after FINA’s founding, women competed in aquatic events in the Olympics for the first time, though not American women.

1917年，在纽约市，一位名叫夏洛特·“埃皮”·爱泼斯坦的法庭速记员创立了女子游泳协会（WSA）。她和一群同样是秘书和职业女性的同事认为，游泳是她们下班后锻炼身体的好方法。在那个女性很少进行剧烈运动或参加体育比赛的年代，爱泼斯坦是一位先驱。

In 1917, in New York City, a court stenographer named Charlotte “Eppie” Epstein founded the Women’s Swimming Association, or WSA. She and a group of fellow secretaries and working women decided that swimming would be a good way to get exercise once they clocked out. In a time when women didn’t perform strenuous activities or compete in sports, Epstein was a pioneer.

尽管她本人并非游泳健将，但爱泼斯坦热爱游泳，并孜孜不倦地致力于提升美国女性在世界赛场上的竞争力。这一目标与她作为女权运动倡导者的工作不谋而合。她决心让女性在体育运动中得到应有的尊重。作为后来被誉为“美国女子游泳之母”的她，最引人瞩目的成就之一是，她成功说服美国业余体育联盟于1917年认可女子游泳——这是该联盟当年唯一认可的女子比赛项目。

Though she wasn’t herself an excellent swimmer, Epstein loved to swim, and she worked tirelessly to establish American women as a force in worldwide competition. The goal dovetailed with her work as a champion of women’s rights. She was determined that women be taken seriously as athletes in sport. In one of her signature achievements as the “mother of women’s swimming in America,” as she was later dubbed, Epstein persuaded the US Amateur Athletic Union to endorse women’s swimming in 1917—the only sport it recognized for female competition that year.

在WSA，爱泼斯坦获得了志愿教练资格。路易斯·汉德利是一位出生于意大利的奥运选手，他利用俱乐部作为实验室，开发并改进了美式自由泳。这种泳姿在当时具有革命性意义——它是澳式自由泳的变体，但采用了速度更快、六拍的打腿动作。自由泳的某种形式自古以来就有人使用，早在公元前2000年的埃及浮雕中就已出现，后来在北美、巴西和所罗门群岛等遥远地区的土著民族中也出现过。如今，自由泳几乎成了自由泳的代名词——由于其速度优势，如果可以选择，自由泳是大多数人在比赛中使用的泳姿。汉德利在WSA（世界游泳协会）教授所有年轻女性美式自由泳，其中包括一位名叫格特鲁德·埃德勒的十二岁女孩。

At the WSA, Epstein acquired the volunteer coaching services of Louis Handley, an Italian-born Olympian who used the club as a lab to develop and refine the American crawl. The stroke was revolutionary at the time—it was a variation of the Australian crawl, but with a faster, six-beat flutter kick. Some form of the front crawl has been employed since ancient times, with appearances in Egyptian bas-reliefs from 2000 BC and, later, among far-flung indigenous peoples across North America, Brazil, and the Solomon Islands. It’s now synonymous with freestyle by default—because of its superior speed, the front crawl is the stroke most people use in competition, if given the choice. Handley taught the American crawl to all the young women at the WSA—including a twelve-year-old named Gertrude Ederle.

当时的泳装简直是累赘：从头到脚都是黑色的羊毛，游泳者不在泳池时还得用浴袍遮盖。男士泳装则相对进步一些；对男士泳装的主要规定是泳衣必须与内衣有所区别。1917年，美国公园管理协会发布了泳装规定，允许男士穿着背心式泳衣，这种泳衣由短裤和一件遮住腹股沟的长衬衫组成，以示端庄。但男女泳装都在迅速发展，面料越来越少（也越来越轻），让运动员在运动中拥有更大的活动自由度。最终，埃普斯坦说服了管理机构，允许女子游泳运动员在比赛中不穿丝袜——在当时，这实际上被视为裸露——她们穿着的是由澳大利亚游泳冠军安妮特·凯勒曼推广的连体比赛服。

The swimming costumes at the time were literally a drag: neck-to-toe black wool, which had to be covered with robes when swimmers weren’t in the pool. Male swimwear was more progressive; the chief stipulation for men was that their bathing attire be distinguishable from underwear. In 1917, the American Association of Park Superintendents published bathing suit regulations that allowed men to wear tank suits, which consisted of shorts worn with a separate long shirt that covered the groin, for modesty’s sake. But swimsuits for both genders were evolving rapidly, with less (and lighter-weight) fabric that gave more freedom of movement in the sport. Epstein eventually convinced the governing body to let female swimmers swim without stockings in competition—at the time, this was actually considered nudity—in the one-piece racing suit popularized by the Australian swimming champion Annette Kellerman.

1920年安特卫普奥运会上，埃普斯坦被任命为美国女子游泳队的领队，汉德利则担任教练。这是美国女子游泳运动员首次获准参赛，埃普斯坦在其中发挥了至关重要的作用。美国女子游泳协会（WSA）的游泳运动员埃塞尔达·布莱布特雷在安特卫普奥运会上表现出色，包揽了女子游泳全部三个项目的金牌。此后，埃普斯坦和汉德利在多届奥运会上继续合作，为格特鲁德·埃德勒的成长铺平了道路，并亲自训练她，使她成为史上最伟大的游泳运动员之一。

Epstein was appointed team manager of the American women’s swim team at the 1920 Olympics in Antwerp, and Handley assumed coaching duties. It was the first time American women swimmers were allowed to compete, and Epstein played a critical role in making that happen. WSA swimmer Ethelda Bleibtrey dominated at the Antwerp Games, winning gold in all three women’s swimming events. Epstein and Handley would continue to work in partnership in subsequent Olympics, paving the way for—and training—Gertrude Ederle to become one of the best swimmers of all time.

鉴于“埃皮的女孩们”所树立的榜样，尤其是在公众心目中女性身着泳装往往带有某种不雅意味的印象，埃普斯坦精心指导她的游泳运动员们在水中和水中都取得成功。她确保她们举止得体，彬彬有礼，衣着考究。

Mindful of the example that was made of “Eppie’s girls,” especially given the risqué association in the public mind with women in bathing suits, Epstein carefully shepherded her swimmers to success both in and out of the water. She made sure they behaved as ladies, had impeccable manners, and dressed well.

埃德勒是爱泼斯坦笔下最成功的案例：1921年至1925年间，埃德勒保持着惊人的29项全国和世界业余游泳纪录——这些纪录的创造涵盖了前所未有的各种距离和条件，从泳池短距离冲刺到数英里长的公开水域比赛——她也因此成为那个时代最受爱戴的体育英雄之一。正如格伦·斯托特在其为埃德勒所作的传记《年轻女子与大海》中所述，“‘埃德勒创造世界纪录’的标题在体育版面上的出现频率，堪比‘贝比·鲁斯击出本垒打’。”

Ederle was Epstein’s ultimate success story: between 1921 and 1925, Ederle held an astounding twenty-nine national and world amateur swimming records—setting those records in an unprecedented range of distances and conditions, from sprints in a pool to miles-long open-water races—and became one of the era’s most beloved sports heroes. As Glenn Stout notes in his biography of Ederle, Young Woman and the Sea, “‘Ederle Sets World Record’ became as common a headline in the sports pages as ‘Ruth Hits Home Run.’”

在1924年巴黎夏季奥运会上，埃德勒克服了诸多不利因素，包括膝伤以及女子队参赛人数不足，最终获得三枚奖牌，一枚金牌和两枚铜牌。她们每天要花五六个小时才能到奥运比赛泳池训练。美国官员不希望这些易受影响的年轻女子与道德观念可疑的巴黎人混在一起——因此她们被流放到巴黎郊区。

During the 1924 Summer Olympics in Paris, Ederle won three medals, one gold and two bronze, despite adverse conditions: an injured knee and the fact that the women’s team had to travel five to six hours a day just to practice in the Olympic competition pool. American officials didn’t want the impressionable young women to mingle with Parisians of questionable morality—hence the exile to the outskirts of Paris.

对自己在奥运会上的表现感到失望后，埃德勒将目光投向了成为首位横渡英吉利海峡的女性。在那个年代，横渡这条冰冷险恶、波涛汹涌、狂风肆虐的海峡被认为是一项惊人的壮举。1925年，埃德勒和爱泼斯坦前往英国，准备进行她的首次尝试。然而，在她游到一半时，他们的英国向导误以为她溺水，碰了碰她，导致她被取消资格。沮丧的埃德勒后来解释说，她当时只是在休息。第二年，埃德勒上演了一场史诗般的逆转，她以两小时的优势打破了男子纪录。伦敦劳埃德保险公司为埃德勒的横渡开出了五比一的赔率，认为她不可能成功。埃德勒的父亲亨利因此获得了丰厚的奖金。她回到纽约后，迎接她的是漫天飞舞的彩带。

Disappointed with her performance at the Olympics, Ederle set her sights on being the first woman to swim the English Channel. A swim crossing in the frigid, forbidding strait, often chopped by waves and wind, was considered a monumental physical feat during that era. In 1925, Ederle and Epstein traveled to England for Ederle’s first attempt. She was disqualified when their British guide, thinking she was drowning, touched her halfway through the swim; a frustrated Ederle later said she was just resting. In the most epic of comebacks, Ederle returned the next year and smashed the men’s record by two hours. Lloyd’s of London took bets on Ederle, laying five-to-one odds against her making it across. Ederle’s father, Henry, collected handsomely. She came home to New York and was greeted by a blizzard of ticker tape.

夏洛特·爱泼斯坦最终带领她的游泳队员创造了五十多项世界纪录。在接下来的十年及更长时间里，《纽约时报》频繁报道女子游泳协会的“女游泳明星”，她们在当时各种游泳锦标赛上的垄断地位无人能及。该俱乐部培养了如此多的“本地美人鱼”，以至于当报纸上出现一位速度飞快的新“水仙女”，被誉为冉冉升起的埃德勒游泳俱乐部新星时，几乎已成过眼云烟。

Charlotte Epstein eventually led her swimmers to more than fifty world records. Through the next decade and beyond, the New York Times wrote frequently about the Women’s Swimming Association’s “girl swim stars,” whose monopoly on various swimming championships during the period was unparalleled. So many “local mermaids” had been turned out by the club that it was almost old news when a speedy new naiad was introduced in the paper’s pages as a coming Ederle.

达拉·托雷斯14岁时就打破了50米自由泳世界纪录，那是在1982年，她宛如一位速度惊人的新星。她参加了1984年和1988年奥运会，分别获得接力赛的金牌、银牌和铜牌。大学毕业后，她便退役了，以为自己的泳坛生涯就此结束。“那时候，人们都觉得我老了，”她说。她当时才刚过二十岁。但是，和埃德勒一样，托雷斯对自己在早期奥运会上的表现并不完全满意。她当时还没有获得过个人奖牌。

Dara Torres first broke the 50-meter-freestyle world record as a fourteen-year-old, back in 1982, the very picture of a speedy new naiad. She swam in the 1984 and 1988 Olympics, winning relay gold, silver, and bronze, and retired after college, thinking that was that. “At that point in my life, I was considered old,” she says. She was barely in her twenties. But, like Ederle, Torres wasn’t totally happy with her performance at those early Olympics. She hadn’t yet won an individual medal.

为了进入电视行业，她在NBC体育频道找到了一份实习生的差事。一天，她正在整理录像带——当时，德高望重的花样滑冰运动员布莱恩·博伊塔诺正在谈论复出，以及这对他的意义。她突然灵光一闪。“我也想那样做。” 1992年美国奥运选拔赛前11个月，她搬到了佛罗里达州开始训练。

Looking to get into television, she took a menial job as an intern at NBC Sports. One day, she was logging tape—the venerable figure skater Brian Boitano was talking about making a comeback, and what it would mean to him to do it. A bell went off in her head. I want to do that. Eleven months before the 1992 US Olympic trials, she moved to Florida to train.

托雷斯当选为1992年巴塞罗那奥运会代表团的队长，并再次赢得接力金牌。“我是队里年纪最大的，当时25岁，”她回忆道，“他们都叫我‘奶奶’。”之后她再次退役，七年间再也没有下过泳池。

Torres was elected a team captain of the 1992 delegation to Barcelona and won another relay gold. “I was the oldest woman on the team, at twenty-five,” she remembers. “They called me Granny.” She retired again and didn’t get in the pool for seven years.

1999年春天，在朋友和母亲的劝说下，她第二次复出，备战2000年悉尼奥运会，并斩获五枚奖牌，其中三枚是个人奖牌。在她完成最后一场比赛后走出赛场时，一位记者拦住她进行采访。“你之前已经七年没游泳了，”他问道，“你觉得你41岁还会复出吗？”

In the spring of 1999, at the coaxing of her friends and her mother, she unretired for the second time, training for the Sydney Olympics in 2000 and winning five medals, three of them individual this time. When she was walking out of the arena after her final event, a reporter stopped her for an interview. “You didn’t swim for seven years before this,” he said. “Do you think you’ll be back at forty-one?”

“我当时想，‘是吗？’”她说。她回家后，在33岁时第三次退休，认为自己已经没有什么需要证明的了。

“I was like, ‘Yeah, right,’” she says. She went home and retired a third time, at thirty-three, thinking that she had nothing left to prove.

那位记者果然很有先见之明。2008年，41岁的托雷斯在赢得第一枚奥运奖牌近25年后重返泳池。她在怀孕期间开始游泳，试图在缓解孕吐的同时进行锻炼。尽管腹部隆起，呕吐的冲动几乎一直伴随着她，她还是忍不住和隔壁泳道的中年男子比赛。输给他让她抓狂。也正是在那时，她开始意识到自己已经准备好再次复出。但这一切发生得比她预想的要快得多：女儿出生几个月后，她出人意料地游出了足以让她获得2008年美国奥运选拔赛资格的成绩。

That reporter showed himself to be prescient. In 2008, at forty-one, nearly two and a half decades after her first Olympic medal, Torres was back in the pool. She took up swimming during pregnancy, in an attempt to get exercise while coping with nausea, and despite her burgeoning belly and the near-constant urge to throw up, she found herself unable to resist racing the middle-aged man in the next lane. It drove her crazy not to beat him. And that’s when she began to suspect she was ready for yet another comeback. But it happened more quickly than she expected: a few months after her daughter was born, she surprised herself by swimming well enough to qualify for the 2008 US Olympic trials.

正如埃德加·爱伦·坡所说，竞争不断地将她逼到悬崖边。这一次，悬崖边是第四道。

Competition kept coaxing her back to the edge of the precipice, as Edgar Allan Poe called it. This time, the precipice was lane four.

第四泳道。镜头再次回到托雷斯所在的北京奥运会50米自由泳决赛出发台。游泳运动员们依次上前，在等待裁判的声音时，最后一次抖动四肢。“各就各位！”随着一声蜂鸣，他们从出发台上腾空而起，在空中划出一道弧线，将自己弹入泳池。

Lane four. We’re back with Torres at the starting blocks of that 50-meter freestyle final in Beijing. The swimmers step up, shaking out limbs one more time as they listen for the race official’s voice. Swimmers take your mark. At the beep, they fly off the blocks, with a mid-air undulation that propels each of them into the pool.

正如其“水花四溅”的绰号一样，50米自由泳是一场疯狂而又泡沫四溅的比赛——在这个比赛中，比赛时间只有24秒。在篮球比赛中，这段时间就是进攻时间。一名NFL球员可以跑完球场全程……着陆后，还有大把时间可以跳个滑稽的舞。国际空间站能飞行一百二十英里。二十四秒足够吃个甜甜圈，把凉的咖啡热一下，给朋友发条生日短信。但在泳池里，你看到的只是八条泳道，一场勉强控制的风暴从一端翻滚到另一端，气泡翻腾。

True to its splash-and-dash nickname, the 50-meter free is a frantic, foamy blur—in this case, it’s one that lasts twenty-four seconds. In basketball, that interval is the shot clock. An NFL player can run the length of the field for a touchdown, with an eternity left over to do a funny dance. The international space station can travel a hundred and twenty miles. Twenty-four seconds is time enough to eat a doughnut, heat up coffee that’s gone cold, compose a birthday text to a friend. But in the pool all you see is eight lanes of a barely contained tempest churning up bubbles from one end to the other.

在北京的比赛中，托雷斯从一开始就保持领先，她强劲的双臂以相对稳定高效的划水频率挥动着。在最后的冲刺阶段，她的指尖似乎率先触到了池壁。然而，在慢镜头回放的水下画面中，德国选手布里塔·斯特芬（Britta Steffen）从托雷斯的左侧强势反击。当托雷斯滑入池中时，斯特芬的手从她身边掠过，用时24.06秒。托雷斯的成绩是24.07秒。斯特芬以百分之一秒的优势夺得金牌。

In that race in Beijing, Torres held the lead from the start, her powerful arms turning over at a relatively controlled and efficient stroke rate. In the final push, her fingertips appeared to be the first to reach for the wall. In the slowed-down underwater footage, though, lane three, Britta Steffen of Germany, comes in strong on Torres’s left. As Torres glides in, Steffen’s hand surges just past, 24.06 seconds. Torres’s time: 24.07 seconds. Steffen won gold by one-hundredth of a second.

百分之一秒。比蜂鸟扇动翅膀的时间还短。比眨眼的时间还短。

One-hundredth of a second. It’s less than a flap of a hummingbird’s wing. Less than the blink of an eye.

托雷斯记得当时她身处泳池，震惊得说不出话来。无论结果如何，她都想表达敬意，于是她潜入泳道线下，祝贺斯特芬获得金牌，坎贝尔获得铜牌。然而，当她潜入水中时，脑海中却充斥着咒骂和疑问。百分之一秒？我到底做错了什么？我这辈子都要为此耿耿于怀。我还能做得更好吗？就差百分之一秒？

Torres remembers being in the pool, dumbstruck. No matter the result, she wanted to be respectful, so she ducked under the lane lines to congratulate Steffen on the gold and Campbell on the bronze. As she went underwater, though, expletives and questions rattled around in her head. One-hundredth of a second? What did I do? I’m going to be thinking about this for the rest of my life. How could I have done this better? One-hundredth?

她打电话给她的私人教练迈克尔·洛伯格，当时他正在马里兰州的一家医院病床上接受血液疾病治疗，她问他……她做错了。“你触碰终点板的力度不够，”他说。在50米自由泳颁奖仪式上领取银牌两分钟后，她又回到泳池边，准备参加4×100米混合泳接力赛的最后一棒自由泳比赛。在那场比赛中，她游出了接力赛历史上最快的100米自由泳分段成绩。她触碰终点板的力度过大，导致韧带撕裂，拇指骨折。她们最终获得了银牌。

She called her personal coach, Michael Lohberg, who was watching from a hospital bed in Maryland, where he was receiving treatment for a blood disorder, and asked him what she did wrong. “You didn’t touch the pad hard enough,” he said. Two minutes after picking up her silver at the 50-meter medal ceremony, she was back on deck again to swim the anchor freestyle leg of the 4 × 100-meter medley relay. In that race, she swam the fastest 100-meter freestyle split in relay history. She hit the touchpad on the finish so hard that she tore a ligament and broke her thumb. They won silver.

托雷斯比起赢球更痛恨失败。我问她是如何从那百分之一秒的失利中走出来的。“那件事确实让我难过了好一阵子，”她若有所思地承认道，“我反复回想了无数遍，最终不得不接受这个事实：那场比赛对我来说是完美的。我必须释怀。我已经41岁了，足够成熟，不会再纠结于那百分之一秒。”她意识到，即使输掉比赛，那仍然是一次完美的游泳。

More than she likes to win, Torres hates to lose. I ask her how she recovered from the one-hundredth-of-a-second heartbreak. “It did stay with me for a while,” she admits thoughtfully. “I had to come to terms with it, after going over it so many times in my head, that the race was a perfect race for me. I had to be OK with it. I was mature enough, at forty-one, to not dwell on one-hundredth of a second.” She realized she could lose a race and still have it be a perfect swim.

12

12

如何像刺客一样游泳

How to Swim Like an Assassin

在体育界，游泳比赛是一种混合形式：个人项目以团队比赛的形式计分。这意味着，尽管你为团队的胜利或失败做出了贡献，但比赛的体验却是孤独的。即使是接力赛，你参与的那部分团队比赛也是独自进行的。

In the sporting world, swim meets are a hybrid: individual events scored as team competition. Which means that though you contribute to your team’s victory or defeat, the experience of a race is a lonely one. Even in a relay event, your particular sliver of team competition is conducted in solitude.

跃入水中，人群的喧嚣瞬间消失殆尽。你仿佛置身于一种感官隔绝的状态，视野受限于泳镜，或许也受限于刺眼的阳光。你急于游到泳池另一端再返回（如果是接力赛，还要将泳棒交给下一位选手），但首先要应对的，是你自己大脑的运转。田径、自行车或体操比赛的形式与之类似，表面上所有人都像在进行一场和谐的交响乐，但游泳比赛的水域环境却将运动员的个人能力发挥到了极致。

Hit the water, and all the sound and fury of the crowd is stripped away. You are swimming in a kind of sensory isolation, peripheral vision limited by your goggles, or perhaps by the glare of the sun. In your haste to get to the other end of the pool and back (and hand off to the next swimmer if it’s a relay race), there is first and foremost your own brain to contend with. A track or cycling or gymnastics meet is similar in format, everyone ostensibly working in symphony, but the swim meet’s aquatic environment enhances the athlete’s solo to the extreme.

我想要了解的是运动员内部的视角。要想在这个运动的最高水平上取得成功，运动员需要具备怎样的心态？我联系了运动心理学家吉姆·鲍曼，他从2004年到2016年，鲍曼与美国奥运游泳队合作了四个奥运周期，深入了解精英游泳运动员的心理状态。许多运动心理学家认为游泳90%取决于心理因素，但鲍曼却认为恰恰相反。“他们谈论正念，但我更倾向于无念的状态， ”他解释道。在他看来，他的工作就是不断缩小心理因素的影响，让游泳运动员在比赛时“就像767客机开启了自动驾驶模式”——他们由生物力学和比赛计划控制，而不是受情绪或担忧的干扰。正如空乘人员所说，心理和情绪的包袱都被安全地“托运”了。

The view from within is what I’m after. What frame of mind does a competitor need to succeed at the highest level of this sport? I call up Jim Bauman, a sports psychologist who worked with the US Olympic swim team over four Olympic cycles, from 2004 to 2016, for a peek inside the elite swimming brain. A lot of sports psychologists describe swimming as 90 percent mental, but in a way Bauman thinks it’s the opposite. “They talk about mindfulness, but I think of it more like mindlessness,” he explains. His job, as he sees it, is to make that mental piece smaller and smaller and smaller, so that when it’s time for the swimmers to race, “the 767 is on autopilot”—they’re controlled by their biomechanics and their race plan, not their emotions or worries. The mental and emotional baggage is, as the flight attendants say, safely stowed away.

日复一日，在同一个泳池里。你能看到隔壁泳道的人，却无法真正和他们交谈。来回游动，目光始终盯着泳池底部的黑线。这段时间里，你会有很多时间思考，稍不留神，恐惧就会占据你的心头。对于精英游泳运动员来说，那条线简直就是个威胁，一个你会逐渐憎恨的东西。比赛当天，你会问自己：这一切真的值得吗？鲍曼说，即使你取得了成功，你脑海中那巨大的空洞也会放大你的自负和自我对话，让这一切不断回响。

Every day, day after day, in the same pool. You can see people in the next lane, but you can’t really talk to them. Back and forth, back and forth, staring down at the black line at the bottom of the pool. It’s a lot of time to think, and if you aren’t careful, fear can take over. Among elite swimmers, that line is a menace, a thing you can grow to hate. You show up on competition day and ask yourself, Was all of that worth it? Even if you’re successful, Bauman says, the cavernous space of your head amplifies the ego and the self-talk and makes it all echo.

目前世界最佳游泳运动员凯蒂·莱德基或许有一种特殊的清空思绪的能力。恐惧是大多数运动员面临的主要问题，但鲍曼认为她与众不同。莱德基目前保持着女子400米、800米和1500米自由泳的世界纪录。在2016年里约奥运会上，她打破了自己保持的纪录。她以惊人的优势打破了400米和800米自由泳的世界纪录。2018年，她又将自己的1500米世界纪录提高了5秒。到21岁时，她已经创造了14项世界纪录。当你读到这篇文章时，她可能又创造了更多纪录。

The best swimmer in the world at the moment, Katie Ledecky, may have a special knack for clearing her head. Fear is a major issue for most athletes, but Bauman thinks she’s wired differently. Ledecky currently holds the world records in the 400-, 800-, and 1,500-meter freestyle. At the 2016 Olympics in Rio de Janeiro, she obliterated her own world records in the 400-meter and 800-meter freestyle races by jaw-dropping margins. In 2018, she beat her 1,500-meter record by five seconds. By the time she was twenty-one years old, she had set fourteen world records. By the time you read this, she may have added even more.

如果你听莱德基谈论游泳，你就会明白她有多么专注。多年前，15岁的她还是个初出茅庐的新秀，备战她的首场国际赛事——2012年伦敦奥运会。她当时就设想过自己的比赛，而她心中只有一个目标：金牌。

If you listen to Ledecky talk about swimming, you begin to realize how single-minded her focus is. Years ago, as a fifteen-year-old upstart preparing for her first international meet, the 2012 London Olympics, she visualized her race. She never visualized winning anything but gold.

“她是那支奥运代表队里最年轻的队员，要在卫冕冠军的主场泳池里与他同场竞技，”莱德基的教练布鲁斯·杰梅尔在马里兰州通过电话告诉我。他在那里执教于首都游泳俱乐部，伦敦奥运会后，他一直在那里训练莱德基，直到里约奥运会。“当被问及是否紧张时，她说她从不让自己去想除了胜利之外的任何事情。”他最喜欢用一句话来形容莱德基的比赛心态。“她不怕失败，”他说，“但失败对她来说永远不是一个选项。”

“She was the youngest on that Olympic team, racing against the reigning champion in that champion’s home pool,” Ledecky’s coach for four years, Bruce Gemmell, tells me by phone from Maryland, where he coaches the Nation’s Capital Swim Club. That’s where he trained Ledecky after London and up through the Rio Olympics. “When asked if she was nervous, she said she never let herself picture anything else but winning.” He has a favorite way to describe Ledecky’s mindset in competition. “She’s not afraid of failure,” he says, “but failure is never an option.”

在备战里约奥运会的日常训练中，杰梅尔说她失败得非常惨烈——而这恰恰也是关键所在。“她总是愿意在训练中全力以赴，她失败的次数比我执教过的任何人都多，但这仅仅是因为我们把标准定得太高了，”他解释道。“她努力去挑战，即使她没能达到规定的时间，或者她状态下滑、力竭，但她至少在尝试中取得了成功。而且她第二天还会回来，继续努力。”

On a day-to-day level in practice as they prepared for Rio, Gemmell says she failed spectacularly—and that, too, was key. “She was always willing to stick her neck out in training, and she failed more than anyone else I’ve ever coached, but that’s only because we set the bar so high,” he explains. “She reached for it, and even if she didn’t achieve the times on the sets, or if she faltered and faded, she succeeded in the attempts. And she came back the next day and did it again.”

莱德基目前是斯坦福大学的本科生，主修心理学。在一门名为“信念如何创造现实”的课程中，她被要求讲述自己如何运用目标设定和心理意象赢得奥运金牌。在一份PPT演示文稿中，她谈到了杰梅尔，并解释了失败如何成为通往成功的关键垫脚石——以及不惧失败如何帮助她相信自己能够实现设定的目标。

As an undergraduate at Stanford University, Ledecky is now a psychology major. For one course, How Beliefs Create Reality, she was asked to talk about how she had used goal setting and mental imagery to win her gold medals. In one PowerPoint presentation, she talked about Gemmell and explained how failure is a critical stepping-stone for success—and how not being afraid to fail helped her to believe that she could accomplish the goals she set.

杰梅尔告诉我，莱德基在比赛中有一种特殊的自信。那不是傲慢。“菲尔普斯在比赛中也展现了同样的自信，”他说。“但与此同时，在备战阶段，凯蒂会痴迷于任何细节，或者说任何能让她进步的关键事项。”

Gemmell tells me that, in competition, Ledecky has a specific kind of confidence. It’s not an arrogance. “Michael Phelps took that same confidence into competition,” he says. “And yet at the same time, in the prep, Katie would be obsessed with any detail, or major thing, that she could in practice do to get better.”

运动心理学家鲍曼多年来一直与海豹突击队合作。他甚至曾带领奥运选手到加州与海豹突击队一起进行障碍训练。“人们总是问我，在如此混乱的情况下，海豹突击队是如何保持专注的，因为各种事情都可能同时发生，”他说道。“海豹突击队的优势在于能够从纷繁复杂的环境中找到关键信息，而不会被无关紧要的事情和噪音所干扰。他们专注于任务和目标，仅此而已。”

Bauman, the sports psychologist, has worked with Navy SEALs for years. He has even taken Olympic athletes to do obstacle-course training sessions with them in California. “People always ask me how Navy SEALs are able to maintain focus in such crazy situations, when so many things can be coming at you,” he says. “What SEALs are good at is being able to find what is relevant in a situation, and they don’t get distracted by all the irrelevant stuff, the noise. They focus on the job, the objective, and that’s it.”

对游泳运动员来说，这些都是无关紧要的事情：我分到哪条泳道？谁在我旁边游？观众席上有什么人？计时器在哪儿？社交媒体上有人怎么评价我？水温是多少？ “这些都与你作为游泳运动员的工作无关，”鲍曼说。训练时，你应该专注于生物力学：你的出发、踢腿、呼吸和节奏。他试图教他的游泳队员在比赛中也这样做。“你的任务是从A点以最快的速度游到B点。你的对手在做什么与你需要做什么无关。这就是海豹突击队的思维方式。”

Irrelevant stuff for a swimmer: What lane did I get? Who’s swimming next to me? Who’s in the crowd? Where’s the clock? What did social media say about me? What’s the temperature of the water? “That has nothing to do with your job as a swimmer,” Bauman says. In training, you focus on biomechanics: your start, your kick, your breathing and rhythm. He tries to teach his swimmers to do the same thing in a race. “Your job is to swim as fast as possible from point A to point B. What your competitor is doing is irrelevant to what you need to do. And that’s the way the Navy SEALs think.”

那些能够随时发挥出色水平的运动员——比如托雷斯、菲尔普斯和莱德基——与海豹突击队员颇为相似，以至于鲍曼在2016年里约奥运会上给美国游泳运动员的口号是：像海豚一样游泳，像海豹突击队员一样思考。 “显然，精英运动员和特种作战人员面临的风险截然不同，”他告诉我，“但他们的思维方式却很相似。”在泳池里，莱德基被形容为“刺客”、“冷酷无情”、“毫不留情”。说到游泳界最优秀的头脑，我想，最顶尖的竞技游泳运动员与最顶尖的战士拥有一些共同的特质，这应该不足为奇。

Athletes who can perform on demand—Torres, Phelps, Ledecky—are enough like SEALs that this was Bauman’s mantra for the American swimmers in Rio, in 2016: Swim like a dolphin, think like a SEAL. “Clearly, the stakes are much different between elite athletes and special operations war fighters,” he tells me, “but the thinking is similar.” In the pool, Ledecky has been described as “an assassin,” “stone-cold,” “pitiless.” When it comes to the best minds for swimming, I suppose it shouldn’t be surprising that the most elite competitive swimmers share traits with the most elite fighters.

托雷斯、莱德基和菲尔普斯之所以能取得成功，其中一个重要原因是他们能够永无止境地刻苦训练，最终达到一种“自动驾驶”状态——鲍曼所描述的那种“无意识”状态。这种持续不断的练习和所需的坚定不移的专注力，本身就是一种耐力。

What sets Torres, Ledecky, and Phelps apart as successes includes the ability to grind it out, forever and ever and ever, in the interest of achieving autopilot—the mindlessness that Bauman describes. The constant rehearsal, and the unwavering focus that’s required, is its own kind of endurance.

菲尔普斯是奥运史上最成功的选手，为了赢得奥运冠军，他进行了大量的心理演练。他会想象比赛的场景、感觉和气味，并以生动的剧本和画面形式描绘出自己希望比赛中发生的一切。他还会思考可能出现的干扰因素以及如何应对。他尤其注重专注于自己的泳道。“专注于自己的泳道”意味着不再关注其他选手的动向。

Phelps, the winningest Olympian of them all, did plenty of mental rehearsals for his Olympic victories. What a race looks like, feels like, smells like. What you want to happen in that race, in the form of a vivid script and images. What distractions may come and how to manage them. He visualized staying in his lane. “Stay in your lane” meant stop worrying about what everyone else was doing.

他的长期教练鲍勃·鲍曼告诉他不要说“不能”这个词。菲尔普斯最近说，鲍曼这样做是为了“让我开阔眼界，相信自己能做到任何想做的事情”。他认为，这正是他们共同取得成功的关键。

His longtime coach, Bob Bowman, told him not to say the word can’t. Bowman did that, Phelps said recently, “so I could broaden my mind and believe that I could do whatever I wanted to.” That, he thinks, was key to their success together.

但我不得不指出，长时间的游泳训练很难保持高度专注。水流终究会侵蚀最坚硬的岩石。在精英级别，游泳运动员每天要下水两次，每次训练游六到十二英里，休息日少之又少。这样的训练强度难以承受。时间一分一秒地流逝。一圈又一圈，景色依旧。多年来，即使是那位最终斩获二十八枚奥运奖牌、意志如钢铁般的冠军也曾崩溃。那条黑线一直困扰着他。在追逐奖牌的过程中，菲尔普斯曾与自杀念头和抑郁症作斗争。竞技游泳是孤独的。随着时间的推移，泳池对他而言仿佛变成了一个无法逃脱的鱼缸。

But I can’t help but point out that hyperfocus is hard to sustain over decades of swimming. Water erodes even the hardest rocks over time. At the elite level, a swimmer is in the pool twice a day, logging six to twelve miles a session, with precious few days off. It is a punishing regimen to sustain. The clock ticks. Lap after lap, the unchanging scenery. Over the years, even the steel-willed champion who ended up with twenty-eight Olympic medals broke down. The black line bedeviled him. In the chase for those medals, Phelps battled suicidal thoughts and depression. Competitive swimming is lonely. As time went on, the pool contracted, becoming a fishbowl he couldn’t escape.

我们当然无法真正了解精英游泳运动员的内心世界。我们只能了解他们告诉我们的。和托雷斯一样，菲尔普斯也曾短暂退役。他开始公开谈论抑郁症和心理健康问题。2014年，他最终进入康复中心接受治疗，以戒除药物滥用。在康复期间，他试图理解持续不断的比赛是如何让他精疲力竭的，以及他是如何质疑自己作为奖牌获得者之外的人的价值的。他记起自己热爱游泳，仍然想继续游泳。但他意识到，自己的人生目标已经发生了转变，从首先成为一名竞技游泳运动员，转变为首先成为一名丈夫和父亲。

We can’t really get inside the heads of elite swimmers, of course. We only know what they tell us. Like Torres, Phelps had temporary retirements. He became vocal about depression and mental health. He ended up in rehab in 2014, to deal with his substance abuse. In recovery, he tried to understand how the constant churn of competition wore him down and how he had questioned his own value as a person apart from the swimmer who won medals. He remembered that he loved to swim. That he still wanted to do it. But he realized that his personal objectives had shifted, from being a competitive swimmer first to being a husband and father first.

康复后，在备战里约奥运会期间——他最终赢得了六枚奖牌，其中五枚是金牌——菲尔普斯大部分训练时间都花在了室外泳池，这对他来说是一种全新的体验。他第一次有了新的视野。“在室外，你会感受到一种截然不同的能量，”菲尔普斯告诉《体育画报》，“游完泳，抬头望去，是万里无云的蓝天。这对我来说太神奇了。”

Post-rehab, in the lead-up to Rio—where he would win six medals, five of them gold—he spent most of his training time in an outdoor pool, which was new to him. For the first time, there was something else to look at. “You have a different energy outside,” Phelps told Sports Illustrated. “You finish swimming and look up, and it’s a blue sky with no clouds. That’s pretty amazing to me.”

一项关于美国流行游泳队名称、其对应的动物特征以及分布地点的非官方调查：

An unofficial survey of popular swim team names, their native animal traits, and where they are found in the United States:

梭鱼：通常广泛分布于温带和热带海域；以其巨大的牙齿、凶猛的行为和滥杀无辜而闻名。加利福尼亚州、佛罗里达州和马里兰州均有游泳队目击到梭鱼。

Barracudas: normally distributed widely in temperate, tropical seas; noted for large teeth, vicious behavior, and indiscriminate killing. Swim team sightings in California, Florida, Maryland.

鳄鱼：除南极洲和欧洲以外，遍布各大洲；某些种类的鳄鱼吼声响亮，尾巴强劲有力，非常适合游泳。加利福尼亚州、印第安纳州、佛罗里达州和德克萨斯州拥有数量可观的鳄鱼种群。

Crocodiles: native to every continent except Antarctica and Europe; certain species have loud roars and powerful tails excellent for swimming. Significant swim team populations located in California, Indiana, Florida, and Texas.

锤头鲨：分布于全球所有热带水域；雄性和雌性大锤头鲨均为独居且对人类具有危险性，而雌性扇形锤头鲨则倾向于成群结队地聚集在一起。游泳队分布广泛，从新泽西州、马里兰州和佐治亚州到加利福尼亚州和俄勒冈州均有发现。

Hammerheads: found in all tropical waters worldwide; male and female great hammerheads are both solitary and dangerous to humans, while scalloped hammerhead females tend to congregate in large schools. Swim teams widely distributed, from New Jersey, Maryland, and Georgia to California and Oregon.

虎鲸：分布于世界各大洋，从北极到南极均有发现；它们是高度社会化的鲸类，通常成群结队地生活。他们一起游泳，协调彼此的活动，包括教导年幼的同伴如何捕猎以及如何成为好父母。游泳队的群体分布范围同样很广，包括佐治亚州、伊利诺伊州和德克萨斯州等地。

Orcas: found in all oceans of the world, from the Arctic to the Antarctic; they are highly social, and whales in a pod swim together and coordinate their activities, including teaching younger pod members how to hunt and how to be good parents. Swim team populations have similarly wide-ranging communities, including locations in Georgia, Illinois, and Texas.

海獭：栖息于俄罗斯、阿留申群岛、加拿大、阿拉斯加、俄勒冈州和加利福尼亚州太平洋沿岸的近海海藻林中；水下游泳速度可达每小时9公里，是优秀的潜水员。游泳队分布区域重叠度很高，尤其是在加利福尼亚州，但分布范围也延伸至威斯康星州等地。

Sea otters: populating offshore kelp forests along the Pacific coasts of Russia, the Aleutian Islands, Canada, Alaska, Oregon, and California; can swim up to nine kilometers an hour underwater and are superb divers. Heavy overlap in swim team distribution, especially in California, but ranging to places including Wisconsin.

龟：通常指菱背龟，一种生活在美国东海岸，在墨西哥湾沿岸也很常见的龟类；它们在陆地和咸淡水沼泽中度过的时间大致相等，但需要饮用淡水。它们逃跑迅速，而且非常擅长游泳。加利福尼亚州、德克萨斯州、纽约州和马里兰州都有很普遍的游泳队。

Terrapins: mostly used to refer to the diamondback terrapin, a species of turtle that lives along the eastern coast of the United States and is also abundant in the Gulf Coast; they spend roughly equal time on land and in brackish, swampy water, though they need fresh water to drink. They are quick to flee and are very good swimmers. Swim teams prevalent in California, Texas, New York, and Maryland.
