团队吉祥物究竟是什么？不就是团队的精神图腾吗？从这些动物学的命名规则中，我们可以解读我们人类的雄心壮志。我们渴望成为游泳健将，成为冷酷无情的竞争者。在野外，速度、力量、耐力和狡猾至关重要，是动物生存成功的关键。泳池里也是如此。

What’s a team mascot, anyway, but a spirit animal for that team? In these zoological naming conventions, we can read our ambitions as a species. We wish to be native swimmers, and merciless competitors. In the wild, speed, power, endurance, and cunning are prized, critical to an animal’s success. And so it is in the pool.

13

13

鲨鱼和小鱼

Sharks and Minnows

从我位于北加州的家到奥尔巴尼水上运动中心不到两英里，在那里，从下午四点左右开始，你可以观察到小游泳运动员的成长历程。在温暖的室内泳池里，孩子们最先下水，他们软绵绵、肌肉松弛的四肢笨拙地游动着，仿佛在进行着一场与协调性截然相反的运动，四肢杂乱无章，像章鱼一样搅动着泡沫般的水花，从泳池边缘游向池中央。有时，他们的前进速度慢得令人难以置信，仿佛他们正逆着物理定律的某个漏洞向后游动。

From where I live in Northern California, it’s less than two miles to the Albany Aquatic Center, where, starting around four in the afternoon, you can observe the life cycle of a young swimmer. In the indoor pool, where the warm water serves as an incubator, the youngest children get in first, their squishy, unmuscled limbs moving in whatever the opposite of coordination is, a sort of octopus-like profusion-confusion of arms and legs churning up foamy water as they convey themselves from the edge of the pool to its middle depths. Sometimes their forward progress slows to such a point that it appears that maybe, just maybe, they are moving backward, through some improbable loophole in the laws of physics.

这些是蝌蚪和海马。至少他们的游泳教练是这么称呼他们的。这位戴着眼镜、活泼开朗的年轻女子，尽管乳胶泳帽和有色泳镜让学生们稚嫩的脸上呈现出统一的轮廓和扭曲的表情，却能准确地叫出每个学生的名字。

These are the tadpoles and the sea horses. Or so they are called by their swimming instructor, a chirpy, bespectacled young woman who, despite the uniformity and distortion that latex swim caps and tinted goggles impose on the tiny faces of her students, somehow knows the names of every single one of them.

半小时后，鳄鱼和短吻鳄入水，随后是海龟和海豚。我喜欢这些组的名字；它们一方面暗示着一种冷酷无情，另一方面又蕴含着一种令人向往的美好品质。但不知为何，这些名字都显得那么真实。年纪稍大的游泳者正在学习仰泳；他们在深水区尝试着基本的跳水动作；他们做出的水下波浪式动作，开始逐渐接近海豚的踢腿动作。

Thirty minutes in, the alligators and crocodiles enter the water, followed by the sea turtles and dolphins. I love the names of these groups; they indicate a ruthlessness on the one hand and a sweetly aspirational quality on the other. But somehow they all feel true. The older swimmers are learning backstroke; they attempt elementary dives in the deep end; they perform the underwater undulations that begin to approximate a recognizable dolphin kick.

一个小时后，真正的游泳健将们到了。他们都是高中游泳队员，个个身形魁梧，宛如阿芙罗狄蒂和阿多尼斯，肌肉线条流畅，体格健壮，岁月似乎并未在他们身上留下任何痕迹。这就是游泳队的样子，至少在北加州是这样。男生们穿着Speedo三角泳裤或紧身及膝泳裤；女生们则穿着各种颜色和款式的吊带连体泳衣或分体泳衣。他们迈着自信的步伐，迈着大步，没有同龄孩子常见的羞涩，从闷热的室内泳池走向凉爽的室外泳池平台。他们一入水，便与水融为一体。他们是水的主人；他们在水中滑行、荡漾，动作和谐。他们努力训练，但看起来却毫不费力。

An hour in, the thoroughbreds arrive. Here are the high school swimmers, broad-shouldered Aphrodites and Adonises all, with their unmarred, smoothly muscled physiques, their sturdy bodies as yet to be marked in any obvious way by life. This is what a swim team looks like, or at least the one here in Northern California. The boys wear Speedo briefs or body-hugging knee-length trunks; the girls have strappy one- and two-piece suits in all manner of color and coverage. They move confidently, in great loping strides, without the self-consciousness so common in kids their age, past the steamy heat of the indoor pool and into the bracing open air of the outdoor pool deck. They get in the water and they are of the water. They are creatures who belong there; they glide and ripple and move in harmony. They work, but it doesn’t look like work.

要判断一个人是否有成为优秀游泳运动员的潜质，可能需要很长时间，甚至长达数年。回顾每一位奥运游泳选手——包括凯蒂·莱德基——她们最初都是那种稚嫩的小游泳健将。甚至有家庭录像带记录了莱德基六岁时在水中奋力游动的场景。在她的第一场比赛中，她全神贯注地在泳池里游，时不时地探出头来，四处张望，寻找对手的身影。最后冲向池壁，然后她脸上绽放出灿烂的笑容。“你在泳池里想什么呢？”有人问她。“什么都没想！”她兴高采烈地喊道，露出一口歪牙。“只是努力游！ ”

It can take a long time to see if someone is going to be a good swimmer, to the tune of years, really. Press rewind on every Olympic swimmer—Katie Ledecky, too—and each starts out as one of those squishy little swimmers. There’s home video evidence of Ledecky as a six-year-old churning away in the pool in her first race, periodically popping her head up and craning around to seek out visuals of her competitors. The final lunge for the wall, then her beaming face afterward. “What were you thinking about in the pool?” she’s asked. “Nothing!” she exclaims, cheerily, crooked teeth everywhere. “Just trying hard!”

我们很多人都曾加入过游泳队，这其中蕴含着值得探讨的共同基础体验。熬过游泳初期那种生死攸关的挣扎阶段，你就会开始体会到水的美好。加入一支队伍，你就会开始珍惜与队友并肩作战的时光。只有当你游泳水平足够高，渴望变得更强时，竞争才会出现。

Many of us have joined a swim team at one time or another, and there is a shared foundational experience here that’s worth examining. Battle past the desperate life-or-death phase of swimming, and you begin to appreciate how good the water feels. Join a team, and you begin to appreciate the company you keep. Competition happens when you get good enough at swimming to want to be better.

从一开始，速度和技巧就至关重要。你一遍又一遍地练习，不断改进泳姿，最终目标是什么？当然是胜利，但胜利转瞬即逝，尤其是在这个阶段。即使是对最年轻的游泳运动员来说，仔细分析胜利的意义，你也会意识到，真正能让你兴奋好几天的，是努力与时机的完美结合。任何游泳队队员，无论水平高低，都能体会到这种感觉。

Right from the start, it becomes about speed, and technique. You work to refine your strokes, over and over again, to achieve—what? The win, yes, but that’s fleeting, especially at this stage. Parse out the win for even the youngest swimmers and you realize that it’s the rare coming together of effort and timing that lifts you for days. That’s a feeling that any swim team swimmer knows, no matter their level.

即使到了现在，我依然能感受到自己身上那种与生俱来的自信，这要归功于游泳队。我个子不高：身高只有五英尺五英寸（约1.65米），而且还得看我有没有记得挺直腰杆。但在水里，我却能感受到自己的力量。

Even now, I can trace a certain kind of physical confidence that I have all the way back to swim team. I am not a big person: five feet five on the days I remember to stand up straight. But the water is the one place I feel powerful.

我至今仍保存着一叠钢笔蜡笔画，用订书钉仔细装订在一起，日期是1984年7月4日。在这些画作——“从我六岁起”——中，我站着在跳板上，身着条纹泳衣，光彩夺目，然后纵身跃入空中。入水和游向梯子的方式多种多样：前跳、后跳、炮弹式跳水、开罐器式跳水、铅笔式跳水……我全都记录了下来。那是夏天。我热爱游泳。事情就是这样。

I still have in my possession a sheaf of pen-and-crayon drawings, carefully stapled together and dated July 4, 1984. In those pages—“From When I Was Six Years Old”—I stand on the diving board, glorious in stripes, before springing boldly into the air. There were so many ways to enter the water and swim for the ladder: forward dive, back dive, cannonball, can opener, pencil drop . . . I documented them all. It was summer. I loved swimming. That was the short of it.

照片展现出一种喜悦和娴熟的自在。但关键在于“熟练”二字。如果你能翻开照片背后的故事，你会发现一段丰富的经历。我之所以能在水中如此自由、自信和强大，是因为我已经花费了数百小时学习游泳。

The pictures show a joy and a practiced ease. But the operative word here is practiced. If you could peek at the pages between those pages, you would find a dense backstory. I could be free and confident and strong in the water because I’d already spent hundreds of hours learning how to swim.

我们学会了仰泳和俯泳：身体在水中平静地悬浮。我们学会了屏住呼吸和踢腿：这是推进的基础节奏。我们学会了基本的仰泳（向上、向外、并拢）和侧泳（摘苹果放进篮子）：这是休息的基本动作。我们学会了自由泳以及如何侧脸呼吸：这是前进动力的来源。我们学会了蛙泳以及如何抬头呼吸：这是安全锁定目标的关键。所有这些，每个夏天的平日，从早上九点到十点半，都通过反复练习牢记于心。那时，我们努力练习，是为了做到毫不费力。

We learned front floats and back floats: the calm suspension of our bodies in water. We learned to hold our breath and kick our feet: the foundation rhythms of propulsion. We learned elementary backstroke (up, out, together) and sidestroke (pick the apple and put it in the basket): the essential strokes of rest. We learned freestyle and how to breathe with our faces to the side: the drive of forward momentum. We learned breaststroke and how to breathe with our heads up: the safe sighting of a destination. All of this was drilled into us by repetition, every summer weekday, from nine to ten-thirty in the morning. We put in effort, then, to be effortless.

我们的游泳队叫弗里波特海魔队。我喜欢所有提高速度的方法：借助浮板上下漂浮，学习如何从出发台上飞驰而出，以及拼命踢腿直到双腿酸痛。大多数时候，努力的回报并不会立刻显现。我和哥哥、堂兄弟们经常和大孩子们一起玩游戏：鲨鱼和小鱼、水球、马可波罗。还有钩梯子游戏，其中一个伙伴会抓住另一个伙伴。两人双腿相接，形成一个弗兰肯斯坦式的游泳者：一人踢腿，一人拉拽，不可避免地导致从泳池一端到另一端滑稽地推拉动作。

Our swim team was the Freeport Sea Devils. I loved all the different ways of getting faster: bobbing along with pull buoys, learning how to soar off the starting blocks, kicking until your legs burned. Most of the time, the payoff wasn’t clear right away. My brother and cousins and I played games with the big kids: sharks and minnows, water polo, Marco Polo. Hook and ladder, in which one partner would hold on to the other’s legs to form a single Frankenswimmer: one person kicking, the other pulling, inevitably resulting in a comically jerky push-pull action from one end of the pool to the other.

我们一年四季都游泳。夏天，早上在奥林匹克规格的室外泳池训练，训练结束后我和安迪就回家看动画片。冬天，放学后在室内训练，一直持续到很晚，我的头发经常在回家的车上冻僵。

We swam year-round. In the summer, morning practices were held in the Olympic-size outdoor pool, after which Andy and I would come home and watch cartoons. In the winter, when practices were held indoors after school and ran late into the evenings, my hair would freeze on the car ride home.

在大赛前，我们会举办意面派对，为我们饥肠辘辘、正在成长的身体补充碳水化合物。用锡纸盘盛着的千层面、肉丸意大利面、烤通心粉，都是队员家长们精心烹制的。年复一年，在分区锦标赛上，我们都屈居亚军，输给了我们的劲敌回声公园队。有一年，我们的教练和我们做了个交易：如果我们整个赛季保持不败，并在锦标赛上击败回声公园队，我们就可以剃光他的头。

We had pasta parties before big meets, to carbo-load our hungry, growing bodies. Aluminum-foil trays of lasagna, spaghetti and meatballs, baked ziti, made lovingly by team parents. Year after year at the division championships, we came in second to Echo Park, our rival team. One year, our coach made a deal with us: if we went undefeated in the season and beat Echo Park at the championship meet, we could shave his head.

那一年，我们赢了。庆祝派对上，我们把他扔进泳池，剃光了他那头棕色的卷发。那天晚上有一张照片，我们整个游泳队都挤在泳池边。小孩子们在前面，高举双臂，欣喜若狂；大孩子们则在跳板的梯子上爬上爬下，欢呼雀跃。照片里，我坐在三米高的跳台上，帮忙展开弗里波特队那面鲜艳的红白黑三色胜利旗帜。

That year, we won. We threw him into the pool and shaved his curly brown locks at the celebration party afterward. There’s a photo from that night, our whole swim team swarming the pool deck. Little kids up front, arms raised in ecstasy, older kids cheering while perched up and down the ladders to the diving boards. There I am, sitting on the three-meter high-dive, helping to unfurl Freeport’s bright red, white, and black team banner in victory.

练习时的背景音乐是​​室内游泳池边水波荡漾的回声，在水中变得模糊不清，只有当我们抬起手臂时，教练的喊叫声才变得清晰可闻。我们抬头呼吸，或者在完成一组艰苦的训练后到达池壁。氯气的味道成了我皮肤的天然气味。高中赛季期间，我每天凌晨训练后走进教室，眼周的泳镜印记都渐渐消退。对同学们来说，除了偶尔从模糊不清的晨间广播中传来的游泳比赛结果之外，这就是我游泳生涯的唯一痕迹。

The soundtrack to practice was the swishing echo chamber of the indoor pool deck, muffled in the water, the yelled instructions that only became clearly audible when we lifted our heads up to breathe or when we reached the wall at the end of a grueling set. Chlorine became my skin’s default scent. During the high school season, I walked into homeroom after predawn practice with goggle marks fading from around my eyes. To my classmates, it was the only evidence of my swimming life, other than the occasional swim meet results that came filtered through the garbled fuzz of morning announcements.

我最终在六岁儿子加入游泳队前后再次加入了一支队伍。我童年的十年都在参加比赛，但这是二十多年来我第一次和别人一起训练和比赛。作为一个成年人，我想记住这一切的意义所在。这次复出时，我刚满四十岁，所以我想我的目标是成为像达拉·托雷斯那样的普通女性。我的队伍是奥尔巴尼舰队队，菲利克斯的队伍是伯克利梭鱼队。

I end up joining a swim team again around the same time my own six-year-old does. I spent a decade of my childhood competing, but it’s the first time in more than two decades that I’ve trained and raced with others in practice. As an adult, I want to remember what it was all for. At the point of this comeback, I’ve just turned forty, so I guess I aspire to be an Everywoman Dara Torres. My team is the Albany Armada; Felix’s is the Berkeley Barracudas.

阿玛达队是一支大师级游泳队，这意味着它隶属于美国大师游泳协会（US Masters Swimming）。该协会是面向18岁及以上游​​泳运动员的竞技游泳队联盟。美国大师游泳协会成立于1970年，目前在全国拥有6.5万名会员和1500支队伍及训练小组，并负责组织地区性、全国性和国际性比赛。无论你是刚从大学游泳队退役的22岁游泳健将，还是80岁以上的游泳新手，这里都欢迎你。有些游泳运动员参加比赛，而另一些则将训练本身作为首要目标。

The Armada is a Masters team, which means that it’s part of US Masters Swimming, the competitive swim team circuit for swimmers eighteen and up. Established in 1970, US Masters now has sixty-five thousand members around the country and one thousand five hundred teams and training groups, and it sanctions regional, national, and international meets. It doesn’t matter if you’re a twenty-two-year-old water rocket just off a college team or a novice swimmer over eighty—there’s a spot for you. Some swimmers compete in meets, while others prioritize training as its own goal.

奥尔巴尼舰队队的主教练卡罗尔·尼普是一位六十岁出头、皮肤晒得黝黑的女士，她穿着……鲜艳的红色唇膏，灿烂的笑容。虽然我在奥尔巴尼游泳池游了四年泳，却从未加入过成人游泳队。这并非卡罗尔教练招募队员不够努力——我明白她为何能凭借卓越的执教和社区建设获得全国奖项——只是我不确定自己是否准备好再次接受别人在泳池里对我的指导。过去二十年，我一直专注于如何享受游泳的乐趣和锻炼，如何轻松完成一个小时的训练，不必过分在意速度，也不必承受比赛的压力。成人游泳让我感到畏惧。

The head coach of the Albany Armada, Carol Nip, is a sun-burnished woman in her early sixties who wears bright-red lipstick and a big smile. Though I’d been swimming at the Albany pool for four years, I’d never swum with the Masters team. It wasn’t for lack of Coach Carol’s recruiting efforts—I see why she has won national awards for superlative coaching and community building—I just wasn’t sure I was ready for someone to tell me what to do in the pool again. I’d spent the last twenty years focusing on how to swim for fun and exercise, to swim an hour-long workout without worrying too much about speed and without the stress of competition. Masters swimming intimidated me.

练习的第一天，我和菲利克斯都感到同样的紧张，胃里像是有蝴蝶在颤抖。那些由来已久的社交焦虑——会好玩吗？我能跟上吗？大家都会不会比我强？ ——在我脑海里不断循环播放。当我走到泳池边时，突然感觉自己仿佛与少女时代的影子同行，这让我感到有些意外。

On our respective first days of practice, Felix and I both feel the same nervous butterflies quivering in our stomachs. Those time-worn social anxieties—Will it be fun? Will I be able to keep up? Will everyone be better than me?—are streaming on loop. As I walk out on the pool deck, I’m startled by the momentary feeling that I’m walking with the shadow of my girlhood self.

小时候，比赛对我来说是一种展现正直、支配地位和权力的方式，即便这些可能并不存在。我能看出这其中蕴含着某种战争的意味——如果说我曾经刻意追求过冲突，那么这里就是我的战场。但伴随肾上腺素飙升而来的，是恐惧，是害怕把自己置于聚光灯下，在众目睽睽之下，与时间赛跑，与其他游泳运动员竞争。我不想在意别人的看法，但我又不得不在意。

When I was a child, competition was a way to assert integrity and dominance and power where perhaps there was none. I can see that there’s something warlike in this—inasmuch as I’ve ever cultivated conflict, this is the arena. But along with that adrenaline rush comes a fear, of putting myself out there, in public, against a clock, against other swimmers. I don’t want to care what other people think, but I do.

回想起来，我早期的游泳生涯中曾有过一段类似“失乐园”的时刻，那时我第一次体会到竞争会如何让人沮丧。当时我读八年级，是校队队员，第一次参加大型锦标赛决赛。那是高中一年一度的游泳锦标赛的晚上。参加郡级比赛，我惊喜地发现自己竟然进入了100码蛙泳决赛。决赛里有个我一直很崇拜的高年级女生，我们一起在同一个俱乐部训练，在我心里她简直就是“女神”。我被分在最外侧泳道，感觉自己希望渺茫。她预赛成绩最快，所以被分到了第四泳道，占据了有利的中间位置。

When I look back on it, there was a kind of “Paradise Lost” moment in my early swimming life, when I first understood how competition could get you down. I was an eighth grader on the varsity team, swimming in my first big championship final. It was the evening of the annual high school county meet, and I was surprised and delighted to find myself in the final heat of the 100-yard breaststroke. There was an older girl I looked up to, a senior. We swam on the same club circuit; I equated her in my mind with “goddess.” I was a long-shot contender in the outside lane. She had the fastest qualifying time and got that favored middle placement in lane four.

比赛开始前，她走到起跑线后面和我打招呼。我兴奋地笑着，很高兴见到她。但当我看到她脸上的表情时，笑容瞬间消失了：她焦虑得让人作呕，而我现在才知道，这种焦虑是会传染的。

In the moments before the race, she came up to me behind the starting blocks. I smiled excitedly, happy to see her. But the smile quickly dropped off my face when I saw the look on hers: she had a sick-to-your-stomach anxiety that was, I now know, contagious.

“我好紧张，”她说着，紧紧抓住我的胳膊。这不再是我认识的那个女孩了，她总是面带微笑，和蔼可亲，同时又散发着一种冷静自信。眼前的她完全变了个人——一个拼命抓住我，仿佛我是她救命稻草的女孩。“这是我高中最后一场比赛了。”然后，她又说了一句让我大吃一惊的话：“求你别赢我。”

“I’m so nervous,” she said, clutching my arm. This was not the girl I knew, who was always smiling and kind but also projected a cool confidence. This was someone else—a someone who was desperately holding on to me like I was her life raft. “This is my last race in high school.” And then she said something that startled me: “Please don’t beat me.”

我们继续参加了比赛，最终她赢了。赛后，她拥抱了我，恢复了往日的活泼，然后和队友们一起庆祝。我很确定我当时也尽力想赢，虽然我不能否认她的话在某种程度上改变了我。那天，我渐渐明白了一个道理：当你习惯了胜利，就会害怕失败。竞争并非全然令人愉悦，即使对一个八年级的学生来说也是如此——对失败的担忧会让我失去那种自由自在、无拘无束的感觉。

We went on to swim the race, and she ended up winning after all. After the race she hugged me, back to her usual effervescent self as she went to celebrate with her teammates. I’m pretty sure I did try to win, although I can’t say that her words didn’t change me somehow. Something crept in that day, an understanding that when you become accustomed to winning, you become afraid of losing. Competition was not a totally happy thing, not even for an eighth grader—and the worry of it could drag down the free-flying feeling I’d come to associate with it.

在和队友们一起训练时，我看着大家在水里穿梭，穿着花哨的泳衣——唯一没变的是，Speedo泳裤依然像以前一样艳俗——我仿佛看到了一群闪闪发光的鱼儿。仅仅几周后，我就意识到自己错过了和团队一起训练、一起游泳的动力。我发现，为了别人而努力游得更快更容易。队友们会鼓励你、推动你前进。在那群鱼儿中，有一种共同的意识和共同的目标。

At practice with the Armada, I look at all of us in the water, flitting back and forth across the pool in our flashy, colorful suits—one thing that hasn’t changed is that Speedos are still as gaudy as they ever were—and I see a school of flashing fish. After just a few weeks, I realize that I’d missed training with a team, the motivation of swimming together. I find that it’s easier to make myself swim fast for someone else. Having teammates picks you up and pushes you along. In that school of fish, there’s a shared consciousness and a shared purpose.

每天中午训练特别累，回到家后，我刚从办公桌前站起来，左肩就隐隐作痛。有时候，右肩也会这样。有时候，我会顾及年龄，睡个午觉。

I go home after a particularly grueling midday practice, and when I rise from my desk, my left shoulder complains. Or else it’s my right. Some days, I give age a concession and take an afternoon nap.

一天早上，卡罗尔教练给我们每人发了一个小笔记本。在她让我们下水之前，她让我们写下来年的两个目标。我该写些什么呢？

One morning, Coach Carol hands each of us a little notebook. Before she lets us get in the water, she makes us scribble down two goals for the next year. What do I write?

1. 做一件让我害怕的事。

1. Do something that scares me.

2. 二十多年来第一次参加游泳比赛？？？

2. Swim in a meet for the first time in twenty-plus years???

训练结束后，卡罗尔教练在泳池边拦住我。“太平洋大师赛短池锦标赛快到了，”她兴高采烈地说，“我觉得你在你们这个年龄组很有竞争力。记得把比赛日期记在日历上！”

Later, after practice, Coach Carol stops me outside the pool. “The Pacific Masters short course championships is coming up,” she says cheerfully. “I think you can be really competitive in your age group. Mark it on your calendar!”

听到这些话，我的肾上腺素飙升，这种巴甫洛夫式的条件反射我以为早已克服了。但我对竞争很感兴趣。我又开始回想起在海魔队的日子。那个曾经在比赛中激动不已的女孩是谁？而我，又会在比赛中展现出怎样的好胜心呢？

At these words, my adrenaline spikes, a Pavlovian response I thought I’d outgrown. But I’m curious about competing again. I find myself thinking back on those Sea Devil days. Who was that girl who once thrilled at a race? And what version of my competitive self would show up at the meet?

比赛日阳光灿烂，碧波荡漾，宛如一座露天泳池。清晨驱车翻越伯克利山前往苏打水上运动中心，我感到一阵紧张。两天前冲浪后，我的左肩还有些酸痛，这让我意识到自己属于40到44岁这个年龄段。为了缓解焦虑，我决定参加两项轻松有趣的比赛：50米蛙泳和100米个人混合泳——蝶泳、仰泳、蛙泳和自由泳各25码。

Competition day glints like an outdoor pool, all dewy blue and sunshine. On the early morning drive over the Berkeley hills to the Soda Aquatic Center, I feel my stomach turning over. My left shoulder is still a little cranky from when I surfed two days ago. Just enough to remind me of my forty-to-forty-four age group. To offset the anxiety, I decided to swim two fast, fun events: the 50-meter breaststroke and the 100 IM, or individual medley—twenty-five yards each of butterfly, backstroke, breaststroke, and freestyle.

苏打水上运动中心的泳池美轮美奂：十八条比赛泳道，可以同时进行两组比赛，每组九条泳道。泳池面积很大，两组比赛之间还留有两条空泳道作为缓冲。一层薄薄的、半透明的雾气笼罩着蔚蓝的池面，等待着被尚未完全苏醒的太阳驱散。泳池左侧，在一组金属看台和电子计时板的后面，还有一个专门的热身池，供比赛间隙使用，让我们放松身心。

The pool at the Soda Aquatic Center is a thing of beauty: eighteen competition lanes that allow two heats to run concurrently, with nine lanes each. The pool is so big that there are two extra lanes in between, left empty as a buffer. A thin, translucent layer of fog hovers above the cerulean water, waiting to be burned off by a still-sleepy sun. Off to the left, behind a set of metal bleachers and a digital timing board, there’s also a dedicated warm-up pool, open for use between races so we can stay loose.

数百名游泳运动员熙熙攘攘地走来走去，他们身穿游泳队特有的及膝连帽派克大衣：厚重的尼龙材质，内衬抓绒，颜色五颜六色，以红色、黑色和宝蓝色为主，饰以金色、黑色和白色滚边，绣着一些晦涩难懂的缩写。MEMO. TOC. EBAT. ALB.（至少最后一个我知道，因为那是我们奥尔巴尼舰队的缩写。）

Hundreds of swimmers are milling about, swathed in the shin-length hooded parkas that are particular to swim teams: bulky, fleece-lined nylon monstrosities in all colors, heavy on the reds and blacks and royal blues, trimmed with gold and black and white, embroidered with inscrutable acronyms. MEMO. TOC. EBAT. ALB. (I know that last one, at least, because it’s us: Albany Armada.)

我仍然记得该怎么做。我在我们队的遮阳帐篷下脱掉身上的衣服，戴上帽子和护目镜，小心翼翼地不让指甲戳破我们队帽那精致的黄蓝相间的乳胶帽。热身结束后，卡罗尔教练递给我一根橡皮筋——提醒我时刻保持身体的柔韧性。她还把一条蓝丝带塞到我手里。“你已经赢了，”她笑着说，“这是你高中毕业后的第一场比赛！”

I still remember what to do. I shed my layers in a heap under our team’s shade tent and snap on my cap and goggles, being careful not to poke a fingernail through the delicate yellow-and-navy latex of our team cap. After warm-ups, Coach Carol hands me a rubber band—a reminder to always be flexible. She also presses a blue ribbon into my hand. “You’ve won already,” she says, grinning. “It’s your first meet since high school!”

在我的第一项比赛——50码蛙泳——的泳道分配处，我环顾四周。我不禁注意到附近站着一位八十到八十四岁年龄组的游泳运动员，她戴着黑色泳帽，穿着红色队服，涂着与之相配的鲜艳口红，精致的妆容上透着一丝宁静。我看着她，她身上那种满足的神态让我感到平静。

At the lane assignment for my first event, the 50-yard breaststroke, I take a long look around. I can’t help noticing a swimmer in the eighty-to-eighty-four age group standing nearby, wearing a black cap, a red team parka, and matching bright lipstick, a serene look on her beautifully made-up face. I look at her, and something about her contented presence settles me.

裁判宣布我的组别，我走上出发台，站在那座壮丽、宏伟、巨大的泳池边。游泳运动员们，各就各位。信号一响，我纵身跃入水中。

The official calls my heat, and I step up to the starting blocks, at the precipice of that gorgeous, glorious, ginormous pool. Swimmers, take your mark. At the signal, I take the plunge.

耳边传来水声，如同大海的轰鸣。水下寂静无声，强劲的划水、踢腿、滑行……这短暂的时光充满了无限可能，我几乎不想浮出水面。当我浮出水面时，却什么也听不见。手臂和腿机械地划动着，忠实地重复着练习已久的蛙泳动作。然而，我的思绪却慢了一步，与身体的节奏不同步。直到两圈比赛的第二圈，我才猛然醒悟——突然间，清醒得惊人——一切都恢复了正常。视线突然清晰起来。最后十五码，我四肢一股劲儿涌上心头，仿佛突然想起要踩油门似的。

The rush of water in my ears, a phroom like the ocean. That delicious silence underwater, strong pull, kick, gliiiiiide. The fragment of time is so full of possibility, I almost don’t want to break the surface. When I do, I don’t hear anything. Arms and legs are moving mechanically now, executing the breaststroke they’ve been practicing so faithfully. And yet my mind is moving a beat behind, not quite there with my body. It isn’t until the second lap of the two-lap race that I wake up—suddenly, and with startling clarity—and everything clicks into focus. The last fifteen yards, a surging in my limbs, as if I’ve just remembered to hit the gas pedal.

之后，除了为队友加油，我便带着傻笑在泳池边闲逛。我还有一场比赛，结果要几个小时后才能出来。（我的两个项目都得了第三名。）我可不是奥运游泳选手。我的目标很普通，比赛的意义也不大。但无论多么短暂，我都记得那种感觉。一种瞬间的轻松，一种竭尽全力的感觉。

Afterward, when I’m not cheering for my teammates, I drift around the pool deck with a foolish grin on my face. I still have another race, and the results won’t come in until hours later. (I place third in both of my events.) I’m no Olympic swimmer. My goals are modest; the stakes are low. But however fleeting it is, I remember what it feels like. A momentary lightness, the feeling of having done my ever-elusive best.

在练习中，卡罗尔教练会不断进行调整。蛙泳时，头部要保持在双臂之间。用力划水。你的头直直地抬起，阻碍了你的前进。仰泳时，你的右臂总是交叉。试着向三点钟方向伸展。蝶泳入水时，双手要分开。这里，双手与肩同宽，不要并拢。自由泳时，伸长右臂，肘部抬高。你的入水距离太短了。

In practice, Coach Carol offers constant calibrations. Keep your head between your arms on the breaststroke. Press. Your head is popping straight up and it’s stopping your forward movement. Your right arm keeps crossing over on backstroke. Try reaching for three o’clock. Keep your hands apart when you enter on the butterfly pull. Out here, shoulder width apart, not together. On freestyle, lengthen your right arm, elbow high. You are entering short.

在训练之外独自游泳时，我也会牢记这些要点。按压。伸展。低头。指尖划水。这是一个不断精进的过程，我开始意识到，这种身体上的重复练习可以是一种冥想，超越了赢得比赛这个简单的目标。我以前从未这样思考过游泳，因为激烈的正面竞争总是掩盖了这一点。现在依然如此。（即使到了四十岁，也没有什么比即将到来的比赛的焦虑更能让我立刻冲进洗手间了。）但在这里，在这些动作中，在泳池里，在《龙威小子》这部电影中，确实存在着一种禅意。 反复“上蜡，擦蜡”，直到掌握为止。这就是游泳作为一种自我提升的方式。

I keep these in mind as I swim on my own outside of practice. Press. Reach. Head down. Fingertips dragging. It’s a constant refinement, and I begin to realize that the physical repetition can be a kind of meditation that transcends the simple goal of winning a race. I’ve never really thought about swimming in this way, since the frenzy of head-to-head competition always eclipsed it. Still does. (Even at forty, there’s nothing like the impending anxiety of a race to send me straight to the bathroom.) But there is a Zen practice to be found here, in the motions, in the pool, in the Karate Kid “wax-on, wax-off” repetition until it’s right. It is swimming as self-improvement.

我们练习出发、转身和流线型姿势。我们登上出发台，练习接力。随着我越来越沉浸于这种有目的的练习中，我开始思考游泳这项运动最吸引我的地方——对手并非真正的对手，尽管对手就在那里，与你并肩游弋。我的意思是，游泳比赛不像击剑或摔跤那样需要智取对手。游泳和跑步一样，有一种基本而原始的感觉。你最大的对手是时间，以及在这种情况下，你必须与之抗衡的水。

We practice starts, turns, streamlines. We get up on the blocks and rehearse relays. As I become more and more immersed in this kind of intent practice, I think about what intrigues me about swimming as a sport—that the adversary is not actually the other person, though that other person is there, swimming alongside you. What I mean by this is that swimming competition is not like fencing, or wrestling, where you outwit the other person. Like running, swimming has a basic, elemental feel. Your chief adversary is the clock and, in this case, the water that you’ve got to work with to beat it.

14

14

武士之道

Ways of the Samurai

想象一下，一位沉默的武士，双肩浸在水中，快速而高效地游过一条河流——同时还穿着重达 45 磅的全套盔甲。

Picture a silent samurai, submerged to his shoulders in water, swimming across a river with speed and efficiency—all while wearing a full forty-five-pound suit of armor.

在日本这个岛国，数百年前的文献中就记载了武士游泳的技艺。封建时代，不同的游泳流派（或称“流派”）应运而生；守护各个地区和地理环境的武士们都拥有各自独特的航行技巧，能够巧妙高效地驾驭当地水域。在1603年至1868年的封建时期，几乎每个氏族都拥有自己的游泳流派。在德川幕府的鼓励下，游泳作为一项军事技艺蓬勃发展。

In Japan, a country of islands, writings dating back hundreds of years describe samurai swimming. In feudal times, different ryu, or schools of swimming, developed; samurai protecting each region and geography had their own ways of navigating the local waters with artful efficiency. Nearly every clan had a ryu during the feudal period, from 1603 to 1868, when swimming as a military art blossomed under the encouragement of the Tokugawa Shogunate.

不同武士流派发展出各式各样的技巧，用于潜行接近敌人、长时间漂浮以及渡过湍急的河流。这些经典的日本游泳武术，即日本泳法（ Nihon eiho），逐渐演变为崇尚优雅和优美，其动作经过精心设计，能够适应水波荡漾等自然条件，使身体与水流和谐统一。

The schools of different warrior groups came up with a diverse array of techniques for sneaking up on an enemy, floating for long periods, and fording fierce rivers. These classical Japanese swimming martial arts, or Nihon eiho, evolved to prize grace and elegance, with deliberate movements that reflected conditions such as ripples and waves, so that the body and the water could move harmoniously as one.

1898年，日本在港口城市横滨举办了首届现代游泳比赛。横滨是日本最早对外开放贸易的地区之一。不难理解，对于这个曾经与世隔绝的国家而言，横滨见证了许多“第一”：第一份英文报纸《日本先驱报》；日本第一个也是最大的唐人街；以及这场日本与包括英国、澳大利亚和美国在内的联队之间的首届国际游泳比赛。

In 1898, Japan hosted its first modern swim competition, in the port city of Yokohama, one of the first parts of the country to be opened up to trade with the rest of the world. Yokohama, understandably, was the site of many foreign firsts for this once-isolated nation: the first English-language newspaper, the Japan Herald; the country’s first and largest Chinatown; and this first international swim meet, between Japan and a combined team that included England, Australia, and the United States.

日本人运用传承数百年的武士泳姿，在100码和440码的比赛中击败了外国选手。要找到任何关于这场历史性体育赛事的英文记录都颇具挑战性，但我找到了一本1935年出版的关于日本游泳史的书籍。书中提到了一位名叫阿尔宾的神秘英国人，他赢得了第三项比赛——880码的冠军。至于为什么会选择这些特定的距离，我不得而知。

Using centuries-old samurai swimming strokes, the Japanese beat the foreigners in the 100-yard and 440-yard races. It’s a challenge to find any English-language record of this historic sporting event, but I tracked down a 1935 book about the history of swimming in Japan. In it, I found a reference to the mysterious “Englishman named Arbin” who managed to win the third event, the 880-yard race. Why those particular distances were selected for the races, I cannot tell you.

但我可以告诉你，横滨游泳比赛在日本游泳史上占有特殊的地位。它不仅仅是一场游泳比赛，更象征着东西方传统和理念的一次正面较量。在那场比赛中，英国选手使用了特鲁根泳姿——想象一下，这是一种抬头交替的前划臂泳姿，但每次划水时腿部都会向两侧摆动。英国人约翰·亚瑟·特鲁根在巴西长大，从土著部落那里学会了这种泳姿，并于1873年在英国首次使用；两年后，他用这种泳姿赢得了当地比赛，并打破了纪录。特鲁根泳姿被誉为一项突破。

But I can tell you that the Yokohama contest holds a special place in Japanese swimming history. More than a mere swim meet, it symbolized a larger, head-to-head measuring up of Eastern and Western traditions and philosophies. In the meet, the English used the trudgen—imagine a head-up alternating front arm stroke, but with a kind of sideways leg thrash with each stroke. The Brit John Arthur Trudgen picked it up from indigenous tribes as a boy growing up in Brazil and debuted the stroke in England in 1873; two years later, he won a local competition using it, in record-breaking time. The trudgen was hailed as a breakthrough.

但日本人拥有自己独特的侧身划水方式，在当时速度惊人。他们的胜利表明，运用日本英法（日本武士阶层十八种武术之一，包括骑术、射箭、击剑和徒手搏斗）的游泳运动员能够与使用西方技术的游泳运动员竞争并取得胜利。这场比赛暗含着民族自豪感，与明治维新时期日本的现代化和统一进程不谋而合。

But the Japanese had their own version of an overarm side stroke that was incredibly fast for the time. Their victories showed that swimmers using Nihon eiho—one of the eighteen martial arts of the samurai warrior class, including horsemanship, archery, fencing, and hand-to-hand combat—could compete and win against swimmers using Western techniques. The competition had an undercurrent of nationalist pride that coincided with the Meiji period and the modernization and unification of Japan.

二十世纪初，日本开始派出更多游泳运动员参加国际游泳比赛。在此期间，西方的泳姿发展迅速，日本人努力追赶。他们学习并采用竞争对手最新的自由泳泳姿，并从英国和美国进口书籍中研究相关技术。

In the early twentieth century, Japan began sending more swimmers to international swimming contests. During this period, strokes in the West were rapidly developing, and the Japanese worked hard to catch up. They adopted the latest versions of the front crawl stroke being employed by their competitors and studied techniques from books that they imported from England and America.

大阪一所中学建起了一座现代化游泳池，学生们在那里学习自由泳。正是在这所中学，一位名叫高石胜夫的年轻人开始参加竞技游泳比赛；1924年，在巴黎奥运会上，他成为第一位在奥运会上崭露头角的日本游泳运动员，在100米和1500米自由泳比赛中均获得第五名，并与三位队友一起在800米接力赛中获得第四名。这犹如一声振奋人心的号角；次年，日本所有分散的游泳团体联合起来，成立了正式的业余游泳协会。

One modern pool was built in Osaka, at a middle school, and students there were taught the crawl stroke. It was at this middle school that a young man named Katsuo Takaishi began to swim competitively; in 1924, in Paris, he became the first Japanese swimmer to garner attention at the Olympics, managing fifth-place finishes in the 100-meter and 1,500-meter freestyle races, and a fourth-place finish in the 800-meter relay with three of his teammates. It was a rallying cry; the next year, all the disparate swimming groups in Japan were united under a formal amateur swimming federation.

高石成为了日本自由泳冠军。1926年，他和其他人受邀前往夏威夷参加比赛。美国最优秀的游泳运动员们正等着与他们一较高下。在那里，高石让打破了约翰尼·韦斯穆勒保持的50米和400米自由泳奥运纪录，令他的同胞们激动不已。这意义非凡：当时，韦斯穆勒是美国泳坛的耀眼明星，也是世界上速度最快的游泳运动员之一，刚刚在巴黎奥运会上斩获两枚金牌，击败了夏威夷传奇游泳运动员兼冲浪运动员杜克·卡哈纳莫库。四年前，韦斯穆勒是第一个在100米自由泳比赛中突破一分钟大关的人。（值得一提的是，他后来在米高梅的卖座电影中扮演了泰山，并成为当时的国际影星。）

Takaishi became Japan’s freestyle swimming champion. In 1926, he and others were invited to a meet in Hawaii, where America’s best swimmers were waiting to race them. There, Takaishi thrilled his countrymen by shattering Johnny Weissmuller’s Olympic records in the 50-meter and 400-meter freestyle events. This was a big deal: At the time, Weissmuller was the famously handsome face of American swimming and one of the world’s fastest swimmers, having just won two gold medals in the Paris Olympics, beating out the legendary Hawaiian swimmer and surfer Duke Kahanamoku. Four years earlier, Weissmuller had been the first to break the one-minute barrier in the 100-meter freestyle. (That he would later go on to play Tarzan in MGM’s blockbuster films and become an international movie star of the era is also worthy of note.)

其他泳姿呢？在同一时期，鹤田义幸成为日本蛙泳的领军人物——在1928年阿姆斯特丹奥运会上，他成为首位获得200米蛙泳金牌的日本游泳运动员。他曾公开表示，日本古典游泳武术对现代蛙泳的影响深远；他将蛙泳描述为“加速版”的平大游（hira-oyogi），平大游是由观海流（Kankai ryu）发展而来的一种泳姿，专为远距离公开水域游泳而设计。他认为日本蛙泳训练技法的悠久传统及其所需的技巧都极具价值。

What about the other strokes? During this same period, Yoshiyuki Tsuruta became Japan’s dominant breaststroker—at the 1928 Amsterdam Olympics, he became the first Japanese swimmer ever to win gold, in the 200-meter breaststroke. He was vocal about the influence of the classical Japanese swimming martial arts on breaststroke as we know it; he described it as a “speeded-up form” of hira-oyogi, a stroke developed by the Kankai ryu that was especially intended for swimming in the open sea over long distances. He saw value in the long tradition of Japanese training techniques in breaststroke and the skills it took to swim it well.

1932年洛杉矶奥运会上，日本冠军队终于以惊人的统治力在世界舞台上崭露头角。高石尚弥担任队长，同时也是教练组成员，鹤田则领衔蛙泳项目。在这一阵容中，日本游泳队队员们以惊人的体能和速度征服了全场。他们共斩获12枚奖牌，超过所有游泳奖牌总数的三分之一；在男子6个游泳项目中，他们赢得了5枚金牌，包揽了100米仰泳的金牌，并在其他3个项目中也几乎包揽了所有金牌。鹤田在200米蛙泳项目中再次夺金，成为首位在同一项目中蝉联金牌的日本游泳运动员。

It was at the 1932 Los Angeles Olympics that Japan’s champions finally broke out on the world stage with extraordinary dominance. With Takaishi as captain and also part of the coaching staff and Tsuruta leading the breaststroke contingent, the team’s swimmers dazzled with their fitness and speed. They took home a total of twelve medals, more than a third of all the swimming medals that were handed out; they won gold in five of the six men’s swimming events, sweeping the medal podium in the 100-meter backstroke and performing near-sweeps in three other events. Tsuruta won gold again in the 200-meter breaststroke, becoming the first Japanese swimmer to win back-to-back gold medals in the same event.

在那届奥运会上，鹤田看到了蛙泳运动复兴的希望，也重燃了日本传统泳坛的自豪感。他的年轻队友前畑秀子在女子200米蛙泳比赛中获得银牌，成为首位获得奥运奖牌的日本女性。四年后，她又摘得了金牌。鹤田的崛起开启了日本在蛙泳项目上近一个世纪的统治时期，并涌现出众多奥运奖牌得主。

At those Games, Tsuruta saw hope for the reinvigoration of breaststroke’s popularity—and pride in Japanese traditions—with his younger teammate Hideko Maehata, who won silver in the women’s 200-meter breaststroke. She was the first Japanese woman ever to medal in the Olympics. Four years later, she’d win her gold. With Tsuruta, the Japanese began a reign of dominance in breaststroke that has lasted for nearly a century and produced an extensive cast of Olympic medalists.

我喜欢把每种泳姿都看作是独具个性的。蛙泳常被认为是速度最慢的泳姿，但它却是我最喜欢的。蛙泳每次划水都需要抬头换气；它不像自由泳和仰泳那样拥有明显的搅动力量，也不像蝶泳那样华丽炫目。（奇怪的是，蝶泳其实是在20世纪30年代从蛙泳演变而来，当时人们发现手臂在水面上划水比在水里划水速度更快。蛙泳就是在蝶泳的基础上发展而来的。）直到1952年，蝶泳才被国际泳联（FINA）认可为一项独立的泳姿；在1956年奥运会上，蝶泳最终成为一项独立的比赛项目。

I like to think that each of the different strokes has its own personality. Breaststroke is often thought of as the slow stroke, but it’s my favorite. It requires a raised-head breath with every pull; it lacks the overt, churning power of freestyle and backstroke, and the flashy, splashy show that is butterfly. (Butterfly, strangely enough, evolved from breaststroke in the 1930s, when practitioners discovered that an out-of-the-water arm pull was faster than an in-the-water arm pull. A variation of the butterfly was used in breaststroke competition until 1952, when it was accepted by FINA as a separate stroke; at the 1956 Olympics, butterfly was finally swum as its own event.)

蛙泳看似沉稳的节奏背后，隐藏着一股静谧的力量。我的哥哥天生就会蛙泳，而我却并非如此。小时候，我努力练习蛙泳，也因此努力培养出我所认为的那种蛙泳特质。我天生就容易急躁，现在依然如此。但蛙泳不允许你急躁；如果你急躁，就会失去滑行的流畅感，以及隐藏在划水动作中的整个速度机制。急躁反而会减慢速度。这就是蛙泳的悖论。然而，放慢速度，你就会像太妃糖一样舒展身体。减少快速的上下摆动，你就会毫不费力地被水流牵引着前进，就像清晨的船身划破河面般流畅。蛙泳的腿部动作，在水面下悄无声息地发挥作用，就是你秘密的推进器。

Concealed behind breaststroke’s deliberate pacing is a quiet strength. It came naturally to my brother but not to me. As a kid, I worked hard to be good at breaststroke and, by extension, to acquire that quality that I associate with it. I had the propensity to hurry, and still do. But breaststroke won’t let you be impatient; if you do, you lose the glide, and the entire mechanism for speed that’s hidden in the stroke. Rush, and you go slower. It’s the paradox of breaststroke. Ease up, though, and you stretch, like taffy. Cut the quick bobs, and you’re pulled along, effortless, smooth as the hull of a boat cutting through early morning glass on a river. That frog kick, working without splash underneath the surface, is your secret propeller.

练习时，我累了就会跟在哥哥身后，利用他的尾流节省体力。“别拖着我游，”他会这么说，但语气里总会带着微笑。蛙泳比赛的节奏就不同了；你必须把握好时机，不能操之过急，否则就什么也得不到。在这个现代社会如此痴迷于速度的时代，这提醒我们，放慢速度，才能发现更多可能性。

During practice, I used to draft behind my brother when I felt tired, using his wake to save energy. “Stop dragging off me,” he’d say, but he’d smile to soften the words. In a breaststroke race, the pacing is different; you must be thoughtful with timing, not hasty, or you get nowhere. In a modern world that is so obsessed with speed, it’s a good reminder of what’s possible when we slow down.

为了提高游泳水平，我一直在和卡罗尔教练一起调整划水动作：伸长手臂，保持头部流线型，双腿并拢。我经常去看儿子的训练，那里就像潮水般涌来涌去的小船。游泳池。每次训练结束后，菲利克斯从水里出来，嘴唇发紫，瘦削的肩膀微微颤抖，他让我想起了我的弟弟。我问菲利克斯游泳练得怎么样，他告诉我他不喜欢冷水。“那比赛呢？”我问。我见过如果有人在泳道里靠近他，他就会立刻加倍努力。“你不喜欢游得快吗？”

In an effort to be a better swimmer, I’ve been tinkering with the mechanics of my strokes with Coach Carol: lengthening my arms, keeping my head more streamlined, pressing my legs together. I attend my son’s practices, where whole tidal waves of little kids churn back and forth across the pool. When Felix emerges from the water at the end of a session, lips blue and skinny shoulders shivering, he reminds me of my brother. I ask Felix how his swimming is coming along, and he informs me that he doesn’t like the cold water. “What about racing?” I ask. I’ve seen the way he ratchets up the effort if someone inches up alongside him in the lane. “Don’t you like going fast?”

他想了一会儿。“我不喜欢别人命令我做事，”他说，“我喜欢自己做主。” 这让我想起了我自己。在任何年龄，追求自我提升的自律都很难，尤其对孩子来说。但我现在年纪大了。我感觉自己可以从日本的游泳武术中学到一些东西，比如如何变得更好——耐心，以及对我们身体如何在各种水域中运作进行更深入、更细致的研究。

He thinks for a minute. “I don’t like it if someone tells me to do it,” he says. “I like it if it’s my choice.” Now he reminds me of me. Self-discipline in the pursuit of self-betterment is hard at any age, especially when you’re a child. But I’m older now. I have the feeling that I have something to learn from Japan’s swimming martial art about what it means to be better—patience, for one, but also a longer, meticulously studied view on how our bodies can work in all kinds of water.

当我得知如今在日本举行武士游泳比赛——想象一下，一位沉默的武士在 25 米长的游泳池中滑行——吸引了远至波兰和英国的游泳运动员时，我便前往东京，寻找日本英法（Nihon eiho）的顶尖实践者。

When I find out that there are samurai swimming competitions being held today in Japan—now picture that silent samurai gliding across a 25-meter swimming pool—that attract swimmers from as far away as Poland and England, I make the trip to Tokyo to seek out the leading practitioners of Nihon eiho.

在日本的一则电视报道中，一位武士缓缓步入游泳池。我仔细观看他演示“甲胄御前大游”（katchu gozen oyogi），即身着全套盔甲游泳。他身姿流畅地横渡泳池，双腿交替划水。他头顶的金属尖顶头盔保持干燥。尽管铆接的皮革鳞甲沉重地压在他的身上，他却像幽灵般滑行。“这身盔甲很重，”年轻人拖着自己和湿透的装备从泳池里爬出来后，带着一丝微笑说道，“但我很高兴我会游泳。”（幸运的是，这条新闻报道有英文字幕。）

In a Japanese television report, a samurai lowers himself into a swimming pool. I watch closely as he demonstrates katchu gozen oyogi, full armor swimming. He moves smoothly on a sideways path across the pool, legs alternately circling. The metal-pronged helmet atop his head stays dry. Despite the blanket of riveted leather scales weighing down his torso, he slides along, wraithlike. “The armor is very heavy,” the young man says with a little smile, after he has dragged himself and his water-logged equipment out of the pool. “But I’m delighted I can swim.” (The news report, lucky for me, is subtitled in English.)

另一位游泳者，身穿泳裤，头戴黑白条纹泳帽，展示了一种截然不同、更具动感的技巧：跳水（inatobi），也称灰鲻鱼跳。他从静止的水下姿势跃出水面，双臂向后挥动，头部向前猛冲，露出精瘦（且肤色黝黑）的腰部。这是游泳时最基本的跳跃方式，可以用来挣脱海藻或其他杂物的缠绕，或者跳上船。

Another swimmer, this one dressed in swimming trunks and a black cap with white stripes, demonstrates a different, more dynamic skill: inatobi, gray mullet jumping. From a still and submerged position, the swimmer surges vertically out of the water, arms whipping back and head thrust forward, exposed to his very lean (and very tan) waist. It is the fundamental method of jumping while swimming to disentangle oneself from seaweed or other debris, or to leap onto a boat.

最后，是最基本的动作：立泳。这位年轻的选手面容放松，目光投向远方。他的头部几乎纹丝不动，面前的水面平静如镜。他仿佛在水面下隐藏着一台极其缓慢的跑步机。他的头和头发完全干燥。不同的流派有不同的变化，但基本原理相同。如今花样游泳运动员和水球运动员用来将上半身有力地推出水面的那种熟悉的打蛋式踢腿动作？它与十六世纪大师详细描述的方法非常相似。小堀流的卷轴，该流派专注于解放双手的技巧。腿部轻柔的循环运动旨在提高效率，并保持上半身的静止和稳定。日本花样游泳队使用的打蛋式踢腿动作直接源自野岛流。

Finally, the most fundamental of all moves: tachi-oyogi, standing swimming. The young competitor’s face is relaxed, his eyes trained on the horizon. His head moves near imperceptibly, the water in front of him as still as glass. It’s as if he is on a very slow treadmill hidden just below the surface of the water. His head and hair are completely dry. Different schools have different variations, but the basics are the same. That familiar egg-beater kick used today by synchronized swimmers and water-polo players to propel their upper bodies so powerfully out of the water? It bears a strong resemblance to the method described in detail in sixteenth-century master scrolls from the Kobori ryu, which specializes in techniques to free up the hands. The muted cycling of the legs is meant to be efficient and to keep the upper body stationary and stable. The version of the egg-beater kick used by the Japanese synchronized swimming team comes directly from the Nojima ryu.

我了解到，如果你擅长站立游泳，你就能在水里做任何事：写书法、装弹射击、剑术决斗。你可以携带武器和旗帜。你甚至可以在几乎完全浸没的情况下精准地射箭。记住，箭羽必须保持干燥才能保证飞行稳定。

I learn that if you’re good at standing swimming, you can do anything in the water: write calligraphy, load and fire a rifle, duel with swords. You can carry weapons and flags. You can shoot a bow and arrow with great accuracy while nearly submerged. Remember that the feathers on an arrow need to be dry to fly true.

新闻片段中，我们看到两名男子搏斗，两人都双手紧握木剑。他们互相叫喊，警惕地绕着对方转圈，仿佛在跳舞。但他们其实是在湖里划水，远离岸边。我们还看到两名女子在用“揖手”（nukite）游泳，这是一种收手式游泳技巧。这种高肘、匍匐前进的游泳技巧用于逆风逆浪或横渡潮汐；它能让你用肩膀劈开波浪，避免被破碎浪花的冲击力吞没。

In the news segment, we see two men fight, each gripping his wooden sword with both hands. They shout and circle each other warily, as if they are dancing. But they’re treading water, in a lake, far from shore. We see two women swimming nukite, the withdrawing hand style. This high-elbow, crawling arm technique is used to swim facing the wind and waves or when crossing the tide; it allows you to cut through the waves with your shoulder and avoid being overwhelmed by the foamy force of a breaking wave.

石引绿是现代武士泳技艺的大师。她由日本游泳联盟委任，是负责传承日本武士泳技的八位人士之一。如同其他武术——例如柔道或剑道——日本泳技也分为不同的等级，每个等级都需要多年的训练和考核才能晋升到下一个等级。

Midori Ishibiki is a modern-day master in the age-old art of samurai swimming. Appointed by the Japan Swimming Federation, Midori is one of eight people who are responsible for preserving the swimming martial art of Japan. Like any other martial art—judo, say, or kendo—Nihon eiho is governed by various levels of practice, and each level requires years of training and exams to move up to the next.

绿在东京长大，现在住在镰仓，一个位于东京以南一小时车程的海滨小镇。她今年五十岁，一头红棕色的波波头衬托着圆润的脸庞，在泳池中游动时几乎不激起一丝涟漪。但日本泳法不仅仅是身体技能的训练：“它也强调精神层面的修行，”她用活泼的、带有英国口音的英语说道，这得益于她在诺里奇多年的生活。“它就像冥想一样。”

Midori grew up in Tokyo and now lives in Kamakura, a seaside town an hour south of the city. Fifty years old, with reddish brown hair styled in a bob framing her round face, she can glide across a pool with barely a ripple. But Nihon eiho isn’t just about physical skills: “It also emphasizes a spiritual path,” she says in her perky, British-accented English, which comes from years of living in Norwich. “It’s like meditation.”

日本古籍教导我们，在冰冷的水中游泳能培养毅力；潜入水中能培养耐心；潜水能增强勇气；身体漂浮能使心灵平静；掌握救援和复苏技能是全心全意行善的体现。

Old Japanese texts teach that swimming in freezing water cultivates perseverance; submergence leads to patience; diving fosters bravery. Floating of the body leads to serenity of the mind. The mastery of rescue and resuscitation is a sign of wholehearted benevolence.

绿从十三岁起就开始跟随师傅学习古典游泳技巧，每年夏天都会去位于东京湾对岸的千叶海滩。她所在俱乐部的现任师傅山口和夫如今已年过八旬，绿每年夏天依然跟随他学习。如今，这位学生也成为了一位老师，在千叶期间，她会在学校的俱乐部里指导两百多名初中生。他们学习的是水风流，这种流派注重在开阔的海域和河流中高效游泳——例如，安全地穿越波浪，或者快速取回附近漂浮的物品。

Midori began studying classical swimming techniques with her master when she was thirteen, during summers at the beach in Chiba, across Tokyo Bay from the city of Tokyo. Her club’s current master, Kazuo Yamaguchi, is now in his mid-eighties, and Midori still studies with him every summer. But these days the student is also a master, and while in Chiba she in turn instructs more than two hundred junior high students from their school’s clubhouse. Theirs is the Suifu ryu, which devised practical ways to swim efficiently on the open sea and rivers—to safely get through waves, say, or to quickly retrieve something floating nearby.

虽然武士泳是日本游泳文化的根基，但其传统正在逐渐衰落。然而，那些肩负保护这项传统重任的人们却认为，这与现代日本游泳队在国际赛场上取得成功有着直接的联系。五月初一个异常温暖的星期里，我四处旅行。去东京看看如今的武士游泳是什么样子，以及人们至今仍在进行这项活动意味着什么。

Though samurai swimming is at the roots of Japan’s swimming culture, its traditions are waning. But those tasked with its preservation see a direct line to modern Japanese swimming success in international competition. During an unseasonably balmy week in early May, I travel around Tokyo to see what samurai swimming looks like today and what it means that people are still doing it.

为了找到石引绿，我来到了横滨的一家室内游泳俱乐部，在泳池边汗流浃背。室内泳池边简直像个超高温的桑拿房。穿着便服站在这么漂亮的泳池边，让我感到很不自在，但这却是我认真记录绿游泳课内容的唯一办法。今天，除了普通学员外，还有五位范士——日本泳法中最高级别的教练——也来上课。其中一位教练，七十三岁的今村正明，日本游泳协会日本泳法委员会副会长，正好奇地打量着我。他也觉得我穿着便服很奇怪。

My pursuit of Midori Ishibiki leads me to an indoor swimming club in Yokohama, where I am sweating profusely on the pool deck. The indoor pool deck is like a sauna turned up to the max. It causes me distress to be dressed in street clothes by the edge of a perfectly nice pool, but it’s the only way I can take proper notes on the happenings in Midori’s swim class. Today there are five hanshi masters—the highest level master there is in Nihon eiho—attending the class along with the regular students. One of the masters, Masaaki Imamura, the seventy-three-year-old vice chair of the Japan Swimming Federation’s committee on Nihon eiho, is examining me curiously. He also thinks it’s weird that I’m wearing street clothes.

“你为什么不去游泳呢？”他用低沉浑厚的声音打招呼，脸上带着迷人的笑容。“天气太热了。”他穿着黑色Speedo泳裤，戴着一顶黑色布泳帽，帽檐上有白色滚边，帽带系在下巴下面。黑色泳帽代表着他在神传流的资历；白色泳帽是给初学者的，就像柔道或空手道等其他武术中的白带一样。不过，不同流派的泳帽颜色等级划分略有不同。我勉强挤出一个笑容，随即又皱起了眉头，真想冲回更衣室，脱掉厚重的棉质连衣裙和紧身裤，也跳进水里。但我不能错过接下来发生的一切。

“Why don’t you swim?” he greets me with a deep, booming voice, as he issues forth a charming grin. “It is very hot.” He is wearing a black Speedo and a black cloth swim cap with white piping and strings that tie under his chin. The black cap indicates seniority in the Shinden ryu; white caps are given to beginners, much like the white belt in other martial arts like judo or karate. The progression of colors, however, varies by ryu. I manage to smile back, then grimace, and I’m tempted to dash back into the locker room to shed my heavy cotton dress and leggings so I can get in that water, too. But I can’t chance missing what happens next.

绿谷班上的十五名男女学生围成一圈，鞠躬致意。然后，他们一个接一个地走向水边，轻盈无声地滑入水中，如同鸭子跃出湖面一般。游了几圈后，今村跳上岸，自告奋勇地担任我的临时体育解说员。“我们为什么要游泳？”今村带着他那迷人的笑容，低声问道。“嗯，这很简单。”他像个教授一样，双手交叉，然后用他那修长的棕色手指一一列举了以下几点：

The fifteen men and women in Midori’s class circle and bow. Then, one by one, they stride to the water and slip in, smoothly and soundlessly, like ducks to the surface of a lake. After a few laps, Imamura hops out and volunteers to be my de facto sports announcer. “Why do we swim?” rumbles Imamura, with another winning smile. “Well, that’s very simple, you see.” Like a professor, he steeples his hands, and then proceeds to tick off the following on his slender brown fingers:

为了生存： “日本当然是四面环水。”

For survival: “Japan, of course, is surrounded by water.”

宗教方面： “在神道教的习俗中，禊（用水进行身心清洁的仪式）是神圣的。”

For religion: “In Shinto practices, misogi—the ritualistic cleaning of body and mind with water—is sacred.”

为了战斗： “武士为了保卫封建领土，发展了具有地域特色的游泳学校。”

For fighting: “The samurai, to protect feudal territory, developed regionally specific swimming schools.”

比赛项目包括：“例如跳水、竞速或花样游泳等。”

For competition: “Disciplines include diving and racing, say, or synchronized swimming.”

为了增强身心力量： “日本英法的最高原则是心与水合一。”

For strength of mind and body: “The topmost principle in Nihon eiho is mind and water, together.”

他说，这最后一个原则可以解释为“水之心”。他一边说着，一边用手指蘸着水在旁边的长椅上描摹着日文汉字。“这是最重要的。原因有很多，但等你年纪大了，就能体会到禅宗的精髓，大师的智慧，以及其中的哲学。”

This last principle, he says, can be explained as mizu no kokoro, or “mind like water.” On the bench next to us, he traces a finger on its surface with water as he speaks, writing out the Japanese characters. “This is the most important thing. There are many reasons, but when you get older, you can appreciate the Zen part, the master part, the philosophy.”

我们停下来观看绿子游过。她穿着……她戴着一顶黑色泳帽，上面有两条白色条纹，表明她是小组的组长。其他学员在泳池边观看，她示范着“划水式”（nukite），这种向后划水的姿势我在日本电视上见过，据说可以劈开涌来的波浪，划向大海。她做这一切似乎毫不费力，脸上始终带着微笑，她在水中的自在让我想起一只友善的海豚在嬉戏。

We pause to observe Midori as she swims by. She wears a black cap with two white stripes that signify that she is the director of her group. As the rest of the class watches from the side of the pool, she demonstrates the nukite style, that withdrawing arm stroke I saw on Japanese television, the one intended to cut through incoming waves as one heads out to sea. Because she does this all with seeming effortlessness, and with a smile, her at-homeness in the water makes me think of a friendly porpoise at play.

“绿小姐，她游得非常好，”今村赞许地说。他称赞她流畅优雅的划水动作，并强调了她推进力的强大。“你认识北岛吗？”他问道，指的是日本蛙泳选手北岛康介——或许是史上最伟大的蛙泳选手。北岛在2004年雅典奥运会和2008年北京奥运会上分别获得男子100米和200米蛙泳双料金牌后，于2016年退役。“北岛的蛙泳就像日本泳法——因为他划水一次就势大力沉，然后滑行很长很长一段距离。”他解释说，这一次划水的力量至关重要——它展现了对节奏和耐心的精湛掌控。

“Midori-san, she is very good,” Imamura says, approvingly. He comments on her smooth, elegant stroke and emphasizes the power of her propulsion. “You know Kitajima?” he asks, referring to the Japanese breaststroker Kosuke Kitajima—perhaps the greatest breaststroker of all time. Kitajima retired in 2016 after winning double gold in the men’s 100- and 200-meter breaststroke in the 2004 Athens and the 2008 Beijing Olympics. “Kitajima swims breaststroke like Nihon eiho—because he has one powerful stroke and then floats: a long, long glide.” The power of that one stroke, he explains, is critical—it shows a mastery of pacing and patience.

“运用这些技巧，你可以跑得很快，但这并非重点，”今村说道。“如今，在日本，日本英法是为那些明白它并非像年轻人那样追求速度或胜利的老年人准备的。我们反复练习，非常非常努力地工作，以达到禅定的境界。它关乎精神的力量。”

“You can go very fast using these techniques, but that is not what it is about,” Imamura says. “Now, in modern Japan, Nihon eiho is for older people who know it is not about racing, or winning, the way it is for young people. We practice, practice, practice, and work very, very hard to get to that place of Zen. It is about strength of mind.”

与绿一样，今村几十年来一直是日本咏唱界的一位资深人物。他从小在学校学习日本咏唱，首先是出于传统。他继续……他练习武术是因为他喜欢动作中蕴含的冥想特质。“这就像太极拳，只不过是在水中进行，”他说。“这个比喻很贴切。在专注的过程中，你会找到内心的平静。”

Like Midori, Imamura has been a senior figure in Nihon eiho circles for decades. He learned Nihon eiho as a child in school, first and foremost out of tradition. He continued the martial arts practice because he liked the meditative quality that came along with the physical movements. “It’s like tai chi, but in water,” he says. “That’s a good comparison. In the concentration, you find a peace.”

课堂上，学员们分成三人一组，每组以三角形队形横渡泳池：抬头挺胸，双臂交替划水，双腿蛙泳。每个人都时刻关注着组内其他成员，并做出细微的调整，以确保全组动作同步。伊玛穆拉解释说，不同的游泳者由于身体条件不同，各有长短。这种三人队形练习旨在培养学员的感知能力——既要感知自身和他人的身体，也要感知不断变化的环境——以及控制力。“你不能与水对抗；你必须与水合作，”伊玛穆拉说道。正如其他一些历史悠久的沿海文化，例如荷兰文化所强调的那样，这里再次体现了水是盟友而非敌人的理念。懂得如何在水中生存，才能将水视为朋友。

The class splits into groups of three, and each group sets off swimming across the pool in a triangle formation: head up, arms alternating in a front crawl stroke, legs frog kicking. Each person is fully aware of the others in the group, making minute adjustments so that the whole group moves in synchrony. Different swimmers have different strengths and weaknesses according to their bodies, Imamura explains. The three-swimmer formation is an exercise in awareness—of your own body and others’, and of the ever-changing environment, too—and control. “You can’t work against water; you have to work with water,” Imamura says. As other longtime coastal cultures, like the Dutch, emphasize, here, again, is the idea of water as ally, not enemy. Knowing how to survive water is what allows us to see it as a friend.

下课后，几位老师热情地邀请我去街对面泳池边的小酒吧喝啤酒。我和绿、今村以及另一位老师小妻咲（一位三十多岁、脸上带着酒窝的年轻女子，她容光焕发，在班上显得格外引人注目）围坐在一张木桌旁。这时，一位身材精干、戴着眼镜、头发梳理得一丝不苟的男士出现在桌角：正是日本英法全国委员会主席日野昭典。（我之前看过一篇关于日本英法的日本新闻报道，认出了他。）那天是星期天。下午，因为绿子告诉他我要来，他特意穿上西装打上领带来见我。

After class, the masters delight me with an invitation to join them for beers in a small pub across the street from the pool. Midori, Imamura, and I crowd around a wooden table along with another master, Saki Kozuma, a dimpled young woman in her thirties who stood out from the rest of the class by virtue of her radiant youth. Then a trim, bespectacled man with neatly combed gray hair materializes at the corner of the table: Akinori Hino, the head of the national committee on Nihon eiho himself. (I recognize him from the Japanese news report I watched about Nihon eiho.) On this Sunday afternoon, because Midori informed him of my visit, he has taken the trouble to put on a jacket and tie to meet me.

在这群杰出的游泳大师齐聚一堂之际，我想请教大家，日本泳技如今的魅力何在？人们为何选择学习这种游泳武术，而不是其他游泳课程？他们究竟在追求什么？

With this eminent group of swimming masters gathered, I ask what allure Nihon eiho holds today. Why do people take classes in the swimming martial art instead of other swimming lessons? What are they looking for?

“太好玩了！”今村惊呼道。绿子笑了。

“It’s very fun!” Imamura exclaims. Midori laughs.

“日本英法就是让自己变得更好，”她停顿片刻后补充道。“也许是健康，也许是生活方式，也许是精神层面的东西。每个人都有自己的水平，你可以选择自己练习的目标。你最好的目标是什么？它可以是时间，也可以是速度，但不仅仅是这些。它也可以是我想让我的划水动作更优美。”

“Nihon eiho is to make yourself better,” she adds, after a moment. “Maybe it’s health, or lifestyle. Or something for your mind. Every single person is at their own level, and it lets you choose your own purpose in the practice. What is your best purpose? It can be time, or speed, but it’s not just that. It can also be that I want to be more beautiful in my stroke.”

日野意味深长地点点头。“我感兴趣的正是其中的耐心、放松和慢节奏，”他说。这时，酒吧老板娘端来一托盘啤酒，他顿了顿。大家碰杯，互道“干杯”，然后我们继续交谈。

Hino nods sagely. “The patience, relaxation, and slowness of it is what I find interesting,” he says. He pauses as the proprietress of the pub brings a tray of beers. A round of cheers and kampai, then we continue our conversation.

小妻老师从幼儿园就开始在学校学习游泳。在日本，学龄儿童必须接受游泳训练。她在大学期间开始学习日本泳法。“我喜欢思考如何踩水、如何抓水，以及如何锻炼身心，而不仅仅是身体。” 她在东京一所大学的游泳俱乐部教授高中生和大学生日本泳法。

Kozuma, the young master, learned to swim in school when she was in kindergarten. School-age swim instruction is mandatory in Japan. She started Nihon eiho at her university. “I liked thinking about how to tread water, how to catch water, how to exercise for your mind, too, not just for body.” She teaches Nihon eiho to high school and college kids at a university swim club in Tokyo.

“水里是人们无法发短信、打电话或找到我的最后一个地方，”她咯咯笑着说——这是她努力……在培养下一代的过程中，她发现日本英语有意想不到的好处。

“The water is the last place where people cannot text, call, or find me,” she says with a giggle—in her efforts to develop the next generation, she finds that Nihon eiho has unexpected benefits.

托尼·坎迪是个身材魁梧的人——身高六英尺五英寸，体重超过两百磅。但当他在水中练习日本泳法时，他几乎只露出下巴。在那里，他能以不同的视角看待世界。最近，在一次伦敦之旅中，他在海德公园游泳，那里有天鹅出没。“当你身处水中时，因为你不会溅起水花，蜻蜓会从你身边飞过，船夫会从你身边滑过，”他告诉我。“你对世界的理解是在水面之上，而不是在水下。”他停顿了一下，思考着。“不过，我曾经被一只天鹅攻击过。”

Tony Cundy is a big guy—six feet five and over two hundred pounds. But when he’s in the water practicing Nihon eiho, he’s mostly hidden away to chin level. He gets a different view of the world there. Recently, on a trip to London, he swam in Hyde Park, swans and all. “When you’re in the water, because you’re not breaking the water or splashing, dragonflies will flit past you, boatmen will glide by,” he tells me. “Your understanding of the world is at the waterline, not underneath.” He pauses, considering. “Though a swan did attack me once.”

坎迪是唯一一位获得日本英法认证的非日本籍教练。他现居东京，担任广告公司高管，但成长于英国著名的海军小镇普利茅斯，从小就热爱游泳。年轻时，他以自己精湛的游泳技艺和速度著称，并以此为傲，其水平堪比奥运选手。1995年，22岁的他移居东京，开始学习合气道。五年后，他开始接触日本英法。“我之前对游泳的认知，”他说道，“全都颠覆了。”

Cundy is the only non-Japanese person ever to be certified to teach Nihon eiho. He lives in Tokyo and works as a top advertising executive, but he grew up swimming in Plymouth, a prominent English naval town. As a young man, he was proud of being an accomplished and speedy swimmer in the Olympian tradition. He moved to Tokyo in 1995 when he was twenty-two to study aikido. Five years later, he began to learn about Nihon eiho. “And everything I thought I knew about swimming,” he says, “went out the window.”

他记得第一次和游泳教练一起在泳池里，教练滔滔不绝地讲述着游泳武术的传统。他的老师站在他面前，双臂交叉抱在胸前，一边点头一边看着他。但他并没有站在泳池底部——他站着。他正在游泳，用的是日式的踩水方式——立泳。他的上半身纹丝不动，坎迪忍不住一直盯着他看。

He remembers being in the pool with his swimming teacher for the first time, talking to him at length about the swimming martial arts tradition. His sensei was standing in front of him, arms folded, nodding his head. But he wasn’t standing on the bottom of the pool—he was standing swimming, tachi-oyogi, the Japanese style of treading water. His upper body was so still that Cundy couldn’t stop staring.

一位老师潜入五米泳池底部，走过池面，然后平静地浮回水面。一位学员举着五公斤重的哑铃，在水中踩水超过一个小时。他的老师在水中射箭，精准地击中各种目标的中心。突然间，他明白了，游泳的关键不在于速度或距离，而在于掌握足够的技巧，以便应对未来生活中可能遇到的任何水上情况。他学会了用臀部和腿部发力，以全新的方式控制动作和动量，大大减少了手臂的使用。这对他来说是一次醍醐灌顶的顿悟。

A teacher dropping to the bottom of a five-meter pool, walking across it, and then floating serenely back up. A practitioner treading water with arms aloft, holding a five-kilogram dumbbell, for more than an hour. His sensei firing arrows across the water to hit the centers of various targets. Suddenly, he saw, swimming was not about speed or distance but about becoming skilled enough to handle whatever water scenarios he might encounter out in the world. He learned to develop movement and momentum in new ways, through the hips and legs, with much less use of the arms. It was a revelation.

“我以前游泳总是低着头，拼命划水，下潜，上浮，下潜，上浮，想着能游多少圈？我从来没注意过其他事情，”坎迪说。“现在我总是抬头挺胸，用鼻子呼吸。我能看到每一道波浪，对周围的环境也非常敏感。”速度只是日本泳法的一个组成部分，并非其根本目标。坎迪认为，在大多数情况下，游泳是一种更敏锐地体验周围环境的方式。

“My swimming was always, Head down, thrash away, down, up, down, up, how many laps can I do? I never noticed anything else,” Cundy says. “Now my head is always up, and I breathe through my nose. I can see every wave, and I’m very aware of my surroundings.” Speed is just one component of Nihon eiho, not the fundamental objective. For the most part, Cundy sees it as a way to experience his environment more keenly.

坎迪曾参加过各种日本英法比赛，包括在日本举行的年度全国比赛。该比赛只有两项是竞速项目，其中一项采用的泳姿正是1898年横滨游泳队击败外国选手时所用的泳姿。考试和比赛项目涵盖了计时赛、举重、挥旗表演和全副武装游泳等。

Cundy has competed in different Nihon eiho events, including the annual national competition in Japan. Only two events in that competition are races, one of which employs the stroke that those Yokohama swimmers used to beat the foreigners way back in 1898. The examinations and competitions range from those time trials and weight holding to demonstrations of flag waving and armored swimming.

我半开玩笑地问他是否准备好战斗了。“哎呀，”他想了一会儿，惊呼道。然后他指出，其中一些原理与海豹突击队的战斗和步法技巧相似（显然，海豹突击队体现了许多理想，例如运动心理学家吉姆·鲍曼所说的超强心理素质）。但是，尽管日本泳姿对体能和运动能力都提出了很高的要求，真正让他坚持下去的，是其中蕴含的思考和精湛技艺——“就像给碗上漆一样精益求精”

I ask him, half-jokingly, if he feels ready for battle. “Crikey,” he exclaims, thinking for a moment. Then he points out that some of the principles are similar to the combat and treading techniques used by Navy SEALs (clearly the SEALs embody a host of ideals, like the superior mental toughness that sports psychologist Jim Bauman spoke of). But for all of Nihon eiho’s physical challenges and athleticism, it’s the degree of thought and refinement—“the same kind of refinement that has been applied to lacquering your bowl, for that matter”—that keeps him swimming.

武士游泳的理​​念在今天依然具有深刻的哲学意义。哲学家达蒙·杨在其著作《如何思考运动》中重拾了古老的运动理念，认为运动应该兼顾人的整体人性，而不仅仅是他所谓的“身体机器”。杨指出，在体力和脑力活动方面，那种二元对立的思维方式——比如运动员与书呆子、运动型与书呆型——是一种错误的划分。

The ideals of samurai swimming have a clear philosophical resonance today. In his book How to Think About Exercise, the philosopher Damon Young revives the ancient idea of exercise as something that takes into account one’s whole humanity—and not just what he calls “the bodily machine.” Young observes that the tendency to think in dualism—jocks vs. nerds, sporty vs. bookish—is a false divide when it comes to physical and mental exertions.

他认为，游泳的益处不仅在于增强体魄，更在于提升智力。理想的现代游泳运动员注重的是整体体验，而非将锻炼视为一种“调教”。同样重要的是，我们对锻炼有多么出色而感到自豪。“我们越是拥有完整的自我意识，”杨格曾对一位采访者说，“我们就越会为此承担责任。”

Swimming’s benefit, he argues, has as much to do with intellectual enhancements as it does the achievements of the body. The ideal modern swimmer focuses on the whole experience rather than the perception of exercise as a “tune-up.” Important, too, is the pride we feel in the well-exercised body. “The fuller sense of self we have,” Young once told an interviewer, “the more responsibility we take for it.”

随着时间的推移，游泳已经从单纯的机械技能和生存技能——一种由男性练习的军事技能——转变为一项能够实现目标的技能。游泳还有一种更深层次的意义：它是一种休闲方式，一种乐趣，能够提升你的精神和身体健康。这种通过游泳来促进身心健康、获得情感共鸣、实现人格完整发展的理念，我深有同感。身体和心理是密不可分的。

Over time, swimming has shifted from mere mechanics and survival—a military skill, practiced by men—to achieve a more intangible significance: a form of recreation, a pleasure, something that can sharpen your spiritual as well as physical health. This idea of swimming for wellness, emotional resonance, whole personhood, rings true to me. The physical is intertwined with the psychological.

在日本，泽井敦弘是一位畅销书作家，他撰写关于身心合一、开发“气”（生命能量）的理论。他还记录了自己学习日本英法（Nihon eiho）的经历。其中最令他印象深刻的是“束缚缠身”（shusoku garami），这种技巧可以让人在双手双脚被捆绑的情况下游泳。我们当中很少有人会面临从敌营逃脱、必须游过护城河才能逃脱的境地，但这其中蕴含着一些道理。“我惊讶地看着一个双手双脚被绑的人在水池里游来游去，他的动作介于青蛙和鳗鱼之间。他可以俯泳，也可以仰泳，头朝前，脚朝后，”敦弘写道。“我的老师让我们大吃一惊，他说：‘你们以为游泳是用胳膊和腿，但你们错了。不用胳膊腿也能游泳。看看鱼儿吧。真正的游泳是用全身。’”

In Japan, Sawai Atsuhiro is a bestselling author who writes about mind and body unification principles that develop ki, or life energy. He has also written about his experiences of studying to be a master in Nihon eiho. The technique that impressed him most was shusoku garami, which allows someone to swim with both hands and feet bound together. There aren’t many of us who will face the possibility of breaking out of an enemy prison, having to swim across the castle moat to escape, but there’s a lesson here. “Astonished, I watch a man with hands and feet tied swim across a pool with a motion that is a cross between a swimming frog and an undulating eel. He is able to swim on his front or on his back, head first or feet first,” Atsuhiro writes. “And my teacher surprised us by saying, ‘You believe you swim with the arms and legs, but you’re wrong. You can swim without them. Look at a fish. Real swimming is using the whole body.’”

在我的脑海中，鲑鱼再次浮现，它们是适应力、韧性和耐力的优雅典范。我们并非鱼类，但我们依然能从它们身上汲取灵感。在这里，鲑鱼提醒我们，游泳可以是一项全身心投入的运动。游泳比赛的严苛磨练，造就了人们对游泳的热爱，将其视为一种身心全面提升的方式。重点从单纯关注身体转向身心合一。想象一下溪流汇入河流，河流最终流入大海。

In my mind, the salmon surfaces again, that elegant example of adaptation, tenacity, and stamina. We are not fish, but from them we continue to take inspiration. In this case, the fish reminds us that swimming can be something to engage your whole self. From the rigor of swimming competition comes a devotion to swimming as holistic self-betterment. The emphasis moves from body alone to body and mind, together. Think of a stream flowing into a river, a river flowing into the sea.

这些水域交汇在一起，让我明白了我为什么会游泳。

These waters run together in a way that helps me to understand why I swim.

流动

FLOW

水是 H₂O ，由两部分氢和一部分氧组成，但还有第三种物质，使水成为一种物质，但没有人知道它是什么。

Water is H2O, hydrogen two parts, oxygen one, but there is also a third thing, that makes it water and nobody knows what it is.

——D·H·劳伦斯，《第三件事》

—D. H. Lawrence, “The Third Thing”

这句话出自《白鲸》的开篇。“是的，正如每个人都知道的那样，”以实玛利宣称，“冥想和水永远是密不可分的。”

It’s in the opening pages of Moby-Dick. “Yes, as every one knows,” Ishmael declares, “meditation and water are wedded forever.”

小说开篇，伊什梅尔便将我们的注意力引向聚集在曼哈顿海岸边，凝望着大海的人群，他们沉浸在一个安息日的午后。瞧，这些人，都微微俯身，仿佛要将我们定格在梦境之中。他们的出现印证了他的观点：大海那如液体般流动的指尖，的确有一种魔力，能让我们沉浸于思绪之中。伊什梅尔指出，古波斯人称大海为圣，希腊人则赋予它一位强大的神祇。处女航仿佛蕴含着某种“神秘的韵律”。但水的魔力究竟是什么？它又对我们产生了怎样的影响？这仍然是个谜。

Here at the novel’s beginning, Ishmael calls our attention to the crowds of dreamy water gazers gathered along the shores of Manhattan on a Sabbath afternoon. See all those people, leaning over ever so far. They prove him right: the ocean’s liquid fingers have a way of transfixing us in thought. Ishmael points out that the ancient Persians call the sea holy, that the Greeks give it a powerful deity of its very own. A maiden voyage sings with a kind of “mystical vibration.” But what exactly is the magic of water, and what does it do to us? It’s a mystery.

当我们凝视湖泊、河流或海洋时，会发现水能激发一种特殊的遐想。或许，如果我们不只是观看，而是跳入水中畅游一番，水的深处更能提升我们的意识。

When we peer into a lake, river, or ocean, we find that water encourages a particular kind of reverie. Perhaps its depths can enhance our consciousness even more if, instead of just looking, we get in and swim.

我们跳入水中，发现自己置身于一个奇特的环境中过渡空间。我们身处其中，悬置却又流动；漂浮却又时刻面临沉没的危险。如果我们顺流而下，而非与之对抗，便能找到一种瞬间的状态，一种运动与悖论式静止并存的状态，那就是流动。

We jump into that water and find ourselves in a curious liminal space. Here we are, suspended, yet moving; floating, yet ever in danger of sinking. And if we swim with the current, instead of fighting against it, we find a momentary state, one of motion and yet paradoxical stillness that is flow.

匈牙利心理学家米哈里·契克森米哈赖（Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi）将“心流”解释为“人们完全沉浸于某项活动，以至于其他一切都变得无关紧要的状态”。他说，这种活动——比如游泳或演奏音乐——带来的愉悦感如此强烈，“以至于人们即使付出巨大的代价，也会为了享受其中而去做”。我想到了冰冷的海水、黎明即起的锻炼、肩伤，还有我花在比基尼上的所有钱。

Flow is what the groundbreaking Hungarian psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi explains as “the state in which people are so involved in an activity that nothing else seems to matter.” The experience of said activity—swimming, say, or playing music—is so entirely enjoyable, he says, “that people will do it even at great cost, for the sheer sake of doing it.” I think of frigid waters, crack-of-dawn workouts, shoulder injuries, all the money I’ve spent on bikinis.

近三十年前，齐克森米哈里首次使用“心流”一词来描述完全沉浸于某种体验之中，以至于自我意识消融，时间流逝的感知也随之消失的感受。他写道：“每一个动作、每一个念头都必然地源于前一个，就像演奏爵士乐一样。”这种毫不费力、全身心投入的专注令人愉悦。对我而言，真正走进水中去追寻这种狂喜的状态有着双重吸引力：它让我同时体验到两种沉浸感。

Nearly three decades ago, Csikszentmihalyi was the first to use the word flow to describe the experience of being so totally immersed that the self seems to fall away, along with any awareness of the passage of time. “Every action, movement, and thought follows inevitably from the previous one, like playing jazz,” he writes. This kind of effortless, deeply engaged concentration is joyful. For me, actually getting into water to chase that ecstatic state of mind has a double appeal: it’s two kinds of immersion experienced at once.

1810年，在齐克森米哈赖（Csikszentmihalyi）对“流动”一词做出定义一个半世纪之前，诗人拜伦勋爵横渡了赫勒斯滂海峡——这条险恶的四英里海峡，如今被称为达达尼尔海峡，位于土耳其北部。他从爱琴海游到马尔马拉海，顺着潮汐从欧洲游到亚洲。在此过程中，他开启了……几个世纪以来，人们对那里的水域一直充满迷恋。时至今日，游泳爱好者们依然对横渡这片象征性海洋充满热情。但我最感兴趣的是，正是这次游泳开启了拜伦的创作灵感。

In 1810, a century and a half before Csikszentmihalyi defined flow as such, the poet Lord Byron swam the Hellespont, the treacherous four-mile strait that is today known as the Dardanelles, in northern Turkey. He crossed from the Aegean to the Sea of Marmara, swimming with the tide from Europe to Asia. In the process, he kicked off a centuries-long fascination with the waters there. To this day, swimmers are enamored with the traverse of these symbolic seas. But what I’m most interested in is the idea that this swim is the thing that unclogged Byron’s creative faucet.

拜伦痴迷于游泳。他患有腿部畸形，严重影响了他的步态；只有在水中，他才能感受到真正的自由和自我。“我热爱大海，”他写道，“每次出水，我都感到一种前所未有的精神振奋。”他甚至幻想自己前世是人鱼。他尽可能地游泳：泰晤士河上的桥到桥，里斯本的塔霍河河口，以及威尼斯大运河。在他横渡赫勒斯滂海峡时，他已经发表了一些诗作，但尚未成为伟大的浪漫主义诗人之一。

Byron was obsessed with swimming. He suffered from a leg deformity, which severely contracted his gait; he never felt so free and himself as when he was in the water. “I delight in the sea,” he wrote, “and come out with a buoyancy of spirits I never feel on any other occasion.” He entertained the thought of having been a merman in a previous life. He swam wherever he could: bridge to bridge on the Thames River, in a Tagus River estuary in Lisbon, down the length of Venice’s Grand Canal. At the time of his Hellespont swim, he had published some poetry but had not yet established himself as one of the great Romantic poets.

然而，他成功横渡赫勒斯滂海峡的经历激发了他的灵感，于是他创作了讽刺诗《从塞斯托斯游到阿拜多斯之后所作》，以此向这次游泳以及希腊神话中希罗和利安德的故事致敬。利安德是一位来自阿拜多斯的年轻人，他爱上了希罗，一位住在塞斯托斯塔楼里的阿芙洛狄忒女祭司。每天晚上，利安德都会游过四英里的赫勒斯滂海峡去拜访希罗，希罗的灯指引着他。一天晚上，灯熄灭了，他被波涛和水流吞没，溺水身亡。希罗从塔楼上纵身跃下，与他一同赴死。

His successful Hellespont crossing, though, got his muse talking, and he produced “Written after Swimming from Sestos to Abydos,” a satiric poem in homage to the swim and to the Greek myth of Hero and Leander. Leander, a young man from Abydos, falls in love with Hero, a priestess of Aphrodite who lives in a tower in Sestos. Every night, Leander swims the four miles of the Hellespont to visit Hero, guided by her lamp. One night the lamp blows out, and he drowns, overcome by the waves and currents. She throws herself from her tower to join him in death.

拜伦轻描淡写地描述了那次艰苦的游泳给恋人和他自己带来的分歧：

Of the strenuous swim, Byron wrote airily of the divergence in consequence for the lovers and himself:

很难说谁表现最好：

’Twere hard to say who fared the best:

可悲的凡人啊！因此，诸神依然在诅咒你们！

Sad mortals! thus the Gods still plague you!

他失去了劳动成果，我失去了玩笑：

He lost his labour, I my jest:

因为他溺水了，而我得了疟疾。

For he was drown’d, and I’ve the ague.

是的，拜伦虽然经历了一阵发烧和寒战，但尽管他语气轻松，他仍然觉得游泳让他摆脱了忧郁，激发了他的创作灵感，让他得以展现自己最好的一面。事实上，赫勒斯滂海峡成了他人生的一个转折点。1819年，他创作了诗歌杰作《唐璜》的前两章；在诗中，他更加自豪地提及了这次横渡。他还写了许多充满想象力的信件给朋友，信中他以英雄和利安德的神话为蓝本，讲述了自己游泳的经历。最终，拜伦加入了希腊反抗奥斯曼帝国的独立战争，并因此成为希腊民族英雄。

Yes, Byron escaped with a bout of fever and chills, but for all his jaunty tone, he felt that swimming coaxed him out of melancholy, opened up his creative stores, and gave him access to his best self. In truth, the Hellespont became a touchstone for him. In 1819, he would write the first two cantos of “Don Juan,” his poetic masterpiece; in it, he makes more proud references to that crossing. He also wrote many imaginative letters to friends riffing on the Hero and Leander myth as it related to his swim. Eventually, Byron joined Greece’s war of independence against the Ottoman Empire, for which he would become a Greek national hero.

随着时间的推移，“拜伦式”逐渐成为我们最富激情的探索者、游泳健将和艺术家的代名词。拜伦代表了文化史学家雅克·巴尔赞所描述的“专注的头脑”，以及“高昂的精神、机智的谈吐、清醒的常识和对真理的热情——简而言之，是智慧活力的独特释放”。横渡赫勒斯滂海峡激发了拜伦的想象力；也正是在那之后，他的文字和他的世界才迸发出如此鲜活的力量，足以触动我们所有人。

In time, “Byronic” would be a label for our most passionate seekers, swimmers, and artists. Byron came to represent what the cultural historian Jacques Barzun once described as a “concentrated mind,” as well as “high spirits, wit, daylight good sense, and a passion for truth—in short a unique discharge of intellectual vitality.” Swimming the Hellespont was the thing that loosed Byron’s imagination; only after did his words, and his world, generate a vivid electricity potent enough to reach the rest of us.

15

15

宗教练习

A Religious Exercise

游泳带来的专注和即时性，让我想起了我的孩子们：一种活在当下的状态。每一个过去的瞬间都被新的瞬间所取代：一个接一个的“现在”，让我没有太多时间去沉湎于过去，也没有太多时间去担忧未来。活在当下，对我忙碌的大脑来说是一种挑战——但我渴望它。游泳是我对抗存在主义焦虑的良药。

The focused immediacy of swimming encourages a mindset that reminds me of how my young children think: it’s an ever-present-ness. Every past moment is immediately replaced by a new one: a constant stream of now, and now, and now that doesn’t allow much room to dwell too long on things past, or what’s to come. Living in the now is a state of being that my busy brain finds challenging—but I desire it. Swimming is an antidote for the existential anxiety from which I suffer.

在罗杰·迪金（Roger Deakin）的著名游历英国水道的著作《水之记录》（Waterlog）中，这位博物学家将游泳描述为一种具有变革性、如同爱丽丝梦游仙境般的体验；这项活动影响着他对自我和时间的感知。“当你进入水中，就会发生某种类似蜕变的事情，”他写道。“离开陆地，你穿过镜面般的水面，进入一个全新的世界……游泳时，你看到和体验到的事物都与以往截然不同。”与其他任何事物都不同。”他补充道，“你对当下的感受是无比强烈的。”

In Waterlog, his celebrated chronicle of swimming through Britain’s waterways, the naturalist Roger Deakin described swimming as having a transformative, Alice-in-Wonderland quality; it was an activity that had power over his perception of self and of time. “When you enter the water, something like metamorphosis happens,” he wrote. “Leaving behind the land, you go through the looking-glass surface and enter a new world . . . You see and experience things when you’re swimming in a way that is completely different from any other.” Your sense of the present, he added, “is overwhelming.”

运动员经常谈到“进入状态”，在这种状态下，表现似乎完全是自动的。研究人员将其描述为一种心理上的时间感知改变，它使你的注意力集中在当下——你完全沉浸在活动中，全神贯注于阅读和对外部刺激做出反应，以至于时间似乎变慢了，当下这一刻被无限延长。

Athletes often talk about “being in the zone,” where performance seems to happen at an automatic level. Researchers have described this as a psychological alteration of time that pulls your focus to the here and now—you’re so consumed by the activity, and so occupied with reading and reacting to external stimuli, that time seems to slow down, so that the present moment is expanded.

心理学家罗伯特·尼德弗（Robert Nideffer）在20世纪80年代率先将运动心理学确立为一门学科，他将“心流”和“状态”定义为两种相似但又截然不同的沉浸式状态—— “状态”指的是身体机能的最佳状态，“心流”指的是心理状态的最佳状态。他认为，处于“状态”的人会感觉时间变慢；而处于“心流”状态的人则会失去对时间的感知，感觉时间飞逝。

The psychologist Robert Nideffer, who first helped establish sports psychology as a discipline in the 1980s, has defined zone and flow as two similar, but distinct, immersive states—using zone to refer to the optimal state of physical performance and flow to refer to the optimal state of mental performance. People who are in the zone, he argues, experience time as slowed down. People who are in a flow state, by contrast, lose awareness of time, so that it seems to fly by.

当然，对于运动员来说，专注于身体表现是全部的精力；在比赛中，目标是游得最快，所以大脑不能偏离这个目标太远。这正是莱德基和菲尔普斯所擅长的那种海豹突击队般的高度专注。即使对于我这样一个在泳池里游来游去的普通人来说，比赛也会让我的注意力紧紧地集中在动作上，以至于形成一种“隧道视野”。神经心理学家大卫·伊格曼已经确定，这种时间感变慢的现象源于在肾上腺素飙升、压力巨大的事件中——无论是比赛还是濒死体验——记忆会更加丰富地形成。（毕竟，比赛是对……的升华。）我们的生存本能转化为竞争。）回想起来，我们对这些事件的记忆更加详细，因此时间似乎被拉长了，从而变慢了。

For the athlete, of course, attention to physical performance is all-consuming; in a race, the point is to go fast, so the brain can’t wander too far from that objective. This is the type of Navy SEAL laser focus that Ledecky and Phelps excel at. Even for me, a mere mortal in the pool, competition fastens my attention so tightly to the action that it creates a kind of tunnel vision. The neuropsychologist David Eagleman has determined that this slowing-of-time perception comes from memories being formed more richly during high-adrenaline, high-stress events—whether it’s a competition or a near-death experience. (Racing, after all, is the sublimation of our survival instincts into a competition.) In retrospect, we remember those events in greater detail, so that time seems expanded, and thereby slowed down.

然而，如果没有比赛，或者水是威胁，我发现，将动作精进到自动化的程度，实际上能让我将注意力转移到其他地方。虽然比赛本身与心流相悖，但训练却能促成心流。当你达到流畅的境界时，那种身体上的轻松和愉悦感会引领你的思维进入未知的领域。突破这层界限，你会发现一种不同的存在方式。这种高度集中的注意力——时间仿佛膨胀，或者加速流逝；感觉时间不再重要，或者说它远没有你想象的那么重要——正是我所追求的心流。

Absent a race situation, or one in which water is a threat, though, I’ve found that the refinement of movement to automation is actually the thing that allows my attention to shift elsewhere. While competition itself is at odds with flow, the training part enables it. When you’ve reached fluency, that physical ease and pleasure grants your mind entry to uncharted territory. Push through the looking-glass, and you’ll discover a different way of being. This heightened attentiveness—the ballooning of time, or the speeding-up of it; the perception that time no longer matters, or that it matters less than you might have thought—is the kind of flow I’m after.

作为人类游泳者，我们永远无法真正成为鱼。你我都明白这一点。我们无需提醒自己周围是水。但我们偶尔会体验到鱼儿的感受。我们会短暂地忘记水的存在。在这种遗忘中，我们可以随波逐流。白日梦对于解决问题和激发创造力至关重要。科学家们现在知道，当我们的思绪漫无目的地游荡时，大脑的“默认模式网络”就会被激活。正是它促成了新鲜、意想不到的联系。这也是为什么你会在淋浴时迸发出一些绝妙的想法。海洋生物学家兼作家华莱士·J·尼科尔斯（Wallace J. Nichols）大力倡导他所谓的“蓝色思维”，强调随波逐流对于发现的重要性，并将水视为实现这种思维的途径。过程。“身处水边，能营造出感官丰富的环境，带来足够的‘柔和魅力’，让我们的注意力得以放松，让默认模式网络启动，”他写道。“阿基米德在浴缸里推导出测量不规则形状物体体积的方法，这绝非巧合。灵光一闪！”

As human swimmers, we can never really be the fish. You and I, we know that. We don’t have to remind ourselves that it’s water around us. But we get glimpses of what it’s like to be the fish. We get flashes of forgetting the water. In the forgetting, we can drift. Daydreaming is critical to problem solving and creativity. Scientists now know that when our minds are wandering without any particular external focus, the brain’s “default-mode network” is active. It’s what makes fresh, unexpected connections possible. And it’s the reason you get some of your best ideas in the shower. The marine biologist and author Wallace J. Nichols is an evangelist of achieving what he calls “blue mind,” which emphasizes the importance of drifting to discovery, and water as a way to enable that process. “Being around water provides a sensory-rich environment with enough ‘soft fascination’ to let our focused attention rest and the default-mode network to kick in,” he writes. “It’s no coincidence that Archimedes was in the bathtub when he deduced a method for measuring the volume of an object with an irregular shape. Eureka!”

琳恩·考克斯向我解释说，游泳能让人进入一种改变的状态，就像吸毒一样。有时，我们会无比清晰地专注于某件事，并能屏蔽掉无关的事物；有时，注意力会变得模糊，一个念头会引出另一个念头，而不会中断。“既然可以去海里游个泳，谁还需要迷幻药呢？”她笑着说。

In its power to produce an altered state, Lynne Cox explains to me, swimming is like a drug. Sometimes we zero in on something with unparalleled lucidity, and we gain the ability to tune out the extraneous stuff; other times the focus is fuzzy, and one thought leads to another, without interruption. “Who needs psychedelics,” she says with a laugh, “when you can just go for a swim in the ocean?”

已故神经学家兼作家奥利弗·萨克斯描述了一种超然的状态，这种状态人人皆可体验，从他那“体型庞大如鲸鱼”的父亲——他父亲直到94岁高龄仍每日优雅地游泳——到孩童皆可达到。萨克斯会在游泳时在脑海中构思书籍。考克斯与萨克斯成了挚友，每当他们恰巧同时身处纽约或加利福尼亚时，便会一起游泳。他们的初次相遇是在曼哈顿的一个游泳池里，两人共用一条泳道。游完泳后，萨克斯从泳池里爬出来，身上还滴着水，便用防水平板电脑记笔记。

The late neurologist and writer Oliver Sacks described a transcendent state that is accessible to all, from his father—with his “great whalelike bulk,” who swam daily and elegantly until ninety-four years of age—to the very young. Sacks wrote books in his head while swimming. Cox became great friends with Sacks, and on the occasions that they ended up in New York or California at the same time, they would go for swims together. During their first meeting, they shared a lane in a Manhattan pool. Afterward, Sacks climbed out of the pool, still dripping, to write notes on a waterproof tablet.

考克斯注意到了这一点。她告诉他，她最好的灵感也是在游泳时产生的。他们一致认为，游泳是思考、随波逐流、在脑海中构思的理想时机。

Cox noticed. She told him that she, too, came up with her best brainstorms while swimming. They agreed that swimming was an ideal time to ruminate, to noodle for noodling’s sake, to compose in one’s head.

考克斯游泳时，她的脑子里在想些什么？“这是一种介于梦境和清醒之间的状态，”她告诉我。她说，或许我们可以称之为“海之梦境”。游泳的节奏会让你的身体放松下来——训练有素的身体似乎会不由自主地继续游动——而你的大脑则可以自由驰骋。

What is it like inside Cox’s head when she’s swimming? “It’s a state between a dream state and an awake state,” she tells me. Maybe, she says, we can call it sea-dreaming. The rhythm of swimming lulls your body—which, well-trained, seems to keep moving on its own—and your brain is allowed to go wherever it wants.

“也许你会闻到码头上有人正在喝咖啡的香味，”考克斯说。“你会注意到水面泛起的涟漪，鹈鹕从身边掠过。也许当你看到一群银色的凤尾鱼在你脚下游动时，你的心跳都会停止。”在静谧的海浪声中，你可以选择过滤掉一些事物，专注于另一些。认知科学家已经证明，水声——海洋有节奏的低吟，瀑布奔腾的轰鸣——能够使人脑平静下来。我们会感到心率和血压下降，α波活动增强——这种脑波与放松和血清素分泌增加有关——同时也能激发创造性思维。有一天，我在Spotify上闲逛时发现，一些白噪音水声是这个音乐流媒体服务上最热门的歌曲之一；其中一首名为“滚滚海浪”的曲目播放量已经接近1500万次。

“Maybe you smell the coffee someone is drinking on the pier,” Cox says. “There’s this awareness of the ripples of water, the pelicans sliding right by. Maybe your heart stops as you see a wave of silvery anchovies swimming below you.” In the hushed oceanic roar, you can choose to filter some things out and to focus on others. Cognitive scientists have shown that water sounds—the rhythmic hum of the ocean, the rush of a waterfall—are calming to the human brain. We experience a drop in heart rate and blood pressure and an increase in alpha-wave activity—those brain wavelengths associated with relaxation and boosted serotonin—as well as that creative thinking.
