While tooling around on Spotify one day, I find that white-noise water sounds are some of the biggest hits on the music-streaming service; one such track, called “Rolling Ocean Waves,” has been played nearly fifteen million times.

漫步林间固然美好，梭罗在其超验主义经典著作《瓦尔登湖》中对此有所阐述。但在1845年至1847年间，梭罗在瓦尔登湖畔的小屋里生活了两年零两个月零两天，期间他每天清晨都会早起游泳；他将其描述为“一种宗教仪式，也是我做过的最美好的事情之一”。每一次游泳都令他身心愉悦。每日的例行活动早起是为了实现他在新英格兰森林中“有意识地生活”的愿望。

Walks in the woods are all well and good, as Thoreau illustrated in his transcendentalist classic, Walden. But during the two years, two months, and two days that he spent living in that cabin at Walden Pond, between 1845 and 1847, he also got up early every morning to swim; he described it as “a religious exercise, and one of the best things which I did.” Each of his swims stimulated body and mind. Each day’s routine of rousing early to do so was a way to enact his desire to “live deliberately” in the New England forest.

人们常常把散步视为伟大思想家的工具：查尔斯·达尔文、阿尔伯特·爱因斯坦、阿莫斯·特沃斯基和丹尼尔·卡尼曼，他们三人曾结伴漫步，彻底革新了决策科学。然而，人们却很少明确提及游泳——一种类似的辅助方式，与其说是工具不如说是媒介——它对于引导内心世界、促进思维流畅至关重要。（尽管爱因斯坦不会游泳，但他热爱水上旅行。在他1922年至1923年写成、最近才出版的旅行日记中，他写道：“海上航行多么有利于思考和工作啊——简直是人间天堂，没有书信往来、拜访、会议，以及其他种种魔鬼的发明！”）

Much has been made of the walk as the instrument for big thinkers: Charles Darwin; Albert Einstein; Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, who famously rambled together and revolutionized the science of decision making. Less has been explicitly made of swimming—a similar kind of aid, more medium than tool—for channeling the inner life and improving the flow of thoughts. (Though Einstein could not swim, he loved to journey by water. In his travel diaries, dating from 1922 to 1923 but just recently published, he wrote, “How conducive to thinking and working the sea voyage is—a paradisaical state without correspondence, visits, meetings, and other inventions of the devil!”)

身体活动与环境同样重要。科学记者费里斯·贾布尔在一篇题为《为什么步行有助于思考》的文章中指出：“我们移动身体的方式会进一步改变我们的思维方式，反之亦然。”由此可见，游泳的节奏，由于其流畅的连续性，能够促进一种特定的思维方式。游泳和陆地运动都会对我们的身体化学产生相同的变化：心跳加快、血液循环增强，从而为肌肉和大脑提供更多的血液和氧气。

The physical action matters just as much as the environment does. “The way we move our bodies further changes the nature of our thoughts, and vice versa,” notes the science journalist Ferris Jabr, in an essay called “Why Walking Helps Us Think.” It follows that the pace of swimming, because of its fluid continuity, encourages a specific kind of thinking. There are the same changes to our body chemistry in swimming as there are in land exercise: faster heartbeat, increased circulation, more blood and oxygen to muscles and brain.

贾布尔援引了弗吉尼亚·伍尔夫笔下经典沉思者、漫游者克拉丽莎·达洛维的漫游经历，称她“不仅感知着周围的城市，更在过往中穿梭”。伍尔夫本人也曾在日记中写道，漫步于城市之中令人精神振奋。伦敦用充满活力、水生的语言来描述这种沉浸式体验，就像“站在最大波浪的最高峰上，身处事物的中心并与之共舞”。

Jabr invokes the peripatetics of Clarissa Dalloway, Virginia Woolf’s classic musing, ambulatory character, as someone who “does not merely perceive the city around her. Rather, she dips in and out of her past.” Woolf herself, writing in her diary about the stimulating energy of walking through London, used energetic, aquatic language to describe the immersive experience as “being on the highest crest of the biggest wave, right in the centre & swim of things.”

贾布尔在详细描述斯坦福大学关于步行与创造力关系的研究实验时写道，步行会让“思绪在翻腾的思想海洋中漂流”。对贾布尔、伍尔夫和其他一些人来说，措辞的选择暴露了他们的真实想法。他们谈到“灵感涌现”，谈到灵感翻滚，谈到思想之流中“波光粼粼的水面”。步行固然有助于思考，但游泳同样也是一种有效的思维途径。

In his detailing of Stanford University research experiments on the relationship between walking and creativity, Jabr writes that walking set “the mind adrift on a frothing sea of thought.” For Jabr, Woolf, and others, the choice of words betrays them. They talk of “ideas bubbling up,” the tumbling of them, the “wrinkling water” in a current of thought. Walking is conducive to thinking, but swimming is just as true a conduit.

像游泳者那样有意识地生活，意味着你是一个追寻者：追逐海洋的蓝色灯芯绒，追随河流的脉络。科学作家弗洛伦斯·威廉姆斯指出，“地点很重要”——从亚里士多德到华兹华斯，诗人和哲学家们早已告诉我们这一点。“我们的神经系统天生就会与环境中的特定点产生共鸣，”威廉姆斯在她的著作《自然疗法》中写道。“科学正在证实浪漫主义者早已知晓的真理。”拜伦深谙此道，并尽可能地追寻着它。我们渴望靠近海洋、湖泊和河流。尽管飓风预警和海平面上升，我们仍然在海滩上建造房屋，因为那景色对我们有着某种特殊的意义。

To live deliberately as a swimmer means that you are a seeker: a chaser of the ocean’s blue corduroy, a follower of river veins. The science writer Florence Williams notes that “place matters”—something that poets and philosophers from Aristotle to Wordsworth have been telling us for ages. “Our nervous systems are built to resonate with set points in the environment,” Williams writes, in her book The Nature Fix. “Science is now bearing out what the Romantics knew to be true.” Byron knew it, and swam after it whenever he could. We want to be near the ocean, the lake, the river. We build houses on the beach despite hurricane warnings and sea-level rise because that view does something to us.

研究发现，心脏手术后康复的住院病人，如果床脚摆放着自然风景图片，所需的止痛药剂量会减少；包含水景的图片比封闭森林的图片更能有效缓解术后焦虑。人类需要亲近自然，威廉姆斯写道，因为“我们的大脑尤其喜爱水”，所以我们需要在城市地区增加更多“蓝色空间”，而不仅仅是绿色空间。威廉姆斯盛赞旧金山湾区独特的水域环境——南端和海豚俱乐部的游泳爱好者们，他们正奋力游向恶魔岛！——但她最欣赏的还是新西兰惠灵顿，那里有一条公共浮潜路线。（现在就预订门票吧！）

Hospital patients recovering from heart surgery have been found to need less pain medication when there are nature scenes at the foot of their beds; an image that includes water is even more effective than an image of an enclosed forest in reducing anxiety during the post-operative period. As humans, we need doses of nature, and because “our brains especially love water,” Williams writes, we need more “blue space,” not just green space, in our urban areas. Williams gives a shout-out to the aquatic specialness of the San Francisco Bay Area—all those South End and Dolphin Club swimmers, stroking to Alcatraz!—but reserves her greatest admiration for Wellington, New Zealand, which has a public snorkel trail. (Book your tickets now.)

在一次游泳时，考克斯问萨克斯能否给他一些仰泳技巧方面的建议。萨克斯欣然同意，因为任何能让他游得更轻松的方法都意味着他不必将太多精力集中在游泳上，从而可以腾出脑力去思考其他事情。

During one of their swims, Cox asked Sacks if she could give him a tip or two on his backstroke. He was happy and agreeable about it, because anything that allowed him to swim more easily meant that he could swim without having to devote too much mental bandwidth to the act, freeing his mind to puzzle over other things.

2015年，萨克斯82岁高龄，身患癌症。但他仍然坚持每天游泳一英里，尽可能地坚持下去，并写作到生命的最后一刻。

In 2015, Sacks was eighty-two and dying of cancer. And yet he still swam a mile a day, for as long as he could, writing until the end.

简而言之，快乐是进入心流状态的必要条件。尼德弗和齐克森米哈里都强调，心理挑战必须是我们热爱去做的事情，否则我们无法达到心流状态。

Joy is, quite simply, essential to the achievement of the flow state. Both Nideffer and Csikszentmihalyi emphasize that the psychological challenge has to be something we love doing, or we can’t get there.

尽管我努力在研究心流时遵循科学家的研究成果，但我仍然忍不住回到诗人那里，寻找游泳益处的最有力证据。游泳当然可以激发创造力，带来发现，但它也是改变心情的一种方式，因为归根结底，如果不能沉浸在事物带来的感官愉悦中，心流就毫无意义。

As much as I try to stick with scientists and studies in the examination of flow, I can’t help but turn back to the poets for the most convincing evidence of swimming’s perks. Swimming can lead to creative output and discovery, certainly, but it is also a way to change your mood, because when you get down to it, flow is nothing if it’s not getting lost in the sensory pleasure of the thing.

新罕布什尔州乡村的一处农场是普利策奖得主、诗人玛克辛·库明（Maxine Kumin）的故乡，她于2014年去世。她也是一位游泳爱好者——这对我们来说真是幸运。她曾担任夏令营教练，并在拉德克利夫学院担任游泳队队长。在她早期的一首名为《少年救生》（Junior Life Saving）的诗中，她描绘了夏日湖畔孩子们的身姿和质感，从“膝盖的等腰线”到“被阳光晒伤的皮肤”。湖水本身仿佛是有生命的，充满智慧；它有自己的节奏。它“对着鱼儿微笑/然后又恢复平静”。对孩子们来说，游泳是神奇的；她不愿告诉他们水中的危险，不愿看到那份神奇慢慢消逝。但她仍然坚持这样做；这是她的工作。她教给他们保持自身和那份神奇所需的技能。

A rural New Hampshire farm was home to Maxine Kumin, a Pulitzer Prize–winning poet who died in 2014. She was also a swimmer—lucky for us. Her particular swimming history included stints as an instructor at a summer camp and captain of the swim team at Radcliffe College. In an early poem titled “Junior Life Saving,” she summoned up the wild angles and textures of kids by a lake in summer, from the “isosceles of knees” to their “sun-killed skin.” The lake itself is sentient, witty; it has timing. It “smiles to a fish / and quiets back to glass.” Swimming, to the children, is magic; she hates to tell them of the perils of that water, hates to watch the magic seep away. But she does it still; it’s her job. She teaches them the skills they need to keep themselves, and that magic, alive.

晚年，库明写道，她每天都会独自一人在她称之为“人造水坑”的地方游泳。那是她和丈夫于1963年在新罕布什尔州自家沼泽地里挖的一个池塘。她热爱这个池塘，并尽可能多地在里面游泳。她看着池塘在冬天结冰，冰层裂开“如同靶子练习”；春天，她看着蝌蚪“从冰冻的冰层中挣脱出来/破土而出”。她观察到，水獭是游泳健将。她把“手在水中抓握和拉扯”比作一首歌的节奏。游泳的配乐：几十年来，她反复在不同的作品中探讨这个主题。

Later in life, Kumin wrote of solitary daily swims in what she called her “invented puddle,” a pond she and her husband had dug into the marshland of their New Hampshire property in 1963. She loved that pond and swam in it as much as she could. She watched it freeze in winter, the ice cracking “like target practice”; in spring, she watched the tadpoles “quake from the jello / and come into being.” The otter, she observed, is a spectacular swimmer. She likened the “cupping and pull / of handholds on water” to the rhythm of a song. The soundtrack of a swim: it was an idea she kept returning to, again and again, in different works, over the decades.

库明最著名、最具代表性的诗作《晨泳》也是她最喜欢的诗：

Kumin’s most famous and iconic poem, “Morning Swim,” was also her favorite:

我身下的鱼儿抽搐着，敏捷而温顺。

Fish twitched beneath me, quick and tame

在他们的绿色区域，他们唱着我的名字

In their green zone they sang my name

并随着游泳的节奏游动。

and in the rhythm of the swim

我哼唱了一首慢速的二四拍赞美诗。

I hummed a two-four-time slow hymn.

在这里，她描写了游泳的韵律。鱼儿游动有节奏，她踢水时也一样。美感源于时机的精准，一切都协调一致，从呼吸到气泡的产生。在这种身体与环境的同步中，二者之间的界限消失了。游泳要求我们将自己的身体融入另一个与我们截然不同的身体——水。她注意到，当她进入水中时，水也进入了她。这种融合彻底完成。

Here, she writes of the musicality of that swim. The fish have a beat, and so does she as she kicks her feet. The beauty comes from the rightness of timing, everything in sync, from breath to bubbles. In this falling into synchronicity between the body and the environment, the dividing line between the two ceases to exist. Swimming is something that requires us to make our bodies a part of another body unlike ours, that of water. She notes that as she enters the water, the water enters her. The conjoining is complete.

阅读库明的文字让我意识到，游泳其实是一种毫不妥协地臣服于自然元素的过程。她对游泳乐趣的记录，加深了我对游泳时自身感受的觉察。比如，绕过岩石岬角，感受那令人屏息的温度变化。那是一种怎样的感觉？又比如，看着溪鳟，先生跟在女士身后。它们要去哪里？再比如，从岩石上跃入水中，渴望“融入那/闪烁的青柠绿光芒”。我是否会焕然一新？

Reading Kumin helps me realize how much swimming is an unflinching giving-over to an element. Her record of the pleasures amplifies my own awareness of what absorbs me when I swim. Something as simple as rounding a rocky promontory into a breath-stealing change in temperature. What does it feel like? Something as simple as looking at brook trout, the mister followed by the missus. Where are they going? Something as simple as diving in from rocks and aiming to come up “into the fizz / of lime-green light.” Will I emerge transformed?

在这些短暂的观察瞬间，时间仿佛凝固了。在我写下这些文字的时候，我和两个朋友去了索诺玛县一处林木葱郁的古老度假区，并在俄罗斯河里游泳。北加州已是晚春，天气干燥，正午的阳光炙烤着大地，蚊子已经开始嗡嗡作响，但微风拂过树冠，预示着凉爽的夜晚即将到来。跳入那片碧绿的河水中，水流湍急却并不令人不适——与其说是一记重拳，不如说是轻轻拍了拍我的下身，让我清醒过来。我绕过鹅卵石滩，逆流而上。突然间，我感觉自己仿佛在跑步机上游泳——就像那种永无止境的泳池，水流不停地将我固定在原地。我注意到，即使在我游泳的时候，树叶也在飞速掠过，被湍急的水流裹挟着。我继续划水，低头看着，看到细小的树枝在空中飞舞。如果我停止游泳，逐渐前进的步伐会立即变成后退的步伐，河流的上游弯道也会以惊人的速度后退。

In these small moments of observation, there is frozen time. In the period that I’m writing this, I visit a woodsy old resort area in Sonoma County with two friends and go swimming in the Russian River. It’s late spring and dry in Northern California, the midday sun hot, the mosquitoes already whining, but the breeze ruffles the tree canopy and hints at the cool evening to come. Entry into that slash of green water is brisk but not unwelcome—more like a friendly pat on the bottom, a little wake-up, than a rude punch to the face. I swim round the pebbled bend and turn upstream. Suddenly it’s as if I’m swimming on a treadmill—one of those Endless Pools with the constant current that holds you in place. I notice the leaves zipping by even as I swim, carried past me by the rushing water. I keep stroking, looking down, and see little twigs flying by. If I stop swimming, the incremental forward progress instantly becomes backward progress, and the upstream bend in the river recedes with shocking speed.

我尝试着如何巧妙地运用水力：游动以保持位置，停下来顺流而下。游动以保持位置，停下来顺流而下。最后，我完全停止了游动，双臂伸向身前，翱翔在波光粼粼的河底之上。一条鱼将尾巴甩入水中，然后我翻身仰望，看着天空飞速掠过。我独自一人，却并不感到孤独。在这片河流中，游泳意味着成为万物的一部分。

I experiment with the hydro-economy of my movements: swimming to hold position, pausing to drift back downstream. Swim to hold, pause to drift. Finally, I stop swimming altogether, holding my arms in front of me as I soar above the rippled river bottom. A fish flicks its tail into the depths, and then I turn onto my back to watch the sky rip by. I am alone, but I don’t feel lonely. Out here in the river, to swim is to be a part of things.

16

16

液态

The Liquid State

我们在游泳时都在想些什么？与陆地运动不同，游泳需要潜入水中，带来一种独特的与世隔绝感。但在这种情况下，这种与世隔绝却是一种难得的恩赐。在如今这个时刻在线的时代，游泳提供了一种逃离现实的方式。事实上，每个泳池都是一个潜在的入口。

What do we think about when we’re swimming? Unlike land-based exercise, swimming requires submersion and that characteristic isolation. But isolation in this context is a rare blessing. In the always-connected modern age, the medium represents a means of disappearing. Each pool is in fact a potential portal.

游泳有时就像一个虫洞，让我得以逃离日常生活的琐碎。我跳进湖里，游向远方，尽我所能。当我游到足够远的地方——无论是字面意义上的还是比喻意义上的——我就知道，因为我会想要回去。这是一种挑战极限的练习。我能承受多少，我需要多远的距离，我能离岸边游多远才会感到害怕，以及我何时会渴望回到岸边。我会反复思考那些看似重要的事情，但游完之后，湖水会冲刷掉大部分的烦恼。游完之后，我的心情和思维清晰度至少提升了48%。

Sometimes swimming is a wormhole through which to escape the grinding machinery of everyday life. I get in a lake and swim away, as far as I can. When I get far enough away, literally and figuratively, I know it, because I find I want to go back. It’s an exercise in thresholds. How much I can take, how much distance I need, how far I can get from shore before I feel afraid, at what point I desire to return to land. I brew and brood over things that seem to be of consequence, but by the end of a swim, the water has washed much of that away. I come out with my mood and mental clarity improved by a minimum of 48 percent.

秋日清晨，天空冰冷如金属，凉雨拍打着泳池水面，泛起阵阵涟漪。我仰泳着，感受着……此刻，温暖的水流让我感到无比惬意。一只乌鸦飞过我的视野。每天有多少鸟在泳池里拉屎？这并非我游泳时最深刻的思考，但却是我最喜欢的一个念头。鸟儿总是从头顶飞过，它们也经常拉屎。我们在自家车道、汽车上、学校停车场都能看到它们的痕迹。那么，当它们飞过水面拉屎时呢？当它们飞过我的身体，落入水中时呢？这种情况何时发生，又有多频繁？我的思绪跳跃着，最终落在泳池边的排水沟里，我希望鸟粪最终能落在那里。我发现自己很享受思考鸟粪这件事。这种思考过程的乐趣源于它奇特的趣味性：意想不到的转折，以及为了思考而思考。其他时候，我会唱歌、列待办事项清单，或者幻想早餐吃什么。毋庸置疑，并非只有深刻的思考才能使人头脑清醒。

Cold metallic sky on a fall morning, cool rain dimpling the surface of the pool. I cruise along in backstroke, feeling the here-and-nowness of the warm water. A crow flies across my field of vision. How many birds poop in the pool each day? This is not the most profound thought I’ve ever had while swimming, but it’s a favorite nonetheless. Birds fly overhead all the time. They poop quite frequently. We see the evidence of this on our driveways, on our cars, in the school parking lot. What about when they let fly over a body of water? What about over my body, in water? When, and how often, does this happen? I follow the skip and jump of my mind to the edge of the pool and into the gutter, where I hope the poop ends up. I find that I’m delighted to be ruminating on bird shit. The pleasure of this whole processional of thought stems from its curious novelty: the unexpected left turns, the thinking for thinking’s sake. Other days, I sing songs or make to-do lists or fantasize about what I’m going to eat for breakfast. Suffice it to say that it’s not just profound thought that can clear one’s mind.

大多数时候，如果我没在清晨去海里冲浪，早上八点半之前我就会去附近的游泳池。即使地面结了霜，水温也依然温暖。除非你是救生员，吹哨示意我上岸，否则我根本感觉不到你的存在。在这美好的六十分钟和三千二百码的游泳时间里，我只有我自己。在泳池里，一旦泳镜起雾，就没什么可看的了。我往里面吐过、喷过各种各样的防雾剂，但都无济于事，雾气就像白内障一样慢慢侵蚀我的视线。不过，我并不在意。声音？水的晃动声几乎盖过了其他一切声音。味道和气味也主要是氯和盐的味道——虽然，在我以前的游泳池，我以前……能闻到楼下咖啡馆飘来的汉堡香味。如今，我常能闻到隔壁高中食堂飘来的煎蛋和薯饼的香味。尽管近几年科技飞速发展，你仍然很少看到游泳运动员佩戴耳机或骨传导耳机：因为它们的效果并不理想。

Most days, if I’m not in the ocean for a surf at first light, I get into the neighborhood pool by eight-thirty a.m. Even when there’s frost on the ground, the water is warm. Unless you’re the lifeguard, blowing the whistle when you want me to get out, I don’t know you exist. For sixty blessed minutes and three thousand two hundred yards, I’m my only audience. In a pool there’s nothing much to look at once the goggles fog over. I have spit and sprayed all manner of antifog fixes into them, and none has kept the mist from creeping up on my vision like cataracts. But I’m OK with that. Sound? The sloshing of water pretty much cancels out everything else. Taste and smell are largely of the chlorine and salt variety—though, at my old pool, I used to smell burgers cooking from the café downstairs. Nowadays I get whiffs of eggs and hash browns from the high-school cafeteria next door. Despite all the tech advances of the last few years, you won’t see many swimmers wearing earphones or bone-conduction music devices: they just don’t work that well.

沉浸其中也能带来内心的平静。有时，游到一片空白才是最终目标。我们通过数圈数进入冥想状态，观察阳光在泳道间移动时光影的微妙变化。思绪在脑海中游动，然后突然间，一片虚无。在那短暂的间隙，我们彻底摆脱了思考的重负。迈克尔·菲尔普斯小时候被诊断出患有注意力缺陷多动障碍（ADHD）；那时，游泳池是他的“避风港”，他说，部分原因是“待在泳池里能让我的思绪慢下来”。最近，退役后，远离了比赛的压力，他谈到游泳池是心灵的庇护所，也是他重获精神健康的场所。

Submersion creates internal quiet, too. Sometimes swimming to blankness is the goal. We enter the meditative state induced by counting laps and observe the subtle play of light as the sun moves across the lanes. We slip from thought to thought, and then there’s a momentary nothingness. In that brief interlude, we are entirely liberated from the weight of thinking. When he was a child, Michael Phelps was diagnosed with ADHD; back then, the pool was his “safe haven,” in part, he says, because “being in the pool slowed down my mind.” More recently, in retirement, away from the stress of competition, he has talked about the pool as a place of sanctuary and renewed mental health.

在约翰·契弗1964年的短篇小说《游泳者》中，内迪·梅里尔游过郊区邻居家的后院泳池回家。为了到达目的地，他必须避开围绕着每一处水域的聚会和社交狂欢。在一个泳池边，内迪“在吧台旁站了一会儿，生怕被任何可能耽误他行程的谈话缠住。当他感觉自己快要被人群包围时，他纵身跃入水中，游了过去。”由此可见，水就像一个气泡，所有社交压力都可轻易地被避开。

In John Cheever’s 1964 short story “The Swimmer,” Neddy Merrill swims home through the backyard pools of his suburban neighbors. To get there, he must navigate the parties and social merriment surrounding every body of water. At one stop, Neddy “stood by the bar for a moment, anxious not to get stuck in any conversation that would delay his voyage. When he seemed about to be surrounded he dove in and swam.” Water, then, is a bubble in which all social pressure is easily eluded.

杰伊教练告诉我，长时间游泳能让他头脑冷静、沉着、有条理，这是其他运动无法做到的。“很难带着怒气离开泳池，”他说，“泳池的环境让你不会有这种感觉。”随着世界充斥着越来越强烈的铃声和提示音，变得越来越歇斯底里，把自己悬浮在水中就显得越来越有吸引力了。

Coach Jay tells me that a long swim leaves his mind calm, collected, and organized in a way that other sports don’t. “It’s hard to leave the pool angry about something,” he says. “It doesn’t lend itself to that.” As the world, with its escalating rings and pings, gets ever more hysterical, suspending yourself in water becomes ever more appealing.

“当我游来游去，或者绕着杰夫湖转圈时，各种理论和故事就会在我的脑海中构建起来，”奥利弗·萨克斯在《水孩子》一文中写道，这篇文章是我最喜欢的散文之一。在泳池里游五百个来回从来不会让人感到枯燥乏味；相反，萨克斯说，“游泳带给我一种快乐，一种极致的幸福感，有时甚至会让我欣喜若狂。”身体全身心地投入运动，而心灵却自由漂浮，不受束缚。除此之外，他还补充道，“游泳还蕴含着丰富的象征意义——它丰富的想象力，它蕴含的神话潜力。”这不禁让人想起拜伦。

“Theories and stories would construct themselves in my mind as I swam to and fro, or round and round Lake Jeff,” Oliver Sacks wrote in “Water Babies,” one of my favorite essays of all time. Five hundred lengths in a pool were never boring or monotonous; instead, Sacks said, “Swimming gave me a sort of joy, a sense of well-being so extreme that it became at times a sort of ecstasy.” The body is engaged in full physical movement, but the mind itself floats, untethered. Beyond this, he added, “there is all the symbolism of swimming—its imaginative resonances, its mythic potentials.” Echoes of Byron.

最近一个工作日的早晨，我在泳池边看着一个八岁男孩和他的十几岁姐姐在我旁边游泳。男孩在陆地上瑟瑟发抖，嘴唇发紫，双腿发软。但当他踏入水中，却自信满满，全神贯注，像海豹一样游刃有余。那一刻，他仿佛只是一个沉浸在水中的男孩。

One recent weekday morning at the pool, I watch an eight-year-old boy and his teenage sister swim their laps beside me. The boy shivers on land, lips blue and knees knocking. But when he hits the water, he is confident, focused, as fluent in the medium as a seal. For a little while, there is just a boy in his buoyancy.

这并不是说游泳运动员很容易成为禅师。比尔·克林顿曾告诉美国公共广播公司（PBS），他和希拉里每天下午都一起游泳；如果其中一人在游泳过程中胆敢提及政治话题，他说：“我们会制止对方。”

This is not to say that swimmers find it easy to be Zen masters. Bill Clinton once told PBS that he and Hillary swim together every afternoon; if either dares to mention a political topic during the course of their swim, he said, “We will stop the other one.”

我问达拉·托雷斯，这位为参加五届奥运会而积累了无数训练时间的运动员，游泳时她在想些什么。“我总是同时做五件事，”她说道。她打电话告诉我（当时她正在开车）。“所以当我下水的时候，我会想所有我要做的事情。但有时候我会进入一种状态——什么都不想。”她说，重要的是时间是属于你自己的。“你可以用它来做任何事。这取决于你的心境——它反映了你的状态。”

I ask Dara Torres, who has amassed countless training hours for her five Olympics, what she thinks about when she’s swimming. “I’m always doing five things at once,” she tells me by phone (at the time, she was driving a car). “So when I get in the water, I think about all the things that I have to do. But sometimes I go into a state—I don’t really think about anything.” The important thing, she says, is that the time is yours. “You can use it for anything. It depends where your head is at—it’s a reflection of where you are.”

它反映了你所在的位置：本质上，这是一份只属于你的状态更新。而且这种体验是人人平等的。你不必是游泳健将也能体会到感官独处带来的益处，以及水所能带来的平衡感。

The reflection of where you are: in essence, a status update to you, and only you. And the experience is egalitarian. You don’t have to be a great swimmer to appreciate the benefits of sensory solitude and the equilibrium the water can bring.

文学、艺术和电影中那些让我们的想象力自由驰骋的著名水域：

Notable waters in literature, art, and movies where our imaginations have gone swimming:

爱奥尼亚海的深处，愤怒的海神波塞冬将奥德修斯扔进了海里，最终在女神雅典娜的指引下，奥德修斯安全地在斯刻里亚岛（据说是今天的科孚岛）的河岸上登陆（荷马，《奥德赛》，公元前八世纪）。

The depths of the Ionian Sea, into which an angry Poseidon plunged Odysseus, who was eventually guided by the goddess Athena to a safe landing on a riverbank on Scheria, supposedly today’s Corfu (Homer, The Odyssey, eighth century BC).

在非洲大西洋沿岸，当地的水神与欧洲的图像融合，产生了玛米瓦塔（Mami Wata），或称“水之母”，是一位拥有双尾的美人鱼神，她与非洲移民一起游到了海地、巴西和多米尼加共和国等地（15世纪后期）。

The Atlantic coast of Africa, where local water spirits blended with European iconography to produce Mami Wata, or “mother water,” a mermaid deity with a double tail who swam with the African diaspora to such places as Haiti, Brazil, and the Dominican Republic (late fifteenth century).

台伯河，卡西乌斯和凯撒曾在这里进行游泳比赛，卡西乌斯救起了疲惫的凯撒，后来以此作为他比凯撒更胜一筹的例证（威廉·莎士比亚，《尤利乌斯·凯撒》，1599 年）。

The Tiber River, in which Cassius and Caesar once had a swimming race, and Cassius rescued a tiring Caesar, later citing it as an example of his own superiority to Caesar (William Shakespeare, Julius Caesar, 1599).

路易斯安那州墨西哥湾沿岸，埃德娜·庞特利尔在那里自学游泳，最终溺水身亡，以摆脱社会期望的残酷束缚（凯特·肖邦，《觉醒》，1899 年）。

The Louisiana coast of the Gulf of Mexico, where Edna Pontellier teaches herself how to swim, and ultimately drowns herself, to free herself from the grim fetters of societal expectations (Kate Chopin, The Awakening, 1899).

（欧内斯特·海明威， 《老人与海》 ，1952 年）年迈的渔夫圣地亚哥在古巴海岸附近的墨西哥湾暖流中经历了为期三天的旅程，期间他被一条不停游动的巨型马林鱼拖着。

A tour of the Gulf Stream, off the coast of Cuba, a three-day journey experienced by the aging fisherman Santiago while being pulled by a giant marlin who won’t stop swimming (Ernest Hemingway, The Old Man and the Sea, 1952).

毛泽东游过长江，这一幕被描绘成共产主义宣传的一部分，并被写成一首据称是毛泽东本人所作的诗（毛泽东，《游泳》，1956年）。

Across the Yangtze River, an actual swim by Mao Zedong that straddles fact and fiction when presented as Communist propaganda, in a poem supposedly written by the Chairman himself (Mao Zedong, “Swimming,” 1956).

加州的一个后院游泳池，象征着一个漫无目的的年轻人的生活就像一张空白的画布，在罗宾逊太太出现之前，他从未想过下一步会发生什么（迈克·尼科尔斯，《毕业生》，1967）。

A backyard swimming pool in California, signifying the open canvas that is an aimless young man’s life, no thought of what’s next until Mrs. Robinson shows up (Mike Nichols, The Graduate, 1967).

法国南部的一个游泳池，为画家与伴侣关系的破裂奠定了基础，与画家标志性的泳池边幸福的同性恋家庭生活场景（大卫·霍克尼，《艺术家肖像[泳池与两个人]》，1972 年）形成鲜明对比，更显意义非凡。

A pool in the south of France, which sets the stage for the unraveling of the painter’s relationship with his partner, even more meaningful when juxtaposed against that painter’s iconic poolside scene of blissful gay domesticity (David Hockney, Portrait of an Artist [Pool with Two Figures], 1972).

暴风雨来临之际，迈阿密海滩上，一个绰号“小家伙”的男孩漂浮在毒贩胡安的怀里，胡安正在教他游泳，这一切都构成了一个激动人心、发人深省的蜕变时刻（巴里·詹金斯，《月光男孩》，2016）。

A beach in Miami as a storm rolls in, where a boy nicknamed “Little” floats in the arms of a drug dealer named Juan who is teaching him to swim, all of it making for a stirring, revelatory moment of metamorphosis (Barry Jenkins, Moonlight, 2016).

人们经常跟我聊起他们的游泳习惯——比如，当他们到一个新的城市旅行或搬家时，第一件事就是清点所有游泳池和开放水域。这是他们了解一个地方的一种方式，也是他们绘制陌生地理地图并将其内化的方式。

People often tell me about their swimming habits—for example, how, when they visit or move to a new city, the first thing they do is account for all the pools and open water. It’s a way to get to know a place. It’s how they map out unfamiliar geographies and make them their own.

我小时候，父亲经常给我讲海南岛的故事，那座位于南海的“中国夏威夷”。对中国人来说，海南岛总是带着一种浪漫的边疆气息。作为中国最南端的岛屿，它是唯一一座热带岛屿，几个世纪以来一直是诗人、政治家流放之地。对我父亲来说，海南岛是一个梦想之地，一个棕榈环绕的世外桃源，是他理想的灵感来源。他是一位出生于香港的画家，与母亲离婚后离开纽约回到中国生活。

When I was growing up, my father told me about Hainan Island, the “Chinese Hawaii,” perched on the South China Sea. To the Chinese, Hainan has always had a romantic, frontier air about it. As the southernmost point in China, it is the only tropical island, and it served for centuries as a place of exile for poets and politicos. To my father, a Hong Kong–born painter who divorced my mother and left New York to go back and live in China, it was a dream of a place, a palm-fringed paradise that represented the ideal inspiration for him.

三十出头的时候，我曾有三年没见过父亲。一天早晨，我深吸一口气，给他打了个电话。那年我的工作要去海南。“再来游泳吧，”我忐忑不安地说，“来南海见我。”他真的来了。

There was a time in my early thirties when I hadn’t seen my father in three years. One morning I took a deep breath and called him up. My work would take me to Hainan that year. “Come swimming again,” I said, my stomach full of butterflies. “Come meet me in the South China Sea.” And he did.

当时海南岛正处于蓬勃发展的时期，但我们仍然能够漫步在空旷的白色沙滩上，感受着薄荷绿的海浪轻柔地拍打着海岸，还可以驱车前往岛屿的乡村腹地。一位中国朋友凭记忆为我写了一首传统诗歌，这是一首用许多汉字写成的长诗，歌颂了海南的……海南风景如画，美不胜收。“海南真美，”他说，“我虽然没去过，但在学校里学过。”我带上了朋友用中文写的那首诗，到了海南后请父亲帮我翻译。岛上那些云雾缭绕的悬崖峭壁和海岸线，仿佛是从古老的书法卷轴和绘画中走出来一般，跃然眼前。

The island was in the midst of a development boom, but still we were able to walk on stretches of empty white beach, with spearmint waves lapping the shores, and take drives to the rural inner parts of the island. A Chinese acquaintance back home wrote out a traditional poem for me from memory, a long verse with many characters about Hainan’s famously striking landscape. “Hainan is very beautiful,” he’d said. “I’ve never been there, but I learned about it in school.” I brought the poem with me, which my friend had written in Chinese, and asked my father to translate it for me when we were in Hainan. The island’s legendary mist-clad cliffs and coastlines, straight out of the old calligraphy scrolls and paintings, came to life.

我努力想要忘记，小时候父亲是我生活中不可或缺的一部分。十二岁那年，他曾告诉我，我是他最好的朋友。想起这些，我心里很不是滋味；长大后，我只能每隔一两年见他一次。第一次我坚持要去中国看他——那是我从澳大利亚的大学交换生项目回来的路上——我冲他又哭又叫，不是因为他离开了母亲，而是因为他离开的方式。那次旅行我没能游泳，但我的眼泪却像泳池里的水一样多。

I tried to forget that as a child, my father was a daily constant in my life. Once, when I was twelve, he told me I was his best friend. It hurt to remember that; as an adult, I saw him only every year or two. The first time I insisted on visiting him in China—on my way back from that college semester abroad in Australia—I screamed and cried at him, not for leaving my mother but for the way he did it. There was no swimming on that trip, but there was a pool’s worth of tears.

在海南岛，我们达成了和解。对我而言，这是一次朝圣之旅，前往一个崭新而宽容的地方。我哄着他陪我去游泳。他，这位前救生员，已经记不清上次游泳是什么时候了。他的蝶泳游得还不错。空气潮湿，海水温暖，令人感到舒畅。他看起来很开心。我仰面漂浮在水面上，凝望着南海上空云朵交错的天空，也感到无比快乐。

On Hainan Island, we came together in a truce. The trip was a pilgrimage for me, to a new, more forgiving place. I coaxed him into accompanying me on a swim. He, the former lifeguard, could not remember the last time he went swimming. His butterfly wasn’t half bad. The air was humid. The water was warm, enveloping, a balm. He looked happy. As I floated on my back and stared at that cloud-streaked sky over the South China Sea, I felt that I was, too.

弗朗茨·卡夫卡曾说过：“真理永远是一个深渊。人必须像跳进游泳池一样，敢于从琐碎的日常经验那颤抖的跳板上纵身跃入，然后沉入海底。”我们潜入深渊，是为了之后再次浮出水面——笑着，挣扎着呼吸——回到如今被双重光芒照亮的事物表面。我们敢于纵身一跃，是为了看到新的事物。有时，我们这样做是为了找回曾经拥有的感觉。

Franz Kafka observed that “the truth is always an abyss. One must—as in a swimming pool—dare to dive from the quivering springboard of trivial everyday experience and sink into the depths, in order later to rise again—laughing and fighting for breath—to the now doubly illuminated surface of things.” We dare to jump so we can see something new. And sometimes we do it to recover a sense of what we once had.

17

17

从一个游泳运动员到另一个游泳运动员

From One Swimmer to Another

从前，我爱上了一个家庭和一个湖泊。在游泳的仪式中，在人与人、身体与身体的连接中，蕴藏着一种别样的流动。

Once upon a time, I fell in love with a family and a lake. In the ritual of swimming, the connection of one body to another, of one person to another, there is flow of a different sort to be found.

我们在一起的第一个夏天，马特带我去拜访他的祖父母，他们住在乔治湖北岸的度假小屋里，距离纽约市以北五个小时车程。泰德和雪莉1939年在湖上的一个游泳筏上相遇，战后结为夫妻。他们安身立命的港湾是银湾这个小村庄，以及自1899年就屹立于此的宏伟的基督教青年会度假村。那次拜访时，我和马特也正值青春年少，刚从大学毕业，还要再过八年才会结婚。但从带纱窗的后廊望出去，那片被常绿树木环绕、宛如明信片般美丽的湖泊，从一开始就成为了我们爱情的象征。

The first summer we were together as a couple, Matt took me to visit his grandparents at their cottage on the northern shores of Lake George, five hours north of New York City. Ted and Shirley met on a swimming raft on that lake, in 1939, and got married after the war. Their safe harbor was the tiny hamlet of Silver Bay and the grand old YMCA resort that had been there since 1899. Matt and I were young ourselves on that visit, just out of college, and would not be married for another eight years. But that liquid-mercury lake—framed by evergreens in the picture-postcard view from the screened-in back porch—would be a touchstone from the first.

家里每个人都有自己独特的过湖方式。爷爷泰德尤其喜欢驾着渔船四处游荡。他一生拥有过三艘渔船：终极号 愚行一号、二号和三号，一个比一个更大更精巧。没人记得他曾经真正钓到过鱼。

Everyone in the family had a particular way of crossing the lake. Grandpa Ted had a special affection for tooling around in fishing boats. He owned three in his life: The Ultimate Folly I, II, and III, each larger and more elaborate than the last. No one could remember him having ever actually caught a fish.

身高六英尺五英寸的克里斯叔叔蜷缩在皮划艇里，然后划过湖面。马特的妈妈罗宾喜欢划着橡皮艇在湖上漂荡——她不常横渡湖泊，但她是个精力充沛的岸边戏水爱好者。她的丈夫简是一名船舶检验员，他喜欢用帆板冲浪，后来又喜欢用立式桨板。乔治叔叔是国家户外领导力学校的教练，也是一位全能的户外运动爱好者，他喜欢帆船；马特的弟弟杰西刚刚拿到驾驶十三英尺波士顿捕鲸船的执照。

Uncle Chris, all six feet five of him, folded himself into a kayak before paddling across. Matt’s mom, Robin, loved to float around in a rubber dinghy—she wasn’t a frequent lake crosser, but she was a spirited shore dabbler. Her husband, Jan, a marine surveyor, traversed the waters on a windsurfer and, later, on a stand-up paddleboard. Uncle George, a National Outdoor Leadership School instructor and all-around outdoorsman, liked to sail; Matt’s little brother, Jesse, had just earned a license to pilot the thirteen-foot Boston Whaler.

一天早晨，爷爷泰德一边吃早餐一边做着他每天的填字游戏，漫不经心地提起他和朋友们以前常常从银湾游过一英里，横渡湖面到达跳水岩。世世代代以来，孩子们都喜欢从那里纵身跃入水中，体验惊险刺激的跳水。“那时候，这可是件稀罕事，就像游过英吉利海峡一样，”他说着，目光瞥了我一眼，然后又回到填字游戏上，每个填好的方格都用墨水清晰地写着。“如果你说你那天游过了湖，那可真是了不起的事。”

One morning over breakfast and his daily crossword puzzle, Grandpa Ted casually mentioned that he and his friends used to swim the mile from Silver Bay across the lake to Diver’s Rock, for generations the spot where children have made a heart-stopping jump into the water. “That was the thing to do back then, like swimming the English Channel,” he said, his eyes sliding over to me before returning to the crossword, each completed square lettered in unwavering ink. “If you said you’d swum across the lake that day, that was something.”

我竖起了耳朵，对他露出微笑。我知道该怎么做，他也知道。我喜欢这种能以我自己的方式加入到前人横渡湖泊的行列的想法。他递给我一份私人邀请。

My ears perked up. I smiled back at him. This was something I knew how to do, and he knew it. I loved the idea of joining the generations of lake crossers before me, in a way that was me. He was handing me a personal invitation.

那天下午，我们从银湾出发，马特我划着奶奶雪莉的旧蓝色皮划艇在他旁边游泳，这样他就不会被快艇撞到。

That afternoon, we pushed off from Silver Bay, Matt swimming and me beside him, paddling Grandma Shirley’s old blue kayak, so he wouldn’t get run over by speedboats.

我们穿过港口里摇曳的帆船和摩托艇；经过海湾海滩的木筏，泰德和雪莉正是在那里初次相遇；经过苏格兰帽岛，马特的父母在那里举行了婚礼；经过一艘船上的人，他用扩音器冲我们喊道：“在湖里游泳对你们的健康有害！”因为湖里到处都是飞驰的船只和摩托艇。四十五分钟后，我们到达了潜水岩，这是一处石质峭壁，马特家族的每一位成员都曾从这里纵身跃入水中。这真是一次在乔治湖畔进行的马特家族历史水上之旅。

We made our way out past the sailboats and motorboats bobbing in the harbor; past the raft at Bay Beach, where Ted and Shirley first set eyes on each other; past the tiny island of Scotch Bonnet, where Matt’s parents were married; past a man in a boat who yelled at us through a megaphone, “Swimming in the lake is hazardous to your health,” what with all the boats and Jet Skis racing about. Forty-five minutes later, we arrived at Diver’s Rock, the stone-faced cliff where each member of Matt’s family has made the jump. It was a veritable water tour of his family history at Lake George.

完成从悬崖跳下的庄严仪式后，轮到我游回湖对岸了。我尽量不去想那些快艇，相信划着蓝色皮划艇的同伴会保护我的安全。湖面平静如镜，完美无瑕。当我靠岸来到银湾岸边时，我感觉自己仿佛完成了某种仪式。我想我终于明白了这个地方对马特以及之前那些横渡湖泊的人的意义。

After we performed the solemn ceremony of jumping off the ledge, it was my turn to swim back across the lake. I tried not to think of speedboats and trusted my man in the blue kayak to keep me safe. The water was pancake-flat and perfect. When I beached myself on the shores of Silver Bay, I felt initiated. I thought I finally understood something about what the place meant to Matt and to the company of lake crossers before us.

八年后，婚礼第二天，我们再次参加了乔治湖的游泳活动，四十位最亲密的朋友组成船队一同前来。我们双方的外祖父母都到场见证了这一刻，我想可以说，我从一个家庭游进了另一个家庭。我们年复一年地参加这项活动。即使后来我们搬到了旧金山，也从未间断。我们一直坚持去——有时在秋季或冬季，但大多是在夏季。游泳的方式也略有不同。有一年元旦，我和马特赤着脚踩在雪地里，冻得脚底生疼，我们召开了银湾北极熊游泳俱乐部的第一次也是唯一一次会议（总共只有两个人）。

Eight years later, we continued our Lake George swim, the day after our wedding, with forty of our closest friends in the flotilla. Both sets of our maternal grandparents were there to witness it, and I suppose you could say that I swam from one family into another. We returned, year after year. Even after we moved across the country to San Francisco, we kept going back—sometimes in fall or winter, mostly in summer. There have been variations on the swim. One New Year’s Day, our bare feet stinging in the snow, Matt and I held the first and only meeting of the Silver Bay Polar Bear Swim Club (total members: two).

这些年，爷爷走了，杰西也走了。现在我们再回去，最让我感动的总是萤火虫和繁星。通往湖边的蜿蜒小路，被茂密的树木和群山过滤，隔绝了现代生活的喧嚣。那些闪烁的萤火虫，在地面上摇曳，密密麻麻地填满夜空，仿佛在传递着某种信息。它们提醒我们放慢脚步，珍惜当下拥有的真挚情感。

In the years since, Grandpa has gone. Jesse, too. When we go back now, it’s the fireflies and the stars that get me every time. Much of modern life is filtered out through the dense trees and mountains on the winding approach to the lake. Those winking lights, bobbing along the ground and filling up the night sky with their impossible density, send a signal. It’s a reminder to slow up and be awake to the real connections we have while we have them.

我最初以为游泳的乐趣在于当下——在于享受当下——但后来我发现，游泳本身也可以是一种仪式。这不仅仅关乎这个家庭，也不仅仅关乎这个湖泊。水域是共享的空间，而这正是与之相伴的神话。古德劳格松德究竟是什么？不就是纪念吗？人们游泳不就是为了与古德劳格以及其他冰岛人建立联系吗？在追寻一个伟大的生存故事的过程中，我发现了什么？是每个游泳者与古德劳格本人之间建立的联系。

I started out thinking that the pleasures of swimming were all about immediacy—about being in the present—but I have found that the act of swimming can serve as ritual, too. It’s not just this family, and it’s not just this lake. Bodies of water are shared spaces, and this is the mythology to go with it. What is Guðlaugssund, anyway, but remembrance? Why do people do it other than to feel a kinship with Guðlaugur and their fellow Icelanders? In pursuit of a great survival tale, what did I find? A swimmer-by-swimmer connection to the man himself.

当你与世界及其力量建立连接时，启示便会随之而来。顺流而下，你会感到所向披靡；逆流而上，你便会突然意识到那些无形的力量在与你对抗。我希望我的孩子们无所畏惧，因为他们知道潮流就在那里。因为他们知道面对这种情况该怎么做。这些都是我珍藏的游泳故事。

When you are tuned in to the world and its forces, revelations follow. Swim with the current, and you’ll feel invincible. Swim against it, and you suddenly become aware of the invisible forces against you. I want my own children to be unafraid, because they know that the current is there, because they know what to do when they face it. These are the swimming stories I carry with me.

巴勃罗·聂鲁达十九岁时就创作了《二十首情诗和一首绝望之歌》，他运用水的意象来描绘恋爱中令人陶醉的美好，以及沉浸其中时失去控制的感受。诗集中的第九首《松醉》是我最喜欢的，因为它生动地描绘了一对游泳者在外海浪中相遇的场景：两个充满激情、彼此交融的身体，一个向另一个屈服，“就像一条鱼与我的灵魂紧紧相连”。

Pablo Neruda wrote Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair, published when he was just nineteen; he uses aquatic imagery to depict the intoxicating gorgeousness of being in love, the loss of control when we’re immersed in it. The ninth poem in the collection, “Drunk with Pines,” is my favorite, for its vivid conjuring of a pair of swimmers caught together in the outer waves: two passionate, parallel bodies, one yielding to the other, “like a fish infinitely fastened to my soul.”

如果这不是爱情故事，那又是什么呢？

What are these if not stories of love?

说到游泳，我们可以理解“心流”不仅指齐克森米哈里所定义的广阔的、永恒的存在状态，还指游泳所带来的思绪洪流，以及我们彼此之间和与我们所居住的星球之间的联系。

When it comes to swimming, we can understand flow to mean not just the expansive, timeless state of being that Csikszentmihalyi defined but also the flood of thoughts that swimming enables, and the connection we have to each other and to the planet we inhabit.

“流动”一词源自古英语flówan；同源词根flo-也出现在古诺尔斯语flóa（意为“淹没”）和荷兰语vloeijen（意为“流动”）中。这个词还蕴藏着其他秘密。拉丁语plōrāre（意为“哭泣”）；梵语plu（意为“游泳、沐浴”）；古高地德语flewen（意为“冲洗”）；希腊语 πλωειν（意为“游泳、漂浮”）。我顺着语言的流向而下，发现它提供了一系列关联：淹没、哭泣、游泳、沐浴、冲洗、漂浮。追溯这条谱系，它揭示了一种解脱，一种卸下重担，无论是身体上的——将身体释放到水中，摆脱惯常的重量和重力——还是情感上的——通过痛哭一场，泪水带来的净化。在大海中，潮水奔涌而下。即使远在千里之外，也能感受到水坝微小的溃决。欣喜若狂或许是心流状态的必要条件，但悲伤也同样重要，它就蕴藏在“心流”一词的历史之中。

Flow: from Old English flówan; from the same root flo- are Old Norse flóa, to flood, and Dutch vloeijen, to flow. The word holds other secrets, too. Latin plōrāre, to weep; Sanskrit plu, to swim, bathe; Old High German flewen, to rinse; Greek πλωειν, to swim, float. I follow the downstream movement of language, and it offers up a raft of connections: flood, weep, swim, bathe, rinse, float. Trace this lineage and it reveals an unfettering, an unburdening, whether physical—a release of the body to water, freed from its customary weight and gravity—or emotional, through a good cry, the cleansing release of tears. In the sea, a tidal flood of water traveling from thousands of miles away can absorb the small individual burst of a dam. Elation may be essential to the flow state, but so, too, is a slice of sorrow, embedded in the very history of the word itself.

即使在悲痛之中——父母离异、流产、朋友去世——我依然以水为媒介，感受时光流逝。我不会沉湎于这些悲伤，因为我并非想说游泳治愈了我，但我必须说，游泳，无论以何种形式——在泳池、湖泊，还是划着冲浪板出海——总能帮助我走出困境。潮汐一天两次，不断变化。水永远处于流动之中。游泳就是见证蜕变，见证环境的蜕变，见证我们自身的蜕变。游泳就是接受生命中所有千姿百态的境遇。

Even in grief—the breakup of my parents, a miscarriage, the death of a friend—I have marked time by water. I won’t linger on these sorrows, because I don’t mean to say that swimming cured me of them, but I will say that swimming, in all of its permutations—in a pool, in a lake, paddling a surfboard out to sea—has always helped me come out on the other side of a difficult time. The tides keep changing, twice a day. Water is in a forever state of flux. To swim is to witness metamorphosis, in our environment, in ourselves. To swim is to accept all the myriad conditions of life.

我想起了最初。我们在子宫里漂浮。当我们第一次学会游泳时，我们首先学会的是漂浮。我看着海浪翻滚，它们如何托起我们所有人，一起漂浮。如果我漂浮在旧金山，而你漂浮在太平洋彼岸的东京，我们难道不是一起漂浮吗？

I think back to the beginning. We float in the womb. When we first learn to swim, we first learn to float. I watch the waves roll in and how they lift us all, together. If I am floating here in San Francisco and you are floating across the Pacific in Tokyo, are we not floating together?

托尼·坎迪住在东京，与他相隔数千英里，他的父母在英国西南海岸拥有一栋房子，可以俯瞰英吉利海峡。每当他在日本的湖泊或河流中游泳，练习日本泳法时，他都感到与父母紧密相连。对他而言，游泳的乐趣很大程度上在于它创造了一个思考自己身处何方的空间。“无论你如何划定界限，”他告诉我，“水将你与你连接起来。”

Thousands of miles from where Tony Cundy lives in Tokyo, his parents have a house on the southwest coast of England, where they look out over the English Channel. Whenever he’s swimming in a lake or river in Japan, practicing the strokes of Nihon eiho, he feels that he is connected to them. The pleasure of swimming for him is in large part the space it creates to think about where he is. “However you draw the line,” he tells me, “water connects you.”

过去几年，我看着我的两个儿子，菲利克斯和泰迪，现在分别是八岁和六岁，逐渐学会游泳。从一开始，我就预料到他们会害怕，但我同时也充满期待，盼望着他们克服恐惧，拥抱其他事物的那一刻。事实证明，他们的恐惧转瞬即逝，尽管偶尔会在参照物发生变化时出现——比如从泳池到大海，或者从温水到冷水。紧接着，他们感受到的是好奇和试探性的探索；是能够独立滑离池壁的兴奋；是纵身跃入泳池；是自发的翻滚。是喜悦。

For the past several years I have watched my two sons, Felix and Teddy, now eight and six, become swimmers. From the beginning, I expected fear, but I was eager and hopeful for the moment when it would give way to something else. It turned out that fear for them was fleeting, though it would register every now and then with a shift in reference point—pool to ocean, say, or warm water to cold. What came, in quick succession, was curiosity and tentative exploration; giddiness at gliding independently from the wall; leaps into the pool; spontaneous underwater somersaults. Joy.

我记得怀着菲利克斯的时候，漂浮在考艾岛北岸隧道海滩波光粼粼的深蓝色太平洋上，被阳光晒得暖洋洋的肚子露出海面，我欣赏着纳帕利海岸红绿相间的悬崖。六年之后，我和马特开始了为期三个月的暑假——暂时摆脱日常的忙碌——回到岛上，来到北岸的小镇哈埃纳。我希望菲利克斯也能感受到这种漂浮感，离开我的怀抱，让他充分感受到海水拍打着他瘦削的小身体。我想要一种穿越时空的感觉：同时把他当作婴儿和男孩一样，抱在怀里。

I remember floating in the glassy ultramarine Pacific at Tunnels Beach, on the north shore of Kauai, while pregnant with Felix, my sun-warmed belly poking above the waves as I took in the rippling red-and-green cliffs of the Nā Pali Coast. Six years later, Matt and I began a sabbatical summer—a three-month break from the daily grind—back on the island, in the little north shore town of Haena. I wanted Felix to feel that buoying for himself, outside of me, fully aware of the pulse of water on his lanky young body. I wanted a kind of time travel: to hold him simultaneously in this place as a baby and a boy.

渐渐地，菲利克斯适应了轻柔的海浪。他随着波浪起伏，练习自由泳和仰泳，寻找着粉蓝色的鹦嘴鱼。他和当地人一起学习冲浪，最终到达沙滩。菲利克斯渐渐爱上了这种感觉：这里的水仿佛充满了生命力，与泳池的静谧截然不同。有一天，他结识了一位身材魁梧、皮肤晒成古铜色的中年冲浪爱好者戴夫。戴夫一边大声鼓励他，一边身姿矫健、优雅地划向岸边。那天晚上，我儿子画了一幅画，画中他正和“新朋友”戴夫一起在海浪中冲浪。多年以后，菲利克斯仍然会提起他。

Little by little, Felix got comfortable in the gently rolling surf. He bobbed. He practiced his freestyle and his backstroke. He looked for brilliant pink-and-blue parrotfish. Alongside the locals, he learned to bodysurf to the sand. Felix learned to love the feeling that the water there was in some way alive and different from the stillness of a pool. One day he befriended a stout, sun-bronzed middle-aged bodysurfer named Dave who shouted encouragement and expertly propelled himself toward shore with élan and grace. That evening, my son drew a picture of himself bodysurfing in the waves with his “new friend” Dave. Years later, Felix talks about him still.

在隧道海滩，每天清晨我都会游上一英里甚至更远，在礁石间蜿蜒穿梭，跟随当地人的脚步，寻找他们能带我看到的景色。有一次，我尾随两位身着暗绿色迷彩潜水服的鱼叉捕鱼者，发现四只巨大的海龟正栖息在海底。它们正被一种名为清洁鱼的小鱼享用；这是一种奇妙的共生关系，清洁鱼通过吸食寄生虫和死皮，为海龟坚硬的龟壳提供清洁。四十五分钟后，年轻的渔民们带着当天的渔获——每人两条巨大的鲯鳅——从海里浮了上来。其他时候，我会跟随一些手臂粗壮的冲浪者，尽可能地游到他们划过外礁之前，那里狂风掀起阵阵白浪。我踩着水，安全地站在礁石内，看着它们优雅地、蜿蜒地穿过每一道破碎的浪头。

Every morning at Tunnels I swam a mile or more, zigzagging between reefs and following the locals to what they could show me. Once I tailed two spearfishermen, clad in their dusky-green camouflage wetsuits, and spotted four large sea turtles resting at the bottom of the ocean. They were being feasted on by tiny fish known as cleaner wrasse; in a marvel of symbiosis, the wrasse detail the turtles’ hard shells by hoovering up parasites and dead skin. An efficient forty-five minutes later, the young fishermen emerged from the sea with the day’s catch in hand: huge mahi-mahi, two each. On other days I swam alongside ropy-armed surfers as far as I could before they paddled beyond the outer reef, where the wind whipped whitecaps across the sea. I treaded water and watched safely from within the reef as they made elegant, sinuous turns across the face of each wave as it broke.

我们和附近住着的一户年轻家庭成了朋友，这些天早上我们经常见到他们。他们家的小女儿喜欢研究我们的零食和玩具，还和泰迪熊玩。爸爸晒得黝黑，坐在海边捡拾婴儿大小的、纹路精美的小贝壳。他说，这些牙齿过去只有夏威夷最神圣的祭司才会收集。

We became friendly with a young family living nearby whom we saw often during these mornings. The toddler daughter liked to investigate our snacks and toys and played with Teddy. The father, nut-brown from the sun, sat by the sea gathering tiny, intricately patterned shells the size of baby teeth that he said were once collected only by the holiest of Hawaiian priests.

一天早晨，我在珊瑚点缀的浅水中游泳时，两个男人指着一条四英尺长的鲨鱼，说它侧卧在齐腰深的水中。他们说，这是一条幼鲨，很可能是在试图穿过近岸色彩斑斓的珊瑚迷宫返回深水区时丧命的——这些珊瑚有的像巨石一样大，有的像仙人掌，还有一些像长着叶状脑组织的巨大大脑。

One morning as I swam in the coral-punctuated shallows, two men called my attention to a four-foot shark resting on its side in the waist-deep water. It was a juvenile, they said, and it had probably died while trying to find its way back to deeper water through the maze of vividly colored near-shore corals—some boulder-size, others cactuslike, still others resembling giant brains with lobes.

随后，一位戴着墨镜、穿着红色泳裤的救生员驾驶着沙滩车疾驰而来，将鲨鱼拖上了沙滩。旁观者纷纷围观，打量着它光滑的灰色皮肤、血淋淋的鼻子和浑浊的眼睛。这件事并没有阻止我们继续游泳，但它再次令人警醒，无论我们是否乐意，海洋中始终潜藏着危险：鲨鱼、离岸流、锋利的礁石。

Later, a lifeguard in sunglasses and red swim trunks roared up in a dune buggy and dragged the shark up onto the beach. Bystanders came around to stare at its smooth gray hide, bloodied nose, and clouded-over eyes. The episode didn’t stop any of us from swimming, but it was yet another sobering reminder, welcome or not, of the ocean’s ever-present dangers: sharks, riptides, razor-sharp reefs.

长大后，我逐渐体会到水——无论是海洋、湖泊还是泳池——都是一种连接内心和外部世界的交通工具。在檀香山市中心，我最喜欢的游泳地点之一是阿拉莫阿纳海滩，它位于市中心的海滨。在城市中心，距离高楼大厦仅几步之遥，阿拉莫阿纳海滩波光粼粼、珊瑚礁环绕的海面，宛如一座天然的公共泳池。在那里游泳，就是在水面上体验这片土地：当你面向大海（makai）呼吸时，会看到冲浪者奋力划向浪尖；当你面向山峦（mauka）时，会看到日本新郎新娘正在拍摄婚纱照。在他们的婚礼当天。从这个角度来看，一切似乎都变得有可能。

As an adult, I have come to appreciate water—an ocean, a lake, a pool—as a mode of inner as well as outer transport. In the middle of Honolulu, one of my favorite swimming spots is Ala Moana Beach, along the downtown waterfront. In the middle of the city, steps from high-rise towers, the glassy, reef-protected ocean at Ala Moana serves as the de facto communal pool. To swim there is to experience the place at water level: Turn your head makai, toward the ocean, to breathe, and there are surfers paddling out to the break; turn your head mauka, toward the mountains, and there are Japanese brides and grooms having pictures taken on their wedding day. From this perspective, everything feels strangely possible.

我为什么游泳？很多页之前，我说过我也是这本书里的一个角色。但也许恰恰相反：游泳一直是我生命中的核心——它既是永恒的，又是变幻莫测的，如同一个变形者。

Why do I swim? Many pages ago, I said that I was a character in this book, too. But maybe it’s the opposite: swimming has always played a central role in my life—constant but mercurial, a shape-shifter.

我曾分别从不同的角度探讨过生存、幸福、社群、竞争和心流。但实际上，它们彼此交织。游泳可以呈现出不同的形式、不同的情绪和不同的功能，这取决于一天中的时间、一年中的季节以及人生的不同阶段。它可以带来光明，也可以过滤光线，甚至完全阻挡光线。它可以让人充满活力，也可以让人精疲力竭。它可以将我带入舒适之地，也可以将我推向恐惧之境。它可以通过仪式提醒我，也可以通过心流帮助我忘却烦恼。

I have written about survival, well-being, community, competition, and flow as separate streams of reasoning. But in truth, they all run together. A swim can take different forms, different moods, and different functions, depending on the time of day, the time of year, the time of life. It can cast light, or filter it, or block it altogether. It can be energizing or enervating. It can pull me to a place of comfort or push me to a place of fear. It can remind me, through ritual, or help me forget, through flow.

游泳让我学会放慢节奏，也学会加速前进。我练习得足够多，懂得如何保持平静，也懂得如何控制自己的怒火。我可以在温暖如浴缸的湖水中忘却自我，也可以在蒸汽缭绕的冰岛泻湖中全然沉浸，让每一个光影都深深烙印在我的脑海里。

Swimming helps me to slow down, and to speed up. I have practiced enough to know how to be calm, and how to generate controlled fury. I can forget myself in a bathtub-warm lake or, in a steam-wisped Icelandic lagoon, be so exquisitely present that every glint and glimmer is seared into my brain forever.

作家丽贝卡·索尔尼特这样描述蓝色：它迷人地“是从这里看到的那里的颜色，是你不在的地方的颜色”。水有一种诱惑力。从远处看，它闪闪发光，宛如一颗闪亮的液体宝石。它充满诱惑。它旋转、飘动、汇聚，拥抱着你。它承载着你，却又无法被你承载。当我们沉浸其中时，某种东西被唤醒了。仿佛视觉或听觉被打开了。一种至关重要的全新感官被发现了。我十几岁时当过救生员，曾救过一个溺水的小女孩。她那双在水下的眼睛，像餐盘一样大。我把她拖到潜水池边，她紧绷的肌肉让她感觉异常沉重，与她瘦小的身躯格格不入。她爬出泳池，立刻嚎啕大哭起来。她的兄弟姐妹跑过来，惊呼她根本不会游泳。“既然不会游泳，为什么还要跳下去呢？”我轻声问她。她只是哭得更厉害了。

Here is the writer Rebecca Solnit on the color blue: it is, bewitchingly, “the color of there seen from here, the color of where you are not.” There is a seductiveness to water. From afar, it gleams and glistens, a shiny liquid jewel. It is inviting. It swirls, fans, and coalesces, embracing you. It holds you and yet cannot be held by you. When we immerse ourselves, something is awakened. It is as if eyesight has been turned on, or hearing. It is a vital new sense discovered. When I was a teenage lifeguard, I once saved a little girl from drowning. Those eyes, underwater, big as dinner plates. As I towed her to the side of the diving tank, the tensed muscles of her body made her feel remarkably heavy for such a small, skinny child. She got out of the pool and promptly burst into tears. When her brothers and sisters ran over, they exclaimed that she didn’t know how to swim. “Why did you jump in if you don’t know how to swim?” I asked her, gently. Her only answer was more tears.

当女孩的兄弟姐妹用毛巾把她裹起来，安慰她时，一种久远的记忆涌上心头，让我回想起多年前在琼斯海滩的那一天。溺水悄无声息，来得又快又急。或许有人会注意到，或许无人察觉。现在回想起来，我们这些救援人员不禁会问：为什么？不会游泳，为什么要跳进水里？为什么要如此不合逻辑地让自己身处险境？小女孩无法解释，就像我小时候在海浪中翻滚时，也无法用语言表达自己的感受一样。但我现在知道答案了。

As the girl’s siblings bundled her away in a towel and comforted her, an old awareness surfaced in me, recalling myself on that long-ago day at Jones Beach. Drowning is quiet and quick. Someone might notice—or no one might. It strikes me now that we responders are moved to ask, Why? Why jump in if you can’t swim? Why endanger yourself so illogically? The little girl couldn’t explain it, just as I couldn’t put into words what I felt when I was her age, tumbling in the surf. But I know the answer now.

蓝色：代表你不在的地方的颜色。

Blue: the color of where you are not.

无论我的思绪飘向何方，水那若隐若现的魅力总在召唤我前往别处。它让我逃离地球的束缚，而且随时可以启程。每当我踏入陌生的水域，渴望观察它在我进入液态水体后的反应时，这种感觉便会油然而生。它会轻易地、平静地接纳我，还是会像波浪般拍打、飞溅，每一次划水都让我感到不适？泳池里柔和淡雅的盐味与海水的粗粝矿物味截然不同。加勒比海薄荷糖般的色泽与爱琴海钴蓝的浩瀚无垠也迥然不同。我想尝遍所有这些味道；我想，我对它们的渴望，正是聂鲁达所说的“我那纯粹的海洋狂热”。

Wherever it is I might be in my head, the winking where-you-are-not-ness of water issues an invitation to go elsewhere. It’s an escape from Earth’s terra firma, with regularly scheduled departures. I am reminded of it every time I slip into an unfamiliar body of water, eager to see the way it behaves once I enter its liquid mass. Will it absorb me easily, imperturbably, or will it chop, splash, resist with every stroke? The soft, muted salt of a pool is different from the gritty mineral flavor of the sea. So is the mint-candy look of the Caribbean versus the cobalt vastness of the Aegean. I want to try all the flavors; I think my thirst for them is what Neruda called “my solid marine madness.”

这种色彩饱和的生活延伸超越了自然界，涵盖了人造世界。在飞往棕榈泉的航班上，我看到以泳池为中心的生活方式的几何图形清晰地呈现在下方，重复的绿松石色矩形、椭圆形和奇特的小曲线构成网格。泳池可以出现在任何地方，在内陆地区尤其必不可少。走进泳池，你的思绪便会飘向远方；例如，走进南加州的特定地理环境，你便能洞察二战后美国人的乐观精神。这里曾是好莱坞的避世之所，人们纵身跃入水中，寻求解脱；这些蓝宝石般的泳池所象征的逃离现实的理念，早已渗透到美国电影和文学的意象之中。或者，在寒冬腊月里，泡在冰岛的温泉中，你会透过缝隙看到一丝温暖，那令人愉悦的暖流将你唤醒，让你重新享受曾经令人望而生畏的黑暗带来的夜色乐趣。我们把泳池建在那些对于应对现代生活压力至关重要的地方。泳池是一种象征。人们可以从水中重获新生，成为一个全新的自己。

This color-saturated expansion of life goes beyond the natural world to encompass the man-made. On a flight to Palm Springs, I see the geometry of pool-centric living clearly laid out below in the repeating grid of turquoise rectangles, ovals, and odd little squiggles. Pools can be anywhere and are especially necessary in a land-locked locale. Enter and you may go anywhere in your thoughts; enter in the specific geography of Southern California, for example, and you gain insight into the American optimism of the post–World War II era. This is where Hollywood once went to get away, where people found escape by diving in; the very idea of these sapphire pools as escape infiltrated the iconography of American film and literature. Or take a dip in a hot pool in Iceland in the dead of winter, and you’ll see through a crack, the delicious warmth reviving you to the nocturnal pleasures of the once-forbidding dark. We have put pools in places where they are necessary for surviving the pressures of modern life. Pools are a symbol. It is possible to emerge from the water reinvented, a new version of yourself.

在一般的游泳池里，跳板和梯子之间的距离或许只有二十英尺，但实际上两者之间相隔的远不止这些。在那片空间里，我们或许能瞥见我们渴望的东西。我记得菲利克斯跳下去的那个夏天。这是他第一次站在跳板上。当他站在跳板上鼓起勇气时，我看到在他瘦小、湿漉漉的身体与下方水面之间，仿佛一片充满无限可能的海洋在他眼前展开。他纵身跃向跳水池边的梯子，我看到自己的倒影映在水中，映在他身上——他腾空而起，双臂伸展，悬停在那辉煌的瞬间。我为他许下什么愿望？一个关于水的基本认知，一个关于水如何成为通往另一个世界的门户的认知。他落入水中，溅起的水花在逆光下显得柔和而轻盈。当他浮出水面时，他停顿了一下，仿佛只是一瞬间。然后，他开始游动。

In a typical pool, the distance between the diving board and the ladder is twenty feet, maybe, but so much more separates the two. In that space, we might catch a glimpse of what we desire. I remember the summer Felix jumped off a diving board for the first time. As he stood there on the plank gathering courage, I saw an ocean of possibility open up in the space that separated his tiny, dripping body from the water below. He sprang toward the ladder at the side of the diving tank, and I saw myself reflected in the water, in him, as he took flight, arms outstretched, suspended there for one glorious moment. What did I wish for him? An elemental understanding of water, of how it can be a portal to somewhere else. He hit the water with a muted, backlit splash. When he bobbed up to the surface, he paused, just for a heartbeat. Then he began to swim.

结语

Epilogue

2018年5月初，金·钱伯斯被诊断出患有格林-巴利综合征，这是一种罕见的神经系统疾病，患者自身的免疫系统会攻击神经，导致麻木和瘫痪，并可能迅速蔓延至全身。一天早上，金的左脚开始出现瘫痪症状，但很快就蔓延到她的四肢，以至于当她最终同意去急诊室时，她已经呼吸困难。后来，医生告诉金，她当时距离呼吸麻痹只有90分钟之遥——如果她没有及时就医，就会窒息而死。离开重症监护室时，她腰部以下瘫痪，说话也十分困难。格林-巴利综合征的病因不明，目前尚无治愈方法；约80%的成年患者在确诊六个月后能够独立行走，约60%的患者在一年内完全恢复运动能力。

In early May 2018, Kim Chambers was diagnosed with Guillain-Barré syndrome, a rare neurological disorder in which the body’s immune system attacks the nerves, causing numbness and paralysis that can quickly spread across the entire body. The paralysis started one morning in Kim’s left foot, but it crept up to her legs and arms so rapidly that when she finally consented to go to the emergency room, she was struggling for breath. Later, the doctors told Kim that she had been ninety minutes away from respiratory paralysis—had she not gone to the hospital when she did, she would have suffocated. When she left the intensive-care ward, she was paralyzed from the waist down and had trouble speaking. The cause of Guillain-Barré is unknown, and there is no cure; about 80 percent of adults recovering from the illness can walk independently six months after diagnosis, and about 60 percent fully recover motor strength in a year.

金入院五周后，在她41岁生日之际，她回到了旧金山湾：她参加了一个五分钟的浸水仪式，需要用到一辆轮椅。三个小时的午睡，以及数不尽的友谊，让她得以恢复元气。她说，身体会跟随思想的指引。这是她人生中第二次全身心投入到康复治疗中，重新学习走路。然而，疲劳、挥之不去的瘫痪和神经疼痛，时刻提醒着她要停下来，抬头看看周围的世界。“第一次遭遇医疗事故后，我成了一名游泳运动员，”她告诉我，“那是我人生中最美好的事情。所以，这一次，我知道未来还会有更美好的事情发生。我很荣幸能去发现它。”她说，当你开始行动，当你下定决心的时候，往往是最可怕的时刻：比如差点失去一条腿后第一次跳进泳池，或者在法拉隆群岛漆黑的夜晚从船上跳入水中，不知道落水点会不会就在大白鲨的嘴里。但金睁大双眼，勇敢地迎接新的生活。和第一次一样，她发现水是她重生的乐于助产士。

Five weeks after Kim entered the hospital, she was back in San Francisco Bay on the occasion of her forty-first birthday: a five-minute immersion that required one wheelchair, a three-hour recovery nap, and an endless circle of friends. The body, she says, follows the mind. For the second time in her life, she has thrown herself into full-time physical therapy to relearn how to walk again. Fatigue, lingering paralysis, and nerve pain, though, are reminders to take a moment to look up every now and again. “With my first medical misadventure, I became a swimmer,” she tells me. “It was the best thing that happened to me. So with this latest one, I just know there’s something else amazing down the line. And I’m humbled to find out what it is.” She says that the moment where you begin, when you commit to yourself, is the scariest moment: jumping into the pool for the first time after almost losing a leg, or jumping off a boat at the Farallon Islands on a dense, ink-black night, unsure if the landing zone is right in the mouth of a great white shark. But Kim is jumping into this new life with both eyes open. And, as with the first time around, she has found the water to be a willing midwife to her rebirth.

致谢

Acknowledgments

这本书的诞生离不开众多杰出人士的慷慨相助和长期支持。我衷心感谢那些慷慨地与我分享时间和游泳生涯的人们——特别是热情好客的古德劳格·弗里德索尔松（Guðlaugur Friðþórsson），他敞开心扉地邀请我到他家做客；金·钱伯斯（Kim Chambers），她用充满感染力的喜悦和惊奇讲述了她的故事；杰伊·泰勒（Jay Taylor），他至今仍是我最忠实的笔友；以及带我走进武士游泳奇妙世界的绿石引（Midori Ishibiki）。

This book came into being with the kindness and longtime support of many extraordinary people. My greatest thanks to those who so generously shared their time and their swimming lives with me—in particular Guðlaugur Friðþórsson, who invited me into his home with an open heart; Kim Chambers, who told me her story with such infectious joy and wonder; Jay Taylor, who remains my most faithful pen pal; and Midori Ishibiki, who introduced me to the miraculous world of samurai swimming.

在报道过程中，我问了很多忙碌的人很多看似烦人的问题，但他们都耐心地解答了我的疑问。特别感谢科学家们——保罗·塞雷诺、田中博文、梶村慎吾、克里斯·斯特林格、雷纳托·本德、妮可·本德、梅兰妮·鲁德、安娜·吉斯伦——以及纪录片导演埃琳娜·库巴尔斯卡，她帮助我描绘了她纪录片《水下行走》中展现的巴瑶族人的形象。我还采访了我心目中的游泳英雄们，问他们在游泳时都在想些什么：达拉·托雷斯、琳恩·考克斯、刘易斯·普格、拉姆·巴凯。谢谢大家！感谢 Bruce Gemmell 和 Jim Bauman 为我们打开了一扇了解运动员内心世界的窗口。还要特别感谢不知疲倦的 Alan Allison 在 Guðlaugssund 档案馆提供的帮助，以及韦斯特曼纳群岛历史博物馆的 Helga Hallbergsdóttir。

Over the course of reporting I asked a lot of busy people a lot of annoying questions, and they entertained my queries with nothing but patient consideration. Special thanks to the scientists—Paul Sereno, Hirofumi Tanaka, Shingo Kajimura, Chris Stringer, Renato Bender, Nicole Bender, Melanie Rudd, Anna Gislén—and to filmmaker Elena Kubarska, who helped me paint a picture of the Bajau depicted in her documentary Walking Under Water. I got to bug my swimming heroes about what they think about when they’re swimming: Dara Torres, Lynne Cox, Lewis Pugh, Ram Barkai. Thank you to Bruce Gemmell and Jim Bauman for opening a window into the athlete’s brain. Huge thanks also to the indefatigable Alan Allison for his help with the Guðlaugssund archives and to Helga Hallbergsdóttir of the Vestmannaeyjar History Museum.

感谢 Aaron Retica 建议我写那篇开启一切的文章。感谢我的早期读者：Sara Houghteling、James Wilson、Ethan Watters、Andrea Walker 和 Caroline Paul。你们的鼓励和支持让我坚持下去，在关键时刻给予我宝贵的建议，并让我始终保持信念。感谢 Civil Twilight 的 Caroline、Sarah McCarthy 和 Harper Honan，感谢你们的陪伴。你们让我保持快乐、理智，并让我无论在冲浪还是生活中都能勇于挑战极限。

Thank you to Aaron Retica, for suggesting I write the essay that started it all. Thanks to my early readers: Sara Houghteling, James Wilson, Ethan Watters, Andrea Walker, Caroline Paul. You cheered me on, offered advice at critical junctures, and kept me believing. To Civil Twilight—Caroline, Sarah McCarthy, and Harper Honan—I thank you for all the dawn patrols. You keep me happy, sane, and taking the high line, in surfing and in life.

致瑞秋·莱文，我的工作伙伴、酒店搭档、姐妹：我永远感激我们一起散步的时光，以及你真挚的友谊。你睿智而充满活力的反馈，一路激励着我前行。致克里斯·科林，我的工作伙伴和写作搭档……感谢你为工作带来幽默、音乐和清醒的思考。我因此变得更加敏锐。

To Rachel Levin, my work wife, hotel wife, sister: I’m forever grateful for our long walks and your bighearted friendship. Your smart, spirited feedback buoys me every step of the way. To Chris Colin, my work husband and co-writing buddy . . . thank you for bringing your humor, music, and clear-eyed thoughtfulness to the table. I am sharper for it.

我由衷地感谢丹妮尔·斯维特科夫，她是一位杰出的经纪人，一股强大的力量，也是一位各方面都非常棒的人。每天知道有你在我身边，我都感到无比兴奋。

My deepest gratitude to Danielle Svetcov, incredible agent, elemental force, all-around wonderful human. I am giddy every day to know you’re in my corner.

上述许多人都是因为旧金山作家俱乐部（San Francisco Writers' Grotto）而走进我的生活，那是我梦寐以求的写作社群。作家俱乐部一直是我人生风暴中的避风港，并将继续如此。特别感谢我的游泳伙伴兼写作邻居：托德·奥本海默（Todd Oppenheimer）、布里奇特·奎因（Bridget Quinn）、约书亚·莫尔（Joshua Mohr）和马修·扎普鲁德（Matthew Zapruder）。感谢 Rebecca Skloot 带我加入 Notto 大家庭，在这里，良好的对话——任何创造性事业的必要燃料——总是唾手可得（我说的就是你们，亮点：Laurel Braitman、Mary Roach、Malia Wollan）。

So many of the aforementioned folks came into my life because of the San Francisco Writers’ Grotto, the best writing community a girl could hope for. The Grotto has been and continues to be a port in the storm of life. Special thanks to swimmers and writing neighbors Todd Oppenheimer, Bridget Quinn, Joshua Mohr, and Matthew Zapruder. Thanks to Rebecca Skloot for bringing me into the Notto fold, where good conversation, the essential fuel to any creative endeavor, is always on tap (I’m talking to you, bright spots: Laurel Braitman, Mary Roach, Malia Wollan).

在此，我要向我出色的编辑艾米·加什（Amy Gash）致以最诚挚的谢意：能有你这样的伙伴，我真是太幸运了。你的智慧和敏锐的眼光帮助这本书臻于完美。能够成为阿尔冈昆大家庭的一员，我感到无比荣幸；你们从一开始就理解并支持我的愿景。你们当中有这么多游泳健将！克雷格·波佩拉尔斯（Craig Popelars），我们情同手足（搬到波特兰只会让我们更加亲近）。感谢布伦森·胡尔（Brunson Hoole）确保一切按时完成，感谢凯莉·波利切利（Kelly Policelli）的精湛文案润色。特别感谢杰森·休尔（Jason Heuer）设计了精美绝伦的封面，感谢史蒂夫·戈德温（Steve Godwin）设计了优雅的内页。感谢迈克尔·麦肯齐（Michael McKenzie）和斯蒂芬妮·门多萨（Stephanie Mendoza）帮助这本书走向世界。

A waterfall of thanks to Amy Gash, my marvelous editor: I’m so lucky to have you. Your smarts and sharp eyes helped shape this book into the best it could be. I am over the moon to be part of the Algonquin family; you all saw my vision and believed in it from the start. So many swimmers among you! Craig Popelars, we are kin (moving to Portland only makes you closer). Thank you to Brunson Hoole, for making the train run on time, and to Kelly Policelli, for working your copy magic. Huge thanks to Jason Heuer, who made the most gorgeous book jacket, and to Steve Godwin, who designed the elegant pages within. Thank you to Michael McKenzie and Stephanie Mendoza for helping to introduce this book to the world.

如果没有衷心的感谢，这一切都将是不完整的：我的早期写作伙伴兼内部神经科学顾问 Tom Davidson；热爱开放水域的快乐爱好者 Steve Dawson；在我最艰难的时候给予我支持的 Jenny Fu、Lynsay Skiba、Melissa Gibson、Esther Chak、Anna Vella、Mara Gladstone、Michele Boruta。

All would not be complete without heartfelt shout-outs to dear friends: Tom Davidson, my earliest writing buddy and in-house neuroscience consultant; Steve Dawson, cheerful enthusiast in all things open water; Jenny Fu, Lynsay Skiba, Melissa Gibson, Esther Chak, Anna Vella, Mara Gladstone, Michele Boruta, for lifting me when I felt most heavy.

很多人跟我讲过一些故事，但都没能写进书里；我真希望都能把它们都收录进去。海伦·加西亚、凯瑟·罗萨彻、简·库尔特、芭芭拉·斯塔克·乔丹、南希·布朗……还有我家泳池的“市长”克里斯特尔·波耶顿！非常感谢。想法的酝酿需要时间，我感谢我的……感谢各位编辑，特别是《纽约时报》的编辑，多年来他们慷慨地给予我机会，让我以不同的形式阐述这些想法。

Many people told me stories that didn’t make it into the book; I wish I could include them all. Helen Garcia, Kathe Rothacher, Jane Coulter, Barbara Stark Jordan, Nancy Brown . . . and Krystel Poyeton, the mayor of my pool! Merci beaucoup. It takes time for ideas to percolate, and I thank my editors, particularly at the New York Times, for providing me with generous opportunities to work those thoughts out in different forms over the years.

衷心感谢琳达和鲍勃·巴尔赞夫妇与我们分享他们在博利纳斯的度假小屋：它一直激励着我们全家。

Warm gratitude to Linda and Bob Balzan, for sharing your Bolinas cottage: it inspires our family always.

致我以前的教练们（Nancy教练、Rob教练、Kevin教练、Kathleen教练！）以及现在的教练们（Carol教练、Keith教练和Lessly教练，我发誓，一旦这该死的书出版，我就会来参加训练）。

To my coaches, then (Coaches Nancy, Rob, Kevin, Kathleen!) and now (Coaches Carol, Keith, and Lessly, I swear I’m coming to practice once this dang book is out).

致安迪、斯蒂芬、克里斯：你们永远是我的团队。

To Andy, Stephen, Chris: you’re my forever team.

献给我的父母，是他们教会了我热爱水。

To my parents, who taught me to love water.

最亲爱的，我要感谢我最重要的三个儿子。菲利克斯和泰迪，你们每天都给我的生活带来快乐，无论是在水里还是在岸上。还有我的丈夫马特，感谢你答应陪我游过乔治湖，就因为爷爷说我们可以。我的“北极熊俱乐部”里，除了你，没有别的比你更合适的人选了。我爱你。

And dearest love and thanks to my three most important boys. Felix and Teddy, you bring joy to my life every day, in the water and out of it. And to my husband, Matt, bless you for saying yes to swimming across Lake George with me, just because Grandpa said we could. There’s no one I’d rather have in my polar bear club of two. I love you.

我们为什么游泳

Why We Swim





远距离游泳，携手同行：徐邦妮的随笔

Swimming at a Distance, Together: An Essay by Bonnie Tsui

***

* * *

讨论问题

Questions for Discussion

远距离游泳，携手同行

——徐邦妮散文

Swimming at a Distance, Together

An Essay by Bonnie Tsui

我从未想过，在大多数人不会游泳的时候，我会出版一本关于游泳的书。

I never imagined that I’d be putting a book about swimming out into the world at a time when most people couldn’t swim.

在《我们为何游泳》出版前一个月，我家附近的游泳池关闭了，孩子们的学校也停课了，几乎所有地方都关门了。全国进入封锁状态，我们一家人原本四处游玩的生活也缩减到了几乎完全待在家里。和所有人一样，我们对这种新型冠状病毒感到担忧和困惑。我一直在思考我们的身体究竟能做到什么，以及我们是如何克服恐惧和痛苦的。对我来说，游泳就是其中一种方式。

A month before Why We Swim was published, my local pool closed, along with my children’s school and pretty much everything else. The country entered a state of lockdown, and my family’s usual wide-ranging peripatetics contracted to an existence largely within the four walls of our house. Like everyone, we worried and wondered about this new coronavirus. I thought a lot about what our bodies are capable of, and about the ways we work through fear and pain. Swimming, for me, is one of those ways.

书出版后不久，信件便纷至沓来。数百封信，字里行间生动地描绘了游泳和水对每一位来信者的意义。这些信件通过电子邮件、推特、脸书、Instagram等平台送达；还有我亲爱的邮递员兰妮特亲自送来的。我每一封都认真阅读。

Then, quite soon after the book came out, the letters began to arrive. Hundreds of them, detailing in sharp relief what swimming and the water meant to each person who took the time to write. The notes arrived over email, Twitter, Facebook, Instagram; they were hand-delivered by my beloved mail carrier Lannette. I read every one.

有时，信箱里会收到一些诗歌。其中一首是来自马萨诸塞州的十岁女孩莉莉丝·埃克布拉德（Lilith Ekbladh）写的，诗中饱含哀伤地表达了她在新冠疫情期间对游泳的思念：“我需要游泳来提神醒脑/没有游泳我会疯掉！”有时，信箱里会收到一些艺术作品：一幅描绘中央公园池塘色彩的习作，或是一幅描绘月光下东河游泳者的画作。有一次，信箱里还收到一个精美的手工吹制玻璃杯，杯底是会发光的蓝色玻璃，注满水后会变色。甚至还有一段令人难忘的录音，是加州冲浪传奇人物罗恩·西泽莫尔（Ron Sizemore）用尤克里里弹奏的。这些令人惊喜的礼物极大地拓展了我对水的认知，远远超出了我从前廊所能看到的范围。

Sometimes there were poems. One, from ten-year-old Lilith Ekbladh in Massachusetts, included mournful lines about how much she missed swimming in the time of Covid: “I need it to refresh my brain / Without it I will go insane!” Sometimes there was art: a color study of the ponds in Central Park, or a painting of a swimmer in the East River bathed in moonlight. Once there was a stunning handblown glass tumbler, with a luminous blue glass bottom that changed color when filled with water. There was even a memorable recording by the California surf legend Ron Sizemore, on his ukulele. These surprising and welcome offerings expanded my aquatic horizon far beyond what I could see from the front porch.

许多人分享了在艰难时期游泳的意义。疫情初期，大多数游泳池关闭，人们便转向能找到的开放水域。他们做了许多以前从未想过自己能做到的事情。

Many people shared what it meant to swim through hard times. With most pools closed in the early months of the pandemic, people turned to open water where they could find it. They did things they’d never thought they could do.

无数报纸文章记录了游泳者的坚持不懈。 《华尔街日报》的一篇标题为“新冠疫情关闭了香港海滩，但却无法阻止游泳者下海”的文章写道：“沙滩几个月都禁止进入，所以热爱游泳的人们想方设法绕过这些限制，冒着被水母、藤壶叮咬和被处以巨额罚款的风险。”在澳大利亚——《 纽约时报》的标题是“在墨尔本封城期间游泳以求保持理智”——游泳者们抓住机会重返户外泳池，即使泳池开放受限，而且是在黎明前的黑暗和恶劣的天气中。

Countless newspaper articles documented the perseverance of the swimmer. “Covid Closed Hong Kong’s Beaches, but It Couldn’t Keep Swimmers Out of the Ocean,” read one headline in the Wall Street Journal: “The sand was off-limits for months, so devoted swimmers found crafty work-arounds and risked jellyfish, barnacles, and hefty fines.” In Australia— “Swimming to Sanity in Melbourne’s Lockdown,” read the New York Times headline—swimmers jumped at the opportunity to return to outdoor pools, even with restricted access and in predawn darkness and miserable weather.

我曾为《纽约时报》撰文，讲述我如何观察我认识的泳池游泳爱好者适应开放水域，穿上潜水服、戴上氯丁橡胶泳帽、系上充气浮标。我坚持在旧金山湾东岸里士满的凯勒海滩游泳。每次沿着小路走向海滩，我都能瞥见金门大桥的一小段桥身，以及双峰山顶苏特罗塔的尖顶，它们像船桅顶端一样耸立着。我观察着海水的状况和天气：有时阴沉灰暗，有时晴空万里。我喜欢海滩上形形色色的人们——散步的、涉水的、游泳的——我也融入其中，成为他们中的一员。

I myself wrote for the New York Times about how I’d watched pool swimmers I knew adapt to the open water, donning wet suits, neoprene caps, and inflatable buoys. I kept up with my swims at Keller Beach in Richmond, on the eastern shores of San Francisco Bay. Each time I walked down the path to the beach, I glimpsed an abbreviated span of the Golden Gate Bridge and the spires of Sutro Tower atop Twin Peaks, poking up like the tops of ship masts. I gauged the mood of the water, the weather: steely and gray one day, bluebird sky the next. I loved the diverse range of beach denizens—walkers, waders, swimmers—and I went to take my place among them.

我们保持了距离，但我们一起游泳。

We kept our distance, but we swam together.

韧性就是每天至少花一个小时，年复一年地把头埋进水里。真正的挑战在于——不是把头埋进水里对世界视而不见，而是把头埋进水里去感受它。即使背负着重担，也要记得如何漂浮。

Resilience is about sticking your head in water every day, for an hour or more, year after year. That’s the challenge— not to put your head down and ignore the world, but to put your head down and absorb it. To remember how to float, in spite of the burdens you carry.

这场疫情让我意识到，人类拥有创造力和坚韧不拔的精神。正如查尔斯·斯普劳森在他的著作《黑人按摩师的幽灵》的副标题中所说，“游泳者是英雄” 。但我们并非孤军奋战。我们在水中寻求慰藉，也在彼此身上寻求慰藉。

What this pandemic year has reminded me is that humans are inventive and determined. “The swimmer as hero,” as Charles Sprawson put it in the subtitle to his book, Haunts of the Black Masseur. But we don’t do it alone. We seek solace in the water, and in each other.

在这几个月的强制隔离期间，每一封信件、每一件水生文物都像漂流瓶一样寄到我家。它们对我意味着什么？简而言之，它们代表着这个世界。

Over these months of enforced isolation, every letter and aquatic artifact has arrived like a message in a bottle. What do they mean to me? Simply, the world.

讨论问题

Questions for Discussion

1. 《我们为何游泳》融合了回忆录、新闻报道、历史和科学元素。你觉得这些元素中哪些最能引起你的共鸣？你认为它们融合得是否成功？

1. Why We Swim is a blend of memoir, journalism, history, and science. Which of these elements resonated most with you? Do you think they all work together successfully?

2. 这本书讲的是游泳，但它也讲的是一些更基本的东西：我们与水的关系，以及我们并非生来就会游泳——我们人类必须学会如何在水中生存。你是否曾经为了生存而游泳，或者在水中感到生命受到威胁？

2. This book is about swimming, but it is also about something more elemental: our relationship with water, and how we don’t know how to swim from birth—we humans have to teach ourselves how to survive in it. Have you ever had to swim for survival, or feared for your life in water?

3. 一旦我们学会游泳以求生存，游泳的意义远不止于此：它还能带来身心健康、融入社群、参与竞技、享受心流体验。你与游泳之间有着怎样的关系？这本书是否改变了你对游泳的看法？

3. Once we learn to swim for survival, swimming can be so much more: well-being, community, competition, flow. What is your own relationship with swimming? Did this book change your thinking about it?

4. 与陆地活动不同，游泳能让我们真正离开熟悉的环境，进入一个全新的世界。长距离游泳运动员常说“梦游大海”。身处漂浮的环境中，有哪些方式能解放思想？还有哪些例子表明，环境的改变能带来全新的视角？

4. Unlike land-based activities, swimming takes us quite literally out of our element and puts us in a new one. Long-distance swimmers speak of “sea-dreaming.” What are the ways that being in a buoyant environment can free your mind? Are there other examples in which a change in environment creates a fresh perspective?

5. 崔指出，游泳能鼓励人们重拾玩耍的乐趣——跳水、跳水、假装自己是水怪——而这些乐趣我们成年人往往会忽略。当你自己或你认识的孩子在水中时，你是否也感受到了这些乐趣？你认为这是为什么呢？

5. Tsui notes that swimming encourages a return to play—diving, cannonballing, pretending to be a mercreature—that we often lose sight of as adults. Do you see this in yourself, or in the children you know, when you are in water? Why do you think that happens?

6. 杰伊·泰勒曾在巴格达战区教了两年游泳课。对他来说，游泳帮助他在危险的地方建立起社群。你经常去游泳池、海滩或湖边，那里有没有你熟悉的社群？它是否帮助你度过了特别艰难的时期？

6. Jay Taylor spent two years teaching swim lessons in a combat zone in Baghdad. For him, swimming helped create community in a dangerous place. Do you have a community at a pool, beach, or lake that you frequent? Has it helped you get through any particularly difficult times?

7. 金·钱伯斯成年后开始游泳，是为了从一次创伤性损伤中恢复。从追求身心健康开始，她逐渐融入了社群，参与了比赛，并体验到了心流的感受。你是否也曾被医生建议通过游泳来康复伤病？效果如何？

7. Kim Chambers was motivated to swim as an adult, as therapy to recover from a traumatic injury. From a quest for well-being came community and competition and flow. Have you ever been prescribed swimming to recover from an injury? Did it work?

8. 《我们为何游泳》探索了许多鲜为人知的游泳故事，包括武士游泳——日本的游泳武术——以及东南亚的海洋游牧民族。你最喜欢的关于游泳及其相关文化习俗的新发现是什么？

8. Why We Swim investigates a number of little-known stories about swimming, including samurai swimming—the Japanese swimming martial art—and the sea nomads of Southeast Asia. What were your favorite new discoveries about swimming and the cultural practices around it?

9. 弗朗茨·卡夫卡写道：“真理永远是一个深渊。人必须像在游泳池里一样，敢于从日常琐事的颤动跳板上纵身跃入深渊，沉入深渊，然后才能再次浮出水面——一边笑着，一边挣扎着呼吸——到达如今被双倍光芒照亮的事物表面。”你认为为什么这么多作家也像游泳者一样呢？

9. Franz Kafka wrote, “The truth is always an abyss. One must—as in a swimming pool—dare to dive from the quivering springboard of trivial everyday experience and sink into the depths, in order later to rise again—laughing and fighting for breath—to the now doubly illuminated surface of things.” Why do you think so many writers are also swimmers?

10. 分享书中你最喜欢的一句话或一段话。它为什么让你印象深刻？你从中获得了什么启发？

10. Share a favorite line or passage from the book. Why does it stand out, and what is your takeaway from it?

邦妮·崔 (Bonnie Tsui) 生活、游泳和冲浪都在旧金山湾区。她长期为《纽约时报》和《加州周日杂志》撰稿，曾荣获哈佛大学简·雷尼·奥佩尔青年校友奖、洛厄尔·托马斯金奖和国家新闻基金会奖学金。她的上一本书《美国唐人街：五个街区的人民史》荣获亚太裔美国文学奖，并荣登《旧金山纪事报》畅销书榜，入选2009年旧金山湾区最佳图书。她的个人网站是bonnietsui.com。

Bonnie Tsui lives, swims, and surfs in the Bay Area. A longtime contributor to the New York Times and California Sunday Magazine, she has been the recipient of the Jane Rainie Opel Young Alumna Award from Harvard University, the Lowell Thomas Gold Award, and a National Press Foundation Fellowship. Her last book, American Chinatown: A People’s History of Five Neighborhoods, won the Asian/Pacific American Award for Literature and was a San Francisco Chronicle bestseller and Best of 2009 Notable Bay Area Books selection. Her website is bonnietsui.com.

A Los Angeles Times and Boston Globe bestseller • A New York Times Editors’ Choice / Staff Pick • An NPR Best Book of the Year • A Time Magazine Must-Read Book of the Year • A Bloomberg Best Nonfiction Book of the Year • A Los Angeles Times Book Club Pick • An Amazon Editors’ Pick for Best Nonfiction • A Goodreads Choice Awards Finalist for Best Science & Technology Book of the Year

“这是一部热情洋溢、发人深省的作品，融合了历史、新闻报道和回忆录的元素……徐女士也赢得了读者的喜爱。她提出的普世问题也是对自身的追问，她对所见所闻的阐述令人动容。”—— 《纽约时报书评》

“[An] enthusiastic and thoughtful work mixing history, journalism and elements of memoir . . . Tsui endears herself to the reader as well. Her universal query is also one of self, and her articulations of what she learns are moving.” —The New York Times Book Review

“邦妮·崔捕捉到了游泳的乐趣、危险和实用性，无论是在她的家庭中还是在不同文明中……她报道的广度和文笔的优美，使得《 我们为何游泳》一书的各个元素和谐统一。”—— 《旧金山纪事报》

“Bonnie Tsui captures the joy, peril and utility of swimming, within her family and across civilizations . . . The breadth of her reporting and grace of her writing make the elements of Why We Swim move harmoniously as one.” —San Francisco Chronicle

“崔女士带领读者穿越时空，环游世界，讲述了数千年来人类与水相处、适应水环境以及与之互动的种种方式。她的书也是对游泳对身心灵魂的变革性影响的一次深刻思考。”—— 《洛杉矶时报》

“Tsui takes readers on a trip through time and around the world, recounting the myriad ways humans have endured, adapted to, and interacted with water over thousands of years. Her book also is a meditation on swimming’s transformative effect on body, mind, and soul.” —Los Angeles Times

“Bonnie Tsui提醒我们，人类曾经源于水，如今依然渴求水源……这是一个令人惊叹的故事。”——斯科特·西蒙，《NPR周末版》

“Bonnie Tsui reminds us that humankind once sprang from and still seeks water . . . An amazing story.” —Scott Simon, NPR’s Weekend Edition

“《我们为何游泳》是一本精彩绝伦的混合体式书籍。你绝对不会后悔沉浸其中。”——卡尔·齐默，《纽约时报》科学专栏作家，《她继承了母亲的笑声：遗传的力量、变异与潜力》的作者

“Why We Swim is a gorgeous hybrid of a book. You won’t regret diving in.” —Carl Zimmer, New York Times science columnist and author of She Has Her Mother’s Laugh: The Powers, Perversions, and Potential of Heredity

“这是一部报道深入、引人入胜的作品，从最早的游泳记录（发现于沙漠中央）到消失的水生社会、海上游牧民族等等，精彩纷呈。这本书仿佛是为邦妮·崔量身打造的。”——丽贝卡·斯克鲁特，《 亨丽埃塔·拉克斯的永生》畅销书作者

“A deeply reported and fascinating story that takes us from the first record of swimming (which lies in the middle of a desert) to tales of vanishing aquatic societies, sea nomads, and so much more. This is a book Bonnie Tsui was born to write.” —Rebecca Skloot, bestselling author of The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks

“在《我们为何游泳》一书中，毕生热爱游泳且文笔出众的邦妮·崔探讨了人类与水的关系，以及我们为何会被水的深处所吸引。”—— 《奥普拉杂志》

“In Why We Swim, Bonnie Tsui—a lifelong swimmer who happens to be an excellent writer—investigates humankind’s relationship to water, and why we are drawn to its depths.” —O, The Oprah Magazine

“前竞技游泳运动员、现任全能作家邦妮·崔的《我们为何游泳》……探讨了我们与这项运动的关系，这项运动本身就代表着平静与流畅（我们多么需要这种感觉，不是吗？），书中列举了一系列形形色色的例子，例如游泳武士和冰岛沉船幸存者。”——《户外》杂志

“Former competitive swimmer and current do-it-all writer Bonnie Tsui’s Why We Swim . . . explores our relationship with a sport that quite literally represents quiet and flow (something we could use more of, no?) by offering a look at a grab bag of eclectic examples, like swimming samurais and an Icelandic shipwreck survivor.” —Outside

“崔的这部关于人类与水关系的著作引人入胜、发人深省，其行文流畅自然，仿佛水流本身也在流动……我从头到尾都被它深深吸引。”—— BuzzFeed

“Tsui’s history of the human relationship with water is compelling and profound, in writing so fluid it mimics the flow of her subject . . . It captivated me from start to finish.” —BuzzFeed

“文笔优美，描写生动……崔的这本佳作不仅吸引体育迷，更能吸引更广泛的读者。对科学和自然感兴趣的读者也会喜欢这本关于疗愈运动的叙事作品，强烈推荐。”—— 《图书馆杂志》

“Lyrical and descriptive . . . Tsui’s beautifully written book will appeal to a wider audience beyond sports fans. Readers who are also interested in science and nature will appreciate this highly recommended narrative work about a therapeutic sport.” —Library Journal

“科学与回忆录的诗意融合。”—— 《发现》杂志

“A poetic blend of science and memoir.” —Discover
